pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Use a fresh experiment directory outside original stores; do not overwrite original PDFs.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

C1.justification: V1's central claims concern empirical causal recovery on two synthetic systems, with video applications proposed as future work. V2's abstract and conclusion additionally claim provable recovery with observed states, identify state-dependent TiMINo and conditional-summary-graph identifiability as contributions, and claim benefits for real NBA forecasting and interpretability. These substantially expand the contribution beyond the retained empirical SDCI claim.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly limits its identifiability results to observed states and leaves guarantees for the trained VAE unresolved. Appendix F.2 newly states that hidden wall-collision states prevent accurate graph recovery and discusses teacher forcing as a limitation for long-term forecasts. V2 also interprets NBA state maps through court regions and offensive/defensive behaviour, and explains nonstationary baseline weaknesses through their mismatch with discrete changes in dynamics.

D1.justification: V2 specifies encoder widths, activations, normalisation and skip connections previously deferred to ACD; discloses synthetic sample counts, noise, initialisation and sample-selection details; and documents NBA access, preprocessing, sample counts and VRNN architecture/training. Existing synthetic optimiser schedules and hardware information largely persist. Conversely, v1's explicit supervised state-transition head and weighted-loss description are omitted despite retaining the wall-collision experiment.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only synthetic linear and spring systems. V2 adds real NBA player-trajectory forecasting, including observed and inferred court states and transfer between Toronto Raptors and Boston Celtics games. Both synthetic families remain; the wall-collision scenario is retained in Appendix F.2.

E2.justification: V1 uses ACD as its external baseline. V2 adds evaluated comparisons with TdCM, CD-NOD and SAEM for linear data, CD-NOD for springs, and VRNN for NBA forecasting. Its observed-spring state-count experiment also includes ACD curves, whereas v1 Table 2 reports SDCI alone. The additional methods in v2's related-work table are not all experimental baselines.

E3.justification: Reported linear settings change from alpha=1 and beta1=0.05 to alpha=0.9 and beta1=0.5, with beta2=-0.5 for three-edge-type experiments. The hidden-state rule changes from p<0 to |x|>2, and the main linear comparison uses T=50 instead of v1's T=40. V2 introduces summary-graph existence accuracy, longer sequences and a 200-sample protocol for nonstationary baselines, revised spring configuration sweeps, and 100-step NBA forecasting after 100 observed steps.

E4.justification: V2 adds data-efficiency sweeps, generalisation across variable counts and NBA teams, learned-state analyses, and graph/forecast case studies including failures (Figures 4, 7, 8 and 11–13). The fixed-decoder ablation remains, but v1's static-versus-temporal encoder comparison and discussion of alternative temporal aggregators are removed.

E5.justification: V1 reports wall-collision outcomes as point estimates in Section 4.2.2; v2 Table 5 adds ± quantities for edge accuracy, MSE and state accuracy. Other v1 tables already used ± reporting, so this is a limited extension to retained results. Neither version specifies repeat counts, seeds or the meaning of these uncertainty quantities; additional runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial linear, spring, NBA and qualitative results while removing temporal-encoder results and many training-set entries. Four methods' two-edge linear test scores are retained exactly in Table 3, including ACD's 66.44% and SDCI-Static/SDCI's 93.84% accuracy. Wall-collision accuracy changes from 79.21% to 79.19% for SDCI and 68.61% to 68.63% for ACD. New linear results use revised settings and therefore do not establish a cross-version performance gain.

M1.justification: SDCI-Static is retained and renamed SDCI, but the alternative temporal encoder from v1 Appendix A.1 is removed. The reported hidden-state procedure changes from probability-weighted edge mixing in v1 Eq. 21 to Gumbel-softmax state sampling and gating in v2 Eq. 11. V2 also adapts the decoder to condition player predictions on ball features, materially changing the offered model family and procedures.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Implementation is reorganised around generative modelling, inference and hidden states; training specifications and some existing experiments move into Appendices C and F. The separate future-work section disappears, terminology is revised, and the author block changes. This is substantial editorial reorganisation beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adds scenario and graph-definition diagrams, multipanel experimental plots, state maps and extensive forecast/graph visualisations. The original overview is redrawn, the static-encoder diagram is retained with revised labels and placement, and the temporal-encoder diagram is removed. Existing results are also reformatted into reduced tables, alongside broad changes to typography, text width and figure wrapping.

R1.justification: V1 mainly positions SDCI against stationary approaches such as ACD and prospective causal-video applications. V2 substantially develops its relationship to nonstationary and regime-based research, including CD-NOD, RHINO, NonSENS, LEAP and Regime-PCMCI, and adds TiMINo foundations. Section 2 and Table 1 distinguish variable-specific states from global regimes and changing causal structures from changing effects within fixed structures.

T1.justification: V1 has an SCM formulation and assumptions but no original identifiability theorems. V2 introduces state-dependent TiMINo, a formal conditional-summary-graph definition, Theorem 1 and Corollary 1, with Markov/minimality lemmas and proofs in Appendix A and extension arguments in Appendix B. Appendix D.1 also changes the VAR stability criterion from eigenvalue magnitudes to singular values, which is not mathematically equivalent.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's limited validation through relevant nonstationary competitors, real NBA forecasting, and data-efficiency, transfer and failure analyses. Its formal treatment also clarifies observed-state assumptions and the absence of guarantees for hidden states or the trained VAE. These gains in evidential support and applicability outweigh the removed temporal-encoder ablation and local documentation problems, particularly retained linear scores alongside revised generation settings and the non-equivalent stability criterion.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SDCI research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original linear and spring simulations, NBA trajectory forecasting experiments, and additional generalisation and qualitative analyses in the appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations on linear systems and directed spring systems, including graph recovery, reconstruction, parameter estimation and state prediction results.

results.title: Causal Discovery from Conditionally Stationary Time Series

C1.justification: V2 presents hidden-state discovery as empirically supported while limiting its guarantees to observed states. V3 makes structural identifiability under determined and recurrent latent states a central contribution. Its abstract and conclusion replace the linear-system emphasis with GRN discovery and biological applicability, and extend the NBA comparison claim to NRI.

C2.justification: V3 distinguishes structural identifiability from unresolved state-distribution identification, adds practical uncertainty about choosing K, and expands the estimator-consistency discussion. It explains recurrent-inference difficulties and weak benefits from supplied GRN states through gradual gene deactivation. NBA interpretation additionally emphasizes interaction sparsity and reduced error accumulation through the no-edge mechanism.

D1.justification: Appendices B–C substantially expand architecture, optimization, baseline-tuning and simulation documentation, including recurrent encoder layers and DynGen generation. NBA-specific training and sparsity settings are newly disclosed rather than establishing changes to previously specified settings. Linear-generator and fixed-decoder instructions disappear. PyTorch, RTX 2080 Ti hardware and the NBA data-access reference remain.

E1.justification: V3 adds DynGen gene regulatory network discovery and spring-plus-magnetic particle interactions, and evaluates recurrent states without supplying them. The linear-system experiments disappear entirely. NBA forecasting remains, but the explicit Toronto-to-Boston transfer scenario is removed; observed-state spring coverage survives in Appendix E.1.

E2.justification: The particle comparison changes from ACD/CD-NOD to ACD/Rhino/Neural Granger Causality. NBA adds Chen et al.'s NRI comparator, called NRI-NPM in the main text and NRI-MPM in Appendix B.4. GRN Table 1 additionally evaluates Regime-PCMCI; TdCM and SAEM disappear with the linear experiments. ACD's 2020-to-2022 citation update denotes the same comparator.

E3.justification: The stated spring training/test counts change from 50,000/10,000, with 200 tests for selected baselines, to 10,000/100. Revised particle experiments introduce fixed-graph controls, micro/macro F1 scoring, different training budgets and batch sizes, and annealed rather than fixed state temperatures. GRN evaluation adds AUROC. These reported settings do not establish that retained appendix figures were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds fixed-versus-variable graph controls that distinguish structure recovery from state-estimation difficulty, compares state-information variants on GRNs, and analyzes extracted NBA interaction graphs. V2's fixed-decoder linear ablations, linear failure examples and NBA data-efficiency/transfer tests are removed. The observed-state spring sensitivity, data-efficiency and generalization analyses are retained as Figure 14.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence levels or significance tests. Spring error-bar reporting remains, including the unchanged analysis moved from v2 Figure 4 to v3 Figure 14. The disappearing plus/minus tables accompany removed experiments rather than a documented change in uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: V2's linear and supplied-state collision results are removed, while v3 adds fixed/variable particle results and GRN scores. V3 Table 1 reports 0.936 AUROC and 0.347 F1 for SDCI-determined, versus Rhino's 0.933 and 0.081. NBA curves also change: v3 shows only a slight hidden-state advantage over ACD. Revised settings prevent treating these as matched cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: V3 introduces hidden recurrent-state inference using a state-transition model, a bidirectional GNN-RNN posterior and a state KL term; v2 supplied states in its collision experiment. V3 also adds recurrent-case edge attention, directly parameterized fixed-graph inference, GRN node embeddings and a revised discrete gradient estimator (Section 3.3; Appendix B.3).

P1.justification: The introduction, method exposition and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. V3 introduces a Background section and a separate theory section, moves Related Work after theory, reorganizes the appendices, and replaces numbered scenario classes with descriptive state categories. The contribution list and author block are also revised.

P2.justification: V3 changes the main text and references to two columns, redraws the graph-representation and inference diagrams, and replaces NBA posterior panels with court overlays. It adds GRN and NBA interaction visualizations, removes the earlier overview and linear-result tables, and relocates retained spring analyses to the appendix. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V3 substantially reframes the work around switching-model and latent-regime identifiability, adding comparisons with Balsells-Rodas et al. (2024), Varambally et al. (2024) and Song et al. (2024). It also develops biological positioning through DynGen and GRN literature. These changes exceed citation updates or relocation of related work.

T1.justification: V2's observed-state full-time and conditional-summary-graph proofs are replaced by a latent-state partial-identifiability framework. V3 introduces Gaussian switching-model and uniqueness assumptions, permutation-based definitions, Theorem 4.3, Theorems A.6–A.7 and Corollary A.8 for structures and edge labels. Appendices B.1–B.2 also add ELBO and state-marginalization derivations.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens investigation of the central hidden-state problem: v2 supplied recurrent states, whereas v3 specifies and evaluates latent recurrent inference and uses controls that expose its remaining difficulties. Stronger comparator coverage, GRN evaluation and fuller implementation details make the method more assessable. The expanded theoretical framework states structural guarantees and limitations explicitly. These gains outweigh the loss of linear ablations and NBA transfer/data-efficiency evidence, although statistical reporting remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SDCI and conditional summary graphs, with matching retained experiments and illustrations. All 23 pages of v2 and 25 pages of v3, including their appendices, support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: V3 reports original particle, simulated gene regulatory network and NBA experiments, including graph identification, state estimation and forecasting results.

before.justification: V2 reports original linear-system, particle-simulation and NBA forecasting experiments, including graph accuracy, reconstruction error and supplementary analyses.

results.title: Causal Discovery from Conditionally Stationary Time Series

C1.justification: The central contributions remain agent-number curricula and critic-loss-based SPMARL. v3 makes high-variance return estimation a headline problem in the abstract and conclusion, and qualifies SPRLM's success as applying to most tasks rather than v2's consistent-success statement. These refine the claims without redefining the approach.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations linking ALPGMM/VACL performance to failure to converge to the target distribution and attributing SPRLM's larger-Protoss failures to sparse-return optimization. Appendix A.3.3 adds an applicability qualification: dense rewards reduce exploration challenges and curriculum benefits. v2's Random-prior discussion is removed; the unresolved necessity of the KL constraint remains.

D1.justification: v2 largely provides qualitative implementation guidance and refers readers to code. v3 adds Tables 3–8 specifying network, optimizer, rollout, episode-length and curriculum-distribution settings, including task-specific thresholds. The code pointer changes from anonymous hosting to a named GitHub repository. These are primarily additional disclosures, not evidence that all underlying settings changed.

E1.justification: v3 replaces the 10-player XOR target with 20 players, adds Protoss 6v6, 7v7 and 8v8, and adds Terran and Zerg 5v5/6v6 experiments. Appendix A.3.3 further introduces dense-reward Balance and Wheel tasks, substantially extending coverage beyond v2's three sparse-reward scenarios.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated ALPGMM and adaptive VACL comparators to the main benchmark comparisons and removes Random. v2 cited VACL but represented prior multi-agent curricula through Linear rather than evaluating this adaptive comparator. SPRL/SPRLM and Linear remain; W/O Teacher remains evaluated in Table 1 despite being omitted from the plots.

E3.justification: The evaluation axes change from environment steps to environment samples proportional to agent count, changing the reported sample-efficiency accounting. v3 also introduces performance summaries averaged during training and controlled VLB sweeps. General VLB guidance changes from the expected target return to approximately 80% of it, although Simple-Spread's explicitly stated threshold of 50 remains.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's descriptive analysis of training and curriculum curves, v3 directly compares objective dispersion across six tasks in Figures 7 and 10. It also adds VLB sensitivity experiments on Protoss 5v5 and 6v6 in Figure 11, providing previously absent evidence about the proposed mechanism and hyperparameter robustness.

E5.justification: The Simple-Spread statement of five seeds and 95% confidence intervals is retained. v3 adds mean/standard-deviation summaries and one-sided Mann–Whitney U tests across the six main tasks in Tables 1–2, plus an explicit objective-dispersion estimator in Appendix A.3.4. No increase in seed count is stated.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results for new tasks, comparators, variance comparisons and threshold sweeps. Table 1 newly reports training-averaged Simple-Spread performance of 33.36 (SD 1.84) for SPMARL versus 27.48 (SD 5.38) for SPRLM; larger Protoss tasks reveal weak SPRLM performance. The 20-player XOR results replace 10-player results, so they do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: Both retain critic-loss prioritization, two-stage KL-constrained curriculum updates, shared-policy MAPPO and discretized Gaussian agent counts. v2 Equations 8–9 match v3 Equations 4–5. SPRL is renamed SPRLM; the expanded TD-error explanation does not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanations and experimental discussion undergo extensive rewriting. Background becomes Problem Formulation, SPRL and SPMARL receive separate sections, and MAPPO and implementation material move into the appendix. SPRLM terminology, organized supplementary sections, acknowledgements and an impact statement further restructure the document.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main text, redraws Figure 1, and combines the XOR payoff matrix and SMAC illustration into Figure 3. Benchmark plots have revised axes, legends and expanded panel grids. New statistical and hyperparameter tables, variance plots and ablation figures substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds ALPGMM-related literature, a comparison with prioritized experience replay, brief connections to unsupervised environment design and numerical continuation, and newer MARL and benchmark references. The principal positioning relative to SPRL and existing agent-number curricula remains intact; the PORTAL entry is updated to its published version.

T1.justification: The core Dec-POMDP, contextual-RL, MAPPO/GAE and curriculum-optimization mathematics is retained, with MAPPO moved to Appendix A.2. No new theorem, proof or formal guarantee is introduced. The added standard-deviation formula and TD-target explanation document the empirical analysis.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves validation and reproducibility through direct ALPGMM/VACL comparisons, broader task coverage, sensitivity and statistical analyses, and explicit experimental settings in Tables 3–8. The dense-reward experiments also clarify where benefits diminish. Removing Random loses some comparison coverage, and Table 2 does not establish superiority in every comparison, but the added evidence makes the paper's effectiveness and limitations substantially more assessable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPMARL research work. Their text, equations, figures and tables are readable and support comparison. v2 ends with references and has no separate appendix; v3 includes Appendix A, which was included in the assessment.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark experiments, objective-variance comparisons and threshold ablations in the main text and Appendix A, including Figures 4–11 and Tables 1–2.

before.justification: v2 reports original training, evaluation and generated-curriculum results for Simple-Spread, 10-player XOR and SMAC-v2 Protoss 5 versus 5 in Figures 3, 5 and 7.

results.title: Learning Progress Driven Multi-Agent Curriculum

C1.justification: The claim of learning universal Sinkhorn initializations remains, but the central contribution is redefined around self-supervised bootstrapping and theoretical generator universality. Standalone use expands from certain applications in v1 to a claimed dataset-independent meta neural entropic-OT solver with a few-percent distance error in v4's abstract and discussion.

C2.justification: V1's explanation that potential errors can cancel in barycenter computations is removed. V4 adds explanations for bootstrapping, translation-invariant loss, generator benefits, and evolving sample sparsity. It also acknowledges that the universality theorem does not directly cover the implemented lower-dimensional generator with unenforced Lipschitz constraints, and identifies higher-dimensional scaling as future work.

D1.justification: V4 documents revised architectures, learning rates, decay schedules, batching, and ten-update targets in Appendix B, and specifies 500 test samples per dataset. Reported training changes from just over three hours on a T4 to about 40 minutes on a V100, and the code pointer changes from SinkhornNNHybrid to learn_sink. V1's explicit Adam and positive-offset test-preprocessing disclosures are not retained.

E1.justification: MNIST, grayscale CIFAR10, and Quick Draw teddies remain, with teddies also called 'bear' in v4. Synthetic random test distributions are replaced by LFW faces, and the distinct Wasserstein-barycenter task in v1 Section 5.4 is removed. V4's random-noise training control does not retain the earlier random test set.

E2.justification: V4 adds Thornton and Cuturi's Gaussian initializer to the reported convergence and iteration-count comparisons, retaining the all-ones initializer. V1's evaluated Amos-inspired transport-distance-loss alternative, plotted against potential loss in Figure 3, disappears. V4 discusses Amos et al. but explicitly excludes their method from its initialization comparison.

E3.justification: Regularization changes from epsilon=0.00025 to 0.01, and training changes from 100,000 unique samples reused for five epochs to 20 million samples. V4 adds single-iteration evaluations and replaces the 0.001 marginal-violation threshold table with a 0.01 relative-error table, retaining the 0.01 marginal-violation threshold. Appendix C introduces a 60-million-sample generator study with skip weight 0.5.

E4.justification: V4 Figure 7 directly tests the generator's contribution against training on upsampled noise. Appendix C extends generator-behavior analysis using longer training and a modified skip weight; v1 already displayed generated samples, so this is an extension rather than the first such inspection. The earlier loss-function comparison and barycenter case study are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions already report 95% confidence intervals. V4 specifies that Figures 1, 6, 7, and 8 summarize five independent training runs and explicitly identifies table uncertainties as standard deviations; v1 leaves these details unspecified. This improves statistical disclosure without establishing that the number of runs increased.

E6.justification: The reported results are substantially replaced. For example, at 0.01 marginal violation, v1 Table 2 reports CIFAR means of 1738 iterations for default and 1422 for the network; v4 reports 47 for ones, 3 for pred, and 17 for gauss. These use different regularization and training settings, so they are not controlled performance gains. V4 additionally reports single-iteration median relative errors below 0.05 across its four datasets and generator-ablation findings.

M1.justification: V1 fits zero-centered, exact unregularized dual potentials using MSE and initializes through a C-transform. V4 learns regularized log-scaling potentials using Hilbert projective loss and bootstrapped targets from ten Sinkhorn updates, then exponentiates its prediction. Algorithm 2 substantially changes, the generator expands from one to three layers, and the approximator's widths and activations change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method narrative, and closing discussion are extensively rewritten. Section 4 is reorganized around Generator, Targets, Loss Function, and Training, with architecture details moved to Appendix B. The experimental narrative gains a dedicated metrics subsection, while the barycenter section disappears and Appendix C and an Impact Statement are added.

P2.justification: Existing convergence and runtime plots are redrawn with revised axes and legends and relocated, including v1 Figures 4–5 becoming v4 Figures 1 and 8. Tables expand from two to three method columns and are reformatted. V4 adds violin plots, an ablation plot, and expanded generator-image grids, while removing the loss-comparison and barycenter displays.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially through new discussions of learned OT distances/maps, OT-based machine learning, and invertible residual networks, including Courty et al. (2018), Bunne et al., Uscidda and Cuturi, and Behrmann et al. Positioning shifts toward dataset-independent meta OT solving; criticism of Amos et al. shifts from potential-learning accuracy toward out-of-distribution generalization.

T1.justification: V1 Proposition 7 and its appendix proof bound the regularized dual objective evaluated at unregularized potentials. These disappear. V4 introduces a conditional generator-density/universality theorem, Hilbert projective loss definitions, and Proposition 4.3 bounding true-potential error by bootstrapped loss, with new proofs in Appendix A.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens the central contribution: bootstrapping addresses v1's costly exact-target training, Proposition 4.3 links its training loss to true-potential error, and the Gaussian baseline and generator ablation address important gaps in comparative and component validation. Independent-run disclosure also improves evidential clarity. Removing barycenters narrows application evidence, and generator universality remains conditional on assumptions not enforced in practice. The stronger methodological and empirical support outweighs these limits; changed settings prevent interpreting raw performance differences as controlled gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same Sinkhorn-initialization work. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison: Appendices A–B in v1 and A–C in v4.

after.justification: V4 reports original initialization comparisons, single-iteration error distributions, and a generator ablation in Section 5, plus extended-training observations in Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 reports original loss-function comparisons, Sinkhorn convergence and iteration-count results, and computed MNIST barycenters in Section 5.

results.title: Universal Neural Optimal Transport

C1.justification: The central claims about universal prediction, bootstrapping, and Sinkhorn initialization remain. v6 explicitly includes experiments across costs and Euclidean/non-Euclidean domains in its contributions, raises the headline speedup from 3.46× to 7.4×, and qualifies the generator contribution by fixed dimension.

C2.justification: v6 interprets near-Meta-OT accuracy on MNIST as evidence of generator coverage and adds an interpretation of learning samples from different generator stages. Lower-resolution performance is described as within-range generalization rather than v5's extrapolation claim. The discussion also explicitly identifies non-uniform grids as future work.

D1.justification: v6 supplies explicit complex spectral tensor shapes and multiplication rules, GeLU activations, named optimizers, and clearer batch/minibatch information. It also documents spherical-grid construction, the Meta OT implementation source, and JAX timing conditions including float32, batch size 64, and NVIDIA 4090 hardware. These substantially improve documentation; the UNOT code-and-weights link was already present.

E1.justification: v5 evaluates image distributions on the unit square with squared Euclidean cost. v6 additionally evaluates unsquared Euclidean cost and image distributions projected onto the sphere with spherical distance, training separate models. This substantially expands tested costs and geometries. Cars and Facial Expressions already appeared in v5's appendix.

E2.justification: v5 explicitly excludes direct evaluation against Meta OT. v6 trains that comparator and reports a four-method comparison with UNOT, Gauss, and Ones across six dataset settings in Table 4. Table 6 additionally compares Gauss and Ones against UNOT for barycenter computation; v5 showed barycenters against ground truth without these comparator results.

E3.justification: The stated training-resolution range changes from 28×28–64×64 to 10×10–64×64, including the variable-epsilon variant. New protocols resize all Meta OT comparison data to 28×28 and evaluate barycenter Wasserstein-2 error after 100 gradient steps. These are substantive reported setting additions and revisions; they do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D.6 adds a diagnostic comparing errors on generated samples at their creation and at training completion (Table 5), testing learning across generator stages. Appendix D.7 extends the existing marginal-constraint analysis with single-iteration distributions and additional costs. The resolution and variable-epsilon analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions average experimental errors over 500 samples and already report distributions and mean-plus-dispersion results, including the unchanged entries in Table 1. Additional v6 tables extend this reporting without introducing a new stated uncertainty-estimation procedure, seed count, repeated-run design, or significance test.

E6.justification: v6 adds results for the additional costs and Tables 4–6. Table 4 reports UNOT versus Meta OT errors of 1.3% versus 23.1% on CIFAR at 28×28, while Meta OT remains slightly better on MNIST. Table 6 reports barycenter errors of 0.021, 0.033, and 0.057 for UNOT, Gauss, and Ones. Table 2 replaces the maximum speedup of 3.46× with 7.4×; matching timing conditions are not established.

M1.justification: v6 introduces a spherical adaptation using SFNOs and the spherical Fourier transform instead of the ordinary Fourier transform (Section 4; Appendix A.5). The adversarial generator, bootstrapping loss, and training algorithm remain. The spectral MLP, fixed-size MLP variant, and variable-epsilon inputs were already documented in v5.

P1.justification: The overall section and appendix structure remains. Changes include localized abstract and discussion rewrites, expanded FNO explanations in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.5, moving training details into Section 4, and revised appendix organization. Author affiliations and proceedings information are also updated.

P2.justification: v6 adds spherical examples, plots for additional costs, marginal-constraint distributions, and three result tables. It restructures Table 3 and redraws many charts with changed styling, legends, and scales, including linear rather than logarithmic marginal-constraint plots. Existing barycenter, geodesic, and architecture illustrations are largely retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v6 adds references for spherical FNOs, Adam/AdamW, and point-cloud applications by Geuter et al. and Fishman et al. Its main positioning against problem-specific neural OT remains. The Meta OT citation's change from 2022 preprint to 2023 publication is an update to the same work.

T1.justification: v6 broadens Proposition 2's cost assumptions to Lipschitz costs, adds Theorem B.3 proving equivalence of pointwise and uniform discretization, and extends Proposition 5's proof to predictions with nonzero mean. Theorem 3 and Corollary 4 are substantively revised around the invertible pre-ReLU residual map, including allowance for lambda equal to one.

improvement.justification: v6 resolves an important comparison gap by directly evaluating Meta OT, adds quantitative support for previously visual barycenter demonstrations, and tests broader geometries. The new discretization proof and extension of the bootstrapping bound to uncentered predictions strengthen theoretical support, while implementation disclosures improve reproducibility. These gains are substantial independently of the higher speedups, whose changed or previously unspecified timing conditions limit direct before-and-after interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UNOT research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–D are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

after.justification: v6 retains original empirical results and adds experiments with additional costs and spherical data, a Meta OT comparison, quantitative barycenter evaluation, and generator-training diagnostics.

before.justification: v5 reports original experiments on transport prediction, Sinkhorn initialization, barycenters, geodesics, and gradient flows, plus resolution and variable-epsilon experiments in Appendix D.

results.title: Universal Neural Optimal Transport

C1.justification: The central dimension guarantee is materially weakened to accommodate a second tail regime. V2 foregrounds the revised concentration result as Theorem 1.2 and expands the streaming contribution to an explicit additive/multiplicative guarantee. The underlying weight-oblivious compression objective remains the same.

C2.justification: V2 adds a similarity-search example, explicitly discusses when high distortion forces k > d, and conjectures that changing the recovery function could improve this limitation. It also adds an incorrect interpretation that equal weights yield distortion 1; its definition gives sqrt(d) for equal nonzero weights.

D1.justification: V2 omits v1 Section 4's footnote explaining coordinate-update streams, coordinate-index hashing, and the interpretation of final coordinate values. The Python implementation, Linux/Xeon W-2245 hardware disclosure, and degree-7 hash construction remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same synthetic sparse-vector norm-estimation scenarios with d = 200,000. The new similarity-search example is theoretical motivation, not an additional evaluated task.

E2.justification: Both compare the proposed estimates with exact weighted norms. Neither introduces an evaluated external baseline; cited JL and AMS constructions are not experimental comparators.

E3.justification: Corresponding experiments retain k = 100, 1,000, 10,000, and 100,000, the same sparse-vector construction, overlap settings, and density settings. Estimated squared norms and estimated-to-true norm ratios remain the reported quantities.

E4.justification: The same analyses examine concentration across random matrices and random input vectors, sensitivity to overlap, and sensitivity to sparsity. Their relocation to Appendix A adds no new robustness or supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: Both report histograms over 250 matrix realizations or 250 random vectors in the corresponding experiments. Run counts and uncertainty-reporting practices are unchanged, with no added seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figures 1–4 retain identical image data for all twelve histogram panels. The findings remain unchanged: concentration improves with k, while increasing distortion worsens relative estimation quality.

M1.justification: The complex random projection, squared-product norm estimator, and streaming counters with mean/median aggregation are retained. Estimator notation and theoretical dimension requirements change, but the PDFs do not establish a revised underlying algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, with numbered contribution theorems and a new outline. Concentration theory becomes a separate section, and experiments move after the references into Appendix A. The title changes and Simone Moretti is added to the author list.

P2.justification: The same four figures are resized and repositioned from v1 pages 10–11 to v2 Appendix A on pages 12–13, with captions reflowed. Typography and running headers change, while the two-column format and figure panel structures remain.

R1.justification: The mathematical positioning shifts from de la Pena–Gine decoupling to Blei–Janson hypercontractivity and Kuchibhotla–Chakrabortty sub-Weibull concentration. The introduction replaces feature-weighting and recommender-system motivation with relevance feedback, while related work adds earlier complex-number estimators and further JL applications.

T1.justification: V1's decoupling-based Gaussian chaos bounds are replaced by hypercontractivity, Orlicz norms, and sub-Weibull concentration in v2 Sections 2–4. The main dimension bound changes from a single Delta^4 log(1/delta)/epsilon^2 term to a maximum also containing Delta^2 log^2(24/delta)/epsilon. The Hoeffding theorem is removed, several coefficient derivations are corrected, and the streaming theorem gains an additive-error guarantee for a chosen distortion threshold.

improvement.justification: V2 replaces v1's faulty Gaussian-chaos argument, including Lemma 5's unjustified even-moment simplification, with a detailed heavy-tail analysis and a correspondingly more conservative main theorem. This substantially improves the mathematical basis of the principal contribution, and the explicit k > d limitation improves scope clarity. The repair remains incomplete: the abstract omits the additional log-squared term, and the new equal-weight distortion interpretation is incorrect.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same complex dimensionality reduction and streaming-sketch work. All pages, equations, references, and experimental figures are readable. V1 Section 5 matches v2 Appendix A, allowing a complete comparison despite substantial theoretical revision.

after.justification: V2 Appendix A retains the original simulations and their outcomes in Figures 1–4.

before.justification: V1 Section 5 reports original simulations on synthetic sparse vectors, with concentration and distortion experiments shown in Figures 1–4.

results.title: Dimensionality Reduction on Complex Vector Spaces for Euclidean Distance with Dynamic Weights

C1.justification: The central claim of unbiased weighted-distance estimation from weight-oblivious linear complex sketches remains. However, Section 1.1 introduces substantially different guarantees and improved compression for near-uniform vectors. The streaming contribution advertised in v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion is removed.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of the accuracy cost of preserving linearity compared with nonlinear JL, the failure of the unpartitioned method to compress near-uniform inputs, and how balanced blocks help. Sections 4.3-4.5 explicitly discuss the need for assumptions or prior knowledge about input distributions. These replace much of v2's distortion-example and streaming discussion.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a public code location and explicit uniform sampling distributions. It removes v2's disclosures of Python, Linux, and the Intel Xeon W-2245 processor; this does not establish a hardware change. v3 also introduces a reproducibility inconsistency: Appendix B specifies weights in [0.1,1.2], whereas the figure captions specify [1.0,1.2].

E1.justification: The empirical coverage changes from sparse inputs with binary weights and controlled support overlap in v2 Appendix A to dense near-uniform inputs and a sparse case with identical supports and continuous weights in v3 Appendix B. The earlier partially overlapping support scenarios are dropped.

E2.justification: v2 describes a nonlinear JL alternative in Section 1.1 but evaluates only its proposed estimator. v3 actually evaluates that nonlinear estimator, attributed to Kaban (2015), in Figure 1 and compares it with the proposed estimators in Figures 2-4. This is a focused addition to the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: The experiments change d from 200,000 to 20,000 and remove k=100,000 from the projection sweep. v3 introduces block configurations with k=1 and varying L, or L=100 and varying k. The earlier fixed-matrix/random-input experiment and estimated-to-true-norm ratio histograms are removed, substantially revising the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2's controlled overlap and sparsity-size sensitivity studies in Appendix A.2 are removed. v3 instead examines the effect of block partitioning and different allocations of k and L in Figures 2-4, alongside sparse versus dense behavior in Figures 2 and 5. These analyses investigate substantially different questions about the estimator.

E5.justification: Reported random-matrix repetitions per setting change from 250 in v2 to 1,000 in v3's redesigned experiments. Both versions report empirical histograms without introducing confidence intervals or significance tests. The larger count does not establish additional repetitions of the same v2 experiments.

E6.justification: The experimental results are replaced rather than merely redisplayed. v2 reports concentration with increasing k and degradation with increasing distortion. v3 adds distributions showing poor concentration for dense inputs without partitioning, substantial variance reduction with block projections, and a narrowing gap to nonlinear JL. These are results for changed methods and conditions, not direct v2-to-v3 performance gains.

M1.justification: The basic map g(x)=Ax/sqrt(k) remains, but the estimator replaces squared projected weights (Aw)_i^2 with sum_j A_ij^2 w_j^2. Section 4.4 adds separate projections of vector blocks and sums their estimates. The AMS-like streaming procedure in v2 Section 5 is removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten, including expanded motivation and explanation of the nonlinear alternative. Related work and the outline exchange order. Many existing proofs move into a new proof appendix, with summaries in the main text. Author order, affiliations, and conference information also change.

P2.justification: The document changes from ACM-style formatting to ICML formatting, with different front matter, headers, typography, and a single-column appendix. v2's four figures, using grids or paired histograms, are replaced by five figures with three horizontal panels and revised axes, captions, and styling. This exceeds renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands the machine-learning motivation and research positioning. It adds Kaban (2015), Kane et al. (2011), and an explicit comparison with Kaski et al. (2025)'s multilinear JL transform, distinguishing the complex construction and near-uniform extension. The AMS and limited-independence hashing references associated with the removed streaming section disappear.

T1.justification: Theorem 1.1 changes the weight factor from ||w||_2^2 to ||w||_4^2, redefines the distortion threshold, and revises the estimator's decomposition and bounds. Near-uniformity assumptions and block-construction proofs are added, while the streaming theorem and proofs are removed. The Rademacher concentration result is largely retained. New Lemma 4.5 inconsistently uses L^3 in the main text and L^2 in Appendix A.4.

improvement.justification: v2 leaves improving its weak compression bounds through a revised estimator as an open question. v3 addresses this with the new weight estimator and an analyzed block construction, supported by targeted comparisons in Appendix B and substantially clearer applicability limits in Sections 4.3-4.5. These strengthen the central contribution and its evaluation. Streaming results and earlier sensitivity checks are lost, and the bound and weight-range inconsistencies need correction, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 13 pages of v2 and 20 pages of v3 are readable, including the mathematical material, experimental figures, and appendices. The substantial revision does not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: Appendix B reports original simulations of the nonlinear JL comparator and the proposed complex estimators on dense and sparse inputs, with empirical distributions in Figures 1-5.

before.justification: Appendix A reports original synthetic weighted-norm estimation experiments, including variation across random projection matrices and input vectors, with results in Figures 1-4.

results.title: Dimensionality Reduction on Complex Vector Spaces for Euclidean Distance with Dynamic Weights

C1.justification: v3's principal claims concern logical reasoning under time pressure, with broader applicability proposed prospectively. v4's abstract, contribution list, and conclusion claim demonstrated applicability across arithmetic, decision making, and learning, including continuous cognitive states and multiple feedback modalities. This substantially broadens the claimed contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive interpretations attributing error variability to user/trial differences and performance benefits to complementary DDM and RL components. It also argues that task embeddings can benefit DRL despite worsening standalone SVM predictions (Section 5). The explicit population-diversity limitation in v3's Discussion disappears, while Appendix A.10 adds possible extensions to neural and physiological evidence trajectories.

D1.justification: v4 newly specifies adaptive-feedback thresholds and the greater-than-three-hour participant exclusion criterion, and supplies extensive baseline architectures, optimization settings, training times, and hardware details. It identifies the text-embedding model used for PeerEdu and replaces the separate OSF/ReactiveAI access statements with a CogReact repository reference. The additional original-study details do not establish that its procedures changed.

E1.justification: v3 evaluates arithmetic reasoning under four time-pressure conditions. v4 retains this coverage and adds CPC18 gambling decisions with numeric feedback (30,489 trials, 240 participants) and PeerEdu learning with textual peer feedback and continuous curiosity outcomes (12,804 samples, 300 students), as documented in Section 5 and Appendix A.11.

E2.justification: Beyond v3's Pure DRL and SVM comparisons, v4 evaluates hGRU, LSTM models with pretrained visual encoders, Transformers, MLPs, decision trees, random forests, and linear regression in the arithmetic comparison (Tables 1 and 4). It also introduces DL-plus-DDM comparators, including an MLP architecture matched to the hybrid agent (Figure 11).

E3.justification: The original general, group, individual, and LOPO evaluation designs remain. Added comparisons introduce five task/feedback encoding configurations and validation-based epoch selection: Appendix A.9 divides the original 80% training portion into 80% training and 20% validation, with 30- or 100-epoch budgets for different baseline families. The new learning evaluation also applies MAPE to continuous curiosity.

E4.justification: The original feature-representation, LSTM-width, and Hybrid-versus-Pure-DRL analyses are retained. v4 adds user/trial aggregation analyses of prediction-error variability, component-removal studies on the new tasks, and DL-plus-DDM controls across all three datasets to investigate the contribution of reinforcement learning (Sections 4.1 and 5; Figures 4 and 11).

E5.justification: v4 substantially expands model-comparison statistics with MAPE standard deviations, distribution percentiles, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov and permutation tests (Tables 3–8; Figure 11). Table 4 labels the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range of individual errors as a confidence interval. These additions concern error distributions and significance reporting; neither PDF establishes repeated-training run counts or an increase in runs.

E6.justification: The original general-level Hybrid/Pure DRL MAPEs of 0.2999/0.3034 remain (v3 Figure 6; v4 Figure 2). v4 adds numerous baseline and ablation results, including numeric-input CogReact MAPE 0.2703 and CPC18/PeerEdu MAPEs 0.357/0.950 (Table 4; Figure 4). These concern added encodings or tasks. The explicit attention/anxiety ANOVA findings from v3 are omitted, although their descriptive plots remain.

M1.justification: The original four-stage arithmetic framework is retained. Appendix A.11.2 adds an LSTM risk-prediction agent for decision making and a text-embedding agent for learning. The learning adaptation introduces median-based curiosity classification alongside continuous-value prediction and adjusts DRL observations, actions, and rewards, substantially extending the procedure and its outputs.

P1.justification: The paper is renamed CogReact and extensively reorganized into numbered Related Work, Methodology, Evaluation, Generalization, and Discussion sections. Much of v3's dataset exploration and Methods material moves into detailed appendices, while the abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten.

P2.justification: v4 changes the single-column presentation to a two-column layout, adds baseline/statistical tables, cross-task result plots, and detailed Hybrid/Pure DRL architecture diagrams. Original figures are matched across relocation and renumbering; notably, v3 Figure 4's SVM bar panel becomes v4 Table 3, while the remaining panels become Figure 9.

R1.justification: v4 substantially updates its research positioning around contemporary cognitive simulation, reaction-time models, and language-model-based cognition, adding works such as Goetschalckx et al. (2024), Binz and Schulz (2024), and PeerEdu. It connects evaluated baselines to these research strands and removes several earlier robotics, interaction, and synthetic-data application references.

T1.justification: The evidence-scaling formula, response-time and termination relations, and reward equations (1)–(2) are retained in Appendices A.7–A.8. v4 adds implementation explanations, including naming Brownian noise, but no new formal theoretical development, derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens comparative validation: relevant additional baselines and DL-plus-DDM controls address alternative explanations left open by v3, while evaluated adaptations to two additional cognitive tasks support previously prospective generalization claims. Expanded implementation details also improve reproducibility. Mislabeling error percentiles as confidence intervals and dropping the explicit population-diversity caveat weaken reporting, but the stronger experimental tests provide a clear, substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same hybrid cognitive-modeling framework and original arithmetic study. Despite the changed title and substantial expansion, their text, equations, figures, tables, Methods, and appendices support reliable matching and comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains those original empirical results and adds model evaluations and ablations on the CPC18 decision-making and PeerEdu learning datasets.

before.justification: v3 reports an original arithmetic user study, statistical analyses of collected responses, and trained-model evaluations, including response-time prediction and training efficiency.

results.title: CogReact: A Reinforced Framework to Model Human Cognitive Reaction Modulated by Dynamic Intervention

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: identifying classifier overconfidence, proposing DRE-BO-SSL with two unlabeled-data scenarios, and demonstrating empirical effectiveness. The revised supporting analyses do not introduce a new headline contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies the justification for unlabeled data: Appendix C acknowledges the theoretical applicability gap, and Appendices C/F replace v1's clear advantage over no-transductive learning with objective-dependent conclusions. Section 5.2 additionally acknowledges cases where GP methods perform better and softens the MNIST assessment from outperforming baselines to satisfactory performance.

D1.justification: V2 discloses SciPy L-BFGS-B with one initialization for learning beta, per-iteration optimization, 2000-point subsampling for nonsynthetic pool benchmarks, and fixed settings for supplementary studies. It also specifies CPU models and clarifies MNIST image construction. These supplement existing implementation details; both versions still promise code release upon publication.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same four synthetic functions, four Tabular Benchmarks datasets, three NATS-Bench datasets and multi-digit MNIST task. Expanded ablations reuse existing functions and scenarios rather than introduce new task or dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain GP-EI, GP-UCB and BORE/LFBO using random forests, gradient boosting, XGBoost and MLPs. Sampling analyses retain the same comparator choices. The newly cited MALIBO work is not added as an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: NATS-Bench evaluation extends from 200 to 500 optimization iterations in Figure 6. The pool-sampling study replaces subset sizes 5–1000 with 10–4000 and adds elapsed-time evaluation using a stated 4000-point pool. These substantially revise evaluation budgets and supplementary experimental settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds learned-beta trajectories (Figure 4) and runtime versus subset-size analysis (Figure 13). Unlabeled-point count and distribution studies expand from label spreading on two functions to both classifiers on all four functions. Beta sensitivity and pool-sampling analyses also expand, substantially strengthening examination of parameter dependence and computational cost.

E5.justification: Section 5 changes the reported experiment count from 10 fixed-seed repetitions to 20, with corresponding caption updates throughout. V2 explicitly identifies the reported statistics as sample means and standard errors; v1 shows uncertainty shading without defining it. This is a paper-wide revision of replication and uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main benchmark and appendix curves are replaced, and v2 adds beta trajectories, runtime measurements and expanded ablation results. Figure 11 newly shows cases where no-transductive learning performs best, such as Branin with label spreading. Updated aggregates and extended NATS-Bench runs should not be interpreted as same-setting performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The optimization loop, label propagation/spreading updates, acquisition maximization and truncated-normal sampling remain unchanged. Entropy minimization for beta already appears in v1 Section 4.1; v2 documents its implementation and use more explicitly without establishing a new method component.

P1.justification: V2 makes local prose edits, expands experimental explanations and switches to author-year citations. The analysis moves from Section 4.3 to Appendix C, and limitations move from Section 6 to Appendix H. Despite these reorganizations, the main narrative and most section content remain recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adds beta-learning and runtime figures, expands several ablation grids, and combines v1 Figures s.1/s.2 into Figure 8. It also extends NATS-Bench axes, revises captions and substantially changes the document template, headings and figure placement. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 adds Pan et al. (2023) to connect the exploration/exploitation issue with MALIBO and cites Virtanen et al. for SciPy. It replaces the expected-improvement reference to Mockus et al. (1978) with Jones et al. (1998). The broader positioning relative to BORE, LFBO and semi-supervised learning remains.

T1.justification: V1 Section 4.3 uses error bounds in Equations 11–13 to support superiority in the proposed setting. V2 Appendix C removes this argument and explains that the cited theory assumes independent, identically distributed data and cannot directly apply to sequential Bayesian optimization. A suitable theoretical analysis is left to future work; the cluster assumption and margin definition remain.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves an important validity problem by withdrawing v1's direct application of non-sequential error bounds and explaining the missing assumptions in Appendix C. Expanded ablations expose limits to the benefit of unlabeled data, while additional repetitions, explicit standard errors and runtime measurements strengthen empirical assessment. Implementation disclosures also improve reproducibility. Although a Bayesian-optimization-specific guarantee remains absent, the paper provides substantially better-supported and more qualified evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DRE-BO-SSL research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, including material moved into v2's appendices.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on the same benchmarks, with updated results, expanded ablations and new parameter-learning and runtime analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original optimization experiments on synthetic functions, Tabular Benchmarks, NATS-Bench and multi-digit MNIST, plus appendix ablations.

results.title: Density Ratio Estimation-based Bayesian Optimization with Semi-Supervised Learning

C1.justification: The claim of faster GRF training with comparable accuracy remains. v2 additionally makes robustness to ill-conditioned Jacobians a central claimed advantage and explicitly claims reduced memory demands and computational savings scaling as O(K²) (Sections 2–3.3 and 8). These extend the contribution beyond v1's acceleration-focused framing.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a substantive explanation connecting correlated regressors, nearly singular Jacobians and smaller deep-tree nodes to unstable gradient splits. Appendix C also discusses empty honest leaves and bias in in-sample predictions. v1's interpretation that speed improvements are not explained by fewer splits is no longer developed.

D1.justification: v2 supplies author implementation and experiment/data repository links, three algorithm listings, explicit line-search and simulation-generator formulas, and housing preprocessing and fitting details (Appendices C and F). However, v1's disclosure that identical separately estimated Y.hat and W.hat values were shared across methods is no longer provided; this does not establish that the control itself changed.

E1.justification: The discrete-treatment and continuous-regressor tasks remain, with the latter reframed as varying-coefficient models. v2 adds nonlinear interaction, dense logistic and random-function regimes, a correlated-regressor scenario, and geographically varying coefficient estimation on California housing data (Tables 2–3, Sections 3.2 and 7, Appendix F).

E2.justification: v1 compares grad, exact-OLS fp1 and approximate-OLS fp2. v2 reports GRF-grad versus GRF-FPT without the separate exact-OLS fp1 comparator. The original gradient baseline and previously introduced approximate fixed-point approach remain.

E3.justification: Accuracy evaluation changes from 2,000 trees, 1,000 test observations and K=2/4/8 to 100 trees, 5,000 test observations and K=4/256, with 20,000 training observations. Timing experiments expand beyond individual trees to forests of up to 1,000 trees and revise the sample-size and dimension grids (Table 1). v2 reports MSE instead of v1's normalized L2-loss presentation.

E4.justification: v2 adds a targeted robustness experiment examining split locations and variance across regressor correlations of 0.80–0.99 (Figure 1), alongside broader scaling analyses. Conversely, v1's exact-versus-approximate OLS comparison and split-count diagnostics, which tested whether acceleration resulted from simpler trees, are removed.

E5.justification: v1 documents 500 timing replications and displays their distributions; v2's timing bars omit corresponding replication counts and uncertainty displays. Accuracy replication counts change from 50 to 40. The new stability analysis reports 250 replications with median split variance and 10th/90th-percentile bands, substantially revising uncertainty reporting across the empirical evidence.

E6.justification: v2 adds or replaces extensive timing, accuracy and stability results. New housing timings are 19.1 seconds for GRF-grad versus 12.6 for GRF-FPT, a reported 1.52-fold speedup (Table 4). Accuracy is broadly similar, although the K=256 VCM Setting 2 panel shows higher FPT MSE, and some HTE timing cases favor grad. Changed protocols prevent interpreting these as same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Both versions use CART splits on Jacobian-free pseudo-outcomes followed by forest-weighted estimating equations. The one-step OLS approximation with exact line search was already described as fp2 in v1. GRF-FPT retains this procedure; expanded pseudocode and GRF implementation explanations do not establish an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background and method exposition are extensively rewritten around a Stage I/Stage II narrative. Terminology changes to GRF-FPT, detailed theory and examples move into appendices, and applications, conclusion and impact sections reshape the document's organization.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main text and substantially redesigns the displays: timing bar-chart grids, stability plots, geographic maps, distribution plots, four tables, algorithm listings and a subsampling diagram replace or supplement v1's figures. Figure 10 also introduces a caption error reversing the dimensional labels relative to its panels.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning within causal machine learning, varying-coefficient models, forest theory and classical fixed-point methods. Added references include Chernozhukov et al. (2018), Hastie and Tibshirani (1993), and Ryu and Boyd (2016). The explicit motivation from Yang et al. (2021) in v1 is removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds an explicit asymptotic-normality theorem and regularity conditions, CART-equivalence derivations, and reasoning about honest weights' conditional independence. It substantially replaces the coupling proof, introduces child-size normalization in the fixed-point approximation, and strengthens the criterion remainder from O_P in v1 Proposition 1 to o_P in v2 Proposition 4.1.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important validation gap: v1 tested accuracy only through K=8 and computational gains mainly through single-tree timings. Accuracy tests at K=256, whole-forest timings, nonlinear regimes, a targeted stability experiment and real-data analysis substantially strengthen evaluation of the intended applications. Reproduction links and implementation details also improve usability. These gains outweigh the loss of exact-OLS and split-count diagnostics, although weaker timing uncertainty reporting, caption errors and overly broad interpretations of some results remain material drawbacks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same fixed-point-tree acceleration of generalized random forests despite changes in title and organization. All 22 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v2, including proofs, figures and v2 Appendices A–F, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original stability experiments, simulation timings and estimation errors, plus an original California housing analysis in Section 7 and Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations measuring training times, tree complexity and treatment-effect estimation accuracy in Section 4 and Figures 1–5.

results.title: Generalized Random Forests using Fixed-Point Trees

C1.justification: v3 retains the coalition-attribution and conflict-mechanism claims but expands the central contribution to evaluating whether grouped variables form faithful coalitions. Its abstract and introduction newly claim validation across synthetic, NLP, image and Go settings, consistency with human intuition, and practical value for Go players. v2 makes no comparable empirical or coalition-evaluation claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations connecting faithfulness scores to coherent semantic units and low-scoring NLP groups to representation flaws. It acknowledges that learned interactions can differ from intended ones and that interaction computation restricts Go analysis to small subsets. Appendix J discusses disagreement with experts and hypothesizes a distinction between human tactical reasoning and the network's longer-term statistical patterns.

D1.justification: v3 adds limited reproducibility details for its experiments, including synthetic-function construction, 8×8 image partitioning, input-selection rules, and Go stone-removal, fixed-background and adjusted-output conventions. It does not provide full training hyperparameters, hardware/runtime information or code-release instructions for the proposed method.

E1.justification: v2 has no empirical dataset or task coverage. v3 evaluates synthetic-function regression, SST-2 sentiment classification, MNIST and CIFAR-10 image classification, and KataGo shape-pattern explanations, including expert assessments. The NLP and image examples in v2 were illustrative rather than evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: Neither version reports empirical comparisons against competing attribution algorithms. v3's Table 1 conceptually compares Shapley, Banzhaf, Joint Shapley and Faith-Shap; these are not benchmarked baselines. Direct Shapley calculations in Table 2 serve as references for checking a mathematical identity.

E3.justification: v3 introduces experimental protocols absent from v2: reconstruction checks across coalition sizes 1–10, three faithfulness metrics, MLP regression on 20 target functions, and meaningful-versus-random coalition controls. Further settings include BERT-large/LLaMA fine-tuning, ten selected input variables, and Go analyses after 40 moves. These are new experiments, not revisions of established v2 protocols.

E4.justification: v3 adds numerical checks of the attribution and output decompositions, controlled tests distinguishing faithful, partially faithful and unfaithful synthetic coalitions, and semantic coalition case studies. Appendix J adds expert analysis of Go patterns and how adding particular stones changes their attribution. v2 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3 introduces averaged point estimates and individual examples, but no uncertainty-estimation practice; the five Go experts are participants, not repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds all empirical result entries. Table 2 reports Shapley reconstruction errors from 3.6×10^-8 to 9.1×10^-7; Table 4 reports mean Q values of 0.948, 0.590 and 0.013 for faithful, partially faithful and unfaithful coalitions. Tables 3 and 5 and Figures 2–7 add further reconstruction, NLP, image and Go findings. There are no corresponding v2 measurements for performance-change comparisons.

M1.justification: The coalition-attribution formula in Equation (6) and sparse AND-OR extraction remain unchanged. v3 adds derived faithfulness scores R, R' and Q, plus selection of Go coalition candidates using top-ranked interaction strengths alongside manual annotation. These extend the framework without redesigning its attribution calculation.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and retained theoretical material is reorganized into separate attribution, conflict-explanation and axioms subsections. v3 adds a dedicated related-work section and conclusion, restructures the appendices, and expands conceptual explanations. The author list also removes Bo Fan.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text from one column to two and redraws and relocates Figure 1 with explicit interaction-allocation and conflict diagrams. It adds Tables 1–5, Go visualizations in Figures 2–3, and image-coalition displays in Figures 4–7. These substantially expand the visual presentation beyond v2's single schematic.

R1.justification: v3 adds a substantial related-work section, Table 1 and Appendix A distinguishing coalition attribution from interaction effects. New discussion covers Joint Shapley, Faith-Shap, Shapley-Taylor, Archipelago and other approaches, positioning the paper's mathematical explanation of conflict against previous engineering treatments. v2 provides much narrower background and positioning.

T1.justification: The principal decomposition results are retained under new numbering. v3 adds anonymity and coalition-level symmetry axioms, strengthens the dummy condition from all coalition members being dummy to at least one, and formally defines three faithfulness measures. Appendices E–G supply additional proofs for decompositions, axioms and efficiency; v2's universal-matching equation is relocated, not newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 makes coalition faithfulness operationally assessable and adds controlled synthetic validation plus concrete NLP, image and Go evidence, substantially improving the practical grounding of v2's theoretical proposal. Additional derivations and clearer organization also make the arguments easier to inspect. Real-world validation remains largely example-based, without uncertainty estimates or complete training details, but the gains in testability and supporting evidence are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same coalition-attribution framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original numerical verification, synthetic-function experiments, NLP and image evaluations, and Go analyses involving five experts. Results appear in Tables 2–5 and Figures 2–7, including Appendices I–J.

before.justification: v2 presents mathematical results, proofs and illustrative examples. Figure 1 is a conceptual illustration; neither the main text nor Appendices A–B report original empirical outcomes.

results.title: Towards Attributions of Input Variables in a Coalition

C1.justification: Composable tasks remain central, but v1's headline contributions of six-dimensional task space, SkillForge and targeted filtering are replaced by claims of fully automated generation, verification and evaluation. V2 additionally claims over 90% agreement with human assessment and experimentally demonstrated limitations of foundation agents under greater task diversity and difficulty (abstract, introduction and conclusion).

C2.justification: V1 interprets task distributions as revealing benchmark bias and guiding representative task selection. V2 adds explanations involving inventory distractions, dependence on demonstration locations, and increased material-use scores from redundant items (Section 4.2.3). It also identifies limitations of video subsampling for detailed crafting judgments (Section 4.1), substantially expanding mechanism and failure-condition discussion.

D1.justification: V2 adds Minecraft version, frame rate, observation/action specifications, inventory-generation procedures, human-video collection details, task success metrics, full prompts and verification/evaluation pseudocode (Appendices B–G). These substantially expand implementation documentation. Conversely, v1's explicit MCU repository link is omitted, and v2 describes annotated tasks as a future release; this establishes changed access information, not repository unavailability.

E1.justification: Minecraft and many atomic goals are retained. V2 adds a trajectory-assessment dataset covering 60 tasks and over 500 human/agent videos, plus agent evaluations on 30 atomic and five compositional tasks under varied initial states and distracting conditions (Section 4). These introduce new evaluated data and task requirements beyond v1's task-list and difficulty analyses.

E2.justification: V1 mentions MineCLIP as a possible metric and surveys prior agents' task lists without corresponding performance comparisons. V2 evaluates its scorer against MineCLIP and a version without generated criteria (Table 2), and introduces comparisons among VPT-bc, VPT-rl, STEVE-1 and GROOT, with human reference performance in Figures 9–10.

E3.justification: V1's six difficulty axes combine trajectory measurements, graph complexity and human ratings. V2 uses five human-rated axes, adding visual diversity and omitting operational effort and planning complexity (Appendix D). It also introduces paired and individual video-rating protocols, F1/Kendall/TrueSkill metrics, three difficulty levels and task-specific success definitions (Section 4; Appendix F).

E4.justification: V1's task-clustering and benchmark-difficulty-bias analyses are removed. V2 adds an ablation testing generated evaluation criteria (Table 2), robustness tests examining harder initial conditions and distractions (Figure 6; Table 5), and detailed pillar-building and snow-golem evaluation cases (Appendix G.8). These address substantially different diagnostic questions.

E5.justification: V2 introduces explicit replication and uncertainty reporting: ten rollouts per task/difficulty, averages from at least three human annotations, named world seeds, Kendall's tau with a p-value, and Gaussian TrueSkill uncertainty with plotted error bars (Section 4; Appendices E–F; Figure 10). V1 has no comparable reporting. This does not establish increased runs for any retained experiment.

E6.justification: V1's clustering and benchmark-distribution results disappear. V2 adds evaluator results: Table 2 reports average F1 of 80.0 with criteria, 73.0 without criteria and 44.0 for MineCLIP; Table 3 reports 90.8 across dimensions. It also adds agent rankings led by GROOT in Table 4 and difficulty-dependent success rates in Figure 6. These are new experiments, without matching performance results in v1.

M1.justification: The composable-task foundation remains, but v2 adds an automated procedure: GPT-4o generates randomized executable environments, Mineflayer verifies tasks and provides revision feedback, and a VLM scores videos using generated task-specific criteria (Section 3). These are substantive new components beyond v1's task construction, difficulty scoring and benchmark filtering.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, changes the author information and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion. The narrative moves from atom/molecule tasks, difficulty scores and task-space analysis to benchmark desiderata, an automated pipeline and empirical validation. The appendices are extensively reorganized and rewritten, beyond changes caused solely by adding experiments.

P2.justification: V1's taxonomy, dependency graph, t-SNE visualization, benchmark-distribution radars and text-interface screenshot give way to automation diagrams, evaluator/agent performance charts, difficulty comparisons and rating-interface screenshots. V2 also introduces five-axis per-task radar charts, expanded tables and formatted prompt/code listings. This substantially changes the visual presentation rather than merely renumbering displays.

R1.justification: V1 concentrates on Minecraft task coverage and MineDojo's shortcomings. V2 substantially broadens positioning to generalist-agent benchmarks, including DmLab, Procgen, Crafter, Xland and DYVAL (Table 1), and adds BEDD and LLM-as-judge research (Section 5). Appendix G also compares prior systems' observation/action simplifications, reshaping the rationale for MCU.

T1.justification: V2 removes the mathematical task-difficulty construction: v1's E+V planning approximation, permutation-entropy formulation and claimed independence from sequence length, and piecewise quantile calibration to [0,5] (Section 3; Appendices A and C). V2 instead introduces goal-conditioned initial-state and stratified-sampling formulations (Section 3.2; Appendix E). Neither version supplies a theorem-and-proof development.

improvement.justification: V2 closes an important practical validation gap: v1 proposes an evaluation framework without direct agent benchmarking or validation against human judgments. V2 adds human validation, a MineCLIP comparison, a criteria ablation and repeated difficulty-controlled agent trials, supported by much fuller implementation documentation. Losing the task-space analyses and project link is a drawback, and reporting issues remain, including broad agreement wording and Table 5's inconsistent efficiency delta. Nevertheless, the new methodological and empirical support substantially improves the paper's overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MCU and retain its foundation of composable Minecraft atomic tasks, despite v2's changed title and substantial revision. All pages, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original agent rollouts, human assessments, automated-evaluator comparisons, difficulty experiments and annotated task profiles (Section 4; Appendices D–G).

before.justification: V1 reports original data analyses: task-space clustering using difficulty features and comparisons of benchmark difficulty distributions (Section 4; Figures 3–4). These qualify even though v1 lacks direct agent-performance experiments.

results.title: MCU: An Evaluation Framework for Open-Ended Game Agents

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a KL detector requiring no manually selected threshold. v3 additionally claims applicability to other world-model architectures and explicitly confines novelty to permanent distribution shifts, leaving responses outside scope. v2's concluding recommendation to combine latent and observation-based detectors is removed.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning exploration-induced false alarms, weak correspondence between policy entropy and world-model surprise, and the inability to apply the KL detector directly to image-generating diffusion models. It also discusses RIQN's delay/false-positive tradeoff and experimenter bias. The earlier conditional recommendations for CMTRE versus PP-MARE disappear.
