M1.justification: The base/meta update framework, trace updates, and Hessian-free, 2×2, and L-approximations remain unchanged. The corrected time index in Equation 2 and explicit scalar/blockwise gradient reduction in Algorithm 3 clarify the existing procedure.

P1.justification: Sections 1–6 undergo extensive rewriting and condensation. The experimental narrative and Appendix D are reorganized around expanded coverage, related work and limitations are revised, and an Impact Statement and conference publication text are added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout, with extensive rearrangement of algorithms, tables, and plots. New figures and a CIFAR100 configuration table are added, metric labels change, and v5 Figure 3 is removed. v5 Figure 6 survives as v6 Figure 10; v6 Figure 8 redisplays Figure 4’s trajectories separately.

R1.justification: Section 8 substantially expands positioning against MADA, gradient-based bilevel optimization, and learned optimizers, adding works including Bengio, Maclaurin, Lorraine, Micaelli, and Metz. It now contrasts single-stream online adaptation with validation-based outer optimization and offline optimizer training. Pearlmutter’s Hessian-vector work and Schraudolph’s Local Gain Adaptation reference are removed.

T1.justification: Section 3 adds a finite-horizon, small-meta-step-size argument relating the forward and backward views. Section 9 explains removing the normalization factor for γ = 1, and Appendix A.2 corrects a missing γ factor. The main derivations and Appendix B special-case results otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v6 substantially strengthens validation by testing the framework in its intended continual setting and adding explicit ImageNet and TinyStories test outcomes, addressing important gaps in v5’s evidence about adaptation and generalization. The approximation qualifications and expanded research positioning further improve assessability. The inconsistent γ reporting and loss of the CIFAR10 trajectory analysis are drawbacks, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MetaOptimize and contain readable main text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D. The retained content can be matched reliably despite substantial reformatting and added experiments.

after.justification: v6 retains original empirical results and adds non-stationary CIFAR100 experiments, ImageNet top-1 training/test accuracy, and TinyStories test loss.

before.justification: v5 reports original CIFAR10, ImageNet, and TinyStories experiments, computational overhead measurements, and robustness and blockwise-step-size comparisons.

results.title: MetaOptimize: A Framework for Optimizing Step Sizes and Other Meta-parameters

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion shift from emphasizing TS's detrimental set-size effect and recommending its avoidance to claiming a useful size–class-coverage trade-off. v2 adds practitioner guidance for choosing separate temperatures and combining adaptive CP with calibration as a central contribution.

C2.justification: v1 treats improved conditional coverage as a relatively minor benefit. v2 makes competing size and coverage objectives central to its interpretation and explains why temperature choice depends on user requirements. It adds substantive limitations concerning unknown metric-versus-temperature curves, numerical breakdown at extremely low temperatures, and interpolation sensitivity when thresholds approach one.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands previously sparse implementation documentation. Appendices B.1–B.2 identify the pretrained ImageNet model source, CIFAR training settings including 300 epochs and SGD hyperparameters, GPU hardware, and approximate experiment runtime. Appendix C specifies a degree-five interpolating polynomial and six anchor temperatures. These are disclosures and new-procedure details, not evidence that retained classifiers were retrained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same image-classification datasets: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. The additional experiments vary temperatures, sample allocations, and coverage targets within this retained coverage; they introduce no new dataset, population, or task.

E2.justification: The main LAC, APS, and RAPS comparison set is retained. Appendix C and Figure 18 add a direct comparison between interpolated RAPS and ordinary RAPS using computed thresholds, providing a limited additional comparison for the new procedure.

E3.justification: The reported TS calibration allocation changes from 20% to 10%; CP allocations expand from 20% to 5%, 10%, and 20%, with 10% becoming the default. v2 adds alpha = 0.05, extends the temperature sweep from 1–2 to 0.3–2, and replaces raw marginal and minimum-class coverage with MarCovGap and TopCovGap. Appendix C adds a small-data interpolation evaluation.

E4.justification: v2 retains the per-sample set-size and ECE-versus-NLL analyses, while adding sensitivity to CP-set size and coverage targets, class-coverage temperature sweeps, and an extreme-low-temperature failure analysis. Appendix C additionally tests threshold interpolation and whether small calibration sets recover useful trade-off curves.

E5.justification: Both versions retain median-of-means reporting over 100 random-split trials for the main experiments. Appendix C newly reports three separate single-trial realizations of the interpolation comparison. This adds run-level reporting without establishing an increase in repetitions of the existing experiments; confidence intervals and significance tests are not added.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1's set-size values reappear in v2 Table 5. v2 adds results for new splits, coverage targets, coverage-gap metrics, low temperatures, and interpolation. Its default CIFAR-100/ResNet50 APS sizes are 5.31 before TS and 9.14 after TS under revised settings, so these are not same-setting gains over v1. The NLL-optimal temperature entry also changes from 1.338 in v1 Table 4 to 1.438 in v2 Table 3.

M1.justification: v1 recommends applying adaptive CP before or after undoing TS calibration. v2 introduces separate calibration and CP branches with independently chosen temperatures, plus optional interpolation of CP thresholds from anchor temperatures. Section 3.3 and Appendix C therefore add a substantive temperature-selection and deployment procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, experimental discussion, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the trade-off and practical guidance. Calibration-loss explanations move into the appendix, Appendix B is reorganized, and Appendix C is introduced. The title changes from 'On Calibration' to 'On Temperature Scaling.'

P2.justification: The main document changes from two columns to one with extensive reflow and repositioning. Separate size and threshold plots are combined with coverage plots in v2 Figure 3, coverage tables are reorganized, and new workflow, sensitivity, low-temperature, and interpolation displays are added. Existing reliability and per-sample plots are retained in reorganized locations.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to prior TS-plus-CP applications, conditional-coverage limitations, and class-conditional evaluation, including Lu, Gibbs, Vovk, Barber, and Ding works absent from v1. It refines the positioning by distinguishing the few CP studies using calibration from the majority that do not, while retaining the claimed gap concerning TS's effects.

T1.justification: Most propositions and proofs are retained. Appendix B.4 revises the mathematical coverage measures, notably replacing minimum-class coverage with the average absolute gap among the worst 5% of classes. Corollary 4.3/A.3 loses its explicit nonrandomized restriction without corresponding randomized-score reasoning. Theorem 4.4's small-step formulation largely restates the earlier ascent-direction result.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the justification and usefulness of the paper's main recommendation: it replaces v1's emphasis on avoiding TS with measured, task-dependent balancing of set size and class coverage. Sensitivity experiments, low-temperature failure analysis, practical validation in Appendix C, and training disclosures strengthen empirical grounding and reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses: interpolation is demonstrated only on one dataset-model pair across three runs, and removing the corollary's nonrandomized qualification reduces theoretical precision.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same temperature-scaling and conformal-prediction study by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite the revised title and expanded scope.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on the same datasets, expanded sensitivity analyses, and an empirical comparison of ordinary and interpolated RAPS in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments with LAC, APS, and RAPS on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, including prediction-set sizes, coverage measurements, and temperature sweeps in Section 3 and Appendix B.

results.title: On Temperature Scaling and Conformal Prediction of Deep Classifiers

C1.justification: The central claims of efficient pairwise losses, gradient alignment and competitive regression performance remain. v3 explicitly narrows the abstract's scope to clean data without noise, outliers or distribution shifts and adds the claim that the two pairwise components are beneficial separately.

C2.justification: The new Limitations section explains that GAR can be misled when training data do not reflect the underlying function. v3 also explains why symbolic-regression comparisons depend on access to suitable function primitives. Benchmark correlations are interpreted primarily as evidence about rank preservation, replacing v1's stronger derivative/shape interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents AgeDB's 12,208/2,140/2,140 split, age range and 224-by-224 crop size, identifies IC50 categorical feature types, and clarifies gradient detachment. The printed code pointer changes from FAR to GAR. Most training details are retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E1.justification: Concrete Compressive Strength replaces Abalone in the benchmark coverage. The two synthetic datasets and the other five real-world datasets remain, including both Parkinson targets and both AgeDB settings. PySR and network-depth experiments reuse the existing synthetic data.

E2.justification: v3 adds PySR as a supplementary synthetic comparator, evaluated with and without trigonometric functions in its search space (Appendix B.5). The original synthetic neural comparators and the eight real-world baseline methods retain their participation in corresponding comparisons.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include all seven nonempty loss-component combinations across six tabular tasks, a five-setting network-depth sweep with GAR alpha tuned over {0.5, 1, 2}, and controlled PySR search spaces. The original synthetic and retained benchmark protocols, including splits, budgets and tuning grids, are otherwise unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 examines alpha sensitivity and efficiency but does not isolate loss components or vary network depth. v3 adds comprehensive component ablations (Table 4), depth sensitivity (Figure 6), and a symbolic-regression prior-knowledge analysis (Figures 4–5). Alpha sensitivity results also replace Abalone with Concrete Compressive Strength and revise Wine Quality.

E5.justification: Appendix B.8 newly specifies five AgeDB repetitions with different random seeds; v1 already reports means and standard deviations without this run-count disclosure. This does not establish an increase in runs. Existing synthetic five-seed reporting and benchmark Student's t-test practice remain.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds Concrete results, removes Abalone and revises Wine Quality scores: FAR/GAR MAE changes from 0.596 to 0.494 and Pearson correlation from 0.503 to 0.613, without a disclosed protocol change. Parkinson through AgeDB entries remain identical. Table 2 replaces timings and expands coverage; new PySR, depth and ablation results include GAR's best overall ablation rank of 2.375 in Table 4.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same MAE, error-variance and normalized pairwise-difference losses, KL-based aggregation and optimization procedure. FAR-to-GAR renaming and the explicit clarification that normalization constants are detached from backpropagation do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution narrative and substantial method discussion are rewritten. A new Motivations subsection precedes the pairwise-loss development, the derivative theorem moves later, a Limitations section is added, and experimental settings are reorganized into expanded appendix subsections.

P2.justification: v3 adds two PySR figures, a 25-panel network-depth figure and the component-ablation table. The runtime table expands from three to five dataset columns. Sensitivity displays are revised and reordered, and the duplicate main-text Wine Quality panel is removed. The original synthetic plots largely retain their visual content.

R1.justification: v3 adds Cranmer and Petersen on symbolic regression, Klivans on outlier-robust regression, and Yeh for Concrete, while removing the Abalone reference. It makes the label-space versus latent-feature-space positioning more explicit; the central comparison with RankSim, RNC and ConR remains.

T1.justification: The derivative-equivalence statement now explicitly limits derivative orders to 1 through K, and Appendix A.3 adds directional-limit and L'Hôpital reasoning. v3 omits v1's general p-norm error-difference corollary and MAE/absolute-error variance derivation. The principal variance, Pearson-correlation and KL-aggregation results remain.

improvement.justification: v1 does not isolate the contributions of its three losses and demonstrates synthetic behavior at only one network depth. v3's six-task component study and depth controls address these important validation gaps, while explicit clean-data limitations improve claim calibration. These are substantial evidential gains, although unexplained Wine Quality revisions remain a documentation weakness and Table 4 supports the best aggregate rank rather than superiority on every metric.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, renamed from Function Aligned Regression (FAR) to Gradient Aligned Regression (GAR). All 24 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v3, including proofs, experimental appendices, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds component ablations, network-depth experiments and PySR evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments, real-world benchmark results, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses and measured running times.

results.title: Gradient Aligned Regression via Pairwise Losses

C1.justification: The abstract is unchanged, and the central contributions remain the logical framework, ConCon dataset, and demonstration that preventing forgetting or accumulating data can fail to prevent confounding. The additional experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 now acknowledges that the continual setup itself may explain part of the performance gap and explicitly notes similar joint/cumulative performance for NeSy. V3 adds interpretations of shuffled training and PNN task heads. Existing overfitting explanations and principal limitations remain.

D1.justification: V3 adds brief PNN architecture information, a training-time exception for PNNs, the ResNet-18-based VAE description, and ImageNet class mappings and hyperparameter cross-references. Existing ConCon implementation details, code/data access, licenses, and datasheet information are largely retained.

E1.justification: V3 extends evaluation beyond synthetic ConCon to natural ImageNet images. The introduction evaluates six ImageNet classes; Appendix E adds 24 source classes grouped into six labels across three tasks. This substantially broadens the represented data and classification tasks.

E2.justification: V3 retains all nine original comparison setups, adds PNNs and shuffled training for both model families on both ConCon variants, and evaluates generative replay in Appendix D. These additions broaden comparison to growing architectures, generative replay, and a dedicated control.

E3.justification: V3 introduces shuffled cumulative training that breaks confounder-to-task alignment, task-aware PNN evaluation, and new ImageNet protocols with three sequential pairs of labels. The existing ConCon splits, accuracy metrics, memory-buffer size, and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new shuffled control tests the contribution of temporal confounder alignment while retaining cumulative training. Appendix C also extends positive/negative error analyses to shuffled training and PNNs. The original convergence and error analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions document five random seeds and report standard deviations in Appendix C. V3 extends the existing reporting convention to additional results without introducing a new statistical procedure or reporting an increase in repetitions for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Retained ConCon table values, including standard deviations, are unchanged. New strict-NN results include 89.5% unconfounded accuracy for shuffled training and 49.2% for PNNs, alongside retained cumulative/joint values of 72.6%/95.7%. Generative replay adds 47.73%/49.26% unconfounded accuracy on disjoint/strict. New ImageNet comparisons report 91.7% joint versus 89.3% cumulative accuracy and a 5.58-point average gap in the expanded experiment.

M1.justification: The proposed ConCon construction, ground-truth rule, confounders, and disjoint/strict generation procedures remain unchanged. PNNs and generative replay are additional evaluated approaches, not revisions to the proposed framework.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten, replacing award-reporting and husky anecdotes with literature-based motivation and an ImageNet example. Related-work and results narratives are reworked, the impact statement moves into the main text, and the appendix organization is revised.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column main layout, replaces Figure 1, and rearranges Figure 2 vertically. V2 Table 1 becomes two expanded tables; its error-analysis Figures 6–7 become Figures 6–9 with added rows. New generative-replay and ImageNet tables further change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V3 expands introductory context with shortcut-learning and confounding literature, including Geirhos, Steinmann, and Ye, and cites the added PNN and generative-replay comparators. Ribeiro's explanation paper is removed with the husky example. The central positioning of ConCon remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The predicate definitions, constraints, derivations, and conditions making the ground-truth rule the unique joint solution are retained. V2 Equation 4 is split into v3 Equations 4 and 5; this changes presentation, not mathematical substance.

improvement.justification: The shuffled control addresses an important weakness in v2's central attribution: comparing 89.5% shuffled, 72.6% cumulative, and 95.7% joint strict-NN accuracy better separates temporal confounding from general cumulative-training effects. PNNs and generative replay broaden the empirical challenge, and the NeSy qualification improves interpretive accuracy. ImageNet mechanisms remain less directly established, and Table 2's blanket statement about old-task failure conflicts with its PNN rows, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial strengthening of the central evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ConCon research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and additional experiments in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds PNN, shuffled-training, generative-replay, and ImageNet results.

before.justification: V2 reports original ConCon experiments with neural and neuro-symbolic models, including benchmark accuracies, repeated-run statistics, learning curves, and error analyses.

results.title: Where is the Truth? The Risk of Getting Confounded in a Continual World

C1.justification: V1 centers its contribution on a 1D guarantee for simple payoff functions and identifies multidimensional extension as an obstacle. V2 makes a conditional multidimensional guarantee for bounded-Natarajan, local policy classes its primary contribution, retains the adversarial 1D result as secondary, and explicitly strengthens the hardness claim to randomized algorithms.

C2.justification: V2 interprets mentor-policy complexity as the central boundary between possibility and impossibility. Sections 4 and 6 add substantive qualifications about computational policy selection, the unresolved locality assumption, and the tradeoff between multidimensional i.i.d. states and adversarial 1D states. V1's discussion of unknown horizons and the failed doubling trick is dropped.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 adds implementation-oriented guidance identifying policy updates and nearest-neighbor distance as the required operations, and discusses nearest-neighbor policies when supported by the policy class. V2 also documents horizon-only tuning for the retained 1D algorithm. These remain mathematical specifications; no code, hardware, or runtime information is supplied.

E1.justification: Neither version evaluates datasets or tasks empirically. The added multidimensional setting and state-distribution assumptions concern theoretical coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods against the proposed algorithms. Related-work discussions do not constitute baseline evaluations.

E3.justification: Neither PDF contains an experimental evaluation protocol. Changes to state sampling, action-space assumptions, and query schedules are mathematical model or algorithm changes.

E4.justification: Neither version reports empirical ablations, robustness tests, or case studies. V1's removed multidimensional failure construction is a theoretical counterexample.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical estimates. The changed concentration inequalities and probability bounds belong to theoretical proofs.

E6.justification: Neither version contains measured performance values, rankings, or empirical result entries. Changes to regret and query bounds are theoretical results assessed under T1.

M1.justification: V2 adds LookBeforeYouLeap (Algorithm 1): collect initial mentor labels, select a consistent local policy, and subsequently query and update the policy when states exceed a distance threshold. V1's DBWRQ bucketing procedure is retained as Algorithm 2, AvoidCatastrophe, with a revised prescribed tuning g(T)=T^c.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, results overview, and conclusion; places hardness before the positive results; introduces a dedicated limitations section; and reorganizes the appendices. The former main-text proof discussion is absorbed into the revised appendix treatment, and terminology shifts from payoff-function simplicity toward mentor-policy simplicity.

P2.justification: The document changes throughout from two-column to single-column layout, with reformatted equations, references, and algorithm displays. V2 adds a new pseudocode block and reformats the retained bucketing algorithm. Figure 1 retains the same mathematical construction but is resized, relocated, and given an expanded caption.

R1.justification: V1's Function Complexity discussion emphasizes individual payoff-function complexity in contrast to class-based measures. V2 removes that positioning and builds its primary contribution around Natarajan dimension and PAC learning, adding relevant references. It also adds a substantive comparison with Barman et al.'s geometric-mean bandit objective, explaining its difference from the product objective.

T1.justification: V2 adds locality definitions and the multidimensional Natarajan-dimension guarantee, supported by PAC-learning, concentration, and packing arguments in Appendix B. It replaces the hardness proof to address randomized algorithms, reformulates 1D simplicity in terms of mentor-policy segments, and corrects the query-bound prefactor from 2+range to 4+range. Remark B.1 adds a suboptimal-mentor extension under modified assumptions. V1's Section 5 multidimensional failure derivation is removed.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's central dimensionality limitation through a distinct algorithm and accompanying multidimensional analysis, while retaining the 1D approach. Its explicit locality and computational qualifications also clarify what the guarantees establish. The extension remains conditional on i.i.d. states and locality, and the detailed 2D failure example is lost, but the broader supported theoretical account and clearer applicability boundaries represent a substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, algorithms, mathematical figure, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: V2 remains a theoretical paper throughout the main text and appendices. Its additional algorithm and probabilistic analyses are not empirical results.

before.justification: V1 reports algorithms, theorems, proofs, and mathematical constructions, including in its appendices. It contains no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: Avoiding Catastrophe in Online Learning by Asking for Help

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: separating discrete and continuous flows, perfect hint-supervised single-task and multitask generalization, and architectural support for verifying learned algorithms.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes ordinary benchmark success from the guarantees requiring hard attention, attributes controlled failures specifically to scalar arithmetic, and discusses operation-selection ambiguity. It also adds qualifications about no-hint DFS difficulty and possible tradeoffs between expressivity and generalization guarantees.

D1.justification: v2 leaves the no-hint search largely unspecified; v3 supplies graph-size and state-count ranges, temperature schedules, validation settings, and the selected configuration. The appendices document replacement architectures, exact scalar operations, state-to-operation assignments, training distributions, and optimization budgets. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the code reference and main hardware disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The six SALSA-CLRS algorithms and four-task CLRS-30 subset remain. v3 adds high-degree complete bipartite graphs for BFS stress testing and standalone scalar-function tasks evaluated under a shifted scalar-input distribution.

E2.justification: Table 2 removes Triplet-GMPNN's comparison column, although Section 4.2 still names it. GIN, PGN, Hint-ReLIC, and G-ForgetNet remain in their corresponding comparisons. Appendix C additionally compares the discrete scalar updater against a two-layer MLP.

E3.justification: The main benchmark settings remain stable, but substantial additional evaluation designs appear: scalar-updater replacements with ground-truth-scalar controls in Appendix A; training on 3–5-node graphs and testing on 160 nodes in Appendix B; and 5000-step, 16-state scalar regression with separate training and testing input ranges in Appendix C.

E4.justification: v2 describes the non-discretized ablation only qualitatively. v3 quantifies it and separately investigates hard-attention failures, scalar-update errors, minimum sufficient training sizes, and extended operation learnability. Section 6 and Appendix E also deepen the existing no-hint error analysis with measured state accuracy and pointer-update examples.

E5.justification: Section 6 newly specifies five differently seeded models per no-hint hyperparameter configuration. This is additional run-count disclosure, not evidence of increased repetitions. The retained benchmark tables preserve their five-seed reporting and existing uncertainty conventions.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark scores are unchanged, while Triplet-GMPNN's four entries disappear. Tables 3–8 add substantial results: no-hint BFS scores of 94/34 at 16 nodes and 79/0 at 64 nodes, attention failures on large bipartite graphs, perfect generalization after training on 4–5 nodes, and scalar-operation outcomes including identity-update success in only three of five runs.

M1.justification: The core DNAR architecture is retained. Appendix C implements an extended ScalarUpdate variant with state-gated combinations of cosine, multiplication, and atan2 operations, expanding beyond the original increment, keep, and push operations. This does not establish changes to the benchmark models.

P1.justification: v3 makes sentence-level language corrections, updates affiliations and publication text, and expands explanations of discretization, metrics, and no-hint behavior. Appendices and an impact statement are added, while the main eight-section sequence and overall narrative remain.

P2.justification: The predominantly single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference main text with full-width appendices. v3 adds Tables 3–8 and Figures 2–5, relocates and resizes Figure 1, removes a column from Table 2, and makes unavailable node-level eccentricity entries explicit in Table 1.

R1.justification: The related-work coverage and central positioning remain stable. Changes to references such as Learning to Reason, Tracr, and Algorithmic Concept-Based Explainable Reasoning update publication or bibliographic information for the same works rather than introducing new research coverage.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 changes the summary ScalarUpdate inputs from next-step to current-step states, aligning them with the component equations. Appendix C formalizes the generalized operation-gated updater, while Appendix D develops the existing verification argument into explicit BFS attention inequalities and state-transition conditions. No broader correctness theorem is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence for the central design rationale: v2's qualitative ablation statement becomes controlled component tests, while training-size experiments and quantified no-hint failures clarify generalization boundaries. Explicit BFS verification conditions and expanded experimental details improve assessability and reproducibility. The removed Triplet-GMPNN column, despite its retained mention, creates a limited inconsistency that does not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DNAR research. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v2 ends with references; v3 additionally contains readable Appendices A–E.

after.justification: v3 retains the original benchmark results and adds quantitative ablations, training-size experiments, scalar-operation experiments, and no-hint analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original DNAR experiments on SALSA-CLRS and CLRS-30, multitask results, and observations from training without hints.

results.title: Discrete Neural Algorithmic Reasoning

C1.justification: The central data-free GINN and generative-PINN claims remain. v2 expands the introduction's contribution description to include evaluation metrics and architecture investigations, while narrowing the connectedness contribution's novelty positioning to a continuous-function alternative to existing topology losses.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking SIREN's spectral bias to diversity and eikonal regularization to more meaningful neural-field distances. It also reinterprets the retained Figure 10 examples: v1 describes failure to structure the bracket latent space, whereas v2 identifies improved interpolation with smoothing and acknowledges that the mechanism remains unresolved.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds GPU-memory estimates of approximately 11 GB for the bracket and 7 GB for the obstacle, identifies Dalmia's SIREN implementation, and documents the added SIREN configurations. Existing GPU types, training-time reports and reaction-diffusion implementation details are retained.

E1.justification: The same geometry, reaction-diffusion and annulus demonstrations remain. The mirror task specification changes from focusing rays at (0,1.5) in v1 to focusing at (0,1) with an additional f(0)=0 interface constraint in v2 Section 4.1.

E2.justification: v2 adds SIREN with first-layer frequencies 1 and 2 alongside softplus-MLP in the obstacle comparison, and bracket variants without normal, diversity or eikonal losses. The separate 2D connectedness comparison from v1 Figure 4(c) disappears. These expand internal comparisons; cited persistent-homology methods are not evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendix B introduces quantitative constraint, diversity and smoothness evaluation, including latent-midpoint comparisons. Table 2 revises reported softplus obstacle training from 2000 to 3000 iterations and its eikonal weight from 1e-2 to 1e-5, and adds 64-wide SIREN configurations. The prescribed obstacle normals are also corrected from (0,±1) to (±1,0).

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands architecture, frequency, diversity and interpolation analyses for the obstacle, and adds normal-, diversity- and eikonal-loss ablations for the bracket. Previously qualitative connectedness and initialization tests gain quantitative assessment. The standalone 2D connectedness illustration is removed, while the annulus diversity analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2 averages metrics across 16 obstacle or four bracket shapes from a generator; this is evaluation aggregation, not repeated-training uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 3–4 add numerical constraint-satisfaction, diversity and smoothness results absent from v1. Table 3 reports softplus diversity of 0.12 with the diversity loss versus 0.0076 without it. Table 4 reports generative-bracket diversity of 0.061 by default, 0.034 without diversity loss and 0.033 without eikonal loss. These are newly reported comparisons, not demonstrated same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The conditional neural fields, constraint-penalty objective, boundary-based diversity distance, minimal aggregation and connectedness Algorithm 1 are retained. The expanded architecture comparisons use existing GINN components rather than introducing a new procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, the connectedness explanation is condensed and partly moved into the appendix, and the obstacle narrative is reorganized around generative-model comparisons. The appendices separate implementation from a new evaluation section, and citations change from author-year to numbered references.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from a bracket-focused illustration into a four-task overview incorporating earlier material. v2 adds architecture/diversity displays, expanded interpolation comparisons, a normal-loss close-up and quantitative Tables 3–4, while expanding Table 2. Figure 10 retains its examples but moves and receives a substantively revised caption.

R1.justification: v1 Section 3.1.1 says connectedness had not been addressed for implicit neural shapes. v2 acknowledges relevant prior approaches, including Mezghanni et al. (2021), and positions its continuous Morse construction against discretized persistent homology. This substantially revises novelty positioning. It also adds PINN-optimization references and condenses the specific topology-optimization discussion.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds formal definitions for constraint-evaluation measures, mean shape-set diversity and clipped smoothness. The Morse-theory assumptions, connectedness construction, Algorithm 1 and existing diversity derivation otherwise remain after relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: v1 relies mainly on qualitative examples; v2's defined metrics, Tables 3–4 and expanded ablations make constraint violations and diversity tradeoffs assessable, substantially strengthening the empirical foundation. The revised connectedness positioning also improves precision. These gains outweigh localized reporting defects, notably Table 3's purported interface fraction exceeding one and prose describing its approximately 16-fold softplus diversity difference as several orders of magnitude.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Geometry-Informed Neural Networks work. All pages, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds quantitative model comparisons and ablations in Appendix B, particularly Tables 3–4.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original neural-shape experiments, Gray-Scott pattern generation and diversity-optimization results.

results.title: Geometry-Informed Neural Networks

C1.justification: The contribution shifts from DirectSAM/SeqAE and preliminary CLEVR learning advantages to EPOC and systematic comparison of adaptive tokenizers. v3 adds central claims about morphology alignment, monosemanticity, token efficiency and advantages over object-level tokenization across recognition and captioning settings (abstract, introduction and conclusion).

C2.justification: v3 develops explanations linking polysemantic tokens to infrequent semantic mixtures and truncation robustness to long-tailed token sizes. Appendix D newly identifies limitations involving thin structures, evaluated LLM scale, segmentation latency and loss of within-token spatial detail. These substantially extend v2's interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: Appendices A–C replace the DirectSAM/SeqAE/Phi-2 recipes with EPOC/VLM implementation information and add comparator checkpoint identifiers, segmentation settings, metric tolerances, optimizer/warmup details, precision and token caps. Conversely, v2's own code/model and demonstration links are omitted; this does not establish that those resources were withdrawn.

E1.justification: v3 adds ImageNet-1K recognition, ShareGPT4V/Pixmo-cap detailed captioning, and intrinsic object/part segmentation evaluation on COCO/COCONut, ADE20K, PPP and PartImageNet++. SA-1B and CLEVR-derived captioning are retained; CLEVR captions additionally describe color. This substantially broadens the represented domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 compares its MobileSAM-v2/SeqAE VLM with one patch-based baseline. v3's downstream comparisons include patch, Mask2Former-tiny/large and SLIC against EPOC. Its intrinsic comparisons additionally evaluate OneFormer, SAM ViT-B/H, FastSAM and MobileSAMv2 (Figures 4–5, Table 1).

E3.justification: CLEVR evaluation changes from 2,000 to 5,000 held-out images, 10 to 30 training epochs, and batch size 32 to 512. Phi-2 with LoRA is replaced by fully fine-tuned SmolLM2/Llama configurations. v3 also introduces token-budget sweeps, intrinsic segmentation metrics and throughput protocols, while replacing caption-attribute accuracy reporting with validation perplexity (Appendices A–C).

E4.justification: v3 adds embedding ablations and token-truncation experiments, using random removal for patches and smallest-segment removal for adaptive tokenizers (Figure 6). It also analyzes segmentation granularity, token-size distributions and inference scaling with process count (Figures 7–13). v2 contains no comparable analysis suite.

E5.justification: v3 Section 5.3 newly clarifies that each plotted VLM point represents an individual run. This is a limited disclosure about result aggregation, not evidence of increased replication. Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2's CLEVR accuracy entries, including 11% patch versus 63% subobject count accuracy, are removed. v3 reports new segmentation, perplexity/token-budget, ablation and efficiency results; Table 1 gives maximum throughput of 17.1 FPS for EPOC versus 12.2 for FastSAM. These are new or replaced results under revised settings, not same-setting improvements over v2.

M1.justification: The boundary-prediction idea persists, but v3 presents a 3.7M-parameter SegFormer-b0/watershed EPOC pipeline, compared with v2's 84.6M-parameter DirectSAM. More substantially, SeqAE's learned autoencoding is replaced by pooled image features, bounding-box-plus-mask position encoding and MLP fusion (v2 Sections 2–3; v3 Sections 3.2.3 and 5.1).

P1.justification: The main narrative is extensively rewritten and reorganized into preliminaries, adaptive segmentation, separate intrinsic/extrinsic evaluations and related work. Implementation material is redistributed into expanded appendices, and terminology and contribution framing are substantially revised. This exceeds routine editing or renumbering.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the introductory analogy and SeqAE/LVLM graphics with a watershed schematic, comparative segmentation panels, an efficiency table and extensive evaluation/ablation plots. The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with further displays in the appendices. These are substantial visual and layout changes.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning beyond the subword analogy and SAM. It adds cognitive recognition-by-components research, tokenization/compression studies, and direct discussion of prior superpixel tokenizers, slot attention and token pooling. Section 6 distinguishes separate segmentation from feature-based grouping and explains compatibility with token-embedding research.

T1.justification: v3 introduces a formal token-index-map formulation and defines token monosemanticity, including its erosion-based operational test (Section 2.1, Section 4.2, Appendix B). These are limited formal additions. The O(N)-versus-O(1) boundary-prediction argument already appears in v2; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2's downstream evidence uses MobileSAM-v2 on synthetic CLEVR, explicitly deferring DirectSAM evaluation. v3 directly tests EPOC's segmentation quality, computational cost and downstream usefulness against relevant alternatives, with token-budget comparisons, ablations and substantive limitations (Sections 4–5, Appendices B–D). Replacing attribute/count accuracies with perplexity reduces direct semantic interpretability, and project links are lost, but resolving the proposed tokenizer's validation gap substantially strengthens the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same subobject-tokenization research, despite substantial revision. Their text and visuals support reliable comparison. v2 has no appendix; v3 includes readable Appendices A–D.

after.justification: v3 reports original segmentation, computational-efficiency and downstream VLM experiments, with additional ablations and analyses in the appendices (Sections 4–5, Appendices B–C).

before.justification: v2 reports original CLEVR captioning experiments, including training curves and object-attribute/count accuracies on 2,000 test images (Section 3, Figure 4).

results.title: Subobject-level Image Tokenization

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction shift from mesh-free observation windows and PIRL to a claimed first united 1D–2D–3D foundation model organized around multi-scale inputs, multi-physics learning, and physical alignment. Fourier encoding and PDE-Aligner become central contributions. V2 explicitly emphasizes in-context learning and expands its advertised state-of-the-art scope to 11 PDE types across PDEBench and PDEArena.

C2.justification: V2 attributes grid flexibility and transfer to Fourier-mode selection and united training, and interprets field-classification accuracy as evidence of physical alignment. Appendix B adds limitations concerning interpretability, data and compute constraints, and abrupt dynamics such as shock waves; Appendix H.7 discusses resource tradeoffs against simpler models. V1's acknowledged 3D and high-frequency zero-shot difficulties are also retained.

D1.justification: Compared with v1's short implementation appendix, v2 provides per-PDE data statistics, baseline hyperparameters, model sizes, batch sizes, learning schedules, fine-tuning budgets, and aligner training steps and GPU hours in Tables 5–10. It adds an access link and statements about supplementary code/scripts. Reproducibility remains imperfect: the main text specifies BERT-base-cased, whereas Appendix F.3 specifies albert-math.

E1.justification: V2 adds training and evaluation on 3D Maxwell electromagnetic fields, physical-field classification, and explicit inference across different grid resolutions. Incompressible Navier–Stokes, Shock/KH/OTVortex zero-shot cases, and forcing/buoyancy inverse tasks already appear in v1; their later placement or PDEArena attribution does not establish new coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds PDEformer-1 comparisons on 1D Advection, Burgers, and Reaction-Diffusion, ORCA-SWIN-B on 2D Reaction-Diffusion and SWE, and MPP-AVIT-B. V1's MPP-L is retained as MPP-AVIT-L alongside FNO, PINNs, and U-Net. The original FNO-versus-OmniArch Burgers rollout comparison is removed.

E3.justification: V2 expands evaluation to Base/Large configurations and new resolution and loss-function protocols. Reported data resolutions change, including 3D CFD Ns from 64 to 128 in v1 Table 1 versus v2 Table 5. The zero-shot context sweep changes from approximately 10–100 to 1–50 observations. The retained SWE prompt plot is relabeled Large to Base; this establishes a reported configuration revision, not a rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds an nRMSE/RMSE/MSE loss ablation, PDE-Aligner classification validation, grid-resolution sensitivity, CFD parameter-condition comparisons, and comparative memory/runtime analysis. It also replaces v1's Burgers rollout illustration with several 2D rollout case studies. The inverse-problem and SWE prompt-efficiency analyses are substantially retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 adds a standard-deviation row to the main benchmark table and states in checklist item 7 that main results average repeated experiments, without specifying run counts or seeds. Existing inverse-result uncertainties remain. Conversely, v1 Figure 5's zero-shot context error bars are absent from the revised v2 Figure 10.

E6.justification: The fine-tuned CFD-1D nRMSE of 0.0392 in v1 Table 2 is replaced by 0.0200 for v2 Large; v2 also reports Maxwell results and numerous new configuration and analysis entries. Zero-shot KH changes from 0.5432 to 0.2763, while U-Net remains better at 0.1677. Architecture and setting revisions prevent interpreting these as controlled version-level gains. The inverse-estimation numbers are retained.

M1.justification: V1's axis/convolution encoding and frame-based PIRL scorer are replaced by truncated Fourier encoding, zero-padded inverse Fourier decoding, and a PDE-Aligner using initial/current-state phase and amplitude relationships. V2 introduces energy regularization and a combined simulation/alignment fine-tuning loss, replacing the stated reinforcement-learning objective. These substantially revise the method, beyond renaming.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and method around three design challenges. Related work is compressed and reordered, the standalone Background section disappears, and substantial implementation and analysis material moves into expanded Appendices A–H. A notation table, limitations section, and checklist further reorganize the document.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a predominantly single-column layout. Architecture Figures 2–3 are redrawn, and the main benchmark table is transposed and grouped by comparator and training stage. V2 adds classification, resolution, loss, and rollout displays, redraws the zero-shot context plot with a logarithmic axis, and duplicates the retained inverse table in the appendix.

R1.justification: V2 reframes novelty around united cross-dimensional training and explicitly positions OmniArch against dimensional and grid restrictions of prior models. It adds PDEformer, ORCA/Swin, convolutional and graph-based PDE approaches, and scientific foundation-model examples such as HyenaDNA and OpenLAM. Earlier positioning through xVal, Decision Transformer, and several broader surveys is removed or replaced.

T1.justification: V2 substantially revises the mathematical formulation through definitions of truncated Fourier representations, phase/amplitude alignment, and an energy-regularized objective. Section 3.1.2 additionally introduces mathematical reasoning relating self-attention updates to time integration. These replace or extend v1's axis-encoding and reward formulation; neither version supplies formal theorems or complete proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1's support for flexibility and reproducibility through direct multi-resolution tests, a loss-function ablation, additional unified-model comparisons, and detailed implementation tables in Appendices D–H. These make central claims substantially easier to assess. The gains outweigh new documentation inconsistencies, including BERT versus albert-math and RMSE versus nRMSE labels for identical inverse results. Broad superiority claims also remain insufficiently qualified: v2 Table 1 still favors FNO on 3D CFD.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniArch, despite changes to the title, architecture, and organization. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's appended checklist.

after.justification: V2 reports original prediction and inverse-problem results, together with additional classification, multi-resolution, ablation, and computational-resource experiments in the main text and Appendices F–H.

before.justification: V1 reports original PDE prediction benchmarks, zero-shot evaluations, inverse-parameter estimates, and prompt-length and rollout experiments in Tables 2–4 and Figures 4–7.

results.title: OmniArch: Building Foundation Model For Scientific Computing

C1.justification: v1 presents superior unconditional generation using ESM-2 and treats conditional generation as future work. v2 claims generality across multiple encoder families, demonstrated conditional and backbone-generation capabilities, and performance comparable to multibillion-parameter models using a 35M-parameter denoiser. This substantially broadens the contribution's scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of encoder quality/diversity tradeoffs, DPLM repetition and domain-length behavior, and the advantage of richer fold-conditioning information. It explicitly qualifies pLDDT in intrinsically disordered regions and discusses infilling failures. Conversely, v1's dedicated discussion of monomer/length restrictions and unexplored scalability is removed, although dataset length filters remain documented.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses batch size, learning rate, gradient clipping, warmup, EMA, four A100 80GB GPUs, and approximately ten days per training session (Appendix C.2). Conditional experiments add adapter specifications, training budgets, sampling settings, and baseline initialization details. These are documentation additions; v1's direct DiMA code-access link is omitted without a replacement.

E1.justification: SwissProt and AFDBv4-90 remain, but v2 adds family-conditioned generation across eight families, sequence infilling, functional-motif scaffolding, joint sequence-structure generation, and fold-conditioned design. New coverage includes the 24-problem scaffolding benchmark and CATH S40, TIM-barrel, and NTF2 fold evaluations.

E2.justification: The SwissProt comparison retains nanoGPT, EvoDiff-OADM, SeqDesign, and ProteinGAN while adding Walk-Jump, RITA, D3PM, DFM, and DPLM (v2 Tables 2 and 6). Separate pretrained and conditional comparisons add methods including ProtGPT2, ProGen2, ProLLAMA, RFDiffusion, and Multiflow. The SUPERFAMILY comparison also changes comparator membership, prominently introducing DPLM.

E3.justification: The reported matched model budget changes from 33M to 35M. v2 describes held-out distributional evaluation where v1 described training-data references, replaces SeqD/30%-identity clustering with repetition and revised clustering measures, and adds novelty, ProGen perplexity, and structural distribution metrics. New tasks introduce masking, success thresholds, and best-of-10 or 100-design protocols. These are reported settings, not proof that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds decoder-finetuning and flow-matching ablations, a generation-step sensitivity study, and encoder-capacity/compression analyses. It extends the existing length-masking analysis with quantitative quality results rather than introducing that question anew. Biological analyses gain domain-overlap comparisons, and conditional experiments add structural case studies and failure observations (Appendices E–F).

E5.justification: The existing out-of-distribution pLDDT plus/minus summaries and secondary-structure dispersion plot are retained. Neither version documents repeated-training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new multiple-design attempts specify sampling and selection protocols rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The SwissProt DiMA row changes from pLDDT 80.8 and FPD 0.41 in v1 Table 1 to 83.3 and FD-seq 0.34 in v2 Tables 5–6. Changed model descriptions prevent treating this as a controlled same-setting gain. Substantial new results include 42.2% infilling success versus DPLM's 40.0%, 19/24 scaffolding problems solved, and the fold-conditioned results in Table 14.

M1.justification: v2 extends the unconditional pipeline with classifier guidance, family-label conditioning, an infilling adapter, and motif/fold conditioning components. CHEAP integration enables joint sequence and backbone outputs. The decoder description also changes from two linear layers plus an activation to one linear layer. The core denoiser, diffusion objective, self-conditioning, and length-sampling approach remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Numbered method subsections become compact thematic paragraphs, experiments are reorganized around components, representations, and conditional applications, and much metric exposition and related work move to the appendices. v2 also adds an appendix contents page and changes 'embeddings' to 'encodings' in the title.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the original combined results presentation with compact main-text summaries and expanded, metric-grouped appendix tables. It adds model-size comparisons, family radar charts, conditional structural examples, and a domain-overlap Venn diagram; noise and length plots are redrawn. The original pipeline overview disappears, while UMAP, architecture, disorder, and secondary-structure graphics are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around protein flow models, DPLM/DPLM2, Walk-Jump, CHEAP, SaProt, and other recent approaches. Its introduction explicitly distinguishes earlier continuous protein models by restricted representations or conditional focus, including newly cited Pro-LDM. This changes the research positioning beyond merely relocating related work to Appendix D.

T1.justification: Appendix B removes the SeqD definitions and introduces mathematical definitions for subsequence repetition, cluster-density measures, and alignment-based novelty. These are limited changes to evaluation mathematics. The central diffusion loss and noise-schedule equations remain equivalent, with no added theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for encoder generality and conditional utility that v1 left untested. The targeted ablations, novelty/diversity assessments, conditional benchmarks, and training disclosures make the framework's capabilities more assessable and reproducible. These gains outweigh the omitted code link and explicit limitations discussion, although reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence in particular comparisons—for example, ESMc CD0.5 is 0.963 in Table 3 but 0.863 in Table 7.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DiMA and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite extensive expansion and reorganization in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original generation experiments and adds encoder comparisons, joint sequence-structure generation, and conditional-design results, including those in Tables 7 and 10–14.

before.justification: v1 reports original protein-generation experiments on SwissProt and AFDBv4-90, including baseline comparisons, architectural ablations, and biological annotation analyses.

results.title: Diffusion on language model encodings for protein sequence generation

C1.justification: The abstract is unchanged, retaining claims of unbiased, more sample-efficient autoevaluation and up to 50% effective human-labeled sample-size improvement with gpt-4. The contribution remains a practical PPI instantiation for metric and pairwise evaluation, including synthetic label distributions. Protein experiments support this existing generality claim.

C2.justification: The protein discussion adds interpretation of unoptimized PPI's failure and the usefulness of PPI++ with mediocre annotators. The previous explanation that naive LLM evaluation exaggerates performance differences is removed with that comparison. The requirement for representative data and the distribution-shift limitation remain.

D1.justification: Supplement A adds the protein assay identifier and normalization, averaging of repeated human annotations, hardware specifications, JAX implementation details for Bradley–Terry experiments, and execution times. These are newly documented details, not established implementation changes. Conversely, v2 removes the dedicated experimental-code repository link while retaining the ppi_py link and identical code snippets.

E1.justification: Section 2.4 adds protein-fitness regression evaluation on the ProteinGym protein G assay, containing 536,962 pairwise mutations, substantially extending coverage beyond ImageNet classification and LLM preferences. The LLM win-rate task already appears in v1 Figure 1; its supplementary expansion is not a new task.

E2.justification: The synthetic-label-only imputation comparator, called naive in v1 Figure 3, disappears from the corresponding LLM evaluation in v2. PPI, PPI++, and classical estimation remain. The new protein experiment uses this retained estimator comparison set.

E3.justification: The Bradley–Terry evaluation expands from the n = 25 example in v1 to budgets of 50–150 labeled observations with MSE, ESS, ranking, and interval diagnostics. Protein evaluation introduces standardized Pearson correlation and held-out VESPA predictions. Section 2.3 also corrects the reported fixed PPI weight from lambda = 0 to 1; this does not establish how the earlier implementation ran.

E4.justification: New Figure 4 tests how eight protein annotators of differing quality affect PPI++ effective sample size at n = 500. Supplement B.1 adds confidence-interval calibration and width analyses for protein correlations and Bradley–Terry coefficients. ImageNet interval diagnostics already existed in v1 Figure 2 and are retained in reorganized form.

E5.justification: v1 specifies 500 random splits for ImageNet; v2 specifies 250 splits throughout, newly documenting repetition counts for the LLM analyses. The asymptotic confidence-interval framework and Bonferroni ranking correction remain. The reported count change should not be interpreted as an increase in replication.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the n = 25 model-specific Bradley–Terry results with aggregate curves reporting a 20–25% ESS advantage for PPI++. New protein results report approximately 50% higher ESS and show unoptimized PPI underperforming classical estimation. Figure S2 adds win-rate MSE results, and Table 1 adds execution times. These are added or revised evaluations, not same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The general metric estimator, synthetic-label weighting, and Bradley–Terry fitting procedure are retained. Protein correlation estimation specializes the existing framework using an external annotator, which v1 already permits. The argmax-to-argmin equation correction matches the minimization procedure already described in v1.

P1.justification: Most introductory and methodological prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 revises experimental summaries, consolidates ImageNet result paragraphs, adds explicit Limitations and Broader Impacts headings, and introduces supplementary sections. Author affiliations and contact information are added, while the acknowledgements and standalone availability section are removed.

P2.justification: ImageNet Figure 2 changes from six panels to three, with interval diagnostics moved to Figure S1 and the individual accuracy-interval illustration removed. The old model-specific LLM plot is replaced by aggregate curves. Protein, annotator-quality, and supplementary win-rate plots and a runtime table are added, alongside extensive figure restyling and document reformatting.

R1.justification: Related Work adds BLEU, ROUGE, automatic-metric statistical advantages, and Chaganty et al.'s control-variate debiasing work. Protein-modeling and JAX references are added, while the ImageNet dataset and Elo references are removed. The central positioning relative to PPI, AIPW, and concurrent autoevaluation research remains.

T1.justification: The Bradley–Terry estimator changes from argmax in v1 Equation 18 to argmin in v2 Equation 15, correcting its inconsistency with the stated loss-minimization argument. The general bias, variance, and confidence-set mathematics remains, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: The protein regression and annotator-quality studies address important gaps in v1's empirical support for general metric evaluation and weak synthetic labels. The expanded Bradley–Terry evaluation assesses error, ranking, and calibration across sample budgets instead of relying on one interval example. Supplement A and the optimization correction improve reproducibility and mathematical clarity. These substantial gains outweigh the loss of the naive comparator and direct experimental-code link.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoEval Done Right and provide readable text, equations, figures, and code snippets. The complete documents were inspected: v1 has no appendix, while v2 includes Supplements A and B.

after.justification: v2 retains original ImageNet and LLM evaluations and adds protein-fitness experiments, annotator-quality analysis, and supplementary results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet model-evaluation experiments and LLM preference analyses, including accuracy, confidence intervals, effective sample sizes, and rankings.

results.title: AutoEval Done Right: Using Synthetic Data for Model Evaluation

C1.justification: The central contributions shift from early-exit continual learning, increased overthinking, and TLC to representation stability, classifier diversity, and static auxiliary-classifier prediction. TLC's claimed contribution disappears. v1's headline improvement of up to 15 percentage points is replaced by an average relative improvement of approximately 10%, alongside the claim of matching baselines using 40–70% of their computation.

C2.justification: v2 develops explanations based on complementary classifier predictions and gradient propagation, and hypothesizes that connecting classifiers reduces useful diversity. It adds capacity-based interpretations of ImageNet and ViT behavior, acknowledges warm-start exceptions, and discusses auxiliary-classifier memory and training complexity. These substantially revise v1's emphasis on overthinking and correcting task-recency bias.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix K adds explicit classifier loss weights, placements for three and twelve classifiers, ViT head construction and optimizer settings, and SSIL's 4:1 new-to-old sampling ratio. Conversely, v1's layer-by-layer architecture tables, tensor shapes, and TLC optimization information disappear. The anonymous code address changes, although neither PDF establishes the resource's actual accessibility.

E1.justification: v2 removes TinyImageNet and the task-incremental/task-aware evaluations reported in v1 Appendix D. CIFAR100 and the first 100 ImageNet classes remain; ImageNet100 is the renamed ImageNet-Subset, not an added dataset. The warm-start experiments repartition retained CIFAR100 data.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparisons add GDUMB, EWC, SSIL, ANCL, and LODE, while removing evaluated iCaRL-CNN and joint-training references. FT, LwF, ER, and BiC remain, and FT-E is retained as FT+Ex. v2 also introduces explicit comparisons against linear probing and final-classifier fallback.

E3.justification: v2 Appendix K changes ImageNet ResNet18 training from 200 epochs with step decay to 100 epochs with cosine scheduling and five warmup epochs. New protocols include a 50-class initial task followed by five or ten tasks, ViT-base experiments, and gradient-propagation controls. CKA and unique accuracy add measurements, while primary benchmark tables switch from fixed FLOPs budgets to static multi-classifier accuracy.

E4.justification: v2 adds CKA stability measurements, unique-accuracy analyses, linear-probing versus joint-training controls, classifier-count and cascading/ensembling ablations, fallback-rule comparisons, and ViT analyses. v1's oracle and per-task classifier investigations are partly retained and expanded in v2 Appendices B and C, rather than simply deleted. The dedicated task-recency-confidence analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v1 already includes graphical error bars and shaded bands, but gives point estimates in its result tables and does not specify seed counts. v2 explicitly reports averaging over three random seeds and systematically adds ± quantities to benchmark and ablation tables. This establishes expanded statistical reporting, not an increase in runs; the precise meaning of ± is not explicitly defined.

E6.justification: Results are substantially replaced and expanded. For CIFAR100 with ten tasks, v1 Table 2 reports BiC NoEE accuracy 46.94 and BiC+TLC accuracy 49.10 at 100% FLOPs; v2 Table 1 reports static Base 42.87±1.51 and +AC 46.19±1.47. These differing method and evaluation conditions do not establish a same-setting gain. New warm-start, probing, architecture, and stability results accompany removal of TLC, TinyImageNet, and task-aware result entries.

M1.justification: v2 removes v1's central Task-wise Logits Correction procedure, which optimizes task-dependent logit offsets after training. It instead uses auxiliary-classifier predictions without TLC. The basic intermediate classifiers, weighted joint training, and maximum-confidence fallback already appear in v1; their renaming and formalization do not constitute new procedures.

P1.justification: The title becomes 'Auxiliary Classifiers Improve Stability and Efficiency in Continual Learning.' The abstract, introduction, contributions, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Representation analysis now precedes the method presentation, IC terminology becomes AC terminology, and the supplementary material is reorganized into Appendices A–K.

P2.justification: v2 removes the network and TLC schematics, introduces stability and unique-accuracy heatmaps, and reorganizes accuracy-computation plots into method-specific grids. Benchmark tables change from dataset-and-budget columns to Base/+AC/difference rows across methods, with additional ablation tables. Typography, text width, headers, and appendix layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from an extensive adaptive-inference and early-exit survey toward intermediate representations and continual learning. New discussion cites CKA, representation probing, PODNet, latent replay, ANCL, LODE, and warm-start research. Many adaptive-computation references and TLC's ICICLE-based motivation disappear, substantially changing the research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 removes TLC's affine task-correction assumptions, equal-response assumption, and optimization development from v1 Equations 2–6. It introduces the unique-accuracy definition in Section 3.3. Its dynamic-inference equation largely formalizes the threshold and maximum-confidence fallback already described in v1; neither version provides a theorem-and-proof treatment.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the explanation and validation of why intermediate classifiers help. CKA measurements, probing controls, diversity analyses, and inference/design ablations address v1's largely indirect mechanism evidence and untested design choices; three-seed reporting makes variability more assessable. Coverage narrows, and reporting inconsistencies weaken some conclusions: for example, the CIFAR100x5 FT improvement is +9.49 in Tables 1 and 3 but +5.70 in Table 4 without explanation. These shortcomings limit particular results, but the central hypothesis receives substantially stronger empirical examination.

A1.justification: Both PDFs identify arXiv 2403.07404 and concern intermediate classifiers in continual learning, with shared authors and retained experimental settings. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reframing.

after.justification: v2 reports original representation analyses, benchmark comparisons, warm-start experiments, and architectural and inference ablations in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original continual-learning experiments on CIFAR100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet-Subset, including accuracy-computation comparisons, forgetting analyses, and task-incremental results in Appendix D.

results.title: Improving Continual Learning Performance and Efficiency with Auxiliary Classifiers

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace v1's broad encoder-decoder versus decoder-only claims about context use and memorization with model-specific noise-robustness findings. Figure 2 now groups FLAN/GPT versus Llama/Claude by observed behavior. The central contribution of a reusable configuration-analysis framework is retained.

C2.justification: Sections 5–6 substantially revise the explanations of reader behavior. v2 introduces multiple supporting passages as possible anchors against noise, biomedical terminology as a possible filtering aid, and explicit gibberish failure conditions. These replace or extend v1's emphasis on memorization conflicts and model size. The limitations paragraph is unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds Llama3 tokenization/truncation details, configurations for the additional readers, and approximately $300 in closed-model expenditure. Appendix B and Table 3 clarify PubMed passage and retrieval units. Existing hardware, batching, dataset licenses, and code/data access information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate English NQ, HotpotQA, and BioASQ using the same Wikipedia and PubMed corpora. Single-hop, multi-hop, biomedical, and gold/non-gold context scenarios are retained. Appendix B preserves the dataset sizes and splits.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude Haiku, Llama3 8B, and Llama3 70B to the existing FLAN-T5, FLAN-UL2, and two Llama2 readers. These participate in the reported comparisons and robustness plots. BM25 and ColBERT remain the compared retrievers.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 replaces exact match with F1 for NQ. Section 2.2 changes the reported k sampling grid from {1,2,3,5,10,20,30} to {1,2,5,10,20,50}. Appendix A changes the stated output lengths from 10 and 256 tokens to 10 tokens only. These are reported protocol revisions, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The retained gold/non-gold robustness analyses are substantially expanded across the additional readers, including Appendix D. v2 replaces the FLAN-T5 conditional same-page case study with a cross-model accuracy comparison and adds observations of gibberish responses from Claude Haiku and Llama3 70B under gold biomedical contexts.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance-testing procedures. Both describe greedy decoding without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive reader results and revises existing curves. BM25 paragraph recall@50 changes from 7.5 to 22.8 on NQ and from 3.0 to 54.2 on HotpotQA (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 3), while corresponding page-recall and ColBERT rows remain unchanged. NQ reader scores now use F1, so their increases cannot be interpreted as same-metric performance gains.

M1.justification: RAGGED retains its retriever–reader pipeline, QA prompt, and analysis axes: component choice, context quantity, and gold-passage data slices. Additional reader models are evaluated within this framework; no new algorithmic component or training objective is introduced.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, framework explanations, and Sections 5–7 are extensively rewritten. No-context evaluation moves from Section 6 to Section 5, Section 6 is reorganized around gold-passage presence, and retriever discussion is consolidated. Appendices C–D reorganize supporting material.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn, and the empirical figures receive expanded model legends and reorganized panels. The separate no-context table disappears while Figure 3 includes k=0 results. The retrieval table moves to Appendix C, and Appendix D redisplays and expands the gold/non-gold plots.

R1.justification: v2 adds Brown et al. (2020) and Enis and Hopkins (2024), replaces the original ColBERT citation with Santhanam et al.'s ColBERTv2 reference, and removes Richardson et al. (2013). Section 8's substantive positioning against prior research remains essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version contains substantive theoretical results, formal assumptions, or proofs. The retained framework uses elementary indexing and standard metrics; the scoring changes do not introduce new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is replacing architecture-wide conclusions drawn from two model families with model-specific guidance supported by broader comparisons and robustness evidence (Abstract; Sections 5–6). This substantially strengthens the paper's main practical takeaway. Reporting weaknesses remain: the BM25 score revisions are unexplained, and Section 6.1's Llama2 threshold statement conflicts with Figure 4, limiting confidence in some detailed numerical claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAGGED study. Their text, tables, figures, and complete appendices—A–B in v1 and A–D in v2—support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original results on the same datasets, retaining and expanding the reader comparisons and robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval and reader evaluations on NQ, HotpotQA, and BioASQ, including context-quantity and gold/non-gold passage analyses.

results.title: RAGGED: Towards Informed Design of Scalable and Stable RAG Systems

C1.justification: The central dynamic-switching contribution and claimed minimum 75% communication reduction remain. V2 revises the headline throughput range from 42.0%–216.8% to 32.2%–10x and makes the high-level API an explicit part of its usability contribution. Presenting DSP as an abstraction largely reframes the retained mechanism.

C2.justification: V1 Section 4.1 extrapolates its findings to language-model training without explicit applicability limitations. V2 Section 6 states that DSP may not suit single-dimensional language models and may lose efficiency on operations involving every sequence dimension. V2 also adds explanations for head-count-independent scaling and superlinear scaling through reduced optimizer and gradient overhead.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly documents benchmark simplification, layers, hidden sizes, attention heads, patch sizes, baseline implementation sources, ZeRO-2 usage, parallel-group settings, resolution processing and four API functions. This substantially expands the sparse implementation information in v1. Both versions retain the same OpenDiT code address; this is not a newly announced code release.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate spatial-temporal, video-style transformer workloads; neither reports evaluation on a named dataset or another application domain. The OpenSora-like benchmark, larger configurations and additional timing measurements change settings and measurement procedures within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: V1 lists Megatron-SP in its setup and discusses Ring-Attention, but Figure 3 reports only DeepSpeed-Ulysses against DSP. V2 Figures 5–9 additionally report Megatron-SP, labeled Megatron-LM in the plots, and Ring-Attention, substantially broadening the empirical comparison.

E3.justification: V1 uses a 724M ST-DiT model with cross-attention on H800 GPUs, batch size one and 2–8 GPUs. V2 uses 720M and 3B cross-attention-free models on H100 GPUs. It adds minimum-feasible sequence parallelism combined with data parallelism on 128 GPUs, weak/strong scaling through 64 GPUs, TFLOPS/GPU reporting, and latency and memory measurements.

E4.justification: V1 Figure 3 already investigates throughput scaling. V2 substantially extends this with separate weak/strong scaling analyses, intra-node and inter-node comparisons, attention-head and memory scaling limits, and allocated-versus-cached memory analysis in Figures 6–9. These investigate practical scalability and memory overhead beyond the original throughput study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's black reference boxes indicate linear scaling, and its shaded memory bars distinguish cached memory; neither represents statistical uncertainty.
