E6.justification: The original Figure 3 results are replaced by substantially expanded results under different hardware, models and protocols. V1 reports 42.0%–216.8% throughput improvement over Ulysses; v2 Section 5.1 reports 32%–75% over Ulysses and up to 10x over other baselines. V2 also adds scaling-limit, inference-latency and memory findings. These are not same-setting performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: Both versions use all-to-all resharding between computation stages so that attention can execute locally along the required dimension. V2 expands the description with Switch/Split/Gather primitives and an API, without establishing a different DSP algorithm. Removing cross-attention concerns the benchmark model.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and background are extensively rewritten. V2 reorganizes DSP into overview, problem definition, primitives and adaptability subsections, separates theoretical analysis, expands the experimental narrative, and adds discussion and an implementation appendix. These substantially change the exposition and structure beyond adding results.

P2.justification: V2 adds conceptual and system diagrams, expanded performance/scaling plots, latency and memory displays, settings tables and an API example. The original Figure 1 is retained as appendix Figure 10, while Figure 2 is redrawn as Figure 4. New plots introduce additional comparator series, different axes, failure markers and scaling references.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including GQA, FlashAttention, Mamba, RWKV, OpenSora and FSDP, while removing Longformer, LongRoPE and Llama. It expands discussion of attention-head limits and Ring-Attention communication costs. The principal positioning against existing single-sequence parallelism methods remains.

T1.justification: V2 adds an explicit communication-minimization problem constrained by GPU memory capacity in Equation 6 and formal sharding-state definitions in Table 2. Its communication analysis revises Ring-Attention from 4M in v1 Table 1 to 2M in v2 Table 3, explaining communication along the sharded temporal dimension. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's sparse empirical support through additional measured competitors, two model sizes, scaling, latency and memory evidence, while providing implementation details and concrete applicability limits. These improve the paper's assessability and support for its systems claims. Tradeoffs remain: the benchmark omits cross-attention, and Table 3 implies only a 50% communication reduction versus Ring-Attention at two GPUs, conflicting with the retained 75% minimum claim. These issues temper but do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DSP and retain the same central sequence-parallelism mechanism. All pages, figures, tables and equations were readable through extraction and visual inspection. V1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendix A.1–A.4.

after.justification: V2 Section 5 and Figures 5–9 report original performance, scaling, inference-latency and memory measurements, with experimental settings supplied in Appendix A.3.

before.justification: V1 Section 4.1 and Figure 3 report original throughput measurements comparing DSP with DeepSpeed-Ulysses on a 724M ST-DiT model.

results.title: DSP: Dynamic Sequence Parallelism for Multi-Dimensional Transformers

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add determinate expert offloading for memory-limited inference as an explicit contribution, including claims of up to 60% memory reduction and 75% migration-overhead reduction. v1's prominent DGMoE and modality-discrepancy contributions give way to a ScMoE-centered account. The central distributed-acceleration and model-quality claims remain.

C2.justification: v1's hypothesis that vision/language differences arise from expert-combination counts is removed. v2 emphasizes shared-expert gating and develops representation-similarity, distinct-expert, and complementary-information explanations for shortcut effectiveness (Section 4.4; Appendix A.3). Section 4.3 also explains why larger models retain more offloading overhead through memory-bound decoding.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the shared-expert gate as a linear layer and documents CPU/GPU module placement and the trigger for asynchronous migration. Appendix A.6 clarifies the 16-expert two-node configuration. Most framework, tokenizer, and training disclosures are retained, while the Swin hyperparameter table loses its parameter-count row.

E1.justification: ImageNet-1K, OpenWebText, and WikiText-103 remain unchanged, but v2 adds memory-limited, CPU-offloaded autoregressive inference on a single A30 GPU as a distinct deployment scenario. The two-node ScMoE evaluation also extends the standard-MoE hardware profiling already present in v1 Figure 1.

E2.justification: The vision shared-expert comparator belongs to v1's Residual MoE family but is substantively modified with SE-Gate. Figure 10 adds GPU-only and blocking Offload comparisons against Offload-Async. DGMoE timing comparisons and the GPT3 DGMoE/DGMoE-2 rows disappear, although DGMoE remains in appendix vision and GPT2 quality comparisons. Pre-gated MoE is discussed, not experimentally benchmarked.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a single-A30 offloading evaluation comparing resident, blocking-transfer, and asynchronous-transfer execution using normalized peak GPU memory and MoE-block latency. It also adds ScMoE timing experiments across two nodes with 16 GPUs and 16 experts. The retained vision and language training budgets and most hyperparameters are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds shortcut-position comparisons (Table 1), shared-expert gate on/off ablations (Table 5), and blocking versus asynchronous offloading analysis (Figure 10). v1's constant-weight sweep and ScMoE-2 vision experiment are removed. The representation/gating plots and DGMoE-Share experiment are retained and reframed rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix A.6 newly states that vision comparisons keep random seeds consistent and efficiency results average multiple samples over different periods. Neither disclosure establishes an increase in runs. Sample counts, seed values, confidence intervals, and significance tests remain unspecified.

E6.justification: The main vision comparison changes from ungated ScMoE/Residual MoE accuracies of 78.98%/79.02% to gated ScMoE/shared-expert accuracies of 79.38%/79.53%; v2 Table 5 retains the ungated values. New results include position/gate ablations, two-node ScMoE latency of 6.8 ms, and offloading memory/latency measurements. Several DGMoE results disappear. Matched language perplexities remain unchanged, and the GPT3 timing-to-speedup conversion is reciprocal redisplay rather than a new performance gain.

M1.justification: v2 adds a learned, input-dependent shared-expert gate (Appendix A.3) and a CPU-offloading inference procedure with asynchronous, determinate expert migration (Section 3.3). These substantially extend the model and execution procedure. The original intermediate-position shortcut, now called Pos-2, and adaptive expert-parallel scheduling are retained.

P1.justification: The introduction, architectural explanation, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around ScMoE. Theory and DGMoE specifications move into the appendix, experimental details move to A.6, and results gain distinct distributed, offloading, and shortcut-analysis sections. Fixed-MLP terminology is replaced by shared-expert terminology.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and extensively redraws and redistributes architectural diagrams. It adds offloading diagrams, memory/latency plots, and ablation tables; expands the overhead figure to three panels; and removes the comprehensive architecture overview. Retained representation plots are resized and their panel labels corrected.

R1.justification: The broad MoE-advancements survey is replaced by focused memory-limited inference positioning, expanding the earlier contrast with Pre-gated MoE and EdgeMoE into speculative versus determinate migration. New citations include SE-MoE, SiDA, DeepSeekMoE, and Qwen1.5-MoE. Earlier coverage including StableMoE, MegaBlocks, and SmartMoE is removed, materially changing research positioning.

T1.justification: The residual-gradient derivation and scheduling bounds are retained through relocation and renumbering. A limited formal addition is the input-dependent shared-expert definition in v2 Equation 20, replacing the ungated MLP contribution in that configuration. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 replaces v1's speculative modality explanation with direct gate ablations, tests the chosen shortcut position, and adds two-node ScMoE measurements beyond v1's single-node comparisons. These address important gaps in architectural justification and validation of the acceleration claim. Offloading results also expose both memory savings and residual latency costs. Although secondary DGMoE and constant-weight studies are trimmed and timing variability remains unquantified, the supporting evidence and scientific explanation improve substantially.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ScMoE research. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable across all 18 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v2, allowing reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original vision and language experiments and reports additional shortcut-position and gate ablations, two-node timings, and offloading memory and latency measurements.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original vision accuracies, language-model perplexities, training and inference timings, and architectural analyses.

results.title: Shortcut-connected Expert Parallelism for Accelerating Mixture-of-Experts

C1.justification: The central contributions—multidimensional training and adaptive path optimization under fixed solver configurations—remain. V2's abstract and introduction qualify training benefits as applying to some models. Its conclusion adds an approximately fifteenfold NFE-reduction claim and claims concerning the importance of x0 conditioning, path dimensionality, and training-time spatial range.

C2.justification: V1 discusses training burden and adjacent-pixel differences. V2 adds a straight-versus-curved vector-field hypothesis for SI/FM versus DDPM, connects high-frequency components to CNN locality, and interprets the new conditioning and dimensionality controls. Section 7 newly identifies limited generalizability, Euler-only testing, optimization time/VRAM costs, and dependence on the training solver configuration.

D1.justification: V2 Section 5.1 and Appendix B substantially expand v1's brief implementation description: network dimensions, path-network and discriminator architectures, kernel and noise-tensor sizes, Adam and EMA parameters, path-training budgets, warmups, and dataset-specific hardware configurations. Best-checkpoint selection using FID every 10,000 steps is newly disclosed. These disclosures do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only CIFAR-10. V2 adds training and evaluation on ImageNet-32, including unoptimized and adaptive-path generation. This substantially broadens the evaluated image distribution, although image generation remains the task.

E2.justification: V1's quantitative comparison uses SIbasic and SImodified as controls for SI-based variants. V2 Tables 1 and 7 add evaluated scalar-time FM and DDPM comparators, including modified-conditioning controls in Table 7. SIbasic is renamed SI, and SImodified remains in the appendix rather than being removed.

E3.justification: V2 specifies 10-NFE path optimization, whereas v1 reports adaptive-path evaluations at 10, 20, and 50 NFE. New experimental designs control kernel width, path-network input, retained output dimensions, and Fourier basis count M=10 versus M=30. Added ImageNet-32 experiments use distinct model sizes and training budgets. The retained CIFAR-10 base-training budget and FID-50k metric remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's scale sensitivity and final-image comparisons, v2 adds kernel-width sensitivity, constant/noise/x0 conditioning controls, and comparisons of training-time spatial range in Tables 2–4. Figure 6 tests path dimensionality and Fourier basis count; Appendix A adds frequency-spectrum analysis, and Figures 5 and 9 examine intermediate trajectories. These directly investigate previously untested method components.

E5.justification: V1 gives point FIDs without repetition or uncertainty information. Appendix B.3 newly states that each FID calculation is performed three times and the minimum reported, describing random variation as generally within ±2%. This is newly disclosed evaluation repetition, not evidence of increased independent training runs; seeds, confidence intervals, and result-specific dispersion remain unreported.

E6.justification: Reported CIFAR-10 scalar-SI FID at 10 NFE changes from 17.20 to 14.43; adaptive LPFI/LPFT with s=0.1 changes from 8.58 to 4.14. These are revised reported outcomes, without established equivalence of all configurations and selection rules. V2 adds extensive FM, DDPM, and ImageNet-32 results, including adaptive ImageNet-32 FID 7.06 and cases where tensor time worsens DDPM. V1's adaptive 20- and 50-NFE entries are not retained.

M1.justification: V2 extends the proposed training construction beyond SI endpoint prediction to flow-matching velocity prediction and DDPM noise prediction with their respective objectives and inference fields. Section 4.1 also revises the low-pass construction from image-sized noise to an enlarged tensor followed by edge cropping. The SI Fourier parameterization and frozen-model adversarial path optimization remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title and terminology change throughout from multidimensional interpolants to tensor-valued time. The introduction and method exposition are extensively rewritten, preliminaries are divided into SI and flow/diffusion subsections, and results become organized discussions of individual effects. A limitations section and structured Appendices A–C substantially revise the document's narrative organization.

P2.justification: V2 adds an input-conditioning schematic and redraws the optimization schematic to expose the Fourier construction. Figure 4 uses logarithmic FID axes, and final-image comparisons become trajectory displays. The main table is reorganized across model families and datasets, with detailed controls in Appendix Table 7. New ablation tables, dimensionality plots, spectrum visualizations, and sample grids substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds DDPM/DDIM discussion and citations for those methods, FID, CIFAR-10, ImageNet/downsampled ImageNet, and U-Net. The existing positioning relative to SI, transport coupling, and prior path optimization remains substantially intact. The expanded PyTorch-FID reference identifies the same resource already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds mathematical definitions of Gaussian conditional paths, FM velocity and loss, and DDPM schedules, loss, and probability-flow inference. The low-pass definition also incorporates edge cropping. The SI transport/score theorem and normalized Fourier path construction are retained in equivalent notation; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation and incomplete implementation documentation. ImageNet-32 and FM/DDPM comparisons establish broader applicability boundaries, including negative DDPM findings; component ablations provide evidence for design choices previously supported mainly by intuition. Appendix B and Section 7 improve reproducibility and explain practical constraints. Minimum-FID and best-checkpoint reporting still leave uncertainty incompletely characterized, but the stronger evidence and clearer qualifications constitute a substantial overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' work on multidimensional interpolation and adaptive inference paths, despite the changed title. Text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison throughout; v1 ends with references, while v2 includes readable Appendices A–C.

after.justification: V2 reports original CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 experiments, model comparisons, controlled ablations, and generated examples in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original CIFAR-10 experiments, including FID-50k comparisons, interpolation-scale sensitivity, and results from optimized inference paths in Table 1 and Figures 4–5.

results.title: Multidimensional Adaptive Coefficient for Inference Trajectory Optimization in Flow and Diffusion

C1.justification: v3 retains adaptive multidimensional path optimization but broadens the contribution from tensor-valued training and frozen-SI path optimization to a plug-in across flow/diffusion frameworks with joint model/trajectory training and optional checkpoint reuse. It newly claims substantial adversarial-training efficiency and state-of-the-art conditional CIFAR-10 generation.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations that nonstraight trajectories can improve transportation even with OT-trained fields and that class conditioning can dominate initial-noise dependence in learned coefficients. It also argues for compatibility without coefficient pretraining. v2's DDPM curvature-based failure explanation is dropped, while fixed-NFE and VRAM constraints remain discussed within future directions and training efficiency.

D1.justification: Much of v2 Appendix B's architecture and training information is retained in v3 Appendix E.2. v3 additionally documents synthetic-model configurations, coefficient filtering/padding/rescaling, EDM time schedules and conditioning, separate optimization hyperparameters, dropout handling, GPU configurations, and training times (Appendices C–E; Tables 14–15). These materially expand reproducibility information for the revised procedures.

E1.justification: v3 retains CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 and adds synthetic transportation among Gaussian, eight-Gaussian, and moons distributions, FFHQ and AFHQv2 image generation, and class-conditional CIFAR-10 and ImageNet generation. This substantially broadens the represented distributions, domains, and task requirements beyond v2's image-generation coverage.

E2.justification: v2 primarily compares scalar/tensor variants of SI, FM, and DDPM. v3 Table 5 adds comparisons with EDM, CTM, consistency models, rectified-flow variants, and StyleGAN models, explicitly computing CTM results at five and six NFE. Conversely, the modified scalar-conditioning comparators in v2 Table 7 disappear from the corresponding v3 Table 10.

E3.justification: v3 introduces random-versus-OT pairing controls, additional optimized NFE settings, five-NFE EDM experiments, and separate 500k-image ablation and 1.5M-image main CIFAR-10 training budgets. It adds FDDINOv2 and explicitly accounts for MAC computation with '(+)' NFE notation. Appendix F reports EDM/EDM2 evaluation software where v2 specifies PyTorch-FID; the 50,000 generated evaluation samples are retained.

E4.justification: Conditioning, coefficient range, filtering, and dimensionality were already analyzed in v2. v3 extends these investigations and adds model-only, MAC-only, and joint-training controls (Table 6), learned-coefficient t-SNE analysis (Figure 8), and measured deviation from linear trajectories (Appendix E.3.3). These substantially strengthen analysis of what MAC contributes.

E5.justification: v2 reports the minimum of three FID calculations and mentions approximate random variation. v3 retains minimum-of-three image-metric reporting and explicitly mentions different seeds. Its new synthetic experiments report means and standard deviations over three separately trained seeds (Table 1; Appendix E.1.2). This is a localized uncertainty-reporting addition, without establishing increased image-training repetitions.

E6.justification: The optimized SI FIDs of 4.14 on CIFAR-10 and 7.06 on ImageNet-32 reappear, alongside many retained scalar-model results. However, v3 revises DDPM entries and adds extensive transportation, benchmark, and ablation results. Table 5 newly reports conditional CIFAR-10 FID 1.37 and ImageNet-64 FID 1.48/FDDINOv2 70.2. These are newly reported outcomes under expanded methods and settings, not same-setting gains over v2.

M1.justification: v2 optimizes a Fourier path network while freezing the SI model. v3 adds joint vector-field/MAC adversarial optimization and optional reuse of conventional pretrained checkpoints. It also revises coefficient sampling and sinusoidal parameterization and introduces inference updates using coefficient increments (Section 3; Appendices C–D). These change training and inference beyond renaming tensor-valued time.

P1.justification: The title, terminology, abstract, introduction, related work, and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten around MAC. Framework background moves into Appendix A, experiments are reorganized into synthetic, image MAC-only, and joint-optimization sections, and appendices expand from A–C to A–G. The change is extensive rewriting and restructuring, beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: v3 switches the main text to two columns and substantially redesigns its illustrations and result displays: new trajectory schematics, grouped benchmark tables, training curves, t-SNE plots, and paired baseline/MAC sample grids replace or supplement v2's displays. Some existing tables are relocated and expanded. Figure 12's FFHQ/AFHQ score assignments conflict with Table 5.

R1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites research positioning around trajectory optimality and diffusion distillation, adding discussion of CTM, consistency and distribution-matching methods, neural flow diffusion, and newer trajectory methods. It explicitly distinguishes joint inference-plan/vector-field optimization from distillation. This replaces much of v2's broader CNF/flow/diffusion survey and changes the novelty argument.

T1.justification: v2 presents SI definitions and a transport/score theorem. v3 introduces formal matrix-valued coefficients and trajectory-conditioned MAC definitions, explicit coefficient hypothesis sets, and separate fixed-field and joint optimization objectives. Appendix D adds a derivation using finite coefficient increments. This substantially revises the mathematical formulation rather than merely changing notation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2's limited validation of optimized paths, previously centered on SI and 32×32 images. Comparisons with strong methods, experiments across additional frameworks and conditional tasks, and controls separating MAC from model adversarial training provide much stronger evidence for the contribution. Expanded implementation details and seeded synthetic results also improve assessability. The Figure 12/Table 5 labeling inconsistency and retained fixed-NFE limitation qualify, but do not outweigh, these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite v3's changed title and substantially expanded formulation. The text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and shared methods and results can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 reports original synthetic transportation and image-generation experiments, including conditional generation, joint optimization, and supplementary analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 generation experiments, FID measurements, path-optimization results, and ablations in Section 5 and the appendices.

C1.justification: The central MDP formulation, DPO-plus-PPO method, and provable sample-efficiency contributions remain. V3 adds a headline empirical claim of matching PPO with approximately one-eighth of the data and continuing to improve after PPO saturates, while making benchmark-specific performance claims explicit in the abstract.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 newly attributes RTO's advantage primarily to reward shaping rather than the aggregate DPO reward. Section 4.2 also explains the additional sentence reward as protection against extreme response lengths and argues that a smaller critic can offset the added computational cost.

D1.justification: V3 adds a code/model availability statement and link. Appendix D documents checkpoints, dataset variants, optimizer scheduling, PPO stabilization, decoding settings, eight 80GB A100 GPUs, and memory-saving techniques for the new study. HH-RLHF implementation details disappear, while TL;DR configurations and evaluation instructions are retained in Appendix E.

E1.justification: The HH-RLHF helpful-dialogue experiments are removed. V3 adds UltraFeedback preference training and conversational instruction-following evaluation on AlpacaEval 2 and Arena-Hard. Reddit TL;DR summarization remains in Appendix E rather than being newly added or removed.

E2.justification: V3 Table 1 newly evaluates R-DPO, SimPO, and TDPO alongside SFT, DPO, and PPO. Figure 3 adds Semi-RTO and RS-PPO ablation comparators. The retained TL;DR comparison still includes SFT, DPO, PPO, and DPPO.

E3.justification: The new main study uses Llama-3-8B, 2048-token training, length-controlled and style-controlled win rates, and benchmark-specific decoding. It specifies an 8B PPO reward model and a 1B auxiliary RTO reward model/critic, and introduces data-fraction evaluations. The earlier HH-RLHF evaluation protocol disappears; TL;DR's 100-prompt GPT-4-0613 protocol is retained.

E4.justification: V3 adds token-versus-sentence-versus-terminal reward granularity tests, an RS-PPO control isolating reward shaping, and a data-efficiency study in Figures 3–4. HH-RLHF temperature and training-curve analyses are removed. The corresponding TL;DR analyses are retained as Figures 5–6.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added tables and curves continue the existing practice of reporting results without quantified experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: HH-RLHF results are removed, while v3 Table 1 newly reports RTO/PPO scores of 27.00/19.47 on AlpacaEval 2 LC and 20.3/16.2 on Arena-Hard SC, plus new ablation and scaling findings. These are new experimental settings, not matched-setting improvements over v2. TL;DR results remain unchanged, including RTO's 61% win rate against DPO.

M1.justification: V2 optimizes DPO-derived token rewards plus KL regularization. V3 Equation (4.7) adds a separately trained sentence-level reward, weighted by beta3 and assigned to the final token. This additional reward model and terminal signal materially change practical RTO, although its DPO-to-PPO framework remains.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized from separate setup/results sections into benchmark results followed by mechanism analyses. Summarization material is consolidated into new Appendix E, and Appendix D is rewritten around implementation. The abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion are also revised.

P2.justification: The empirical displays are substantially rebuilt with a new benchmark table, an ablation table captioned Figure 3, and a new three-panel Figure 4. HH-RLHF displays are removed; the TL;DR matrix and plots are relocated and resized as Table 2 and Figures 5–6. Figures 1–2 remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 expands its concurrent-work discussion to TDPO and SimPO and discusses subsequent implicit-reward work by Cui et al. and Yin et al. References also change with the datasets, benchmarks, and implementation. This is a focused update that preserves the main distinction from prior preference-learning approaches.

T1.justification: Equation (4.7) revises the formal practical reward definition, accompanied by a new coefficient-rescaling argument. The MDP formulation, assumptions, Proposition 3.2, Theorem 4.2, and mathematical material in Appendices A–C remain unchanged; no new guarantee or proof establishes the added reward component.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens empirical validation through verbosity-controlled benchmarks, broader baseline comparisons, and controls that investigate reward shaping and data efficiency. These address v2's limited evidence about why RTO works, while Appendix D materially improves reproducibility. Removing HH-RLHF evidence reduces continuity, and naming/cross-reference inconsistencies remain, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger experimental support and implementation guidance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RTO research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained theory and relocated summarization experiments.

after.justification: V3 reports original Llama-3-8B benchmark and ablation experiments, while retaining the original TL;DR results in Appendix E.

before.justification: V2 reports original Pythia-2.8B alignment experiments on HH-RLHF and TL;DR, including GPT-4 comparisons, reward evaluations, temperature analyses, and training curves.

C1.justification: The foundational claim of reconciling equivariance and nonlinear expressiveness remains. v3 expands the central empirical contribution beyond Hamiltonian accuracy on six crystal benchmarks to demonstrated molecular extrapolation and downstream physical-quantity accuracy, explicitly claiming up to 76% improvement in orbital-energy prediction and 17% in wavefunction similarity.

C2.justification: v3 adds specific interpretations of size/trajectory extrapolation, robustness to thermal motion, SOC modeling and downstream physical utility. The trace/gradient complementarity explanation remains essentially unchanged. The earlier argument that success with HarmoSE demonstrates compatibility with approximately equivariant architectures is removed.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies a hidden width of 1024, per-dataset learning rates, Adam with batch size 1 for the crystal datasets, and AdamW with batch size 16 for QH9. Appendix C adds atom-count ranges and molecular split statistics. This substantially expands implementation documentation beyond v1's activation, normalization and loss-weight details, without establishing changes to retained experiments.

E1.justification: v3 retains the six crystal datasets and adds QH9-Stable and QH9-Dynamic molecular systems containing C, H, O, N and F. Coverage expands to molecular size and trajectory extrapolation, together with evaluation of downstream occupied-orbital energies and electronic wavefunctions.

E2.justification: v3 adds QHNet as the evaluated comparator on QH9 and removes v1 Appendix A's MoS2 comparison involving HarmoSE and DeepH-2. DeepHE3, renamed DeepH-E3, and its component-ablation variants remain. Thus an entire comparison branch is removed while a different backbone comparison is introduced.

E3.justification: The new QH9 evaluations use atom-count-disjoint 'ood' and trajectory-disjoint 'mol' splits, diagonal/interatomic Hamiltonian-block MAEs, orbital-energy MAE and wavefunction cosine similarity. They introduce a batch-16 AdamW configuration and conversion of cited baseline MAEs to meV. Existing DeepH splits and metrics remain unchanged; newly disclosed crystal training settings do not establish protocol revisions.

E4.justification: v3 adds distribution-shift evaluations of molecular atom-count extrapolation and unseen thermal-motion trajectories. It removes the approximately equivariant HarmoSE compatibility case study from v1 Appendix A. The original Trace-only/Grad-only ablations, twisted-crystal tests and block-error analyses are retained, with the ablations and complete block plots moved to Appendices E–F.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten repeated experiments, mean-only result tables and a standard-deviation bound around 0.007 meV for Hamiltonian errors. v3 omits v1's explicit seed value of 42 while retaining the fixed-seed statement. No increase in repeated runs or new uncertainty-estimation procedure is reported.

E6.justification: The crystal and component-ablation values are unchanged. v3 Tables 3–4 add QHNet versus QHNet+TraceGrad Hamiltonian MAEs of 1.962 versus 1.191 meV on QS and 4.733 versus 2.819 meV on QD. QD orbital-energy MAE is 264.483 versus 63.375 meV, and cosine similarity increases from 0.792 to 0.927, contrary to Section 4's 'lowers' wording. The earlier HarmoSE comparison results are removed.

M1.justification: The trace supervision, gradient-induced equivariant features, weighted Clebsch–Gordan construction, residual connections, decoders, adaptive two-term MSE loss and inference procedure remain unchanged. QHNet instantiates the existing general backbone interface; no TraceGrad-specific procedural adaptation is described. The newly stated hidden width is implementation disclosure.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: the related-method analysis and theorem proofs move to Appendices A–B, the lengthy application section is condensed into the introduction/results, and ablation descriptions move to Appendix F. The abstract, results discussion and future-work section are extensively revised.

P2.justification: v3 separates main comparisons from full ablation tables, adds QH9 and dataset-statistics tables, splits the structural illustrations, and recolors and rearranges the block-error plots. A selected-panel summary appears in the main text while complete plots move to the appendix. The HarmoSE table and plot are removed; retained plot data remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds QHNet, QH9, KAN, Transformer-survey and twisted-material references. It removes the detailed hybrid-method discussion of Yin et al. and expands the EquiformerV2 critique to tensor-order pruning. Yin et al.'s retitled reference is the same retained work; the overall equivariance–expressiveness positioning remains similar.

T1.justification: The two equivariance theorems, their proofs and the weighted Clebsch–Gordan construction are mathematically retained despite relocation and equivalent notation. Section 6.3 adds a brief complexity argument that featurewise TraceGrad processing preserves the backbones' O(N) scaling; v1 discussed linear scaling only for deep-learning approaches generally.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the framework's generality and physical usefulness. Tables 3–4 test another strictly equivariant backbone on molecular size/trajectory extrapolation and evaluate downstream quantities absent from v1's matrix-error-only experiments. Added training details also improve reproducibility. Removing the HarmoSE/DeepH-2 study narrows comparative evidence, and the missing seed value and incorrect similarity-direction wording are regressions, but the new validation resolves important gaps in the earlier paper's support for broad applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TraceGrad research. All 22 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v3, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables and figures that can be matched across the reorganization.

after.justification: Tables 1–4 report TraceGrad experiments using DeepH-E3 and QHNet across eight benchmarks, including downstream physical quantities. Appendix F retains the component-ablation results.

C1.justification: The central trace-supervision/gradient-induction contribution and the headline accuracy improvements of up to 40% and 76% are retained. V4 adds a prominent claim of improved DFT convergence acceleration in its abstract, introduction, and new conclusion, extending the claimed practical contribution.

C2.justification: V4 explains that applications requiring especially high numerical precision may still require DFT, with learned Hamiltonians serving as initializations. It also interprets the measured inference overhead as an acceptable accuracy tradeoff and the HarmoSE experiment as evidence of broader compatibility. The existing explanation of Trace/Grad complementarity is retained and relocated.

D1.justification: V3's brief training appendix expands into detailed implementation information in v4 Appendices D–F: GPU hardware, PyTorch versions, encoder depths, placement on edge features, invariant-channel and decoder dimensions, lambda search ranges, and learning-rate schedules including warm-up. V4 also adds a QHNet backbone-code link. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation, although v3's explicit instruction about omitting the invariant decoder during inference is not retained.

E1.justification: The eight databases and their thermal-motion, twist, size-extrapolation, and trajectory scenarios are retained. V4 adds the downstream task of using predicted Hamiltonians to initialize DFT convergence on 50 molecules (Table 3). The HarmoSE case study uses the existing Monolayer MoS2 dataset.

E2.justification: DeepH-E3 and QHNet remain the principal comparators. V4 Table 8 adds quantitative comparisons with HarmoSE and DeepH-2 on Monolayer MoS2; these works were already cited in v3 but were not evaluated as comparators there. The new DFT evaluation also includes 1e and minao initialization references.

E3.justification: V4 Appendix F changes the stated QH9 training batch size from 16 to 32 and lambda from 0.3 to 0.2. It also introduces a 50-molecule PySCF convergence protocol with achieved/error-level ratios and a batch-size-one GPU timing protocol. Dataset splits remain unchanged. These are substantial reported setting and evaluation-design changes, although the PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original Trace-only and Grad-only ablations are retained. V4 adds analyses of inference overhead on four datasets (Appendix I) and a case study testing whether TraceGrad benefits an approximately equivariant HarmoSE backbone (Appendix J). These substantially extend the analysis to computational cost and compatibility beyond strictly equivariant backbones.

E5.justification: The principal accuracy experiments still report ten repetitions. V4 clarifies that seeds match the respective backbone implementations, reports per-condition means and standard deviations across 50 molecules in Table 3, and specifies 50 timing repetitions per sample. No increase in the principal training-run count is established.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and ablation table values are unchanged. V4 adds substantial results: Table 3 reports QS/1e achieved ratios of 0.400 ± 0.030 for QHNet and 0.345 ± 0.038 for QHNet+TraceGrad; Appendix I reports MG inference times of 0.247 and 0.264 seconds/sample for DeepH-E3 and its TraceGrad extension; Table 8 reports MM average MAEs of 0.21, 0.233, and 0.178 meV for DeepH-2, HarmoSE, and HarmoSE+TraceGrad. The reported QH9 repeat-run SD bound also changes from 0.007 to 0.009 meV.

M1.justification: V4 Section 5.1 expands the invariant construction into multiple channels, sums their gradients, and feeds invariant features from all encoder layers into the trace decoder; v3 Section 6.1 specifies a scalar construction and final-layer decoder input. The prescribed losses also change: v3 uses MSE for both targets, whereas v4 uses MAE for trace prediction and combined MSE/MAE for QH9 Hamiltonians. These materially revise the described architecture and objective while retaining the TraceGrad principle.

P1.justification: V4 substantially reorganizes the narrative: methods precede experiments, related work moves into the main text, and future work and complexity discussion move to appendices. It adds a conclusion, ethics statement, and background section, rewrites explanatory passages, and revises front matter, including removing Feng Wu from the author list. A new Section 6.1 summary sentence mistakenly reverses the mol/ood descriptions, although the detailed split descriptions remain correct.

P2.justification: V4 adopts an ICLR layout and substantially rearranges displays. V3 Tables 1–2 and 3–4 become merged v4 Tables 1 and 2; DFT Table 3 and HarmoSE Table 8/Figure 7 are added. The framework diagram shows channel-summed gradients, and the Hamiltonian illustration is redrawn and moved to the appendix. The representative main-text block-error panel is removed while its results remain in the appendix; existing plot annotations are repositioned without changing their values.

R1.justification: V4 adds references to PySCF and Wang et al.'s universal materials Hamiltonian model, develops its relationship to the already-cited HarmoSE work, and removes several references including KAN and vision surveys. Much of the new main-text Related Work section reworks v3 Appendix A, so relocation does not represent an entirely new literature review.

T1.justification: The two central theorems and their proofs remain mathematically unchanged. V4 Appendix A adds formal definitions of groups, representations, equivariance, and invariance. Appendix I additionally develops the scaling argument by distinguishing quadratic pair counts in small dense systems from asymptotically linear counts under a fixed cutoff.

improvement.justification: V4 addresses important gaps in practical validation and reproducibility: Table 3 and Appendix I provide DFT convergence and inference-overhead evidence absent from v3, while Appendices D–F specify the architecture and training much more concretely. The HarmoSE case study adds a useful check of broader applicability. These gains substantially strengthen the paper despite localized wording errors, including the reversed mol/ood summary. The original accuracy tables remain unchanged, so the improvement rests on stronger documentation and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TraceGrad research. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V4 retains those original experiments and adds DFT convergence results, inference-time measurements, and a HarmoSE-based experiment.

before.justification: V3 reports original TraceGrad experiments on eight Hamiltonian benchmarks, downstream physical-quantity predictions, and component ablations in Appendix F.

C1.justification: v1 presents a sensible absolute timescale range, roughly between one epoch and the training duration, and agreement with published LLM settings as central claims. v2 drops this contribution and narrows its prescription to transferring timescales across scales. The EMA identity and directions of dataset- and width-dependent weight-decay scaling remain.

C2.justification: v2 removes the absolute-timescale rationale based on dataset coverage and forgetting early updates, together with the explicit limitation that transfer to Lion and Sophia was untested. Section 5 adds substantive interpretations connecting EMA timescales to minibatch noise, critical batch size, and sublinear learning-rate scaling with dataset size.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix F adds GPT architecture specifications, 256-token context lengths, microbatch and gradient-accumulation settings, hyperparameter grids, and code sources; Appendix G adds corresponding licenses. Hardware reporting also expands. Some new documentation remains inconsistent: Figure 4 defines the width factor reciprocally to Equation 12.

E1.justification: v2 retains CIFAR-10 and downsampled ImageNet classification and adds autoregressive language-model pretraining on OpenWebText. The new experiments examine dataset-size transfer with 124M NanoGPT and width transfer with eight-layer GPTs (Figures 2 and 4).

E2.justification: Fixed-weight-decay μP scaling remains the comparator to the proposed width-dependent decay, and the existing scale-invariance controls are retained. v2 extends these comparisons to GPTs and additional schedules without introducing a distinct evaluated baseline method.

E3.justification: The reported ImageNet dataset-size experiment changes from 50 epochs in v1 Figure 2 to 100 in v2 Figure 1; this does not establish that every panel was rerun. New protocols include approximately four-epoch GPT dataset sweeps, 250,000-iteration GPT width sweeps, constant and cosine-to-zero schedule controls, and a 1,000-epoch weight-magnitude experiment.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix C and Figure 11 directly test inverse-weight-decay scaling of learned weight magnitudes. Figures 12–13 and 15–18 add schedule-sensitivity tests for dataset and width transfer. The earlier normalization and initialization ablations remain as Figures 7–10.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages across three random seeds. v2 retains three-seed reporting for image classification but explicitly reports only one seed for the new language-model experiments because of resource constraints. Neither version provides confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: New GPT validation-loss curves show optimal weight decay decreasing with dataset size and increasing with width; new weight-magnitude results approximately follow 1/λ, and schedule-specific results are added. The ImageNet ResNet curves change alongside the reported 50-to-100-epoch revision, while the corresponding ViT panel is retained. v1 Table 1's Llama and Stable-LM timescale entries are removed.

M1.justification: The AdamW update, EMA-timescale parameterization, and proposed dataset- and width-dependent weight-decay rules are retained. Appendix A's normalization, initialization, and separate normalization-parameter learning-rate modifications already appeared in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively recast, including an explicit contribution list. Theorem 1 moves from the appendix into Methods, the natural-range results section and standalone Limitations section disappear, and the results narrative and related-work discussion are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one column to two, and retained appendix plots move onto separate pages. GPT, weight-magnitude, and schedule figures are added, while v1 Figure 1 and Table 1 disappear. Many existing plots are retained with changed placement and numbering, including v1 Figures 6–9 becoming v2 Figures 7–10.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands to discuss follow-up work by Blake and Bjorck, concurrent work by D'Angelo, and batch-size scaling research. v2 more explicitly distinguishes its model/dataset transfer contribution from earlier parameterization, effective-learning-rate, and noise-based interpretations.

T1.justification: The existing scale-invariance theorem and proof now explicitly cover scheduled learning rates with matched ηtλ trajectories. Epsilon rescaling, already present in v1's proof, becomes explicit in the theorem statement. The underlying proof strategy and Appendix B's EMA derivation are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 motivates LLM applications but supplies original training experiments only in vision under one scheduling approach. v2 adds direct GPT dataset/width tests and schedule and weight-magnitude checks, substantially strengthening evidence for the central transfer rules. These gains outweigh the loss of absolute-timescale guidance, although single-seed GPT results and inconsistent width-factor documentation limit confidence in that new evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original image-classification experiments and adds OpenWebText language-model experiments, weight-magnitude measurements, and learning-rate-schedule analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original ResNet-18 and ViT experiments on CIFAR-10 and downsampled ImageNet, including hyperparameter sweeps and scale-invariance ablations.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes direct symbolic PDE solving, high-frequency or steep solutions, and heat-equation skeleton recovery. v2 centers broader DE solving, an asserted greater-than-fourfold RSCO speedup, arbitrary-variable parameterization, and recursive recovery of higher-dimensional PDEs, with superiority over multiple machine-learning solvers. These substantially redefine the principal contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting RSCO to avoiding expensive optimization of unsuitable skeletons and recursion to reducing search complexity. Appendix E introduces gradient interference and missing variables as explanations for comparator failures. It also explicitly discusses approximate symbolic answers when analytical solutions are unavailable, while v1's physical-case and PNN-specific interpretations are removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed algorithms, CPU information, RNN architecture, hyperparameters, grid-search settings, PINN training epochs, and baseline implementation sources in Appendices A-C. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation beyond v1's brief pseudocode and benchmark configurations. However, v1's explicit collocation counts are no longer provided for the retained suite.

E1.justification: v2 adds the nonlinear Van der Pol problem, Poisson problems with three independent spatial variables, and heat problems with two or three spatial variables. It removes v1's periodic-potential, point-charge, and two one-spatial-dimensional heat cases. The twelve Nguyen-derived problems remain as the Γ dataset; their renaming does not constitute new coverage.

E2.justification: KAN and PR-GPSR become evaluated comparators on the five DE benchmarks in v2 Table 2, substantially expanding comparison beyond v1's PINN-based pipeline. PINN+DSR corresponds to the earlier DSR* method. The retained Γ comparison still includes only the proposed method and that pipeline.

E3.justification: v2 replaces reward/R2 reporting with Lphy and uses a common recovery criterion requiring equivalent expression structure and MSE below 1e-8; v1 used different recovery checks for SymPDE and DSR*. It also changes reported benchmark domains, including Nguyen-7/Γ7 from [-1,1] to [0.5,1.5], and introduces equal-time component ablations.

E4.justification: v2 Figure 2 introduces ablations testing the contributions of RSCO and recursive exploration under equal execution time. Table 10 documents intermediate recursive solutions, and Appendix E analyzes missing variables and nonsparse comparator expressions. v1's physical case studies and associated error-distribution analyses are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report twenty independent experiments. v2 adds 95% confidence intervals derived from standard errors for Lphy in Tables 2 and 4, whereas v1 reports averages and recovery rates without intervals. This refines uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports 90% average SymPDE recovery; v2 Table 4 reports 100% for every Γ problem. DSR*/PINN+DSR recovery on Nguyen-2/Γ2 changes from 5% to 100%. Changed methods and recovery rules prevent interpreting these as controlled performance gains. v2 additionally reports 100% SSDE recovery on four PDE benchmarks and 0% on Van der Pol, alongside new expressions and errors; v1's physical case-study results disappear.

M1.justification: The RNN and risk-seeking policy-gradient backbone remain, renamed SSDE. v2 adds two-stage risk-seeking constant optimization, hierarchical entropy, and recursive symbolic substitution across variables, extending v1's time-parametric skeleton approach beyond its PNN coefficient model. Appendix A also introduces PINN-derived partial constraints during recursion.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and retained methodological exposition are extensively rewritten. The system-specific narrative becomes separate preliminary, methodology, experimental-settings, and research-question-based results sections. Appendices are reorganized into algorithms, infrastructure, baselines, datasets, and results; the title, method terminology, and author text also change.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main text, redraws the framework diagram, removes the earlier case-study curves and heatmaps, and adds an ablation chart. Tables are substantially restructured: retained benchmark results display equations and uncertainty intervals, while new tables present conditions, hyperparameters, explicit solutions, and recursive steps.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning by discussing direct symbolic DE solvers from Oh et al., Cao et al., and KAN, distinguishing their computational cost, scalability, and symbolic accuracy. v1's computer-algebra/SymPy discussion is removed. The revision therefore changes the relationship to prior research beyond citation or bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 adds an explicit closed-form solution definition encompassing special functions and neural operators, a combinatorial search-space bound of |L|^|τ|, and a revised filtered policy-gradient formulation for RSCO. These are limited mathematical additions; neither version provides theorems or convergence proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited comparative evidence through direct symbolic-solver baselines and component ablations, supported by confidence intervals and much fuller implementation documentation. These additions make the contribution substantially easier to assess. Inconsistent heat initial conditions between Tables 1 and 7 and the greater-than-fourfold speedup claim without a corresponding timing comparison limit confidence in parts of v2, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in evaluation and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reinforcement-learning framework for symbolic differential-equation solving, retaining the Nguyen-derived benchmarks despite renaming and substantial expansion. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark comparisons, recovered expressions, and component ablations in Tables 2-4, Figure 2, and Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original recovery rates, symbolic solutions, numerical errors, and physical case-study outcomes in Section 4, Tables 1-2, and Appendix B.

C1.justification: The central claim that SST improves memory efficiency while approaching full-rank performance is retained. v2 explicitly focuses its contribution on pre-training and narrows the hyperbolic-space novelty claim from parameter-efficient training to parameter-efficient pre-training. The abstract's headline example changes from OPT-125M to LLaMA-1.3B without fundamentally changing the contribution.

New discussion acknowledges deviation from true SVD factors, explains sampling and optimizer-reset trade-offs, and discusses extra frozen-parameter storage and longer convergence at low ranks. Sampling results are interpreted as showing that visiting all vectors matters more than the particular sampling scheme. The earlier qualification about Adam mitigating enhanced-gradient benefits disappears.

E2.justification: v2 adds DoRA and VeRA to IWSLT'14 comparisons and GaLore to OPT-350M perplexity and the 16-task zero-shot comparisons. Corresponding GaLore appendix tables omit the previous LoRA/ReLoRA* columns, although those methods remain elsewhere; the component-ablation table adds LoRA and ReLoRA* comparison rows.

The original pruning and singular-value-distribution analyses remain. However, v1's enhanced-gradient ablation, reporting 22.87 BLEU without enhancement versus 22.80 with SST, is removed from the corresponding v2 table.

E5.justification: The three-seed HGNN experiments and their plus/minus reporting remain unchanged. Added image-classification results also average three seeds and use the existing reporting practice. Neither version introduces confidence intervals or significance testing, and v2 does not report increased run counts for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Original main benchmark outcomes are retained; Table 1's NaN failures merely change display from dashes to 0.0. New results include LLaMA-1.3B perplexity of 14.59 for SST versus 14.54 for full training, and OPT-350M GaLore perplexity of 1994 versus SST's 27.72. Numerous classification, sensitivity, and resource results are added. The enhanced-gradient ablation and GaLore's alpha=0.25 result of 37.08 are removed.

M1.justification: SST retains singular-value updates, sampled and normalized singular-vector updates, enhanced gradients, periodic re-SVD, and active/frozen storage. The mixed sampling distribution already appears in v1 Appendix F.1. Clipping added to v2 Algorithm 2 matches v1 Equation 4, resolving a documentation inconsistency rather than establishing a new procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and method motivation undergo substantial rewriting. LoRA limitations are folded into Section 3.1, the sparsity and memory-implementation subsections exchange order, and related work moves into the reorganized appendices. The specific Broader Impacts paragraph becomes a generic Impact Statement, and acknowledgements are added.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout and redraws Figure 1 as a four-method comparison. It adds gradient and vector-swapping diagrams, resource charts, and numerous new or restructured tables. v1 Figures 2–4 survive as v2 Figures 4, 5, and 8; the singular-value plots are enlarged and rearranged from two rows into three.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning against relevant alternatives: PLoRA joins the generalized ReLoRA* account, PiSSA is contrasted with SST's dynamic sampling, GaLore receives a dedicated limitations subsection, and DoRA/VeRA receive substantive discussion in Appendix L. Corresponding citations and new dataset/model references are added. The other parameter-efficient training discussion moves to Appendix B rather than disappearing.

T1.justification: v2 removes Theorems 4.1–4.3 and their proofs from v1 Appendices C–E, covering gradient alignment, enhanced-gradient advantage, and zero-distortion initialization. The chain-rule gradient derivation survives as v2 Appendix D, while empirical gradient comparisons replace the theorem-based motivation. Appendix K also introduces the efficiency-ratio definition.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central efficiency argument: Tables 20–23 add memory consumption, wall-clock time, SVD overhead, and reduced-training-budget evaluations where v1 mainly supplied parameter counts and effective-step plots. Additional comparisons, sensitivity studies, and implementation disclosures make the practical claims easier to assess. Removing the theoretical account and the unfavorable enhanced-gradient ablation reduces theoretical coverage and component transparency, but the direct resource evidence and broader empirical scrutiny provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SST research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds C4 pre-training, image classification, additional comparisons, sensitivity studies, and resource measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original translation, language-modeling, zero-shot evaluation, and graph-learning results, plus pruning analyses and component ablations.

results.title: Sparse Spectral Training and Inference on Euclidean and Hyperbolic Neural Networks

C1.justification: The central contributions remain relational attention and its integration with sensory attention for efficient learning across modalities. v2 adds an explicit parameter-efficiency claim to the abstract and contribution list, extending v1's emphasis on data efficiency without redefining the central architectural contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets learned relation activations as semantic structure, adds a scaling-law interpretation, and discusses trade-offs against specialist architectures with stronger inductive biases. It removes much of v1's Tiny Stories ablation-based discussion of symbol choice and syntax. The configuration and hardware-optimization limitations remain, with mechanistic interpretability added as a substantive research direction.

D1.justification: v2 expands parameter and tensor descriptions, documents a memory-saving contraction order, and supplies technical recipes for the new experiments. It reports a new implementation repository, a Python package, and publicly available pretrained weights. Conversely, detailed Tiny Stories settings disappear despite retained Appendix D results, and the mapping between mathematical decoder configurations and reported results remains unclear.

E1.justification: v2 adds FineWeb-Edu language modeling and CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 image recognition, while removing ImageNet evaluation. Relational Games and the five mathematical tasks remain. Tiny Stories remains in Appendix D.3, although its broader main-text evaluation disappears.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated PrediNet, CoRelNet, and Abstractor comparisons on Relational Games (Figure 7), substantially expanding comparison with specialist relational architectures. These are distinct from the DAT-with-RCA substitution comparisons retained from v1 in Appendix D.

E3.justification: Relational Games gains Transformer head-count and width controls; mathematical evaluation expands from two-layer models to two–four-layer comparisons with additional wider Transformers. New CIFAR protocols use 4-by-4 patches, 100 epochs, and alternative augmentation procedures. FineWeb-Edu introduces approximately 350M–1.3B models, GPT-2 tokenization, 1,024-token contexts, and a 10-billion-token budget. These are expanded or new settings, rather than matched reruns of v1's experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds CIFAR symmetry and augmentation studies (Tables 3–4) and a learned-relation interpretability case study (Figure 5). It removes the mathematical extrapolation analysis and Tiny Stories symbol-assignment and symmetry ablations. Relational Games symmetry and both RA-versus-RCA analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Five-seed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals remain for Relational Games and mathematics. v2 adds mean-plus-standard-error reporting in the mathematical results table and reports ten-seed CIFAR experiments; v1's ImageNet results lacked comparable uncertainty reporting. This extends reporting practices without establishing an increase in runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Substantial result blocks are added or replaced. v2 Table 1 reports CIFAR-10 accuracy of 89.7% for ViDAT versus 86.4% for ViT; Table 5 reports FineWeb-Edu perplexity of 16.09 for 343M DAT versus 16.94 for the 353M Transformer. Mathematical model-size results and specialist-baseline findings are also added, while ImageNet and broad Tiny Stories results disappear. These new-setting comparisons do not establish v1-to-v2 performance gains.

M1.justification: The relational-attention operation, three symbol assignment mechanisms, and dual-attention blocks remain. v2 incorporates Grouped Query Attention into its vision and language DAT variants (Appendices C.3–C.4), introducing parameter sharing beyond v1's documented ordinary multi-head configurations.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the method exposition systematically introduces 'sensory attention' terminology. Repeated symbol-motivation text is removed, Appendix B is reorganized and expanded, and the vision and language subsections exchange order. These changes substantially reshape the narrative beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 replaces mathematical epoch curves with parameter-size plots and introduces language-scaling plots, token-relation visualizations, dataset examples, and mathematical/CIFAR tables. Relational Games plots gain comparator curves and parameter-count legends. The symmetry and RA-versus-RCA plots are reused and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through cognitive and inductive-bias literature, neural scaling laws, visual reasoning, and mechanistic interpretability. Appendix C.1 adds substantive discussion of DAT's generality versus specialist relational architectures. The existing RA–RCA distinction remains; citation renumbering itself is only stylistic.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 and Appendix A's assumptions and proof remain substantively unchanged. Appendix B.1 adds a memory-complexity argument: aggregating relations before projection avoids an O(b n² dmodel) intermediate, using O(b n² dr) relation storage instead, with a stated connection to standard-attention memory scaling.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by addressing v1's explicitly untested language-model scaling and adding parameter-count controls and specialist relational baselines. Replicated CIFAR results and expanded implementation/access information further improve assessability. These gains outweigh the loss of ImageNet, mathematical extrapolation, and several Tiny Stories ablations, although DAT-only Grouped Query Attention and unclear mathematical configuration reporting still limit attribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Dual Attention Transformer research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 reports original Relational Games, mathematical problem-solving, CIFAR, and FineWeb-Edu experiments, alongside retained Tiny Stories results and additional analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Relational Games, mathematical problem-solving, Tiny Stories, and ImageNet experiments, including appendix ablations.

results.title: Disentangling and Integrating Relational and Sensory Information in Transformer Architectures

C1.justification: The main contributions—complete PDE conditioning, decoupled Transformer subspaces and strong generalization—remain. However, the introduction replaces v1's assertion that correct prediction without complete PDE information is theoretically impossible with a qualified account allowing implicit information extraction while emphasizing its difficulty.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations connecting embedding geometry to PDE complexity and coefficient variation, and broadens applicability discussion to missing components and equivalent symbolic representations. Similar performance across LLMs is now attributed to sufficient mathematical knowledge, replacing v1's tentative explanation involving limited ablation data and prompts. The periodic-boundary Concat-P qualification is removed; the grid-data limitation remains.

D1.justification: V3 substantially expands reproducibility information: ICON's five prompting trajectories, PINO's 0.1 physics-loss weight, checkpoint selection, INR decoder depths, dataset sample counts and interpolation, 576 symbolic formulations with prompt examples, and the 32-A100 hardware configuration. It also changes the HeterNS access link. Many additions disclose existing implementation details rather than establish procedural changes.

E1.justification: The three benchmark collections and represented PDE families remain. V3 adds partially observed HeterNS evaluation, changing the available input information (Figure 7). The equation-order transfer experiment repartitions the existing 1D family rather than adding a new dataset or domain.

E2.justification: HeterNS comparisons expand from FNO, Factformer and ViT to also include PINO, ICON and MPP, including the double-unseen comparison (v1 Table 12; v3 Table 13). This substantially broadens comparator types. PDEformer-L and DPOT-S remain, despite shortened names in v3.

E3.justification: V1 describes 1D evaluation using two 10,000-sample subsets selected from pretraining data; v3 describes 10,000 generated in-distribution test samples. Factformer's reported size changes from 9.4M to 5.1M despite unchanged listed architecture settings. New protocols include component masking and equation-order transfer with 200-epoch fine-tuning versus 500-epoch scratch training. These are reported setting changes, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds a random-vector control for symbolic embeddings, PCA analyses, HeterNS component ablations, missing-information robustness, equation-order transfer and full-trajectory case studies. Conversely, v1's subspace-ratio sensitivity study and separate 1D Concat-D/Concat-P analysis are removed or replaced (v1 Appendix E.2–E.3; v3 Section 4.4 and Appendix G).

E5.justification: V1 provides no repeated-run counts or uncertainty estimates. V3 Appendix G.5 reports three repetitions and introduces HeterNS standard deviations and 99% confidence labels in Tables 18–19. This establishes new uncertainty reporting, not an increase from a known earlier run count; the confidence calculation and baseline variability are insufficiently specified.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive baseline and analysis results. Table 16, for example, reports 0.1624 after fine-tuning versus 0.3308 from scratch with 5,000 target examples under different training budgets. Factformer's Table 3 error at viscosity 1e-5 and force coefficient 2 changes from 0.0438 to 0.0571 alongside its changed reported size. Most primary Unisolver scores remain; fine-tuning evidence moves to Appendix A rather than disappearing.

M1.justification: The core embeddings, decoupled conditioning and Transformer architecture remain intact. V3 adds an adaptation for incomplete PDE information: replacing components with learnable tokens at 30% probability and permitting inference with missing components (Section 4.4).

P1.justification: Substantial paragraph rewriting spans the introduction, method explanations, experiments and benchmark descriptions. V3 standardizes the narrative around joint training, in-distribution testing and zero-shot generalization, moves fine-tuning discussion into a dedicated appendix, and reorganizes supplementary material extensively.

P2.justification: V3 expands Table 1 with inputs and examples, groups HeterNS columns by evaluation setting, and converts fine-tuning table entries into appendix bar charts. It adds benchmark illustrations, PCA plots, robustness charts, trajectory displays and uncertainty tables, while also changing the document typography and layout.

R1.justification: V3 adds ICON to the generalizable-solver discussion and Poseidon to the limitations comparison, alongside supporting references on PCA, mathematical background and physics-informed learning. Some references, including the explicit T5 and LLaMA-2 entries, disappear although those models remain evaluated. The overall research positioning remains recognizable.

T1.justification: The vibrating-string solution, two supporting lemmas and odd-periodic-extension proof are retained (v1 Appendix B; v3 Appendix D). Renumbering, notation edits and the standard relative-drop reporting formula do not substantively change the theoretical analysis.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens v1's generalization evidence through broader HeterNS comparators and targeted missing-component and unseen-equation tests. Expanded implementation details and run-variability reporting improve assessability. These gains outweigh the removed ratio-sensitivity study and reporting weaknesses, including underexplained 99% confidence labels and the retained 41.3% double-unseen summary, which disagrees with the revised Table 13 average of about 38.5%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Unisolver, and their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison. Retained material can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V3 retains original experimental results and adds baseline comparisons, missing-component experiments, embedding analyses and equation-transfer results.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, ablations, generalization experiments and scaling analyses for Unisolver.

results.title: Unisolver: PDE-Conditional Transformers Towards Universal Neural PDE Solvers

C1.justification: The abstract and four principal contributions retain their meaning. The introduction revises its quantitative speed claim for FairSquare timeout cases from under ten seconds to under one minute, and updates the ACAS Xu mean runtime from 18 to 21 seconds. The overall claims of faster probabilistic verification and conditional completeness remain.

C2.justification: v1 discusses a non-clipped fairness timeout as potentially reflecting proximity to the fairness threshold. v2 instead investigates the remaining clipped-distribution timeout and suggests an intricate decision boundary in a region of substantial probability mass. It also explicitly distinguishes empirically effective BaBSB from the completeness-compatible hybrid. Existing sampling and population-model limitations remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix C documents CROWN's bounding rules, layer-bound construction and the distinction from CROWN-IBP, where v1 mainly names the employed routine. The HW2 description disappears with its experiment. The code and benchmark access information, main hardware, training hyperparameters and deterministic tie-breaking details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate FairSquare demographic parity and parity of qualified persons, including clipped distributions; ACAS Xu safety and robustness; and MiniACSIncome. The fuller fairness comparison already exists in v1's appendix. The Gaussian and polytope extensions do not introduce evaluated datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: The external comparator sets remain FairSquare, SpaceScanner, ProVe_SLR, ε-ProVe and enumeration in their respective benchmarks. Internal comparison methods change: the SelectProb versus SelectProbLogBounds study is replaced by comparisons involving LongestEdge, BaBSB, BaBSB-LongestEdge-10, interval arithmetic and CROWN.

E3.justification: The main experiments switch from SelectProbLogBounds to SelectProb. FairSquare uses unbounded inputs instead of v1's finite limits chosen at machine precision. The replacement appendix studies use FairSquare on HW1, whereas v1's selection study used several benchmarks on HW2. Main metrics, time budgets and MiniACSIncome training splits remain.

E4.justification: v1 Appendix D compares branch-selection heuristics. v2 Appendix E replaces this with controlled tests of splitting heuristics and interval arithmetic versus CROWN, directly examining the performance cost of the completeness-compatible hybrid. Appendix D.2 also adds investigation of the remaining clipped-distribution timeout, including alternative splitting heuristics.

E5.justification: Both retain five training restarts for MiniACSIncome, fixed-seed tie breaking for BaBSB, and ε-ProVe's 99.9% confidence reporting. Neither adds repeated-verification run counts, confidence intervals for runtime, or significance tests. PV's deterministic probability bounds remain distinct from statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Under revised settings, v1 Table 4's NN3,2/Bayes Net 1 qualified-persons timeout becomes a fair result in 40 seconds in v2 Table 3. NN2,2/Bayes Net 1 changes from 622.2 to 11 seconds, reversing its ordering against FairSquare's approximately 60 seconds. ACAS Xu and MiniACSIncome values also change, and new ablations report substantial differences in solved instances. These are revised-configuration results, not isolated same-setting gains.

M1.justification: v2 extends bounded-input splitting to unbounded continuous and integer inputs, introduces BaBSB-LongestEdge-k, and adds adaptations for multivariate Gaussian distributions and polytopal domains. It removes SelectProbLogBounds and generalizes PV's outer interval-arithmetic call to ComputeBounds. These are substantive procedural extensions, although the central probability-bounding framework remains.

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative remains recognizable. Related work is subdivided and reordered, the interval-arithmetic primer is condensed, and terminology and explanatory prose are edited throughout. The new input-distribution section and theoretical appendix expand the structure, while much of the benchmark and training documentation is retained.

P2.justification: The main FairSquare table is replaced by a cumulative-runtime plot using the fuller appendix comparison. The old selection-heuristic plot is removed, two ablation plots and CROWN pseudocode displays are added, and the interval-arithmetic pseudocode display disappears. Most existing figures and table designs remain, with relocation and modest layout adjustments.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated discussion and multiple references on Bayesian neural-network verification, explaining its different source and dimensionality of uncertainty. It substantially develops the comparison with FairSquare and ProVe_SLR, especially exact probability computation versus iterative bounds, and updates verification and learned-branching references. These changes extend research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v1's completeness argument concerns SelectProb, interval arithmetic and LongestEdge. v2 introduces explicit convergence and alternation definitions, generalizes the completeness theorem, and develops proofs covering unbounded inputs and the hybrid heuristic. New Appendix C supplies a CROWN non-isotonicity counterexample and a convergence argument using the CROWN Interval Extension.

improvement.justification: v1's completeness argument covered interval arithmetic with LongestEdge, while its effective experiments used CROWN and BaBSB. v2 substantially strengthens the connection between theory and practice through the CROWN convergence analysis, a completeness-compatible hybrid, and experiments showing that hybrid solves all 18 FairSquare instances. Explicit unbounded-input handling also removes v1's truncation workaround. These gains outweigh the loss of the broader branch-selection study.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same probabilistic neural-network verification work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable and support comparison, including the rotated results tables.

after.justification: v2 reports original results on the retained benchmarks and adds controlled comparisons of splitting heuristics and bound-propagation procedures.

before.justification: v1 reports original verification experiments on FairSquare, ACAS Xu and MiniACSIncome, plus an appendix comparison of branch-selection heuristics.

results.title: Solving Probabilistic Verification Problems of Neural Networks using Branch and Bound
