C1.justification: The main molecular-generation, contrastive-representation and downstream-task contributions remain. v2 adds the broader claim that LDMol is among the first diffusion models to surpass autoregressive models in text generation and suggests implications for natural-language diffusion. The zero-shot generation claim disappears from the abstract but remains in Section 4.1.

C2.justification: v2 develops a substantive explanation connecting SMILES enumeration, structural invariance and mutual information, and interprets the new KL, stereoisomer and guidance analyses. It newly prioritizes ground-truth agreement over validity when stronger baselines have higher validity. The conclusion removes v1's editing-hyperparameter-sensitivity limitation while retaining the difficulty with biological-property prompts.

D1.justification: v2 specifies MolT5large, expands DiT embedding and conditioning details in Appendix A.1, and documents null-source editing and scenario hyperparameter ranges in Appendix A.3. However, Table 4 removes GPU hardware and training-time information, and the ChEBI-specific fine-tuning description disappears. This establishes lost documentation, not that fine-tuning was actually discontinued.

E1.justification: v2 substantially extends editing coverage from structural examples to eight property-directed scenarios involving solubility, drug-likeness, permeability and hydrogen bonding on ZINC15 molecules. ZINC15 also replaces PubChem as the source of unlabeled diffusion-training molecules. The principal paired datasets remain; the MoMu retrieval test set is the earlier Su et al. custom set under another name.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds T5large, MolT5large, MolXPT, bioT5 and bioT5+, and removes SciBERT from that comparison. Table 2 adds MoleculeSTM and MolCA. Figure 5 adds an editing comparison against MoleculeSTM(Graph), while Figure 3 and Table 3 introduce a KL-regularized autoencoder comparator. These substantially strengthen and broaden the comparison methods.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: unlabeled training samples decrease from 100,000 to 10,000, DiT batch size increases from 16 to 64 per GPU, and ChEBI-20 guidance changes from 3.5 to 2.5. Editing examples change from 200 iterations, learning rate 0.4 and guidance 2.0 to 150, 0.1 and 2.5. New protocols include 200-molecule editing evaluations, normalized feature distances for 1,000 random and 1,000 enumerated pairs, and additional ablation metrics. Guidance selection now explicitly uses the reported test-set sweep.

E4.justification: v2 adds an encoder-invariance diagnostic comparing enumerated and random SMILES pairs (Figure 3), ablations of stereoisomer negatives and KL regularization (Table 3), and a classifier-free guidance sensitivity study (Appendix B.1). The original contrastive-pretraining and compression ablations remain. Appendix retrieval cases expand from two to four, and generation/editing examples are revised.

E5.justification: Figure 5(a) newly reports means and variability error bars over three separate editing runs, described as 'standard variation' in its caption. v1 has no corresponding run-based uncertainty reporting. The retrieval averaging over n=10 or n=25 noise evaluations is retained.

E6.justification: LDMol results are revised throughout Tables 1–3. Table 1 exact match changes from 0.363 to 0.530 and FCD from 0.25 to 0.20. At n=25, Table 2 PCdes paragraph accuracy changes from 90.82% to 90.3%, and MoMu paragraph accuracy from 81.13% to 87.1%. Changed training and sampling settings prevent interpreting these as controlled same-setting gains. New results include KL-regularized generation with 0.492 exact match, stereoisomer ablations, guidance curves and editing hit ratios favoring LDMol in five of eight scenarios.

M1.justification: The contrastive SMILES encoder, stereoisomer negatives, compression layer, autoregressive decoder, conditional DiT, retrieval scoring and DDS editing procedure are retained. Specifying MolT5large and adding architecture diagrams and pseudocode clarify implementation rather than establish a changed method. The new editing benchmark uses a null source prompt within the existing DDS procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory motivation, encoder rationale and experimental narrative receive substantial rewriting. Appendices A–C are reorganized into Experimental Details and Additional Results with new subsections. The title, terminology, author presentation and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws overview and example figures, adds encoder-distance, DiT-block and guidance figures, and combines editing examples with a new error-bar chart. Table 1 gains a model-family column, and Table 3 gains grouped reconstruction/generation columns. The downstream pipeline is retained as Figure 7, while retrieval examples are redesigned and expanded as Figure 9. The document template and layout also change throughout.

R1.justification: Beyond v1's emphasis on TGM-DLM, v2 positions LDMol against geometric latent diffusion by Xu et al. and language latent diffusion by Lovelace et al. It develops its relationship to SMILES enumeration and contrastive augmentation through additional cited work, and adds references supporting new comparators. This substantially expands research positioning beyond the switch to author-year citations.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations and contrastive/reconstruction objectives remain substantively equivalent. v2 makes the decoder's latent conditioning explicit and expresses the existing guidance and downstream procedures in pseudocode. Its added invariance and mutual-information discussion is conceptual motivation, without new formal assumptions, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central representation-learning claim through the regularized-latent comparison, encoder-invariance diagnostic and stereoisomer ablation missing from v1. Stronger baselines and quantitative editing results with repeated-run variability also address important weaknesses in the earlier evaluation. These gains outweigh the lost hardware/fine-tuning documentation and removed editing-sensitivity caveat, although selecting guidance using ChEBI-20 test results weakens benchmark independence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LDMol by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, including material renamed or moved between versions.

after.justification: v2 reports original LDMol measurements and adds encoder-feature analysis, quantitative editing comparisons and guidance-scale experiments, including appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LDMol generation, retrieval and ablation measurements in Tables 1–3, together with generation, editing and appendix retrieval examples.

results.title: LDMol: A Text-to-Molecule Diffusion Model with Structurally Informative Latent Space Surpasses AR Models

C1.justification: The introduction now calls a latent domain essential for effective diffusion on complex molecule-generation tasks, strengthening v2's beneficial-design framing. AR superiority and applications without task-specific training were already claimed in v2; their increased prominence in the title and abstract does not establish new contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations connecting temperature to hard-negative sensitivity and complex compression to disruption of informative features. It discusses the reconstruction–cost tradeoff behind latent width 64, identifies very long molecules among reconstruction failures, and describes boundaries under ambiguous or contradictory prompts. The biological-property limitation remains.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a training/sampling code-access link, specifies 12-layer BERT-based encoder/decoder implementations, reports eight 40-GB A100 GPUs, and discloses 320,000 diffusion-training examples. These supplement existing implementation information; they do not establish changed training data or default hyperparameters.

E1.justification: Table 1 adds text-to-molecule generation evaluation on PCDes, previously used for training and retrieval. Figure 11 adds ambiguous and contradictory input scenarios. The existing training datasets, ChEBI-20 generation, retrieval tasks, and editing coverage remain.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds MolT5large and bioT5+ comparisons to the previously LDMol-only handwritten-prompt studies; Table 8 also compares their computational costs. Comparator membership in the retained ChEBI-20 and retrieval benchmarks is unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 substantially expands evaluation through uniqueness, novelty, substructure-based alignment, and V×U×A metrics for the 1,000-sample prompt studies. New analyses introduce temperature and latent-width controls, reconstruction testing on 1,000 unseen SMILES, and scaffold-group UMAP sampling. Existing generation and retrieval settings remain intact.

E4.justification: Appendices A.2 and B add temperature, compression-width, training-placement, and transformer-compression ablations; scaffold visualizations; quantitative prompt analyses; ambiguous/contradictory-input tests; and efficiency analysis. Earlier compression and stereoisomer ablations are retained in Table 7. The brief random-versus-fixed initialization comparison in v2 is omitted.

E5.justification: Editing results retain error bars and the description of means and standard deviations over three runs, moved from v2's Figure 5 caption to v3's Appendix A.3. No new seed disclosure, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run reporting practice is introduced.

E6.justification: v3 newly reports PCDes generation results, including LDMol's 0.464 exact match and 0.32 FCD. Tables 5–8 add reconstruction, prompt-quality, compression-ablation, and runtime/memory outcomes. Original ChEBI-20 and retrieval scores remain identical; v2's qualitative finding of marginal sensitivity to random versus zero-vector initialization is removed.

M1.justification: The contrastive SMILES encoder, stereoisomer hard negatives, linear compression, autoregressive decoder, text-conditioned DiT, and downstream algorithms are retained. Newly documented architectural details and alternative compression experiments do not establish a change to the proposed LDMol procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, motivation, and background receive localized rewrites. Hard-negative details move into implementation, detailed ablations move into Appendix B.6, and acknowledgments and an impact statement are added. The overall section sequence and much of the existing exposition remain.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a predominantly two-column conference paper. Figure 1 is redrawn, Figure 4 panels are rearranged, editing examples move from Figure 5 to Figure 12, and the original ablation table is split. New plots and tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Background coverage expands to discrete and embedding-based text diffusion and molecular LLMs, including Austin et al., Li et al., and DrugLLM. New analyses add supporting citations. InfoNCE attribution changes from Chen et al. to Oord et al.; the central positioning around structurally informative latent diffusion remains.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations, contrastive and reconstruction losses, and Algorithms 1–2 retain the same mathematics, apart from notation corrections. Added mechanism explanations and empirical metric descriptions introduce no substantive formal assumptions, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 supported broad-prompt generation largely through examples and validity. v3 adds quantitative diversity and alignment comparisons, novelty measurements, and explicit failure cases, substantially strengthening and qualifying that evidence. Additional PCDes evaluation, latent-space/design analyses, and implementation disclosures further improve validation and reproducibility. The stronger necessity claim and underspecified timing comparison remain weaknesses, but the overall evidential gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LDMol research. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–B support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added material in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds generation benchmarks, latent-space analyses, prompt evaluations, additional ablations, and computational-efficiency results.

before.justification: v2 reports original molecule-generation, retrieval, editing, and ablation results in Tables 1–3 and the main-text and appendix figures.

results.title: LDMol: A Text-to-Molecule Diffusion Model with Structurally Informative Latent Space Surpasses AR Models

C1.justification: V2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion add the claimed first causal merging scheme for transformer decoders and prediction of merging benefits from spectral properties without downstream evaluation. These substantially extend the contributions beyond v1's encoder-focused investigation. The headline Chronos acceleration claim is retained.

C2.justification: V2 extends the existing low-pass-filter hypothesis with interpretations involving spectral noise, learned token similarity, tokenization, and temporal inductive biases. Dynamic merging is recommended for small batches beyond v1's single-sample recommendation. The limitations remove the encoder restriction and also drop the acknowledgment of untested distribution-shift/adversarial robustness without adding such tests.

D1.justification: V2 specifies decoder insertion between self-attention and cross-attention, separate encoder/decoder merging parameters, and reuse of Hyena settings for Mamba. Resource estimates change from 80 to 100 A6000 hours for pretrained-model experiments and from 6 to 12 A100 hours for state-space experiments. Most existing training and hardware details are retained.

E1.justification: The five forecasting datasets and mouse genomic-classification task are retained. V2 adds controlled linear-trend and periodic-signal inputs for tracing merges in Chronos base (Appendix B.2, Figure 8), providing a limited expansion of test scenarios.

E2.justification: V2 adds an evaluated local-pruning comparator against merging for Chronos small on ETTh1 (Appendix E.2, Figure 16); v1 discussed pruning without reporting this comparison. Existing unmerged-model, global-merging, and Gaussian-filter comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: The main transformer evaluation changes from encoder-only to encoder-plus-decoder merging, with separate merging parameters and 185 inference-search trials instead of 180. V2 adds batch-size-10 dynamic evaluation, best-accuracy state-space configurations, and Mamba/PatchTST settings. Core data splits, forecasting horizons, and validation/test separation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds spectral-entropy/THD and token-representation analyses, cosine-versus-L1/L2 ablations, pruning comparisons, patch-tokenization tests, and tracing of merges on trend and periodic inputs. These substantially expand investigation of when and why merging works. The earlier smoothing, input-length, and positional-embedding analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seed 2024, two timing warm-ups, two measurement runs per batch, and timing standard deviations generally below 2%. These disclosures move partly into Appendix C; no new confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-training uncertainty reporting appear.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises numerous results under the decoder-enabled procedure: for example, 10-layer Non-stationary Transformer acceleration on ETTm1 changes from 3.60× to 3.80× under changed merging conditions. Table 3 adds accuracy-oriented Hyena results (1.68×, 80.6%) and Mamba results, including 4.09× at 74.4% accuracy. PatchTST and diagnostic results are new; Chronos Table 2 is unchanged.

M1.justification: V1 restricts transformer merging to encoders. V2 introduces decoder merging using adjacent-token merges with k=1 and final unmerging by cloning tokens. It also extends the existing single-sample dynamic procedure to batches by averaging threshold-derived merging counts across batch elements.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract and contribution framing, reorganizes experiments into Results and Further investigations, and condenses the main related-work section while retaining an expanded appendix version. The appendices are reorganized into A–E, and the input-token redundancy discussion moves out of the main text.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout. Retained plots are resized, rearranged, and relabeled; the combined redundancy/dynamic figure is separated. Table 3 expands to two architectures and two objectives, alongside new diagnostic tables and figures.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused comparisons with sparse attention, token skipping, and spectrum-preserving merging, citing Child, Raposo, and Tran respectively. It also distinguishes its decoder unmerging from Bolya and Hoffman. Most earlier related work survives in Appendix A; the Geisler graph reference and two Schwinn robustness references are removed.

T1.justification: The local-similarity definition, complexity formula, and attention-only speed-up bound retain the same derivations (v1 Appendix A.1; v2 Appendix B.1). The added causality and Markov discussion supplies conceptual arguments, without new formal proofs or revised mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses the explicit encoder-only restriction with a documented decoder procedure and empirical evaluation. New pruning, similarity, tokenization, and Mamba comparisons substantially strengthen support for applicability and design choices. These gains outweigh the qualifications: reliable spectral prediction remains supported only by associations across five existing datasets, and the removed robustness caveat remains unresolved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same token-merging research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and reports additional decoder-merging evaluations, Mamba and PatchTST experiments, and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original forecasting and genomic-classification experiments, including MSE, accuracy, acceleration measurements, and ablations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Efficient Time Series Processing for Transformers and State-Space Models through Token Merging

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes explaining observed truthful bidding through value-maximizing behavior, universal feasibility and its cost. v2 makes polynomial-time online learning and approximate regret against richer clairvoyant strategy classes central contributions. The valuation-based safe-strategy characterization remains, but the paper's principal claims and scope substantially change.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of learnability through avoiding bid discretization and interprets approximation factors through comparator-class richness. It clarifies that Figure 4's descending ratio uses an m-independent numerator upper bound, discusses consequences of tie resolution, and adds time-varying valuations and cumulative RoI constraints as future extensions.

D1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and Appendix B.3 provide initialization, update and sampling procedures, explicit learning rates, and computation of bandit marginal probabilities. These substantially expand implementation guidance beyond v1's learning discussion. Conversely, v2 removes Appendix C.2's explicit simulation ILP formulation and the statement that this solver formulation generated the results.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same bidding scenarios using semi-synthetic EU ETS data from 2022–2023 and uniformly sampled valuations. The expanded theoretical comparator classes and learning algorithms are not evaluated on additional datasets or scenarios.

E2.justification: Figure 4 retains the same comparisons: optimal safe versus history-feasible bidding, and safe m-pair versus safe one-pair bidding. The former retains an upper bound for the history-feasible optimum. Renamed strategy classes and newly cited algorithms do not add experimentally evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: The documented simulation settings remain T sampled from 100–300, M from 10–80, m from 1–10, normalized bids and uniform valuations. Reconstruction retains tolerance 0.05 and mixture fraction 0.97. v2 does not establish that the retained experiments were rerun using its new optimizer.

E4.justification: The sensitivity analysis over m and the data-reconstruction checks are retained. No additional empirical ablation, robustness test or error analysis appears. Appendix F provides analytical discussion of ties, rather than a new experimental robustness test.

E5.justification: Both versions retain averaging over 100 simulations and the shaded bands in Figure 4. However, v2 removes v1's explicit explanation that these bands represent one standard deviation on either side.

E6.justification: Figure 4 retains the same plotted findings: the safe/non-safe value-ratio upper bound is approximately 1.05 by m=4, and the m-pair/one-pair ratio reaches approximately 1.25 at m=10. Reconstruction findings, including 341 retained auctions and regression coefficient 1.01 with intercept −0.008, also remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v1 Section 7 uses enumeration-based Hedge/EXP3 and proposes submodular optimization with a (1−1/e) approximation for large m. v2 Section 4 introduces an exact DAG optimizer and efficient online algorithms using edge updates, path sampling and a bandit estimator. The underlying valuation-based bidding rule remains equivalent after renaming UF policies as safe strategies and normalizing RoI.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. UF policies become safe strategies, the performance measures are reorganized around richness ratios, learning moves into a central section, and proofs and simulation details are redistributed across reorganized appendices with a new contents page.

P2.justification: v2 adopts substantially different typography, spacing and running headers. It removes the NZ ETS interface screenshot and v1 Table 1, adds a DAG figure and three algorithm displays, and relocates or relabels retained diagrams and proof tables. Figure 4 is reformatted with new notation while retaining its plotted results.

R1.justification: The research positioning shifts toward efficient online learning and comparisons with quasilinear-bidder algorithms. v2 adds works including Potfer et al. (2024), Castiglioni et al. (2024), Aggarwal et al. (2025), and Takimoto and Warmuth (2003), while removing substantial truthfulness-motivation and general auction-optimization literature.

T1.justification: v2 adds the DAG decomposition and correctness proofs, regret upper and lower bounds, and tight m′/m and 2m′/m guarantees generalizing v1's comparisons against one bid pair. It adds deterministic tie handling in Appendix F and omits v1's separate homogeneous-valuation theorem and downward-minimality result. The new bandit proof contains an incorrect sum bound in Appendix B.3.2.

improvement.justification: The exact DAG optimizer and polynomial-time full-information learner resolve v1's reliance on exponential enumeration or approximate optimization, while the general m,m′ analysis substantially broadens the guarantees. These gains outweigh the reduced simulation documentation. A material qualification remains: Appendix B.3.2 bounds a sum growing as Theta(M^4) by O(M^3), leaving the advertised bandit regret dependence on M unsupported as written.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on RoI-constrained bidding in repeated uniform-price auctions. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures and tables, support comparison despite substantial changes in title, organization and theoretical scope.

after.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendix E retain the original EU ETS data reconstruction and simulation results. Retained results still qualify as original empirical work.

before.justification: Section 8 and Appendix C report original data reconstruction and numerical simulations using EU ETS auction statistics, with results averaged over 100 simulations.

results.title: Learning Safe Strategies for Value Maximizing Buyers in Uniform Price Auctions

C1.justification: The central claims about flexible policies, explained safety assessments and dataset/model safeguarding remain. v2 explicitly foregrounds an open framework encompassing preprocessing, augmentation and training, and changes the advertised safeguard range from 7–34B to 0.5–7B. These refine the contribution scope while preserving the main research proposition.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for guided rationale generation, attributes ImageGuard's weak policy responsiveness to overfitting, and interprets human agreement as evidence of alignment. It emphasizes handling ambiguous cases and presents smaller checkpoints as addressing computational costs. v1's LoRA-capacity explanation and 13B deployment recommendation disappear; the context dependence of safety and synthetic-rationale limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies concrete guided-generation prompts and prefilled-JSON instructions, expanded dataset accounting, and the human-study procedure and interface. Training documentation changes batching and hardware from four to five A100-80GB GPUs, while retaining three epochs and the learning rate. LoRA and 34B offloading details disappear. Access instructions now point directly to a repository and explicitly include the pipeline.

E1.justification: v2 retains the SMID-derived dataset, ImageNet and I2P applications, and adds audits of CC12M, COCO and Stylebreeder (Appendix C, Figure 6). Human evaluation also covers multiple datasets. Its exact synthetic coverage is uncertain: Section 7 lists I2P-generated images, whereas Appendix J lists GenAI-Bench.

E2.justification: v1's Llava-7B/13B/34B, Idefics2-8B and GPT-4 Turbo comparisons are replaced by Llava-OV-0.5B/7B and GPT-4o, with LlamaGuard-3-Vision, OpenAI Omni-Moderation and ImageGuard added (v2 Table 2). v2 also adds Llava as an ImageNet audit comparator. NSFW-1, NSFW-2 and Q16 remain in the appendix comparison.

E3.justification: v2 reports 4571/71/824 train/eval/test samples and 5592 training instances after oversampling. v1 instead describes 4940 training and 599 test samples, although Figure 7 shows 734 test samples. Batching changes to size 1 with 25 accumulation steps. Comparisons introduce precision and PES, and new protocols include ImageGuard policy controls and three human evaluators assessing 105 images each.

E4.justification: v1's full-tuning versus LoRA ablation is removed. The extreme-rating analysis is retained and extended with ambiguous-only results (v2 Table 4). New analyses examine ImageGuard under default versus custom policies, Llava's ImageNet classification errors, and human agreement with ratings, categories and rationales. Qualitative policy-following examples are also revised.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed information, run-to-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new human-agreement study reports point estimates without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v1 Table 3 reports 89.46–90.74% balanced accuracy across its safeguard models; v2 Table 2 reports 88.70% for 0.5B and 90.84% for 7B under revised models and settings, preventing a direct performance-gain interpretation. ImageNet unsafe detections change from 16,640 to approximately 20k, and I2P detections from 996 to approximately 2.2k. New human agreement is 88%, 87% and 81% for ratings, categories and rationales.

M1.justification: The safeguard suite changes from Llava-based 7B/13B/34B models to Llava-OneVision-based 0.5B/7B models. Rationale construction changes from zero-shot generation, filtering and template augmentation to guided generation using prefilled human labels for default policies and category-focused prompts for exceptions (v2 Sections 4–5, Appendix G). The taxonomy and basic policy-exception augmentation remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution list and substantial portions of the background and evaluation narrative are rewritten. v1's Building LlavaGuard section becomes separate Dataset Creation and LlavaGuard Model Suite sections. Appendix organization and terminology are extensively revised, beyond the insertion of new experiments.

P2.justification: The main text switches from one to two columns. Qualitative panels and comparison tables are redesigned, audit charts add dataset-size bars, and new audit, rationale and user-study displays appear. Figures 4–5 retain their example images with rearranged panels; Figure 8 partly redisplays the ImageNet audit alongside a new baseline comparison. The LoRA table disappears.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates positioning around contemporary visual moderation systems, discussing LlamaGuard-3-Vision, ImageGuard and Omni-Moderation and claiming a distinctive combination of openness and policy flexibility. It adds newer VLM and AIR 2024 references while removing literature associated with the earlier model-selection, LoRA and rationale-generation discussion. This exceeds bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the mathematical definition of PES as the harmonic mean of PER and balanced accuracy (Equation 2). Equation 1 explicitly formulates the existing PER metric. No substantial theoretical development, theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central promise of reliable, policy-sensitive assessments and explanations. Where v1 supports rationale quality mainly through examples and informal probing, v2 adds component-level human evaluation, explicit competitor policy controls and an ImageNet baseline error analysis, alongside broader real and synthetic dataset validation. Removing the LoRA ablation and retaining reporting inconsistencies, particularly the human-study dataset discrepancy, limit interpretation and reproducibility. Nevertheless, the gains materially strengthen validation of the paper's practical utility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LlavaGuard, with matching research aims, taxonomy and dataset lineage. The text, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies create localized uncertainties but do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of revised models, additional dataset audits, policy comparisons and a human-agreement study.

before.justification: v1 reports original held-out evaluations, LoRA and extreme-rating analyses, and ImageNet and I2P safety audits.

results.title: LlavaGuard: An Open VLM-based Framework for Safeguarding Vision Datasets and Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the claims of an open safeguarding framework, customizable taxonomy, annotated dataset, flexible policy adherence, superior safety performance, and dataset/model auditing applications. The new evaluations support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: Section 7.1 adds the qualification that stable aggregate recognition accuracy can conceal losses in heavily filtered classes. The limitations and Appendix K identify decision-boundary and embedded-text failures. Appendix J additionally interprets retained human agreement in light of demographic differences between annotators and participants.

D1.justification: Appendices I–J newly disclose annotator and participant demographics and consensus handling of ambiguous annotations. v3 also supplies training settings for the new ResNet experiment. Existing LlavaGuard training, hardware, and oversampling details remain. The access pointer changes from the repository to a project page; public training resources were already described in v2.

E1.justification: The safety dataset and existing real and synthetic audit coverage are retained. Section 7.1 adds downstream ImageNet object classification using original versus safety-filtered training data, extending task coverage beyond image-safety assessment. Newly disclosed annotator demographics do not establish a population change.

E2.justification: The held-out comparison expands substantially from v2 Table 2 to v3 Table 3: it adds InternVL2.5 at 1B/8B/78B, Qwen2.5-VL at 3B/7B/72B, QVQ-72B-Preview, and the fine-tuned Siglip2Guard baseline. Existing comparison methods remain.

E3.justification: v3 introduces two substantial evaluation designs: GPT-4o scoring dataset rationales on a 1–10 scale, and controlled ResNet-50 training on unfiltered versus filtered ImageNet. The latter uses 50 epochs, AdamW, learning rate 0.001, and top-1/top-5 evaluation overall and on the ten most heavily filtered classes. Existing safety splits and metrics are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds guided-versus-base rationale and generator-size analyses (Table 2), downstream filtering utility and class-specific impact analysis (Section 7.1), and false-positive analysis addressing boundary ambiguity and embedded text (Appendix K, Figure 13). Existing ambiguity, policy, and qualitative analyses remain.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports ± quantities for the downstream ImageNet accuracies in Section 7.1. Their statistical meaning and the number of runs or seeds are unspecified, so this establishes added uncertainty reporting but not a documented increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: Existing matched benchmark and human-agreement values are retained. Substantial new results include comparator scores, QwenGuard-3B/7B balanced accuracies of 88.72%/89.71%, and guided/base Llava-34B rationale means of 9.1/3.8. Within v3's filtering experiment, unfiltered/filtered top-1 accuracy is 67.2%/67.4% overall but 53.6%/46.9% on the ten most heavily filtered classes. These are added results, not revised same-setting scores.

M1.justification: Section 5.3 adds QwenGuard-3B and QwenGuard-7B using Qwen2.5-VL backbones alongside the existing Llava-OneVision variants. The taxonomy, policy augmentation, guided-rationale construction, and structured assessment procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 introduces numbered subsections throughout Sections 3–7, makes local language corrections, updates affiliation and publication information, and reorders acknowledgements and the impact statement. The main narrative and section sequence are largely preserved.

P2.justification: v3 adds rationale Table 2 and failure-case Figure 13, expands and reformats the main comparison as Table 3, and replaces the former human-agreement table with unchanged values in prose. Figure 8 rearranges the same examples from a four-by-three to a two-by-six grid. Other displays are largely retained or relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to Bai et al. (2023) on Qwen-VL and Tschannen et al. (2025) on SigLIP 2, supporting the added models. The broader positioning relative to existing safeguards, general-purpose VLMs, and rigid NSFW classifiers remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The Policy Exception Rate and Policy Exception Score definitions, including Equations 1–2 and the harmonic-mean formulation, are unchanged. No new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 lacked a quantitative guided-rationale comparison and a downstream test of dataset filtering. v3 adds both, substantially strengthening support for central framework components, while broader baseline comparisons reinforce the performance evidence. Reporting class-specific accuracy losses and concrete false positives also makes applicability limits clearer. These address important validation gaps, although undefined ± quantities and incomplete details for some new experiments remain weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LlavaGuard work and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. v3 retains Appendices A–J and adds Appendix K. The material supports reliable comparison, including relocated content.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds model comparisons, quantitative rationale evaluation, downstream ImageNet experiments, and failure-case analysis.

before.justification: v2 reports original safety-benchmark evaluations, large-scale dataset and generated-image audits, ablations, and human-agreement results.

results.title: LlavaGuard: An Open VLM-based Framework for Safeguarding Vision Datasets and Models

C1.justification: DAG reasoning changes from future work and an acknowledged tree-only limitation in v1 to a central claimed capability in v3's abstract and introduction. V3 also explicitly claims discovery of solutions absent from competing methods and extends its stated applicability to spatial and abstraction reasoning. The central minimal-data, diversity-seeking training claim remains.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations for program-search failures and attributes GPT-4o/o1-mini's Game24 advantage to stronger reasoning capabilities, including self-verification. Appendix G removes the tree-only limitation and identifies costly trajectory collection and long-horizon reasoning as remaining barriers. These qualify applicability while retaining the main interpretations concerning diverse exploration and generalization.

D1.justification: V3 discloses the separate, greedily decoded Llama-3-8B state-transition model, a 0.5 offset for the zero-augmented-reward ablation, and prompts/settings for the added tasks. It identifies the 1D-ARC transformation-function source and reports training times. Most existing LoRA settings, exploration procedures, A100 hardware information, and code-access disclosure are retained.

E1.justification: V3 retains BlocksWorld, Game24, and PrOntoQA and adds spatial planning with a 2x2 Rubik's Cube and transformation-program induction on 1D-ARC. The latter covers movement, filling, and denoising tasks. These additions introduce distinct data and reasoning requirements.

E2.justification: BlocksWorld Table 1 adds SFT with diverse beam, nucleus, and typical sampling, SFT+GFN-CoT, and o1-mini/o1-preview. Game24 Table 2 adds XoT, GPT-4o CoT, and o1-mini; PrOntoQA adds GPT-4o CoT. The new tasks also evaluate GoT and IO/program-only/hypothesis-search comparators. GFN-CoT's source was cited in v1, but its evaluated comparison is new.

E3.justification: V3 introduces creativity as an evaluation metric. The reported BlocksWorld training budget changes from 20 to 10 iterations (v1 Appendix B.2; v3 Appendix C.4). Game24's test selection changes from 100 randomly selected examples to difficulty-ordered indices 910–1010, and the 100-sample condition disappears. These are reported protocol revisions; the PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 Table 6 adds replay-buffer and epsilon-sampling ablations alongside the retained local-search and reward ablations. It adds a training-cost comparison, a two-trajectory probability check, and a comparative Game24 case study (Tables 7–8 and Figure 1). V1's Game24 100-sample sensitivity result is removed. The existing reward-weight and data-efficiency analyses remain in Figure 3.

E5.justification: V1 supplies no repeated-run counts or result uncertainty. V3 Section 4.1 introduces three-repetition reporting, with means and standard deviations for FOR and many baselines and ablations, subject to stated cost-based exceptions. Creativity uses one repetition, and training times average three runs. This establishes new reporting rather than an increase from a known v1 run count.

E6.justification: V3 adds creativity scores and results including FOR accuracies of 10.87% on Rubik's Cube and 50.37% on 1D-ARC. Six-step BlocksWorld accuracy changes from 71.71% to 78.44%, alongside revised training-budget and averaging reports. PrOntoQA in-distribution prediction accuracy changes from 90.10% to 88.73%. Game24 adds o1-mini at 94% and GPT-4o at 59%, versus FOR at 41%, and removes FOR@100's 65% accuracy and 2.06 diversity.

M1.justification: V1 restricts reasoning to trees with backward probability PB=1. V3 Sections 3.1–3.2 allow merged paths in DAGs and use PB=1/|Pa(s)| in the objective. V3 also introduces task-specific rewards based on remaining solution distance for Rubik's Cube and Hamming-distance reductions for 1D-ARC. The log-variance loss and random-policy local search already appeared in v1's appendices.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work is split between Section 2 and Appendix A; the log-variance formulation moves into the main method section; and ablations move from the BlocksWorld subsection to Section 4.7. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned around five task panels and a comparative case study, and the appendix BlocksWorld diagram is redrawn as a merged graph. Results tables gain creativity columns, uncertainty entries, and comparator groups; ablations become a separate table. New benchmark, timing, and probability tables are added. Existing prompt tables become styled figures, while Figure 3 is resized, relabeled, and relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the new Appendix A substantially expand positioning around divergent thinking, self-correction, inference-time computation, program search, and newer GFlowNet applications. V1's explicit first-work claim is removed. V3 emphasizes higher-level DAG reasoning as its distinction from token-level GFlowNet sequence generation and search-based LLM reasoning.

T1.justification: The formal assumptions expand from unique-parent trees to DAGs with uniform-parent backward probabilities. V3 also explicitly assumes distinct actions produce distinct next states when equating action and transition probabilities. Appendix C.2 introduces the set-based creativity definition in Equations 13–15. The log-variance formulation is retained from v1 Appendix A rather than newly derived.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central diversity and efficiency claims. V1 lacked evaluated diversity-focused comparators and uncertainty estimates; v3 adds GFN-CoT and diverse-decoding comparisons, repeated-run statistics, diagnostic ablations, and training-cost accounting. The additional tasks test distinct reasoning requirements. These gains outweigh remaining reporting problems, including Section 4.6.1's blanket superiority claim despite Table 5 placing FOR below STaR on in-distribution prediction accuracy.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Flow of Reasoning by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: V3 reports original experiments on five tasks, expanded ablations, and appendix results measuring training costs and trajectory probabilities.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on BlocksWorld, Game24, and PrOntoQA, including component ablations, sensitivity studies, and generated examples.

results.title: Flow of Reasoning: Training LLMs for Divergent Reasoning with Minimal Examples

C1.justification: v3 adds formalization and proof of learnable loss attenuation as a central contribution and emphasizes improved epistemic uncertainty through fully heteroscedastic ensembles. Its abstract and conclusion strengthen v2's claim of matching or exceeding Gaussian methods to outperforming the evaluated baselines in accuracy, calibration, and OOD detection. The conclusion also newly claims uncorrupted epistemic estimates.

C2.justification: v2 presents beta primarily as an accuracy-versus-calibration/OOD tradeoff; v3 argues it can improve both MAE and CRPS and positively interprets beta ensembles' OOD behavior under the revised evaluation. New explanations connect aleatoric misspecification to epistemic error and attribute performance to loss attenuation and discrete inductive bias. Appendix A.3 specifies approximation deterioration at small means with large target variance.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a Length of Stay training recipe, explicit dataset sizes, revised hardware and trainable-layer details, and additional reproducibility instructions. The advertised code location changes from an anonymous repository to a named GitHub repository, with configuration-file pointers and instructions for obtaining prepared splits. Some information is lost: v3 no longer states the COCO epoch budget or Inventory split proportions explicitly.

E1.justification: v3 replaces Bikes and Collision with hospital Length of Stay, substantially changing tabular task coverage. COCO-People, Inventory, Amazon Reviews, and the Reviews-versus-Bible OOD scenario remain. The synthetic recovery experiments add Poisson-generated data alongside the existing negative-binomial scenario.

E2.justification: v3 adds beta=1 Gaussian comparisons and ensembles of Faithful, Natural, and beta-Gaussian models, substantially expanding the ensemble comparator set. It also adds GLM ensembles in Table 5 and removes the multiclass NN comparisons on Inventory and Reviews. Faithful, Natural, and beta=0.5 Gaussian match v2's Stirn, Immer, and Seitzer baselines rather than representing new methods.

E3.justification: Calibration evaluation changes from continuity-corrected NLL to CRPS, and checkpoint selection changes from validation MAE to validation loss. COCO learning rate and weight decay change; Reviews training changes from updating the backbone to freezing all but its final transformer block. OOD evaluation becomes variance-threshold classification with a 20% ID holdout and AUROC, AUPR, and FPR80. These are substantive reported protocol revisions.

E4.justification: v3 adds empirical moment-approximation error maps, initialization sensitivity with and without beta weighting, median-precision analysis, and Length of Stay CDF case studies. It revises the simulation to analyze ensemble uncertainty components and expands qualitative model comparisons. The COCO beta grid search and multiclass pathology analysis disappear, while the existing three-beta convergence illustration is retained.

E5.justification: The main regression experiments retain five trained models and mean/standard-deviation reporting. OOD permutation tests using 1,500 permutations and associated p-values are replaced by means and standard deviations across ten holdout-resampling evaluations; these are not ten training runs. The GLM appendix additionally describes its reported spread as standard error, inconsistently with the main text's standard-deviation convention.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and added. For example, beta=1 DDPN ensemble MAE changes from 1.701 to 0.959 on COCO-People and from 0.281 to 0.344 on Reviews (v2 Table 3; v3 Table 2). Training and selection changed, so these are not same-setting gains or losses. v3 adds CRPS, sharpness, Length of Stay, and OOD classification results while removing the earlier NLL, entropy-gap, and multiclass results.

M1.justification: The Double Poisson predictive head, approximate NLL objective, stop-gradient beta weighting, and uniform-mixture ensemble procedure are retained. Renaming inverse dispersion from phi to gamma, explicitly writing head biases, and explaining the omitted normalizer do not establish a change to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related-work subsections are reordered, real-world experiments are consolidated, misspecification recovery moves into the main text, and the appendices are reorganized around derivations, experimental details, proofs, and case studies. The title changes from Flexible to Fully Heteroscedastic.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns, and major displays are redesigned. The introductory simulation gains separate aleatoric and epistemic panels; the architecture schematic depicts ensembles. Benchmark reporting is consolidated, new OOD and sharpness tables appear, and appendix case studies are extensively rearranged. The old beta schematic, grid-search plot, and entropy KDE displays disappear; the Inventory point-cloud illustration is retained.

R1.justification: v3 substantially develops positioning around deep ensembles, uncertainty entanglement, and the claimed first formalization of learnable loss attenuation. It adds relevant literature including Mucsanyi et al., Osband et al., scoring-rule work, and OOD detection references. Its treatment of prior Double Poisson regression now acknowledges joint GLMs with separate dispersion covariates, refining v2's blanket description of follow-up models as using constant dispersion.

T1.justification: v3 introduces formal definitions of unrestricted variance, full heteroscedasticity, and learnable loss attenuation, with propositions and proofs in Sections 2–3 and Appendix C. Appendix A.3 adds moment-deviation functions and their derivation, explicitly qualifying DDPN's heteroscedasticity through approximate moments. These substantially extend v2's loss derivation and standard mixture formulas.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's central uncertainty claims through direct OOD detection metrics, broader ensemble comparisons, and investigation of the moment-approximation gap explicitly acknowledged in v2. Initialization and sharpness analyses add useful diagnostic evidence. Removing Bikes, Collision, and multiclass comparisons reduces breadth, and OOD evidence still covers only one task, but the more direct evaluation and clearer treatment of assumptions outweigh these losses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DDPN research. Their main texts and complete appendices are readable, with figures, tables, and equations available for reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original simulations, experiments on four real-world datasets, OOD detection results, and appendix analyses of moment approximations, initialization sensitivity, and predictive sharpness.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulations, experiments on five real-world datasets, OOD analyses, and appendix results covering beta sensitivity and multiclass alternatives.

results.title: Fully Heteroscedastic Count Regression with Deep Double Poisson Networks

C1.justification: v1 principally claims an empirically motivated coupling that accelerates training and often improves generation. v2 makes a persistent scaled continuous-time training/distillation discrepancy a central contribution and claims theoretical and empirical support for reducing that discrepancy and transport costs. Its abstract, contribution list and conclusion are substantially redefined around these claims.

C2.justification: v2 reframes GC as changing the target flow to improve velocity estimation, extending v1's interpretation of proximity to PF-ODE updates. It develops the distribution-shift explanation for GC-only failure and identifies endpoint-predictor quality as a constraint. v1's explicit lack-of-theory limitation disappears, while v2 states ideal-generator and scaling assumptions and acknowledges that GC does not fully solve alignment.

D1.justification: v2 supplements the existing implementation documentation with TorchMetrics, 50,000-image evaluation sets, resizing/cropping/scaling instructions and a Lion implementation source. Gaussian and bridge-process details are removed. Both abstracts retain the same code URL, although v2 additionally describes supplementary code and release upon publication, leaving inconsistent availability wording.

E1.justification: v2 retains CIFAR-10, ImageNet at 32×32 and CelebA at 64×64, and adds LSUN Church at 64×64. It also replaces the learned 1m-2m and 2m-2m Gaussian experimental settings with a one-dimensional two-Dirac setting using a closed-form generator, substantially revising the synthetic coverage.

E2.justification: IC and batch-OT remain the main image-generation comparators, renamed iCT-IC and iCT-OT. v2 adds batch-OT to the CIFAR-10 alignment diagnostic, previously comparing IC and GC, and adds an OT panel to the CelebA qualitative comparison in Figure 7.

E3.justification: v2 adds KID and IS, equal-wall-clock and frozen-predictor controls, and coupling-specific denoisers for its revised velocity-alignment evaluation. Corresponding hyperparameter tables change minimum noise from 0.001 to 0.002 and revise learning rates, dropout settings and some network block counts. Transport evaluation also changes from intermediate-point-to-endpoint cost to noise-to-predicted-data cost; these are not interchangeable measurements.

E4.justification: v2 adds timestep-wise distribution-shift diagnostics, strong versus weak frozen endpoint predictors, dropout ablation and an equal-time control. It replaces the Gaussian gradient-variance and score-update-distance analyses with velocity-discrepancy and revised transport analyses. The optimizer/forward-process ablation disappears, fixed-step scheduling coverage narrows, and EMA analysis is reduced from three datasets to CIFAR-10.

E5.justification: v1 reports performance curves and point scores without performance uncertainty intervals. v2 introduces intervals throughout its primary FID/KID/IS table and specifies five evaluations resampling real and generated images from the same trained model. This adds systematic sampling-uncertainty reporting, not independent training-run uncertainty; the confidence level and interval calculation are unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive numerical and diagnostic results. Table 1 reports CIFAR-10 FID of 5.95 for GC, 7.42 for IC and 6.75 for OT; new LSUN results show GC trailing OT in FID, 9.88 versus 9.71. Table 2 adds equal-time and dropout results, while several earlier ablation and Gaussian result entries disappear. Revised settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The generator-induced endpoint construction, consistency loss, EMA option and IC/GC mixing procedure are retained. Section 5.2 adds a tested variant using a separately pre-trained, frozen endpoint predictor. The change from 'coupling' to 'flows' does not itself alter the main algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, related-work discussion, experimental narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the discrepancy argument. Experiments are reorganized into training from scratch, frozen predictors and mixing, with numbered findings. Appendices are restructured, and the title, terminology and author information change.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the introductory schematic with probability-density and trajectory plots, replaces several diagnostic displays, and introduces a structured multi-dataset, multi-metric results table. The mixing plot narrows to CIFAR-10, while the CelebA comparison moves to the appendix and gains an OT panel. Table organization, typography, headers and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises its relationship to Song et al. by questioning the interpretation that continuous-time training closes the distillation gap. It reframes minibatch OT around approximation error and loss of the no-collision property, supported by added references including Fatras, Sommerfeld and Nurbekyan, and incorporates newer coupling work such as Li et al. These exceed bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v1 contains background equations and an unscaled asymptotic-equivalence statement but no comparable theoretical development. v2 adds Theorem 1 on scaled continuous-time loss and gradient discrepancies, Theorem 2 on asymptotic velocity-estimation discrepancy, transport-cost lemmas and corollaries, and proofs in Appendix A. These introduce substantial definitions, assumptions and derivations.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked theoretical support and only hypothesized the cause of GC-only degradation. v2 adds conditional analyses and proofs, directly tests the distribution-shift explanation, and strengthens evaluation through broader metrics and an equal-time control reporting FID 6.38 versus IC's 7.42. These substantially improve the paper's explanatory and empirical support despite lost Gaussian and ablation coverage. The theory remains idealized, and reported intervals capture image-sampling rather than training variability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same generator-induced consistency-training work despite the revised title and expanded contributions. All 14 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic and image-generation results, including four-dataset comparisons in Table 1 and additional experiments in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian simulations, training diagnostics and image-generation experiments on CIFAR-10, CelebA and ImageNet, including additional Gaussian results in Appendix C.

results.title: Improving Consistency Models with Generator-Augmented Flows

C1.justification: The central claims of efficient domain adaptation and strong downstream performance remain. V2 broadens claimed generalization to agricultural imagery and adds representation analysis as an explicit third contribution. It also revises the claimed linear-probing margin, including 7% to 7.5% in the abstract and approximately 8% in the introduction.

C2.justification: Section 6.3 and Appendix A.2 add substantive explanations linking middle layers to local information and deeper layers to global semantics, using these observations to motivate block selection. Appendix A.4 argues that excessive decoder capacity can fail to improve encoder representations, while A.5 discusses diminishing returns from larger backbones. Earlier SpaceNet and iWildcam limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies shared-head initialization and dimensions, crop and masking settings, teacher EMA and temperatures, initial head freezing, and MAE loss options. It first discloses 32 gradient-accumulation steps and an effective DinoV2 batch size of 1024; this alone does not establish an increase over v1. It also adds Detectron2 implementation information, a GlobalWheat license reference, and a project-page code-access statement.

E1.justification: V2 adds GlobalWheat wheat-head detection in agricultural photographs, extending evaluation beyond the previous classification and segmentation tasks to bounding-box detection. All earlier dataset coverage remains, including EuroSAT, which moves to Appendix A.1.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds substantial PEFT comparisons involving VPT variants, GVPT, SA2VP, and AdaLoRA, including SA2VP applied after ExPLoRA. GASSL and fully fine-tuned MAE disappear from that comparison, and the BOFT row changes its reported initialization from MAE to DinoV2. GASSL also disappears from the SpaceNet and RESISC-45 comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes the reported DinoV2 pretraining learning rate from 0.001 to 0.002 and the RGB MAE rate from 0.00015 to 0.00045. New experiments introduce ViT-B/G configurations, decoder-rank controls, patch-level probes, and detection AP/AR evaluation. These reported revisions do not establish which experiments were rerun. EuroSAT's r64 label in v2 conflicts with its retained reference to the r32 model in Table 4.

E4.justification: V2 adds layer-wise PCA and position/class prediction probes in Section 6.3, attention-map case studies in Appendix A.2, decoder-rank sensitivity in A.4, and backbone-size analysis in A.5. Table 3 expands block-selection and VPT controls. The convergence comparison already existed as v1 Figure 3; v2 updates it and moves it to Appendix A.3.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for benchmark performance. V2's eigenvalue summaries and attention-score filtering describe feature analyses rather than uncertainty in the reported performance estimates.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces ExPLoRA's fMoW-RGB linear-probing scores of 75.77/76.53 with 76.86/77.48, and several Table 3 ablation scores change. RESISC-45 linear-probing accuracy changes from 97.16 to 97.32. V2 adds detection, downstream comparison, and appendix ablation results; GlobalWheat reports 82.7 accuracy, 54.5 AP, and 59.2 AR. The main fMoW-RGB fine-tuning score remains 79.15. Revised pretraining settings prevent interpreting updated scores as established same-setting gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 restates v1's selective block and normalization unfreezing, Q/V LoRA updates, pretrained initialization, and continued self-supervised objective. The expanded head, decoder-rank, and storage descriptions provide implementation and configuration details without establishing a different ExPLoRA algorithm.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the problem setup, method explanations, and portions of the introduction and discussion. It introduces explicit pseudocode, shortens configuration names, adopts source/target terminology, and reorganizes training details by training phase. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adds three representation-analysis plots, an attention-map grid, and new experimental tables. It expands Tables 1 and 3, combines SpaceNet and RESISC-45 into one table, relocates EuroSAT, and redraws and relocates the convergence plot. The document also adopts different title, heading, and running-header formatting.

R1.justification: Related work expands locally to visual prompt tuning and its inference costs, adding VPT, GVPT, SA2VP, and E2VPT citations. V2 also adds GlobalWheat, Detectron2, and medical self-supervised learning references, while removing VideoMAE and point-cloud MAE citations. ExPLoRA's positioning as complementary to existing PEFT remains.

T1.justification: Equation 1 corrects the final expression from W + BA to W0 + BA, fixing the weight-decomposition identity. Otherwise, source/target notation and equation ordering change without substantive changes to the formal assumptions or factorization; no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's limited PEFT comparisons and largely heuristic explanation of block selection through Table 1, Section 6.3, and Appendices A.2, A.4, and A.5. Expanded implementation details make the work more reproducible, and detection results test broader applicability. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses, including conflicting EuroSAT rank labels and overstated PEFT margins: Table 1's 79.15 versus AdaLoRA's 78.87 supports only a 0.28-point advantage. The improvement rests on stronger scrutiny and documentation, not merely higher reported scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ExPLoRA and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–C. Renamed configurations and relocated experiments can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds GlobalWheat detection results, representation analyses, attention visualizations, and decoder-rank and backbone-size ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original ExPLoRA classification and segmentation experiments, parameter-unfreezing ablations, convergence results, and additional NAIP results in Appendix A.

results.title: ExPLoRA: Parameter-Efficient Extended Pre-Training to Adapt Vision Transformers under Domain Shifts

C1.justification: The main method and contribution claims remain. The introduction now explicitly claims advantages of up to 16-fold fewer trainable parameters and eightfold less compute, and strengthens the WILDS description from generalization to outperforming baselines and prior work. The abstract's linear-probing headline changes from 7.5% to 8%.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning limited final-accuracy benefits beyond 50k pre-training iterations, eigenvalue variance as evidence of local/global information encoding, and ExPLoRA's complementary role as a UDA initialization. Existing qualifications about SpaceNet and reduced iWildcam linear-probing performance remain.

D1.justification: New experiments document checkpoint-specific GPU-hour costs, fine-tuning control configurations and the VisDA initialization recipe. Section 5 explicitly explains merging updates into the original ViT. The earlier training hyperparameters, hardware descriptions, code-access statement and dataset-license information are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: Appendix B.7 adds VisDA-2017 synthetic-to-real classification using ExPLoRA initializations for TVT and SSRT, extending evaluation to a conventional UDA setting. Existing satellite and WILDS coverage is retained. Office-Home and FireRisk are discussed but not newly evaluated.

E2.justification: Tables 1/4 add GFM and GDA; Table 1 adds ScaleMAE with LoRA; Tables 1/16 add Mona and Adapter+ comparisons. Table 4 removes the ImageNet-supervised ResNet152 comparator. New VisDA comparisons include CDTrans, PMTrans and alternative TVT/SSRT initializations. Earlier MAE PEFT rows are retained in Table 16.

E3.justification: Appendix B.2 introduces total-compute comparisons using 50k–200k pre-training checkpoints and direct fine-tuning controls with different trainable-parameter budgets. Appendix B.7 adds pre-training on both VisDA domains followed by TVT/SSRT evaluation with ViT-B and classwise/mean accuracy. Existing training schedules and preprocessing remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The new compute-allocation study tests whether extended pre-training is preferable to spending resources on direct fine-tuning. Table 3 adds an MLP-only LoRA ablation, and Figure 4 newly displays eigenvalue variance. Earlier convergence, decoder-rank, backbone-size, attention-map and patch-probing analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added eigenvalue-variance plot concerns feature representations, not uncertainty across experimental runs; the existing attention-score truncation procedure is unchanged.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial baseline, compute-curve and VisDA results, including TVT/ExPLoRA at 88.2% and SSRT/ExPLoRA at 90.9%. Table 3 adds the 48.55% MLP-only result. Table 1 updates ExPLoRA's listed fMoW-RGB accuracy from 79.15% to 79.28%, while Table 4 removes the 54.46% ResNet result. Most retained benchmark scores are unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains selective block unfreezing, trainable normalization layers and LoRA updates to frozen blocks' Q/V matrices. The DinoV2, MAE and multispectral adaptations remain the same. New optimization notation and use as an initialization for UDA do not establish a changed ExPLoRA procedure.

P1.justification: v3 refines domain/task notation, consolidates method and storage explanations, promotes the analysis subsection to Section 7 and reorganizes appendix material. Much of the existing introduction, experimental discussion and limitations retains its wording and narrative sequence.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from one-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is rearranged vertically and moved to the first page; Figure 2 gains explicit block-set annotations. Tables are restructured, MAE comparisons receive an appendix continuation, and new comparison tables, a variance plot and a compute plot are added.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially revises domain-adaptation positioning and expands adapter-related coverage. New Appendix A contrasts ExPLoRA with GFM/GDA and traditional UDA using architecture preservation, objective flexibility, source-data access and label restrictions. Several classical adaptation citations and the ReLoRA discussion are removed.

T1.justification: Equations 5–6 add explicit constrained-optimization formulations and parameter-space definitions for pre-training and downstream adaptation. Appendix A.2 adds formal UDA assumptions, including target/source label-set containment. These are limited formal additions; the existing weight decompositions remain and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central efficiency argument through direct GFM/GDA comparisons and a total-compute study separating extended pre-training from additional fine-tuning, both absent in v2. The UDA experiments and Appendix A also improve applicability evidence and research positioning. New reporting inconsistencies need correction: the stated TVT improvement conflicts with Table 17, and claimed parameter matching conflicts with Figure 7's labels. These localized problems limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial gains in relevant evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same ExPLoRA research work, with readable text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices. Corresponding content can be matched despite substantial layout changes and appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds experiments including compute-allocation comparisons and VisDA-2017 evaluations in Appendix B.

before.justification: v2 reports original ExPLoRA results on satellite and WILDS datasets, together with ablations, representation analyses and appendix experiments.

results.title: ExPLoRA: Parameter-Efficient Extended Pre-Training to Adapt Vision Transformers under Domain Shifts

C1.justification: The introduction changes the assertion that unlearning 'inevitably leaks' membership information to introducing leakage risks, and explicitly qualifies the over-70% detection finding as a worst-case result. The abstract, research questions and central conclusions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 explains how repeated queries could reveal an unlearning event and expands the justification for classification tasks and synthetic data, including difficulties establishing pretraining membership and the models' release ordering. These refine applicability and methodological interpretation without changing the main conclusions.

D1.justification: v3 makes extensive reproducibility information available where v2 supplies only appendix references: dataset construction thresholds, AdamW training settings, unlearning configurations, shadow-model allocation, attack-classifier hyperparameters and padding conventions. Section 4.3 also explains cosine-based decoding. These are documentation gains, not demonstrated changes to the underlying implementations.

E1.justification: Both versions retain SynthPAI-age and SynthPAI-inc classification tasks and the same attack-access scenarios. v3 Appendix A also reports a text-completion check for pretraining exposure. Because v2's referenced dataset appendix is missing, whether this diagnostic task was added cannot be established.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain U-LiRA for auditing and LiRA and ULeaks for relaxed membership inference. Retrain, GA, KL, NPO and TaskVec remain the evaluated unlearning methods. The later appendices introduce no additional comparison method against the proposed attacks.

E3.justification: Shared settings remain unchanged, including model sizes, unlearning ratios, attack metrics and the default 1,000-sample training/single-sample reconstruction setting. v3 specifies a 100-sample, half-prefix completion check and detailed supplementary configurations, but v2's missing appendices prevent determining whether those protocols changed or were merely disclosed.

E4.justification: v3 presents batch-size sensitivity, cosine-versus-Euclidean reconstruction ablations, regularization/clipping ablations and reconstruction examples. v2 already refers to batch experiments, ablations and examples in absent appendices, so their additions or revisions cannot be reliably identified. The earlier status of v3's memory-extraction diagnostic is also unresolved.

E5.justification: v3 Appendix D explicitly reports 100 shadow models, with 85 used for distribution estimation and 15 as tested models. These evaluation-replication counts are unavailable in v2, which gives symbolic counts and refers to its missing appendix. This is additional reporting, not evidence that more runs were performed; confidence intervals and seed details remain unreported.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 2 are identical, and the original plotted results are retained across v3 Figures 3–6. However, v3 supplies substantial concrete results unavailable in v2: memory extraction, training/test accuracy, additional strict attacks, batch reconstruction, ablations and reconstructed texts in Tables 3–21. This is a substantial expansion of available results, without establishing new experiments or same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 3 changes TULA-DR's stopping condition from convergence to reaching a maximum iteration count N. The reconstruction objective, regularization and clipping remain unchanged. The added decoding explanation documents an existing step rather than establishing a new component.

P1.justification: The introduction and dataset rationale receive limited rewriting, decoding and metric explanations are expanded, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added. The principal section sequence and most main-text prose remain stable.

P2.justification: v3 adds an opening overview figure, redraws the attack diagram, and splits the two crowded four-panel result figures into larger plots distributed between the main text and appendices, with revised colors, axes and legends. Table 2 becomes full-width, and the supplied appendices add extensive tabular displays.

R1.justification: v3 adds an introduction paragraph positioning the study alongside concurrent work, including Huang et al. and Shumailov et al., and cites Zhang et al. on membership-evidence limitations. Additional references identify the SynthPAI source and implementation components. The main related-work discussion remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The likelihood-ratio formulation and reconstruction, regularization and clipping equations retain their mathematical content. Appendix C spells out previously described unlearning objectives; no new theorem, proof or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves an important deficiency of the supplied v2 PDF: implementation details and supporting analyses repeatedly referenced but absent are now inspectable. Dataset definitions, training and attack settings, ablation evidence and reconstruction examples substantially improve completeness and reproducibility, while redesigned plots improve readability. The shared headline results are unchanged; the gain is in documentation and assessable evidence rather than demonstrated performance improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, and their main text, equations, tables and figures are readable. However, v2 ends after the references despite citing appendices; v3 includes Appendices A–J. This limits comparison of the supplementary experiments and settings.

after.justification: Section 5 retains the original empirical results, and the appendices provide additional numerical results, ablations and reconstructed examples.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original unlearning-audit, membership-inference and text-reconstruction experiments on Pythia-1.4b and OPT-1.3b.

results.title: Textual Unlearning Gives a False Sense of Unlearning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion shift from a language dataset validated through oracle trajectory-prediction improvements to a multimodal dataset and benchmark with Motion-LLaVA as a central contribution. Claims of learned factual and interaction-reasoning capabilities replace the headline forecasting improvements, while the dataset-size and interaction-coverage claims persist.

C2.justification: The interpretation shifts from language-induced yielding and caution in oracle forecasts to hypotheses about information loss in BEV inputs, alignment between motion pretraining and factual QA, and factual grounding through CoT. v2 also acknowledges the simulated-to-real visual domain gap. The original oracle-information-leakage qualification disappears together with that experiment.

D1.justification: v2 adds model and implementation identification, GPU/time information, simulation generation details, the GPT evaluation prompt, and CoT context examples. It provides explicit code/prompt repository and vision-extension access instructions, whereas v1 promised a future code release. The removed forecasting experiment's T5 configuration, batch size, learning rate, and missing-caption handling are no longer documented.

E1.justification: Model training and evaluation shift from language-conditioned trajectory forecasting to factual and interaction/intention question answering, including vector-input and BEV-image models. The whole-WOMD and language-covered-subset forecasting evaluations disappear. The underlying 63k-scene dataset and its Q&A category coverage remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The v1 comparison of MultiPath++ with and without language disappears. v2 Table 4 instead compares Motion-LLaVA with shuffled ground-truth answers, non-fine-tuned LLaVA, and fine-tuned LLaVA. MultiPath++ remains an encoder component, rather than retaining its earlier role in the forecasting comparison.

E3.justification: The forecasting protocols using MR6 and minFDE6 are replaced by one-epoch LLaVA-v1.5-7b fine-tuning and sampled validation-Q&A evaluation. v2 introduces six language/GPT metrics and a 130-question numerical evaluation using Acc1.0 and Median Error. These are protocols for new experiments, rather than revised scores under v1's settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds ablations of motion-encoder pretraining, direct versus CoT reasoning and factual contexts, and projector alignment versus encoder freezing (Tables 5, 7, and 14). Appendix A.4 adds comparative answer-error examples. The original forecasting case analyses are removed, while the dataset's illustrative interaction cases largely persist.

E5.justification: Both versions report identical category-level standard errors for the same three-evaluator, 501-Q&A study in Table 3. v2's new model benchmarks report point estimates without adding repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
