C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations connecting similarity blocks to redundant knowledge, explaining absent amplitude localization through normalization, and describing model-dependent steering calibration and excessive-steering failures. It also discusses practical applications and task-dependent pruning degradation. The limitation concerning transfer of synthetic steering matrices to real-world, out-of-distribution signals remains.

D1.justification: v3 adds code-access instructions, hardware specifications, model descriptions, exact visually selected pruning blocks, steering-strength guidance, and fine-tuning settings. Synthetic-data documentation is replaced with scenario-specific parameter ranges, although v1's explicit synthetic sample-count configuration is no longer supplied. These substantially change reproducibility information without establishing external resource availability.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic constant, sinusoidal, and triangular signals, including steering transfer to linear and exponential trends. v3 removes the triangular and exponential cases while adding explicit trend, periodicity, and amplitude discrimination, compositional steering, real-data forecasting and imputation, UCR classification and anomaly detection, and ECG5000 steering.

E2.justification: v3 adds unpruned controls for pruning and comparisons with methods including AnomalyTransformer, DGHL, GPT4TS, and TimesNet in Table 9, and TS2Vec, DTW, and ResNet in Table 11. v1's mean-based/LDA/SVM comparison for layer separability is no longer reported; the later SVM-based ECG experiment is a different comparison context.

E3.justification: v3 introduces multiple model families and sizes, four imputation masking rates, forecasting horizons, additional task metrics, and inference timing protocols. Table 6 specifies three training epochs and selection by best test-set performance. The reported synthetic configuration also changes: v1 Appendix B uses amplitude [-1,1] and period [128,164], whereas v3 Appendix A specifies amplitude 50 and period 128 for its seasonal cases.

E4.justification: v3 adds cross-size representation analyses, reported checks using cosine similarity and SVCCA, individual-block versus all-block pruning, compositional-steering sweeps, and an ECG case study. The intervention ablation changes from single versus all layers in v1 Figure 4 to single versus multiple tokens in v3 Figure 11. The original exponential-trend transfer analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v1 provides no explicit repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. v3 introduces five masking-seed runs with means and standard deviations (Tables 3 and 5), timing statistics from 100 passes (Table 7), and cross-dataset dispersion and correlation summaries (Tables 8 and 10). These are new reporting practices for the expanded evaluations.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results absent from v1. Within its new pruning comparison, MOMENT's estimated size changes from 1301.76 to 615.76 MB and inference time from 20.88 to 19.82 ms (Table 7), while mean classification accuracy falls from 0.794 to 0.781 (Table 10). It also reports larger anomaly-detection losses and class changes for all 30 selected normal ECG samples after steering.

M1.justification: v3 adds representation-guided block-wise pruning that preserves block endpoints and zeros intermediate layers (Algorithm 1), plus an optional block-identification algorithm (Algorithm 2). It also extends additive steering to combinations of trend and periodicity directions. These substantially expand v1's identification, localization, and steering pipeline.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten around three contributions and seven research questions. v1's separate Setup section disappears, Future Work becomes part of Discussion and Limitations, and the appendices are reorganized. Reproducibility and impact statements are added.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws the methodology overview, and replaces or expands many original plots with pruning schematics, similarity heatmaps, token-level localization displays, and steering panels. It adds eleven tables and algorithm boxes, while removing the original synthetic-distribution histograms and triangular-pattern figures.

R1.justification: v3 introduces a substantial representation-similarity and pruning literature discussion, including Kornblith, Raghu, Nguyen, and Phang, and positions its pruning approach relative to that work. It also expands TSFM coverage with newer scaling, long-context, and reasoning research, moving beyond v1's primarily concept-probing positioning.

T1.justification: v3 adds a formal definition of contiguous redundant layer blocks and threshold-based identification conditions (Appendix C). Its mathematical signal specification is narrowed to affine and sinusoidal signals, replacing v1 Appendix A's broader waveform, exponential-trend, and noise definitions. Neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the empirical grounding and reproducibility of v1's single-model, mainly graphical synthetic study. Cross-family analyses are connected to controlled pruning evaluations with quantified accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs, repeated-seed results, and downstream failure cases. Expanded steering experiments and implementation disclosures add practical value. Table 6's test-set-based epoch selection and broad accuracy-preservation claims despite anomaly-detection losses weaken parts of the argument, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TSFM representation and steering work, despite the changed title and expanded scope. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original representation-similarity analyses, pruning evaluations, synthetic and ECG steering experiments, and downstream forecasting, imputation, classification, and anomaly-detection results.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data experiments on MOMENT, including layer separability, steering outputs, alternative interventions, and generalization to different input trends (Figures 3–14).

results.title: Exploring Representations and Interventions in Time Series Foundation Models

C1.justification: The personalization and joint data/resource-heterogeneity claims persist. v3 adds conditional convergence guarantees, quantified resource efficiency and a released collaborative-LLM codebase as explicit contributions. The abstract and conclusion consequently claim theoretical support and practical resource efficiency beyond v1's predominantly empirical contribution.

C2.justification: v3 expands explanations of layer-dependent expert specialization and attributes negligible Llama fine-tuning gains on Wikipedia/SlimPajama to likely pretraining overlap. v1's explicit validation-data scarcity warning disappears; v3 instead emphasizes fresh training batches as an in-distribution fallback. The limitations concerning overfitting on easy tasks and vulnerability to attackers remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds an explicit project-code release statement and access link, Llama-specific training schedules, Common Corpus token counts and resource-accounting assumptions. Most existing hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain. Conversely, v1's exact GPT-2 module-name list and explicit attention-LoRA aggregation detail are omitted. The PDFs establish the new access disclosure, not the repository's actual contents.

E1.justification: v3 retains Multilingual Wikipedia, SlimPajama and AG News, and adds Common Corpus evaluation using YouTube-Commons, public-domain books, EU tenders and Harvard US patents. This substantially expands represented domains, particularly transcripts, procurement documents and patents. The existing languages and next-token prediction task remain unchanged.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated pFedMoE and FDLoRA comparisons to Table 1, and FedSA-LoRA and pFedMoE to the extended appendix comparison. pFedMoE was only discussed in v1. FFA-LoRA was already evaluated in v1 Appendix C.1, while the heterogeneous-model comparison retains HetLoRA and FlexLoRA.

E3.justification: v3 adds Llama 3.2-1B alongside GPT-2-124M, with 10 communication rounds for AG News and 20 for Common Corpus (Appendix B.1). It also introduces matched-parameter resource accounting for GPT-2 with bfloat16 assumptions (Table 3). The stated GPT-2 splits, training budgets, batch size and context length are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds an AG News layer-wise routing comparison against pFedMoE (Figure 4) and fills previously unavailable AG News results for training-batch router-update ablations (Table 5). The update-frequency sweep, load-balancing ablation, expert-count/data-quantity studies and token-routing case studies largely carry over.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across three seeds for the principal and extended benchmark comparisons. No changed run-count policy, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure is documented; additional rows follow the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: The original GPT-2 CoMiGS scores are retained, but several baseline scores change: Table 1's Multilingual Local perplexity changes from 55.49 (0.64) to 54.38 (0.32). v3 adds numerous comparator and Llama results, including CoMiGS-1G1S perplexities of 18.37 (0.03) on Common Corpus and 16.31 (0.05) on AG News, plus resource-cost results in Table 3. These additions do not establish same-setting CoMiGS performance gains.

M1.justification: The main CoMiGS architecture and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix F.3 introduces an analytical linear-expert variant with auxiliary routing distributions, a KL-penalized relaxation and three alternating minimization blocks (Equation 28). This is a limited methodological extension; the PDFs do not establish its use in the language-model experiments.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around on-device motivation and hierarchical optimization. Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A, user-specific analysis becomes Section 4.4, and terminology, headings and appendix organization change substantially. These revisions exceed the prose needed simply to insert new results.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout, adds a chat illustration, redraws the method diagram and removes v1's data-split bubble figure. Tables gain model/distribution groupings and new entries; plots gain descriptive user labels. Existing learning curves and routing panels are relocated or split between the main text and appendices, alongside the new pFedMoE comparison.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning through on-device LLM literature and optimization foundations, including Stackelberg, Chen et al. (2021), Nesterov, and Jordan and Jacobs. It adds substantive relationships to FDLoRA and FedSA and revises the comparison with pFedMoE. Several earlier MoE references, including Wu et al. and Zadouri et al., are removed.

T1.justification: v1 contains the bilevel objective and load-balancing equations but no convergence theorems. v3 Section 3.4 and Appendix F add fixed-point and contraction assumptions, linear-convergence theorems and proofs, quadratic/local analyses, and a strongly convex relaxed linear-expert construction. The guarantees concern idealized optimization under additional assumptions.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical support by moving beyond a single small backbone and directly comparing closely related personalized methods. Resource accounting and the project-code disclosure also make practical claims easier to assess. The new theory exposes assumptions, although it does not establish convergence of the actual federated training runs. Reporting drawbacks include unexplained pFedMoE SlimPajama values of 25.40 in Table 1 versus 22.91 in Table 5 and removal of the explicit validation-scarcity warning. These weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger empirical coverage and comparative scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoMiGS research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds Llama 3.2 evaluations, additional baseline comparisons and router analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-2 fine-tuning results, routing analyses, ablations and resource-heterogeneity experiments in Section 4 and Appendices C–E.

results.title: On-Device Collaborative Language Modeling via a Mixture of Generalists and Specialists

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion shift from existence and conditional benign/harmful convergence to SNR-based guarantees for joint attention training. v2 adds delayed-generalization/grokking claims and real-data support as contributions. These materially redefine the paper's main results and scope.

C2.justification: v2 explains delayed generalization through slow signal learning and the exponential training-time term, adding a grokking interpretation absent from v1. Remark 4.2 discusses harmful behavior outside the guaranteed SNR regime. Section 5 also adds dataset-specific interpretations, including BreastMNIST's failure to overfit and AG-news results suggesting harmful overfitting.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's synthetic settings, v2 Appendix G.2 documents ViT/BERT configurations, disabled dropout, separate clean-data classifier-head training, subset sizes, image processing, and AdamW with learning-rate scheduling. These substantially expand reproducibility information for the new experiments. Both versions provide the same code-repository link.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic noisy binary classification. v2 retains that coverage and adds MNIST, CIFAR-10, PneumoniaMNIST, BreastMNIST, AG-news, and TREC, extending evaluation to image recognition, medical classification, news topics, and question types. The theoretical multiclass discussion already existed in v1.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically compares the proposed procedure against competing methods. ViT and BERT are backbones for v2's experiments; its new Table 1 compares theoretical literature rather than evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Synthetic experiments change weak-signal strength from 0.2 to 0.1, learning rate from 1e-4 to 5e-3, initialization, and some dimension/signal settings. The loss heatmap changes from 20,000 to 1,000 iterations. New real-data protocols train final attention query-key weights for 2,000 epochs with label-noise rate 0.1 and training subsets ranging from 20 to 1,000 examples.

E4.justification: The empirical checks of v1's trajectory conditions, Equations 9 and 10, are removed with Figures 4 and 6. The dimension/signal sensitivity heatmap is revised, and v2 adds training-size sensitivity across six real datasets to investigate transitions between fitting regimes (Section 5, Table 2).

E5.justification: v1 mentions trials and training runs without explicit run counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 Table 2 newly reports means and standard deviations over three runs. This is a localized addition of uncertainty reporting, not evidence of increased repetitions for the retained synthetic experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds the six-dataset results in Table 2 and revises synthetic trajectories and loss heatmaps. For example, Figure 3's harmful-overfitting test accuracy changes from 0.91 at d=4500 to 0.87 at d=5000, alongside other setting changes, so this is not a same-setting decline. The old trajectory-condition diagnostic results are removed.

M1.justification: v1 optimizes only the token p from zero while fixing an orthogonal query-key matrix W. v2 jointly optimizes W and p from Gaussian initialization (Section 3.4). This substantially changes the training procedure and dynamics, although the attention formula and cross-entropy objective are retained.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related-work emphasis is reordered, data/model subsections exchange positions, and the main-results narrative changes from existence/convergence/difficulties to a theorem followed by key techniques. The appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are redesigned or reorganized, including SNR annotations and changed noisy-sample panels. v2 adds theoretical-comparison, experimental-results, and dataset-detail tables. The old condition-diagnostic heatmaps disappear; the retained loss heatmap is redrawn as Figure 4 rather than constituting an entirely new analysis.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through Table 1 and Appendix A, including comparisons with Jiang et al., Magen et al., and Sheen et al. It distinguishes label noise, token types, optimized parameters, and training horizons, and adds grokking literature. v1's broad first-study positioning is replaced by explicit differentiation from recent and concurrent attention work.

T1.justification: v1's existence construction and trajectory-conditional convergence results are replaced by finite-time, SNR-based benign and not-overfitting results. v2 introduces attention-gap definitions and staged inductive proofs in Appendices D–E, with substantially revised parameter and data assumptions, including isotropic noise, single relevant/confusing tokens, and constant-order sequence length. The multiclass appendix is adapted; the earlier fixed-head ETF lemma and formal harmful-overfitting proof are removed.

improvement.justification: Under revised assumptions, v2 addresses v1's central reliance on assumed attention trajectories with explicit SNR-based finite-time analysis and detailed staged proofs (Section 4, Appendices D–E). Real-data experiments, uncertainty reporting, and implementation details substantially strengthen empirical grounding. The narrower token/noise assumptions and loss of the formal harmful-overfitting branch limit the extension, but the more explicit convergence conditions and training-time analysis provide a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' study of benign overfitting in attention token selection. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive scientific revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic experiments and experiments on six real datasets, including training losses and test accuracies in Table 2 and supplementary material in Appendix G.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments on attention dynamics, training/test losses, and theorem-condition diagnostics in Section 5 and Appendix I.

results.title: Benign Overfitting in Token Selection of Attention Mechanism

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution paragraphs and conclusion retain the central claims: SNR-dependent benign overfitting can arise solely through token selection, and generalization can follow fitting after a substantial delay. The added analyses support and qualify these existing claims.

C2.justification: Appendix E.2 newly discusses why training the head on the same samples invalidates an independence argument and how separate data changes that situation. Appendix F interprets encoder behavior through capacity, learnable token scores and distributed noise memorization, and explicitly discusses real-data attention patterns and architectural differences outside the analytical setting.

D1.justification: The added experiments document the encoder's single-head attention, nonlinear feedforward layers, normalization and skip connections, and specify the CLS-attention readout and noise-sweep setup. Existing pretrained-model dimensions, optimizer settings, separate head-pretraining data and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic classification distribution and MNIST, CIFAR-10, PneumoniaMNIST, BreastMNIST, AG-news and TREC. The additions vary model configuration and training-label corruption within this retained dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix F.1 adds a one-layer transformer encoder as an architectural comparator, explicitly comparing its attention trajectories and loss heatmaps with the analyzed model. The additional Magen et al. row in Table 1 is a literature comparison, not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The original experimental settings remain. New protocols include joint optimization of the encoder, real-data controls at label-noise levels 0 and 0.2, a noise sweep with training size 200, and tracking maximum CLS-token attention. These supplement the existing experiments rather than replace Table 2's protocol.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained synthetic attention trajectories and SNR heatmap, v3 tests architectural sensitivity through the encoder experiments, sensitivity to label-noise severity through Table 6 and Figure 8, and attention concentration on real datasets through Figure 9. These substantially broaden the diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: Table 2 reports means and standard deviations over three runs in both versions. New Table 6 follows the same practice; no changed run counts, seed-reporting practice, confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: Table 2, Figure 3 and the original synthetic heatmap remain unchanged. New Table 6 reports, for example, AG-news accuracy at n=1000 of 85.5±0.3 with no label noise and 69.6±1.1 with noise 0.2. Figures 6–9 add encoder, noise-sensitivity and attention findings. These are results under added conditions, not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The analyzed model remains single-layer attention with a fixed classifier head and gradient descent on W and p using binary cross-entropy. The added encoder experiments and head-gradient proposition extend evaluation and theoretical justification without changing this procedure.

P1.justification: v3 substantially expands the explanatory narrative around the fixed head and proof techniques, adds an appendix contents list and proof roadmap, and extensively edits proof prose. It also consolidates high-probability events into the preliminaries and groups the multiclass extension with further discussion.

P2.justification: The main text and references adopt a two-column conference layout with running headers. Figure 1 gains explicit SNR annotations; v3 adds the proof illustration in Figure 4, experimental Figures 6–9 and two-panel Table 6. Original Figures 2–3 and the heatmap, renumbered from Figure 4 to Figure 5, are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds Papyan et al. (2020), removes Yun et al. (2020), and includes already-cited Magen et al. (2024) in Table 1. Appendix A revises the Magen comparison, removing the two-token characterization and adding discussion of experimental validation, while retaining the broader research positioning.

T1.justification: Section 3.5 revises assumptions A1–A4 and A8, including changing A1's signal-norm exponent from 3/2 to 4/3. The signed head condition becomes k cos(theta_k)>Theta(1), and Theorem 4.1's non-overfitting time gains a denominator factor d, with corresponding proof revisions. Remark 4.8 adds a rho-dependent timescale qualification, and Appendix E.2 adds Proposition E.1 and its head-gradient geometry proof.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the justification and assessability of the central analysis through the corrected head-alignment condition, revised mathematical bounds, an idealized head-alignment derivation with explicit limitations, and a proof roadmap. Added noise controls, encoder comparisons and real-attention diagnostics address gaps in v2's connection between theory and practical behavior. The gains concern better-supported and more clearly bounded conclusions; the original benchmark scores remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Benign Overfitting in Token Selection of Attention Mechanism. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: The original empirical results remain, and Appendix F adds transformer-encoder experiments, label-noise sensitivity results and measurements of attention dynamics on real datasets.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original synthetic experiments and classification experiments using ViT and BERT on six datasets. Appendix G includes an additional synthetic loss heatmap.

results.title: Benign Overfitting in Token Selection of Attention Mechanism

C1.justification: The central claims remain learning from task-agnostic sub-optimal data, efficient reward-guided adaptation, and superior downstream manipulation performance. The added experiments support these existing claims. Adroit remains in the abstract and evaluation despite being omitted from the introduction's contribution summary.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation beyond the original regularization and pre-training discussion. It attributes offline-online baseline failures to biased value learning and inadequate multimodal priors, explains differing responses to augmented data, and interprets offline fine-tuning and transfer results. Appendix C.4 also adds the qualification that Adroit hammer may require stronger pre-training priors.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly specifies the BC weight as lambda = 1.0. Appendices C.4 and D add visual Meta-World data-collection instructions and implementation sources and architecture details for new baselines. Core SODP implementation details remain, although v1's explicit disclosure that Adroit baselines use expert demonstrations is omitted.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates state-based Meta-World and visual Adroit. v2 additionally evaluates image/point-cloud Meta-World MT-10, extending visual manipulation coverage to ten Sawyer tasks using collected visual data (Appendix C.4, Table 8). Both original evaluation settings remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated RLPD, IBRL, Cal-QL, MTSAC, and MTDQL comparisons while retaining the earlier comparator rows. In particular, the first three substantially broaden comparison to methods combining offline pre-training with online fine-tuning.

E3.justification: The original main training budgets remain, but v2 introduces substantial new protocols: 100k-step online fine-tuning with augmented-data controls for offline baselines (Section 5.3), MT-10 versus basketball pre-training for held-out tasks (Section 5.5), offline fine-tuning using 200 successful episodes per task, and equal-size comparisons of pre-training data quality (Appendices C.1 and C.3).

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of online versus offline fine-tuning and training from scratch on high-quality data (Table 4), BC-only fine-tuning (Table 5), pre-training data quality (Table 6), and multi-task versus single-task pre-training for transfer (Table 3). The original scratch and BC/KL/PL regularization ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three-seed mean/standard-deviation reporting, five-seed comparative learning curves, and per-task return statistics over 50 episodes. Additional result tables use the existing uncertainty-reporting approach; no new statistical testing or revised repeated-run practice is documented.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 scores, Adroit results, and appendix per-task returns are unchanged. v2 adds substantial results, including SODP's 59.26% success under the 100k-step protocol (Table 2), 80.93% after near-optimal versus 65.27% after sub-optimal pre-training (Table 6), and 47.5% on visual MT-10 (Table 8). These are newly reported settings, not improvements over v1 under identical conditions.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same diffusion pre-training, policy-gradient fine-tuning, and proficient-trajectory BC regularization procedure. Visual Meta-World uses the encoder approach already employed for Adroit; the newly disclosed regularization weight does not establish a method change.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized around offline-online comparisons, limited-sample efficiency, and transfer. Existing Adroit results, pre-training ablations, multi-task learning curves, and longer regularization explanations move into organized appendix sections. The introduction receives localized edits, while the method and conclusion remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: The main text changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout. v2 expands Table 1, adds six result tables and a new learning-curve figure, and relocates several existing displays. All original figures remain, including v1 Figure 4 as v2 Figure 8. Algorithm 1 is compressed into fewer, less clearly separated lines.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations and positioning for RLPD, IBRL, and Cal-QL, connecting SODP more directly to offline-online RL. The broader diffusion literature discussion and comparison with DPPO remain substantially unchanged. Updated bibliographic entries for existing works do not represent additional research coverage.

T1.justification: The MDP formulation, policy-gradient and importance-sampling derivations, NLL surrogate derivation in Appendix A, and regularization formulas remain mathematically unchanged. Shortened sampling notation and omission of the explicit noise-reconstruction expression do not alter the retained definitions or reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support beyond v1's primarily offline comparisons. Offline-online baselines and the augmented-data control in Section 5.3 address whether SODP's advantage merely reflects additional online experience. Transfer experiments and targeted appendix ablations better test generalizability and the fine-tuning mechanism. These gains outweigh limited reporting regressions, including the now-inaccurate statement that MTBC performs worst in Table 1 and less explicit Adroit baseline training-data disclosure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SODP research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline evaluations, limited-data experiments, transfer experiments, visual Meta-World results, and further ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original SODP results on Meta-World and Adroit, learning curves, regularization and pre-training ablations, and per-task returns in Appendix F.

results.title: Task-Agnostic Pre-training and Task-Guided Fine-tuning for Versatile Diffusion Planner

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds an average 1000-fold OOD improvement and PCOC expressivity. v2 redefines the contributions around MPC expressivity, in-distribution learnability, and task-dependent OOD performance. Its abstract and introduction explicitly acknowledge learning tradeoffs and poor induction-head generalization, narrowing the practical superiority claim.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a depth-versus-parameter-norm tradeoff in sample complexity and hypothesizes that dynamic communication makes induction-head optimization difficult. New ablations support interpretations about positional-encoding placement. Section 7.3 also explicitly cautions that mixed-input results do not establish superiority on general-purpose textual reasoning.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds substantial reproduction information, including token/numeric encoding instructions, mixed-task batch size 1024, and GPT2 digit formatting, BPE tokenization, and fine-tuning on 50,000 samples for three epochs. However, v1's explicit experiment-code link is absent from v2; this establishes removed access information, not repository unavailability.

E1.justification: The five numeric tasks and fixed/variable-length coverage are retained. v2 adds k-hop induction heads with unseen-symbol testing and mixed textual/numeric conditional aggregation with unseen categories and changed distractor patterns. Appendix D.1.9 also evaluates integer inputs for rounding-based accuracy.

E2.justification: v2 retains standard Transformer, compact-model, and RoPE comparisons while adding GCN and GAT on cumulative sum and sorting using complete/star graphs (Table 1). It also adds fine-tuned GPT2-large comparisons on mixed-input tasks (Figure 34), substantially expanding the comparator families.

E3.justification: The reported numeric-task learning rate changes from 1e-4 to 5e-4; the PDFs do not establish reruns. New protocols include length-30 induction heads with at most three hops and cross-entropy evaluation, rounding/tolerance-based whole-list accuracy, and GPT2 MSE/MAPE scoring that excludes unparseable outputs (Appendix D).

E4.justification: Beyond retained compact-model, RoPE, and attention-map analyses, v2 adds binary/sinusoidal encoding tests and seven architectural configurations examining input representation and positional-encoding placement (D.1.6–D.1.7). New depth and sample-size analyses investigate induction-head failures and mixed-input generalization (D.2–D.3).

E5.justification: Both versions report medians over ten runs with 10th–90th percentile bands. v2 extends this practice to additional plots, including Figure 34, without reporting a changed run count, seed policy, or uncertainty-estimation method.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial findings: standard Transformers achieve near-zero induction-head in-distribution loss with three layers, while positional Transformers perform worse and both generalize poorly to unseen symbols (Figures 3 and 5). Mixed-input, GNN, encoding, ablation, accuracy, and GPT2 results are also newly reported. These additions are distinct from retained numeric curves.

M1.justification: The core layer and positional-only attention equations remain unchanged. Appendices D.2–D.3 introduce limited task-specific adaptations: causal masking and token-output logits for induction heads, and separate token embeddings and numeric projections for mixed inputs.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. PCOC definitions move into Appendix A, learnability becomes a main section, and experiments are reorganized from fixed/variable-length regimes into in-distribution, OOD, and mixed-input sections. The appendix structure is substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adds a Beneš-network diagram, the GNN results table, and numerous induction-head, mixed-input, ablation, and accuracy plots. Existing figures are redistributed or reformatted: v1 Figure 2 becomes v2 Figure 19, existing in-distribution panels receive main-text prominence, and appendix charts adopt shared legends and explicit in-distribution/OOD labels.

R1.justification: v1 motivates PCOC partly through its differences from Sanford et al.'s MPC approach. v2 positions PCOC as a bridge to MPC and standard Transformers, and adds substantive engagement with norm-based learning theory through Edelman et al. and Bartlett–Mendelson. Beneš networks, induction-head work, GPT2, and newer algorithmic-reasoning studies add further research connections.

T1.justification: v1's PCOC simulation theorem is retained as Lemma B.2. v2 adds MPC simulation with logarithmic depth overhead, simulation of standard Transformers, and accompanying routing constructions and proofs (Theorem 5.1, Remark 5.1, Appendix B). Theorem 6.1 and Appendix C introduce a norm-based generalization bound with covering-number and Rademacher-complexity analysis.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper through the MPC connection and explicit learnability analysis, while new ablations and negative induction-head results better establish the mechanism's applicability boundaries than v1's broad advantage claim. These gains outweigh reporting drawbacks: the explicit code link disappears, and Appendix D.3 inconsistently names a mixed-input variant as max while Figures 6, 32, and 34 label it sum. Those issues limit reproducibility but do not erase the substantial theoretical and evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same positional-attention architecture and retain matching numeric experiments. Their main texts, equations, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial expansion.

after.justification: Section 7 and Appendix D retain numeric experiments and report additional original results on induction heads, mixed textual/numeric inputs, architectural ablations, and additional baselines.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix C report original training and generalization experiments on five numeric algorithmic tasks, including sample-size, input-length, and architecture comparisons.

results.title: Positional Attention: Expressivity and Learnability of Algorithmic Computation

C1.justification: v1's abstract advertises a theory bounding example-forgetting time for any training run with known AdamW hyperparameters. v3 replaces that advertised guarantee with an empirical relationship between forgetting and cumulative weight decay. This substantially narrows a central theoretical contribution while retaining the main conclusion that contamination can be forgotten.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly recognizes influence through subsequent gradient trajectories and makes large-model forgetting estimates conditional on an empirical hypothesis. It adds that weight decay is unnecessary for forgetting and interprets OLMo-7B forgetting as slower than OLMo-1B. It also removes v1's learning-rate tuning recommendation and categorical dismissal of individual-data attribution in the forgetting regime.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.4 provides a paper-specific code link, explicit codebase and dataset access links, and a reproducibility statement covering contamination positions. It discloses 8×A100 training hardware and three weeks on an 8×H100 node for OLMo-7B. v1 names underlying tools and data but lacks this project-code access and computational-resource documentation.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same pretraining data sources, seven-benchmark mixture in Section 3.2 and Table 2, and four OLMo benchmarks: HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, and PiQA. Additional model sizes and optimizer configurations retain the represented data and tasks.

E2.justification: Both versions measure contamination against holdout questions or uncontaminated model controls. No competing comparison algorithm is introduced or removed; the new weight-decay configurations are experimental ablations.

E3.justification: v3 adds a 1.6B Chinchilla-scaled condition and OLMo-7B continual pretraining from step 300,000. OLMo-1B follow-up is extended from a reported 0.5% to 1% of remaining training. Section 5.2 replaces the 0.01/0.1/1 weight-decay sweep with interventions at a common contaminated checkpoint using 0.1/1/5/50; Appendix Figure 8 additionally tests zero weight decay.

E4.justification: The weight-decay analysis is redesigned to isolate its causal effect by continuing from the same contaminated checkpoint. New Figure 8 tests whether weight decay is necessary and shows substantial forgetting without it. The novel-data, repeated-data, contamination-position, and duplicate-filtering analyses are retained; the earlier OLMo-1B empirical-versus-decay overlay is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report bootstrapped 90% confidence intervals for the principal contamination plots and 95% intervals for duplicate-filtering validation. No new repeated-run counts, seeds, or statistical estimation procedures are documented. Additional significance statements concern new outcomes.

E6.justification: The retained 1.6B/7B-token plot changes: its four-repetition accuracy gap rises from roughly 19 to 29 points, although v3 Section 4.1 still says 20. Table 1 adds a 1.6B row, including 52.06% holdout and 67.61% four-repetition accuracy. New OLMo-7B results report a 17-point contamination increase and 87% reduction after 13% of remaining training. Extended OLMo-1B results report 96% reduction after 1%, versus 84% after 0.5% in v1. Weight-decay result curves also change.

M1.justification: The exact-contamination and duplicate-filtering framework, standard language-model training, and likelihood-based evaluation are retained. Larger model configurations and weight-decay interventions change the experiments, without introducing a proposed algorithm, architecture component, loss, or inference procedure.

P1.justification: Section 5 is extensively rewritten and reorganized into cumulative decay, controlled empirical evaluation, and conditional large-scale extrapolation. The abstract, introductory contribution discussion, Section 4.3, and discussion are revised accordingly. The appendix structure changes through replacement of the extended theoretical analysis with reproducibility information and supplementary experiments.

P2.justification: The duplicate-question illustration and OLMo-1B plots move to the appendix, while the scaling figure moves earlier. v3 adds OLMo-7B and zero-weight-decay figures, redesigns the weight-decay panels and axes, and extends the Chinchilla plot. Table 1 is expanded and reformatted, and Table 2 receives rotated column headings despite retaining its data.

R1.justification: The same 74 references and substantive related-work discussion are retained. The relationships to contamination detection, natural forgetting, and data attribution research remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 removes v1 Appendix A.5's projection-based forgetting definition, two orthogonality assumptions, and Proposition 3 with its proof. It corrects the gradient-expansion sign and cumulative-product indexing. The retained decay proposition becomes an explicit sufficient bound, proved using log(1−x) ≤ −x instead of the earlier small-x approximation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central weight-decay argument through controlled interventions, a zero-decay ablation, corrected mathematics, and explicit acknowledgment that gradient decay does not itself guarantee example forgetting. OLMo-7B evidence and new reproducibility information further strengthen the paper. The formal scope is narrower and large-scale extrapolation remains hypothetical; the revised scaling plot also conflicts with unchanged prose. These reporting limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and qualification of the conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same contamination-and-forgetting study. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable, allowing relocated content and substantive revisions to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and reports additional OLMo-7B experiments, extended OLMo-1B results, and revised weight-decay experiments, including an appendix ablation without weight decay.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training, contamination, forgetting, and weight-decay experiments in Sections 4–5, plus duplicate-filtering validation in Appendix A.3.

results.title: How Much Can We Forget about Data Contamination?

C1.justification: V1 broadly presents symbolic forward chaining and the computation graph as GPU-vectorized. V2's abstract and introduction explicitly place symbolic manipulation on CPU and neural/probabilistic computation on GPU, materially narrowing the acceleration claim. The headline efficiency claim changes from 0.33%–37.17% of baseline training time to 1.71x–62x faster convergence on simpler benchmarks, while retaining the claim of scalability on harder cases.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive discussion of overlapping-proof double counting, preserved top-k semantics, remaining combinatorial growth, and unsupported nondeterministic symbolic programs. Appendix D.7 newly hypothesizes that backend autodifferentiation differences explain Mugen convergence, explicitly marking this explanation as unconfirmed. These extend v1's limitations concerning batched programming and unexplored generative-model support.

D1.justification: V2 adds detailed HWF neural/symbolic code, recursion examples, tensor-storage and execution details, and richer PathFinder, CLUTRR, and Mugen implementation descriptions beyond v1's existing hyperparameter appendix. Its main hardware description now agrees with v1's RTX 2080 Ti appendix disclosure. Conversely, v1's statement that framework and benchmark code are supplied in supplementary material disappears without replacement access instructions.

E1.justification: The original five task families and their benchmark variants remain, with Small/Medium/Large renamed using explicit sizes. V2 Appendix G adds MNIST ProductN for N = 4, 8, 16, and 20, introducing multiplication requirements beyond the existing digit-summation task.

E2.justification: V2 adds Logic Tensor Networks as an evaluated comparator on SumN: Table 3 reports 92.54 seconds for SumN-5 and out-of-memory outcomes for SumN-10/15. Scallop, ISED, and IndeCateR+ retain their previous comparison coverage. Discussion of other frameworks does not establish additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V2 makes total-time speedup the main comparison, replacing v1's per-epoch ratio while retaining per-epoch comparisons in Appendix D. PathFinder's stated top-k changes from 3 to 1. New protocols compare sequential CPU execution with GPU tag computation for HWF and batch sizes 64 versus 256 for ProductN. The main data splits and ten-hour timeout remain.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained provenance ablation and Mugen convergence analysis, v2 Appendix B isolates HWF's CPU user-function and tag-computation costs, comparing sequential and parallelized execution. Appendix G tests combinatorial scaling and batch-size sensitivity using ProductN. These directly investigate the mechanisms and limits underlying scalability.

E5.justification: Both versions report three trials and average best accuracy and training time. Error bars already appear in v1's accuracy and provenance figures and remain in v2. No new seed policy, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Many reported results change. DOLPHIN's SumN-5 total time changes from 78.33 to 53.86 seconds; IndeCateR+ on SumN-15 changes from a timeout in v1 Table 2 to 548.28 seconds in v2 Table 3. IndeCateR+ accuracy bars also change substantially in Figure 5. V2 adds LTN, HWF timing-breakdown, and ProductN outcomes. PathFinder's revised results accompany its changed top-k setting.

M1.justification: Table 1 revises the reported DTKP-AM zero/unit tag initialization. V1 gives zero a positive-infinity first row and makes the unit entirely positive infinity; v2 makes zero entirely negative infinity and represents the unit with one empty proof. This is a limited provenance-component correction. The five primitives, training objective, and overall framework remain; expanded execution and recursion explanations do not establish a redesign.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around CLUTRR and the CPU/GPU division. The overview and framework exposition are condensed and reorganized, benchmark names become explicit sizes, and existing experimental details and convergence discussion are integrated into a substantially reorganized appendix structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is replaced by a CLUTRR illustration; the original SumN component diagram moves to Appendix D. V1 Table 2 is reorganized into v2 Tables 2, 3, and 5. The provenance plots move to Figure 10 with a logarithmic timing axis, and new timing-breakdown and ProductN tables are added.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against GPU tensor-based frameworks, including LYRICS, LTN, and TensorLog, discussing their grounding requirements and expressivity in the introduction, Section 5, and Appendices F/H. It also adds discussion of probabilistic-circuit and variable-elimination work and specialized recurrent models. This broadens v1's emphasis on CPU-based frameworks and proof-search optimizations.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix A adds an upper-bound argument for the add-mult WMC approximation and a dependent-input equality counterexample: DAMP yields a sum of squared probabilities, whereas DTKP-AM yields probability one when the distribution has at most k symbols. It also explains absent-symbol/proof representations. Table 1 revises zero/unit definitions, and the DAMP prose corrects the previously reversed conjunction/disjunction operations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the scalability argument by clarifying CPU/GPU responsibilities, adding an evaluated GPU-based comparator, and directly measuring execution costs and combinatorial scaling. The approximation analysis and implementation details also make the contribution more assessable. These gains outweigh localized new defects: Table 5's SumN-5 Scallop ratio is 3.43 although 184.76/10.77 is approximately 17.15, and the HWF listing contains incomplete conditions. Those errors still limit numerical reliability and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DOLPHIN and retain matching methods and experiments. All pages, including v1's appendices A–B and v2's appendices A–H, are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports the retained benchmark experiments plus original LTN comparisons, HWF execution-time measurements, and MNIST ProductN experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original training times, benchmark accuracies, provenance ablations, and Mugen convergence curves in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: Dolphin: A Programmable Framework for Scalable Neurosymbolic Learning

C1.justification: The abstract’s methodological contribution changes from pretrained graph featurization followed by supervised classification to jointly trained graph and target prediction with statistical features. The introduction strengthens unseen-cell-line generalization from maintaining decent performance to minimal performance drop. V1’s separately claimed contribution of preparing seven benchmark datasets is omitted.

C2.justification: V1 briefly flags poor doxorubicin performance. V2 explains the mismatch between drug effects on proteins and measured mRNA, discusses undetected off-target effects, and explicitly frames chemical evaluation as a proof of concept. It also introduces interpretations of transferable perturbation characteristics, node-statistics failures on drugs, and potential overfitting to familiar intervention types.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands architecture and training documentation, including edge embeddings, sparse/dense attention, validation selection, stopping criteria, hidden dimension, weight decay, CPU workers and training times. It also specifies a UT-IGSP commit and additional simulation details. Raw-data accession codes remain, but v1’s explicit source-code release promise is omitted.

E1.justification: The seven biological datasets, six drug cases, and seen/unseen cell-line settings are retained; trivial perturbations remain evaluated in the appendix. Synthetic coverage expands through sigmoid test mechanisms and soft-shift training interventions, alongside the existing linear/polynomial and hard/scale-intervention settings.

E2.justification: V2 adds DGE to the genetic and chemical comparisons and MB+CI to the synthetic comparisons. These introduce substantial statistical competitors missing from v1. Existing learned baselines remain, while the explicit RANDOM rows in v1 Table 2 disappear.

E3.justification: Candidate padding changes from random genes to genes with greatest log-fold change. V2 adds Spearman correlation, removes tabular R20, and replaces absolute-k recall with fraction-based recall. Synthetic training expands from approximately 4,000 hard-only datasets to 8,640 including soft interventions and switches to correlation features. Real finetuning changes batch size, learning rate and precision.

E4.justification: V2 adds synthetic-only versus finetuned comparisons, a node-statistics ablation, combined removal of pretraining and graph supervision, learning curves, and comparisons of training with versus without scale interventions. New correlation-difference case studies appear in Figures 6–7. V1’s CDN-MLP accuracy comparisons and marginal/global-feature ablation tables are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard deviations over five synthetic datasets and five rounds of cell subsampling using the same 80%-with-minimum-50 rule. V2’s reference to five seeds describes the retained subsampling procedure; it does not establish additional training runs or a new uncertainty estimator.

E6.justification: Reported nontrivial, seen-cell-line CDN ranks span 0.55–0.72 in v1 Table 2 and 0.92–0.98 in v2 Table 1, under revised models and settings rather than an isolated same-setting comparison. Numerous baseline, sigmoid and ablation results are added. V1’s six drug scores survive, rounded, as v2’s CDN (no μ) row; the new full-model drug results are mixed.

M1.justification: V1 freezes the causal featurizer and trains a single-layer differential network. V2 jointly trains both modules, introduces graph supervision alongside target prediction, adds node-level mean and variance features, and supports concatenation or subtraction of graph representations. Its differential networks use three or two layers, respectively.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. The problem statement becomes a dedicated subsection, methods are reorganized, and appendices gain separate architecture and training sections. The standalone conclusion and reproducibility statement disappear, while an impact statement replaces the ethics statement.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns. Figure 2 is substantially redrawn; recall plots expand from two K562 panels to five datasets with normalized axes. Tables are restructured, trivial results move to the appendix, and new heatmaps and training curves appear. Existing dataset-statistics plots are merged and relocated.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens the perturbation-modeling and causal-discovery discussion, adding works such as CellOT, AttentionPert, GIM, Petersen et al. and Montagna et al. It explicitly positions CDN as a supervised counterpart to DCI’s difference-based reasoning and adds drug-target literature. Several earlier citations, including Chevalley et al. and Reisach et al., disappear.

T1.justification: The intervention-capacity constructions and assumptions move from v1 Appendix A to v2 Appendix C with essentially unchanged mathematics. V2 Section 3.1 adds a limited computational-cost derivation: ordinary attention over graph edges costs O(N^4), whereas axial attention costs O(N^3).

improvement.justification: Adding DGE resolves an important benchmarking weakness: it surpasses v1’s learned comparators, while v2’s revised CDN still exceeds it on genetic data. Intervention-type controls, fuller implementation details and explicit chemical limitations substantially strengthen evaluation and interpretability. These gains outweigh the removal of some earlier ablations, although the abstract’s seven-dataset superiority claim remains broader than the mixed chemical results support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe causal differential networks for perturbation-target prediction. All 22 pages of each version, including appendix text, equations, tables and figures, support comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendix E report original biological and synthetic results, including revised model evaluations, additional baselines and new ablations.

before.justification: V1 Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendix D report original biological and synthetic experiments, including target-prediction results, ablations, runtimes and uncertainty estimates.

results.title: Identifying biological perturbation targets through causal differential networks

C1.justification: v2 reframes novelty around a practical diffusion autoencoder and makes computational efficiency a central contribution. Its abstract and introduction add explicit claims of 22% better generation quality and 2.3× inference throughput, alongside stronger positioning against existing autoencoders. The throughput claim depends on increased compression; the basic denoising-as-decoding claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 explains how shorter latent sequences accelerate generation, interprets the added ADM comparison through conditional posterior approximation, and notes a quality cost from omitting the downstream variational-bound loss. The original discussion of stochasticity, perceptual fidelity, resolution generalization, and memory limitations is retained in Appendix A.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies encoder parameter counts, omission of the downstream DiT variational-bound loss, and H100 timing hardware. Existing optimizer, loss-weight, augmentation, and JAX/TPU details are largely relocated. v1's 10,000-image evaluation disclosure and V100 timing details disappear. The loss disclosure alone does not establish a change to the retained experiments.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ImageNet reconstruction and unconditional generation. v2 adds COCO-2017 reconstruction and class-conditional ImageNet generation (Tables 2–3). The original unconditional tasks remain in Appendix D; higher-resolution reconstruction was already covered in v1.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained controlled VAE comparisons, v2 evaluates VQGAN, LlamaGen, SD-VAE, SDXL-VAE, and LiteVAE in reconstruction comparisons, and Asym-VAE and Omni-VAE in generation comparisons. Appendix D also adds a plain diffusion ADM comparator. Newly discussed diffusion autoencoders are not automatically counted as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce the 34M-parameter SD encoder configuration, target-resolution fine-tuning, PSNR/SSIM, full ImageNet 50K and COCO 5K reconstruction evaluation, and H100 generation-throughput measurements. These extend the protocol substantially. The PDFs do not establish that v1's retained 10K-image evaluations were rerun using the new sample counts.

E4.justification: v2 adds a plain ADM control, examines the benefit of higher-resolution fine-tuning, and supplies SD-VAE case studies emphasizing faces and text. v1's extended decoder-scale, compression, and seed galleries are removed, but the original quantitative ablations and main compression/seed examples remain. These are focused changes to an otherwise retained analysis suite.

E5.justification: Both versions show qualitative variation across reconstruction seeds, without quantitative repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Removing additional example images does not change the statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: Substantial new results appear in v2 Tables 1–3. At 8× downsampling, Table 2 reports ImageNet rFID 0.47 for ε-VAE-SD(M) versus 0.74 for SD-VAE; Table 3 reports class-conditional FID 9.39 versus 11.63. These are added comparisons under new configurations. v1 Tables 1–3 and 5 retain their numerical results as v2 Tables 7, 8, 4, and 6. The original V100 decoder timings are removed.

M1.justification: The conditional diffusion decoder, latent concatenation, velocity prediction, perceptual and trajectory-matching losses, and noise/time schedules remain unchanged. ε-VAE-SD introduces an experimental encoder configuration, without establishing a new proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: discussion moves to Appendix A, original scaling and unconditional-generation evaluations move to Appendix D, and standard-configuration comparisons become central. The introduction and generation section are rewritten, ε-VAE-lite/SD terminology is introduced, and visualization and impact-statement sections are added.

P2.justification: The document switches from single-column to double-column layout, adds three benchmark tables and two SD-VAE comparison figures, and relocates and reformats retained displays. v1 Figures 4–5 become v2 Figures 5–6, while v1's three extended appendix galleries are removed. Table highlighting, captions, sizing, and placement change substantially.

R1.justification: A substantial new diffusion-decoder discussion covers DiffusionAE, DiVAE, Würstchen, distillation/consistency approaches, and DiTo, with explicit distinctions concerning objectives, sampling efficiency, and resolution generalization. The introduction now acknowledges prior diffusion autoencoding and repositions the contribution around practical joint design. Several generic language-model and tokenization references are removed.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–13 are substantively retained. Notation corrections and the new verbal interpretation of conditional posterior approximation do not introduce a theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on a lightweight encoder configuration and controlled generic-VAE comparisons. Standard SD configurations, modern baselines, COCO evaluation, distortion metrics, and class-conditional quality/throughput comparisons strengthen practical validation (Tables 1–3), while original controlled results remain available. Expanded related work also clarifies the contribution. Removed decoder-only timings and incomplete fine-tuning details limit transparency, but the broader, more relevant evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ε-VAE research, with matching methods and identifiable retained experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original ImageNet and COCO reconstruction, class-conditional generation, and supplementary experiments, while retaining the earlier empirical results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet reconstruction, unconditional generation, and ablation results in Tables 1–3 and Appendix C.

results.title: Epsilon-VAE: Denoising as Visual Decoding

C1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden TimeDART from a forecasting-focused method to a representation-learning framework claiming effectiveness across forecasting and classification. The central contribution of combining global autoregressive modeling with local diffusion modeling remains.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the mechanism argument around diffusion counteracting autoregressive overfitting to noise and anomalies. It adds interpretations of shared embeddings, redundant decoder context and TCN behavior, and attributes weaker Weather transfer to shared hyperparameters. v2's discussion of Exchange distribution mismatch and overfitting is removed.

D1.justification: v3 adds dataset split and input-size details for the new tasks, baseline repository links, and specifies that decoder parameters match the encoder except for depth. Reported RTX 4090 memory changes from 16 GB to 24 GB. Most original optimizer and hyperparameter information, and TimeDART's code-access information, are retained.

E1.justification: v3 retains the eight original forecasting datasets and adds four PEMS subsets containing five-minute traffic measurements, plus HAR, Epilepsy and EEG/Sleep-EDF classification tasks. Its pooled pre-training evaluation also expands from energy datasets to targets spanning energy, weather, finance and transportation.

E2.justification: The original forecasting comparator set is retained. v3 newly evaluates FormerTime for classification and adds SimMTM, self-supervised PatchTST, TimeMAE and CoST to the pooled pre-training comparison. That comparison previously contained only TimeDART and random-initialization variants, making the expanded comparison substantively stronger.

E3.justification: Pooled pre-training changes from five energy datasets to all forecasting datasets. New PEMS experiments use a 96-step input and 12–48-step horizons, with selected normalization omissions; classification introduces accuracy and F1 evaluation. v3 also reports native supervised baseline architectures instead of unified encoders and changes Traffic pre-training from 30 to 50 epochs. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds backbone substitution, decoder masking-ratio tests, independent versus common noise-step tests, and shared versus separate embedding comparisons (Tables 5, 14 and 17). Existing module ablations and sensitivity analyses are extended to PEMS and classification. ETTh2 is removed from the reported noise-step/scheduler sweep.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. Forecasting averages across prediction horizons remain aggregation across settings, rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive classification, PEMS, backbone and component results; HAR accuracy is reported as 0.9247 in Table 4. Some retained baseline scores change: CoST's Weather 96-step MSE changes from 0.216 in v2 Table 2 to 0.162 in v3 Table 9. Pooled pre-training results use changed conditions. Some averages change inconsistently: v3 Table 13 reports ETTm2 w/o AR MSE as 0.271 instead of v2's 0.281 despite unchanged constituent values.

M1.justification: The core autoregressive patch/diffusion pre-training procedure is retained. v3 adds a max-pooling classification head optimized with cross-entropy in Section 3.3 and evaluates a causal TCN encoder variant in Section 4.2. These are limited adaptations of the existing framework.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around representation learning, related work is reorganized, and the methodology is condensed and restructured. Task definitions move to the appendix, while implementation details and full results receive a substantially reorganized appendix structure.

P2.justification: The main text switches to two columns and adds a training overview, task-comparison scatterplot, masking diagram and classification/backbone tables. Architecture and sensitivity figures are revised. Detailed forecasting results move to Appendix H, with averages displayed in the main text; the existing forecasting showcases are retained.

R1.justification: The broad forecasting survey is replaced by dedicated autoregressive representation-learning and time-series diffusion discussions. Newly cited works include CSDI, TimeDiff, AutoTimes and denoising autoregressive representation learning. This substantially changes the explanation of TimeDART's relationship to prior research.

T1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds a mean/variance derivation for same-step Gaussian corruption after instance normalization, motivating independent noise steps. Appendix C.1 adds representation-learning and classification task definitions. The original forecasting definition and diffusion/ELBO derivation are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for transferable representations and previously asserted design choices through classification, backbone substitution, and direct masking/noise/embedding controls. Adding competing self-supervised methods to pooled pre-training also improves validation. Reporting errors temper this gain: Table 13 introduces an incorrect ETTm2 ablation average of 0.271 where the listed values and v2 give 0.281. These errors reduce numerical reliability, but the broader validation and targeted component evidence provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TimeDART and retain matching core architecture and optimization objectives. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original forecasting and classification results, backbone comparisons and component analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original forecasting experiments, pooled pre-training comparisons, ablations and hyperparameter analyses in Section 4 and Appendices C–F.

results.title: TimeDART: A Diffusion Autoregressive Transformer for Self-Supervised Time Series Representation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims: additive-energy CRM enables discriminative compositional generalization within discrete affine hulls and improves robustness. The new theory and experiments strengthen support without redefining these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the additions as showing larger advantages with multiple spurious attributes and good synthetic generalization at 20% or 10% group retention. Existing bias/prior interpretations and affine-hull restrictions remain. G.3's added balanced-accuracy superiority claim conflicts with Table 12: CRM scores 90.1 versus 91.7 for LC and sLA.

D1.justification: v2 adds a PyTorch-style implementation covering priors, logits, bias extrapolation, and training/testing (C.2), plus attribute-coding and Gaussian-generation details (G.3 and G.6). These substantially expand documentation beyond v1's pseudocode and training settings. The listing contains discrepancies with the equations, including summing logits rather than probabilities during inference.

E1.justification: The six original benchmarks remain. v2 adds five-attribute CelebA coverage using eyeglasses, hats, and earrings alongside hair color and gender, producing 32 groups (G.3). It also adds Gaussian classification scenarios, including settings with seven to nine attributes (Appendices E and G.6).

E2.justification: v1 evaluates ERM, G-DRO, LC, and sLA. v2 additionally evaluates IRM, VREx, and Mixup in the corresponding compositional-shift and standard benchmark comparisons (Tables 5–11 and 14), substantially expanding the comparator families.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark splits, metrics, backbones, and hyperparameter grids remain. New protocols include leave-one-group-out evaluation over 32 CelebA groups, pooling four spurious attributes into a 16-valued attribute for baselines, and controlled 100-dimensional Gaussian experiments varying attribute counts, category counts, and training-group retention (G.3 and G.6).

E4.justification: The original bias/prior ablations are retained. v2 adds Gaussian decision-boundary case studies comparing CRM and ERM (Figures 2 and 7) and extensive sensitivity analysis of training-group coverage (Figures 8–9). v1's separate random affine-hull membership experiment in Table 12 is removed.

E5.justification: Benchmark reporting retains means and standard errors over three seeds. v1's separate 1,000-run affine-hull frequency estimation is removed; v2's new predictive-simulation curves report three-seed means and standard errors. These are different experiments, not a stated reduction in repetitions for retained benchmarks.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive baseline and simulation results, including five-attribute CelebA WGA of 63.2 for CRM versus 34.3 for LC (Table 12). Retained reports also change: MultiNLI CRM WGA becomes 58.7 from 57.7 in Table 1, while CivilComments CRM WGA when dropping (1,7) becomes 63.0 from 65.0. Several ablation estimates also change.

M1.justification: The proposed additive-energy classifier, joint likelihood objective, bias extrapolation, prior adjustment, and marginalization remain unchanged. The generalized pseudocode and additional attribute heads instantiate v1's existing m-attribute formulation; the original two-attribute algorithm moves to Appendix C.

P1.justification: v2 shortens and moves related work near the end, edits the abstract and mathematical motivation, and replaces the detailed main algorithm with an overview while relocating the original to Appendix C. Most existing theoretical and experimental exposition is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds decision-boundary Figures 2 and 7, sensitivity Figures 8–9, and new aggregate and multi-attribute tables. Existing comparison tables gain baseline rows, and the compact CivilComments table is split into Tables 10–11. Original hull illustrations are retained and renumbered; v1's numerical hull table is removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hinton (2002), Krueger et al. (2021), Zhang et al. (2017), and Bayat et al. (2025). Appendices B and D.7 refine the relationship to additive decoders and newly position the hull analysis as providing sharper characterization and sample bounds than Dong and Ma. The broader research positioning remains.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the general-m conjectural treatment with a hull-growth proof giving O(md + d log d) scaling (Theorem 3 and D.4), and adds additive-function extrapolation reasoning in D.7. The two-attribute proof is retained in D.3. The new statements contain a consistency defect: Theorem 8 omits the factor c used in Theorem 7.

improvement.justification: The general-m proof advances v1's conjecture and numerical check, while broader baseline comparisons, five-attribute CelebA, and controlled group-coverage experiments address important validation gaps. These substantially strengthen theoretical and empirical support. The gains outweigh new consistency problems, including mismatched theorem constants, the Table 12 balanced-accuracy overclaim, and errors in the implementation listing.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Compositional Risk Minimization. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and adds baseline evaluations, five-attribute CelebA results, and Gaussian classification simulations.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on six benchmarks, bias/prior ablations, and a numerical affine-hull membership experiment.

results.title: Compositional Risk Minimization

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction qualify the performance claim as state-of-the-art ACR on CIFAR-10 and competitive ACR on ImageNet. Summary recommendations foreground ECDF, although Section 7 retains the certified-accuracy alternative. The central criticism of ACR and recommendation to discontinue it remain.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 now distinguishes ACR's sensitivity to easy-sample improvements from whether those improvements are easier to optimize, presenting the latter argument as an empirically supported hypothesis. V3 also explicitly limits its study to Cohen et al.'s certifier and acknowledges sound approaches using variable noise scales.

D1.justification: V3 extends the training documentation with ImageNet settings and adds repository access information for code, models, and ECDF data. It also clarifies that the gradient analysis concerns model parameters. However, Appendix C.1 omits v2's batch-size disclosure of 256; this does not establish an actual batch-size change.

E1.justification: V2 evaluates only CIFAR-10. V3 adds ImageNet training and certification, including comparative performance and selection-bias analysis (Table 4 and Appendix E.2), substantially broadening the empirical coverage.

E2.justification: V3 Figure 9 extends Appendix B's four-model ECDF comparison by including SmoothAdv, SmoothMix, and MACER. These methods already appeared elsewhere in v2, but their participation in this comparison is added. The main CIFAR-10 baseline set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: V3 adds ImageNet-specific settings: ResNet-50, 90 training epochs, learning-rate decay every 30 epochs, noise-sample counts of 1/1/2 across the three noise levels, and 50 samples for pretrained-model data selection. The retained CIFAR-10 settings and certification budget N = 100000 with alpha = 0.001 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix B.3 expands the ECDF case study to examine dominance across more methods and noise levels. Appendix E.2 checks whether hard-sample selection bias also occurs on ImageNet. Existing component, hyperparameter, attack-norm, and certification-budget analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same means and standard deviations from three independent random-seed runs on CIFAR-10 (v2 Table 5; v3 Table 8). V3 adds no corresponding uncertainty analysis for ImageNet. Correcting the table caption from certified radius to certified accuracy does not change the statistical reporting.

E6.justification: V3 Table 4 newly reports ImageNet ACRs of 0.529, 0.842, and 1.042; the respective best baseline values are 0.532 for SmoothAdv, 0.846 for SmoothMix, and 1.071 for CAT-RS. Expanded ECDF comparisons add qualitative findings. All ten matched numerical result tables, including CIFAR-10 ablations and seed statistics, retain identical data.

M1.justification: The core CIFAR-10 method remains unchanged. V3 adds an ImageNet adaptation that omits data reweighting and uses a Gaussian-pretrained model for data selection with discarding epoch zero (Appendix C.1, Table 7). The relocated Algorithm 2 otherwise has equivalent control flow.

P1.justification: V3 edits the abstract and selected paragraphs, retitles Section 4.2, adds appendix subsections, and introduces reproducibility and acknowledgements statements. The main section order and overall narrative structure remain largely intact.

P2.justification: V3 adds the literature-survey table, ImageNet results and hyperparameter tables, and two multi-panel ECDF figures. Algorithm 2 moves from the main text to Appendix C.1, and appendix displays are rearranged. This substantially expands the visual presentation while retaining the original plots and result tables.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a structured survey of 13 works from 2020–2024, classifying ACR use, universal accuracy improvements, SOTA claims, and model customization (Table 1). Additional certification and variable-noise literature substantially expands the positioning. Publication updates to existing references are separate bibliographic edits.

T1.justification: Theorems 1–2, their Appendix A proofs, and the ECDF conversion arguments retain the same mathematical substance. V3 explicitly identifies the Gaussian quantity in Theorem 2 as a probability density, consistent with the density formula already used in v2's proof.
