improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens support for the field-wide critique: ImageNet results and selection-bias analysis test generalization beyond v2's single empirical dataset, while the literature survey provides an explicit basis for the research positioning. The optimization qualification in Section 4.2 and broader ECDF comparisons also improve the argument's precision and practical usefulness. Losing the batch-size disclosure is a limited documentation regression that does not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable matching across additions, moves, and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains these original results and adds ImageNet experiments and expanded empirical-distribution comparisons.

before.justification: V2 reports original CIFAR-10 experiments, gradient analyses, component and hyperparameter ablations, and results from three independent random-seed runs.

results.title: Average Certified Radius is a Poor Metric for Randomized Smoothing

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same four contributions and the claim that CursorCore outperforms comparably sized models. The additional evaluations broaden support without redefining these headline claims.

C2.justification: v3 Appendix P removes v2 Appendix M's explicit Python-only evaluation limitation following the multilingual extension. New passages interpret the added benchmarks as supporting broader effectiveness, while retaining limitations concerning HumanEval-derived coverage and repository-level assistance.

D1.justification: v3 documents manual translation of APEval and specifies execution tools, judging procedures, and settings for the added evaluations. Training details move unchanged from v2 Section 5.3 to v3 Appendix E; the prompts and code, model, and data access information are retained.

E1.justification: APEval expands from 164 Python samples to 984 samples across Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, Go, and Rust. v3 also evaluates historical-edit assistance on Zeta, data-science code on DS1000, and class-level generation on ClassEval. Earlier benchmarks and training sources are retained.

E2.justification: All 49 earlier Python APEval model rows remain across v3 Tables 4 and 7; several were relocated from the main table. The other existing comparisons retain their comparators, and the added benchmarks reuse previously evaluated DeepSeek, Yi, and Qwen comparator families.

E3.justification: v3 adds protocols for the new evaluations: bigcode-evaluation-harness for non-Python APEval, GPT-4o judging against assertion text for Zeta, and Inline/Tab settings and a class-generation subset for DS1000/ClassEval. Existing Python testing, greedy decoding, and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The data-selection, edit-format, target-area, thought-process, and sliding-window analyses retain their comparisons and findings. In particular, v2 Section 6.2 is preserved in v3 Appendix H, rather than removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Parenthesized values in the retained result tables continue to denote extra-test scores.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive multilingual results in Tables 8-13 and new benchmark results in Table 6. For example, CursorCore-DS-1.3B scores 45.5, 21.2, and 17.0 on Zeta, DS1000, and ClassEval. All 49 earlier Python APEval rows and 30 existing other-benchmark rows retain identical numerical values.

M1.justification: The Assistant-Conversation interface, code-first outputs, Programming-Instruct procedure, model families, and training approach remain unchanged. Expanded role names and the instruction to analyze before judging clarify behavior already specified in v2's appendix prompts.

P1.justification: v3 clarifies role terminology and the meaning of conversation, moves training details and data-selection ablation into appendices, and adds acknowledgments and an impact statement. Most explanatory prose and the overall argument are retained.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout, with widespread resizing and relocation of figures and tables. Table 1 is redesigned, baseline rows are redistributed between tables, and seven new result tables are added, including six multilingual displays.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for ClassEval, Zeta, and the evaluation harness, and extends Appendix A's coverage of knowledge tracing, data mining, code retrieval, and program repair. These additions broaden the background without substantially changing the central research positioning.

T1.justification: The framework's symbolic specification retains its meaning despite expanded terminology. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 explicitly identifies Python-only evaluation as a limitation. v3 addresses that important applicability gap through six-language APEval and adds evaluation of historical-edit use, data-science code, and class-level generation, substantially strengthening validation while preserving earlier results and ablations. The translated HumanEval tasks and Table 6's restriction to the DeepSeek 1.3B family still limit the breadth of the conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CursorCore work. Their text, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and content relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds multilingual APEval results and evaluations on Zeta, DS1000, and ClassEval.

before.justification: v2 reports original CursorCore evaluations on APEval and other programming benchmarks, together with data-selection, representation, reasoning, and history-retrieval experiments.

results.title: CursorCore: Assist Programming through Aligning Anything

C1.justification: The central contribution broadens from diagnosing delusions and improving target-directed HER training to a general feasibility-based rejection mechanism for decision-time and background planning. V6's abstract and introduction claim a combined learning-rule, architecture, and relabeling solution applicable across three representative planning methods.

C2.justification: V6 develops applicability conditions involving state-set targets and the embedding/indicator functions, and explicitly leaves targets lacking the required state correspondence for future work. Non-singleton evidence is limited to estimation after inadequate control performance. Conversely, v5's explanation of the difficulty of learning estimates originating from hallucinated states is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix I.3 adds Dyna's equal-sized real/simulated minibatches and 0.05 rejection threshold, implemented by zeroing rejected-transition errors. Most Skipper/LEAP implementation details remain, but v5's explicit SSM maximum episode length of 128 is no longer stated. Both versions already provide the same code repository link.

E1.justification: SSM and RDS remain the experimental environments. V6 additionally evaluates neighborhood targets containing up to five states, replacing exact-state completion in these added tests (Appendix G). This introduces a limited new goal specification and feasibility-evaluation scenario without expanding environmental domains.

E2.justification: V6 adds evaluated Dyna baselines against DynaX on SSM and RDS (Figures 4 and 16). Existing Skipper/LEAP relabeling comparator memberships remain after matching names such as F-E to E. Other planning methods listed in Table 2 are discussed applications, not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V6 adds background-planning evaluation using errors against optimal Q values, training-task success, and update-rejection rates. Its non-singleton tests use random-walk training data and modify both the termination indicator and ground-truth DP solver (Appendix G). These are substantial new evaluation designs; the original decision-time training budgets and OOD task sampling largely remain.

E4.justification: V6 adds controlled tests of whether feasibility estimation withstands non-singleton target semantics (Appendix G), while removing Skipper's detailed error decompositions for estimates originating from versus pointing toward G.1 states on both environments (v5 Figures 5 and 8). Generator-strategy and OOD-difficulty analyses are retained despite relocation.

E5.justification: V5 specifies 50% confidence intervals for the SSM behavior plots in Figure 3c/g and 95% elsewhere. V6 states that all presented intervals are 95% (Section 5). Both report 20 seeds; this changes stated uncertainty reporting without establishing additional runs.

E6.justification: V6 adds DynaX-versus-Dyna value-error, success, and rejection-rate results (Figures 4 and 16), plus non-singleton estimation results favoring E+P+G over E (Figures 17–18). Some retained curves are revised, including Skipper's SSM E.1 errors in Figure 3b. V5's directional E.1 breakdown results are removed.

M1.justification: V6 extends the proposal with an explicit feasibility evaluator using a TD hitting-time update, C51-style distributional outputs, and horizon-dependent rejection. Its DynaX adaptation suppresses infeasible simulated-transition updates. V5 primarily proposes relabeling and separate generator/estimator training while assuming suitable update rules; generate, pertask, and their mixture mechanisms are retained.

P1.justification: The title changes, Romain Laroche joins the author list, and target-directed/estimator terminology becomes TAP/evaluator terminology. The introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten, experiments are reorganized, and the appendices are divided into three thematic parts.

P2.justification: V6 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws Figures 1–2, and redistributes v5 Figure 3 across main-text and appendix displays. It introduces target-categorization and method-application tables, adds Dyna and non-singleton plots, and removes the directional error-breakdown figures. These changes substantially alter visual organization.

R1.justification: V6 substantially expands positioning around background planning, generative-model hallucinations, distributional learning, and temporal abstraction, including Dyna, GSP, Dreamer, and MuZero. Several earlier HER-focused references disappear. V5's explicit explanation that generate adapts auxiliary training from Zhao et al. (2024) is also omitted from the corresponding strategy description.

T1.justification: V6 introduces formal set-valued targets, hitting times and tau-feasibility, a target-value decomposition (Equation 1), and Result 4.1 on removing infeasible members from target sets. The TD boundary conditions and distributional feasibility/discount construction add substantial mathematical development beyond v5's mostly conceptual treatment.

improvement.justification: V6 addresses an important specification gap: v5 largely assumes suitable evaluator update rules, whereas v6 supplies an explicit feasibility-learning construction and tests rejection in Dyna. This strengthens methodological clarity and evidence for applicability beyond the original decision-time agents. Useful directional diagnostics are lost, and non-singleton experiments do not establish effective control, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in specification and empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on hallucinated targets, generate/pertask relabeling, and SSM/RDS experiments. Their readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial retitling and restructuring.

after.justification: V6 retains original Skipper/LEAP experiments and additionally reports Dyna/DynaX comparisons and non-singleton-target feasibility experiments.

before.justification: V5 reports original controlled experiments with Skipper and LEAP on SSM and RDS, including estimation errors, behavior frequencies, and generalization performance over 20 seeds.

results.title: Rejecting Hallucinated State Targets during Planning

C1.justification: The central claims remain offline, zero-shot imitation from one rough, partial demonstration through occupancy matching, with reduced myopia. The clearer terminology and additional comparisons support the existing contribution without redefining its scientific scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for FB performance involving limited data and degenerate reward-maximizing solutions. It interprets unseen trajectories as combinations of states within training-data support and discusses ZILOT's non-Markovian policy space. The existing limitation from world-model accuracy and finite horizons is retained.

D1.justification: Appendix C.10 and Table 8 document FB implementation adaptations, goal inputs, normalization, representation sizes, learning rates, batch sizes and discounts. Appendix C.3 adds matched-hardware MPC+Cls timing of 12–35 Hz alongside ZILOT's retained 0.5–3 Hz. Original ZILOT settings and code access remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 30 tasks across three Fetch environments, HalfCheetah and PointMaze, with the same WGCSL, curiosity-collected and D4RL datasets. Single-goal evaluation already appears in v1; the new coverage analysis examines existing data and tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds ERFB and RERFB to the retained Pi+Cls and MPC+Cls comparisons, introducing a distinct Forward-Backward method family. The single-goal comparison also adds these methods and the three ZILOT ablations, expanding from three to eight methods.

E3.justification: Existing experimental settings are retained. The added FB comparisons introduce a two-million-step training budget, evaluation every 50,000 steps and best-checkpoint selection (Appendices C.10 and D.2). Appendix C.8 adds selection of the five closest training trajectories for coverage analysis.

E4.justification: Appendix C.8 adds dataset-support and nearest-trajectory analyses addressing whether demonstrations reproduce training trajectories. Appendix D.2 adds FB training-length sensitivity curves, and the single-goal study gains ablation controls. The original component, horizon and classifier-threshold analyses remain.

E5.justification: The 20-trial, five-seed mean and standard-deviation reporting and Welch tests at p=0.05 are unchanged. Appendix C.8 newly introduces kernel density estimation of training goal occupancies, a limited addition of statistical estimation rather than increased runs or new uncertainty tests.

E6.justification: All retained numerical entries in Tables 1 and 2 are unchanged. v2 adds extensive FB results, expanded single-goal results, training curves, coverage findings and baseline timing. For example, Fetch Slide aggregate Wmin is newly 0.250/0.251 for ERFB/RERFB versus retained ZILOT 0.098; on HalfCheetah backflip, both new baselines achieve 2.002 versus ZILOT 2.625.

M1.justification: ZILOT retains the same learned dynamics model, state-goal and goal-goal value functions, Sinkhorn objective, finite-horizon planning and goal-conditioned TD-MPC2 implementation. The newly described Forward-Backward adaptations concern comparison methods.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main argument sequence remain intact. v2 clarifies rough versus partial demonstrations, renames Conclusion to Discussion, shortens selected passages and reorganizes the appendices, including moving the qualitative gallery after the hyperparameter searches.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch to two columns. Table 1 moves into the appendix and gains FB columns; baseline, density and training-curve displays are added. Figure 4 removes the Pi+Cls panel, ablation plots are restyled, and retained trajectory galleries are redistributed across pages.

R1.justification: v2 recognizes Forward-Backward methods as an exception to v1's broad statement about zero-shot RL and distribution matching. New Appendix B extensively positions ZILOT against Pirotta et al. (2024), explaining applicable and excluded variants. Jeen et al. and additional reward-based imitation references are also added.

T1.justification: The myopia proposition, its proof and ZILOT derivations are unchanged. Appendix B adds formal definitions of the FB reward objectives, including the expert-to-data density ratio and its regularized counterpart. This is limited mathematical elaboration, without a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important comparison gap by evaluating a distinct, closely related FB method family and documenting its adaptation and checkpoint selection. The training-data analyses better substantiate what unseen-trajectory imitation demonstrates, while runtime and limitations discussions expose practical costs. These additions substantially strengthen the empirical case, although conclusions about FB remain specific to the adapted, limited-data setting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ZILOT research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds Forward-Backward baseline evaluations, training curves and analyses of the training-data distribution.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation results across 30 tasks in five environments, including baseline comparisons, ablations, single-goal evaluations and qualitative trajectories.

results.title: Zero-Shot Offline Imitation Learning via Optimal Transport

C1.justification: The central LDHD framework, need for suitable inductive bias, CoT interpretation, and embedding-design principle remain. The introduction reformulates the architecture-specific contribution by explicitly claiming min-degree convergence for both APE and RPE, replacing v1's emphasis on APE failure and RPE's min-degree characterization.

C2.justification: The explanation of APE failure changes from a low-rank attention bottleneck to vanishing coefficients outside the observed training block. V2 also adds the substantive qualification that priming with even a few long examples differs from strict LDHD generalization, and extends its format-based interpretation to the new embedding comparisons. The all-task interpretation of Abacus exceeds the evidence in Figure 3.

D1.justification: V2 adds the copy data-generation and training recipe, formats for the additional tasks, and associated hyperparameters. The original addition sampling instructions, GPT-2 implementation information, optimizer settings, and two-RTX-3090 hardware disclosure are retained. No new code or data release information is provided.

E1.justification: V2 retains URF addition and adds unaligned copy, ParityCoT, single-digit-by-multidigit multiplication, multidigit-by-single-digit division, and AdditionMod10. These substantially expand evaluated task requirements. V1's brief empirical ARF-versus-URF observation is no longer reported; ARF remains a conceptual example.

E2.justification: V1's reported addition comparison uses RPE against RPE-Square. V2 Figure 3 adds evaluated RoPE, NoPE, ALiBi, and Abacus comparators to that task, with the expanded comparator set also appearing in Figures 4–7.

E3.justification: V2 introduces training on lengths 1–5 and evaluation on lengths 1–10, a copy protocol with 2,000 examples per training length and stopping at 1,000 steps, and a 0.0001 learning rate for AdditionMod10. The original addition protocol is retained. Appendix E.1 reports batch size 256 for additional comparisons, whereas the retained addition recipe specifies 128, leaving its claimed setting reuse ambiguous.

E4.justification: V1 Example 1 reports an empirical format contrast: RPE helps ARF addition but provides little benefit for URF addition. V2 drops this brief diagnostic observation. The original extended-training and digitwise addition analysis remains in Figure 2d; the additional benchmark comparisons do not themselves constitute new component ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the empirical results. V2's additional curves retain the same reporting practice.

E6.justification: The original addition curves are unchanged, moving from v1 Figure 1 to v2 Figures 2c–d. V2 adds extensive task, length, and comparator results in Figures 2–8. Figure 8 shows near-perfect RPE-Absolute accuracy through length 10, while Figure 3 shows Abacus addition accuracy near zero, contrary to Appendix E.1's statement about nontrivial generalization on all five tasks.

M1.justification: Appendix E.2 adds RPE-Absolute, a task-specific embedding that uses attention-weighted distances to special tokens for AdditionMod10. The existing RPE-Square, RFMP, and PLAA architectures remain unchanged; their expanded explanations do not establish redesigns.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites and reorganizes the introduction into a structured account of the main work, renames Assumption 1 as Abstraction 1, and expands explanations of existing PLAA and RPE-Square constructions. New background and explanatory appendices precede the relocated proofs. Author, affiliation, and publication information also changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout. V2 adds a three-panel conceptual Figure 1, incorporates the original addition plots into the four-panel Figure 2, and adds substantial comparison displays in Figures 3–8.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including Huang et al., Teney et al., O'Donnell, and the RoPE, ALiBi, and Abacus works, while removing Arora et al., Krueger et al., and Ye et al. The basic positioning against input-length-only formulations and architecture-independent min-degree bias remains.

T1.justification: V1's nuclear-norm conjecture, conjecture-dependent APE theorem, and rank-based failure corollary are replaced by v2 Theorem 3 and Appendix C.4's conditional min-degree analysis under vanishing isotropic initialization and zero training loss. V2 also adds a proof of Corollary 1 and Example 3. The GRPE theorem and corollary are retained under new numbering.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses two important weaknesses: v1's narrow empirical validation against RPE alone and its conjecture-dependent APE analysis. Broader synthetic-task comparisons and a self-contained conditional APE proof strengthen the evidence and theoretical documentation. These gains outweigh localized problems, including Example 3's incorrect interpolator, which does not match the target on x2 = 1, and Appendix E.1's Abacus claim contradicting Figure 3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LDHD generalization research. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains the addition experiments and reports original copy, parity, multiplication, division, and addition-modulo-10 results in Figure 2 and Appendix E.

before.justification: V1 Figure 1 reports original GPT-2 experiments on URF addition, including training curves and digitwise accuracy. Appendix B.1 describes the experiments.

results.title: Low-Dimension-to-High-Dimension Generalization And Its Implications for Length Generalization

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add a central contribution concerning when routing and cascading are useful, distinguishing ex-ante from post-hoc estimator requirements and explicitly rejecting the necessity of varying model sizes for cascading. The introduction also expands its headline empirical claims to the added evaluation settings. The original optimality and unification claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops the interpretation of estimator accuracy, explains threshold cascading's failure with binary SWE-Bench feedback, and recommends depth restriction under suitable conditions. However, v1's explicit limitation concerning cascade routing's greater training-data and hyperparameter-fitting requirements is omitted. The appendix explanation of suboptimal five-shot cascading remains.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds substantial reproduction information: SWE-Bench log provenance and agent identifiers, exact QWEN models, LiveCodeBench version 5, evaluation-harness use, and benchmark-specific estimator features and cost calculations. Existing classification/open-form implementation details are retained or relocated. The declared code access remains unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds SWE-Bench Verified software issue resolution and a combined Minerva Math Algebra/LiveCodeBench evaluation. These substantially extend the evaluated data and task coverage. The original RouterBench, classification, and open-form reasoning coverage remains, including MISTRAL results moved into the appendix.

E2.justification: The main comparisons retain linear interpolation, routing, threshold cascading, and the authors' cascading strategy. The new runtime comparison adds MAX-DEPTH alongside standard cascade routing, SLOW, GREEDY, and NO-EXPECT. The added agent and QWEN pools are model configurations rather than new competing selection methods.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 50/50 training/calibration partitions, SWE-Bench agent pools, four QWEN models, ground-truth post-hoc SWE quality feedback, and costs measured through execution time or tokens multiplied by model size. Runtime scaling uses 100 random inputs per model count. The original splits, shot settings, and three standard noise configurations are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds a two-dimensional noise sweep examining the distinct effects of ex-ante and post-hoc estimation accuracy (Figure 2). Appendix F.2 adds scalability testing up to 80 models and examines depth restriction. The original eleven-model design ablation is retained in Appendix F.1 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V1 provides no comparable statistical intervals. V2 introduces sample-bootstrap intervals for AUC scores and paired AUC differences in Tables 4–6, together with significance-related table markings. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting; it does not establish additional model runs, and bootstrap resample counts and seeds are unspecified.

E6.justification: V2 adds SWE-Bench, Math+Code, noise-sweep, scaling, and benchmark-specific results. Existing entries also change: eleven-model low-noise cascade-routing AUC becomes 87.24 instead of 87.28, and MISTRAL open-form AUC becomes 58.73 instead of 58.69. Some new reporting is inconsistent: Table 5 gives a −0.64 five-shot difference where Table 10 implies +0.64.

M1.justification: The core routing, supermodel selection, pruning, and hyperparameter optimization procedures remain intact. Appendix F.2 introduces MAX-DEPTH, an optional variant that restricts cascade routing to three computed models, constituting a limited inference-procedure change.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract and introduction, adds method-section overviews, and reorganizes practical experiments around accurate versus poor quality estimation. Ablations move into the appendix, the standalone limitations and reproducibility sections disappear, and an impact statement is added. These constitute substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. The original quality-cost Figure 2 is replaced by noise heatmaps, a runtime scaling figure is added, and Table 2 is restructured. New confidence and benchmark-specific tables substantially expand the displays, while existing ablation and MISTRAL tables are relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds targeted discussion of confidence-token routing, routing during token generation, and multi-objective cascading, citing Chuang, Pichlmeier, and Zhang respectively. It also adds references supporting the new evaluations and challenges prior assumptions about model-size variation. The overall positioning around routing and cascading remains recognizable.

T1.justification: Equation (1) replaces the joint expectation over queries and model indices with an explicit probability-weighted model sum inside the query expectation, aligning the main objective and budget expression with the existing Appendix A formulation. The theorems, assumptions, corollaries, and proofs in Appendices A–C otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1 showed limited practical gains and examined runtime only at eleven models. V2's contrasting estimator regimes, noise sweeps, and scaling analysis substantially clarify applicability and computational limits, while bootstrap reporting makes statistical support more assessable. SWE-Bench still assumes ground-truth post-hoc feedback. Removing the explicit training-data limitation and introducing reporting conflicts, notably Tables 5 versus 10, weaken particular claims, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in explanatory and empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated ablations and MISTRAL results.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds SWE-Bench data analysis, math/code experiments, estimator sensitivity experiments, and runtime scaling results.

before.justification: V1 reports original routing and cascading evaluations on RouterBench, classification, and open-form reasoning tasks, plus runtime ablations and five-shot appendix results.

results.title: A Unified Approach to Routing and Cascading for LLMs

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on a practical CG+ algorithm attaining optimal breakdown up to an additive constant. v2 centers a unifying F–RG framework and claims near-optimal practical breakdown. Exact optimality is assigned to an oracle rule, while practical attainment remains open (abstract, introduction, and Section 3.4).

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the unresolved practical/oracle optimality gap and attributes it to threshold selection (Sections 3.4–4.1). It adds an explanation of why aggregating parameter differences handles heterogeneity and interprets low-heterogeneity MNIST results as exposing connectivity limitations. These materially qualify and expand v1's interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 documents the per-node attack-search objective, unit edge weights, CIFAR-10 architecture and learning rate, and synthetic initialization procedure. Conversely, it removes v1's explicit project-code link and MNIST CNN architecture description. The expanded attack-search description alone does not establish that the underlying search procedure changed.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates MNIST classification only. v2 retains MNIST and adds CIFAR-10 classification and synthetic five-dimensional approximate averaging (Appendices B.2–B.3), substantially extending dataset and task coverage. The four attack types and honest graph topology are retained.

E2.justification: The trimming comparator MoNNA/NNA and adaptive ClippedGossip correspond to GTS–RG and CSHe–RG in v2's unit-weight experiments. However, the unattacked D-SGD reference in v1's MNIST Figure 1 is absent from v2's MNIST Figures 1–2; it appears in the new CIFAR-10 comparison instead.

E3.justification: v1 Figure 1 shows MNIST accuracy trajectories through 200 iterations at b=6. v2 Figures 1–2 measure loss and accuracy after 300 steps over b=1–10. Added protocols include CIFAR-10 training for 2000 iterations at b=5 and communication-only averaging evaluated by relative MSE after 100 steps.

E4.justification: v1 compares four attacks at one corruption level. v2 adds corruption-level sweeps that examine where methods break down, plus controlled averaging experiments that isolate communication behavior from model training (Figures 1, 2, and 4). These substantially expand robustness and sensitivity analysis.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 1 contains shaded bands without explaining their meaning or reporting run counts. v2 specifies five MNIST seeds and ten averaging initializations, reporting means and minimum–maximum ranges, and discloses that CIFAR-10 uses one seed. This clarifies statistical reporting without establishing an increase from a known v1 run count.

E6.justification: The fixed-corruption MNIST trajectories are replaced by loss and accuracy results across corruption levels. New CIFAR-10 results show GTS–RG failing under SpH while CSours–RG and CSHe–RG fail under FOE (Figure 3); Figure 4 adds averaging-error results. These are new or replaced results under changed conditions, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v1's CG+ uses the stated (b+1)-st largest neighbor difference as its clipping threshold. v2 introduces weighted F–RG and CSours with a tail-weight threshold of 2b, corresponding to the 2b-th largest difference for unit weights. It also introduces oracle clipping and an asynchronous adaptation (Sections 3–4).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten around the general framework. The lower bound moves into Section 3.4, attack-centering details move to Appendix A, and the former proof appendix is reorganized into Appendices C–F alongside a new experimental appendix. This exceeds terminology or numbering changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. v1's theoretical comparison table disappears; its MNIST learning-curve display is replaced by corruption-sweep plots. CIFAR-10 and averaging figures are added, and the lower-bound topology illustration is redrawn and relocated as Figure 5.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from an improved hybrid of NNA and ClippedGossip to a framework encompassing these and other robust aggregators. v2 adds the concurrent ARC comparison and Pillutla et al. (2022), while removing several contextual references. The changed dates for ClippedGossip and bucketing identify the same works, rather than new citations.

T1.justification: v2 introduces weighted graph definitions, (b,rho)-robust summation, general convergence results, and oracle/asynchronous guarantees. The practical guarantee changes from 2(b+1)<mu_min to 4b<mu_min, with revised clipping proofs in Appendix E. The lower bound is generalized to weighted neighborhoods. However, v2's Clipped Sum definition includes a 1/n normalization absent from its Appendix E.1 analysis.

improvement.justification: Replacing v1's invalid clipping-error argument in Lemma 7 and practical-optimality claim with a revised threshold, analysis, and explicit practical/oracle gap substantially improves scientific reliability. Corruption sweeps and isolated averaging tests directly examine breakdown, while CIFAR-10 exposes failures of the proposed method. These gains outweigh the removed code link and unresolved normalization/sign inconsistencies between v2's main definitions and appendices.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, retaining the decentralized learning problem, spectral attack, and substantial theoretical material. All 22 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including figures and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original MNIST, CIFAR-10, and synthetic averaging experiments in Figures 1–4 and Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original MNIST classification experiments comparing aggregation methods under four Byzantine attacks in Figure 1.

results.title: Unified Breakdown Analysis for Byzantine Robust Gossip

C1.justification: The reversed-development observation is retained, but v3 adds central claims about missing human-like dependencies between abilities, weak scaling of low-level cognition, and shortcut-taking or illusory understanding instead of acquired core knowledge. Concept Hacking becomes a principal contribution in the abstract and conclusion, substantially expanding v1’s benchmark-and-prompting contribution.

C2.justification: v3 develops distinct shortcut and illusion interpretations of control/manipulation outcomes and offers a mechanism for concept-description prompting benefits. Section 6 newly considers whether human-level intelligence requires human core knowledge, discussing multiple realizability, grounded cognition, and world models. This substantially extends v1’s interpretation of reversed performance and counting failures as evidence against genuine understanding.

D1.justification: Appendices B–D substantially expand documentation of task construction, media handling, matching procedures, Llama3.1-70B/DeepSeek judging, and inference on eight A100 80GB GPUs with size-dependent allocation. These are newly documented details, not proof that all underlying procedures changed. Conversely, v1’s resizing specification and human recruitment/skip instructions are omitted.

E1.justification: The original 12 concepts remain, but v3 adds 45 paired standard/manipulated Concept Hacking scenarios and data analyses covering 26 other benchmarks and nine SEED-Bench abilities. These substantially extend evaluation conditions and analytical coverage. Appendix B’s omitted video-image-text row does not establish removal of that format, which remains illustrated in Figure 9.

E2.justification: The model comparison expands from approximately 46 models in v1, whose counts vary between passages, to 231 tested and 219 retained in v3. Table 2 verifies additional comparators including Qwen2.5-VL, NVLM-D, and LLaVA-Video models absent from v1 Figure 5. Appendix D.2 also adds comparisons of Exact, In, Template, and LLM matching against the hybrid matcher.

E3.justification: Circular zero-shot evaluation is retained, while v3 adds chance-normalized log accuracy, modality-dependent evaluation subsets, paired manipulation controls, and a reported 20% matching-failure exclusion threshold. Reported question screening changes from 95% reviewer correctness to over 80% across 20 human answers. Appendix B lists 2,299 questions, conflicting with v3’s main-text total of 2,519, so the exact revised sample remains unresolved.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained prompting study, v3 adds within-benchmark and cross-benchmark correlation analyses, parameter-scaling analyses, systematic Concept Hacking tests, and output-matching diagnostics. Appendix E examines GPT-4o’s explanations across manipulated examples. These substantially broaden the investigation of dependencies, scalability, evaluation failures, and shortcut reliance beyond v1’s single conservation/counting case.

E5.justification: v3 supplements v1’s point accuracies with distributions across models/prompts and scaling-fit error bars or bands, alongside regression R-squared values (Figures 3, 6, and 13). The uncertainty conventions are not adequately defined. Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, or formal significance tests; expanded model and prompt coverage does not establish additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds model scores and extensive correlation, scaling, and manipulation results. New empty-prompt scaling fits report R-squared values of 0.304 for mechanical reasoning and 0.015 for perspective-taking (Figure 6). The prompting finding changes from most prompts helping in v1 Section 4 to most not improving performance in v3 Appendix F. Changed model pools and settings limit direct performance comparisons.

M1.justification: v3 introduces Concept Hacking, a systematic diagnostic procedure that reverses ground truth through task-relevant manipulations while preserving irrelevant conditions (Section 5.1). This substantially extends v1’s isolated conservation/counting example into paired tests distinguishing conceptual understanding, shortcuts, and illusory understanding. The benchmark renaming and retained ten prompting techniques do not themselves change the method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The narrative is reorganized into benchmark construction, experiments, Concept Hacking, and discussion. Much existing cognitive background moves to Appendix A, technical material is reorganized and expanded in Appendices B–D, and prompting moves to Appendix F. These are substantial structural changes beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text switches from one to two columns. The cognitive map and example panels are redesigned, while v1’s accuracy bar chart and model heatmap give way to normalized distributions and a selected-model table. New correlation, scaling, manipulation, and matching displays are added. Prompt results become boxplots, and the original interleaved-media example moves to Appendix B.

R1.justification: v3 replaces the brief architecture-focused overview with benchmark-focused related work and substantially expands positioning around innate knowledge, grounded cognition, world models, and scaling. Added references include Moravec, Barsalou, Lake and colleagues, and Kaplan and colleagues. Much Piaget/Spelke background is retained, while the contribution is repositioned around diagnosing core knowledge deficits.

T1.justification: Appendix D.2 introduces an explicit mathematical definition of matching fail_rate, absent from v1. Its numerator counts valid matches, contradicting its interpretation as a failure rate. This is a limited formal addition; the expanded cognitive-science framework remains conceptual, with no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1’s broad claims about understanding relied mainly on accuracy patterns and one counting example. v3 substantially strengthens their empirical basis through paired interventions, quantitative dependency/scaling analyses, and much fuller curation and evaluation documentation. These changes make the hypotheses more testable and the procedures more auditable. The gains outweigh remaining weaknesses, including inconsistent dataset totals, the contradictory failure-rate equation, undefined uncertainty displays, and scaling conclusions stronger than the reported comparisons establish.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 12-concept benchmark study despite changes to the title and benchmark name. Text, figures, and tables are readable throughout, including v3 Appendices A–F; v1 contains no appendix. Internal reporting inconsistencies limit some exact comparisons but do not prevent reliable assessment of the revision.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark evaluations, correlation and scaling analyses, and Concept Hacking results comparing models and humans, with additional analyses in Appendices D–F.

before.justification: v1 reports original model and human evaluations in Figures 4–5, prompting experiments in Table 2, and a GPT-4o conservation/counting case study in Figure 6.

results.title: Core Knowledge Deficits in Multi-Modal Language Models

C1.justification: v1 presents a multimodal, nonexpanding LLaCA method and emphasizes zero-shot preservation with few additional costs. v2 presents a general continual-instruction framework for language and multimodal models, makes instruction grouping and limited expansion central contributions, and drops the headline emphasis on zero-shot preservation. The contribution's scope and resource-efficiency claim are substantially redefined.

C2.justification: The efficiency rationale changes from maintaining one parameter set to grouping instructions and using inexpensive TF-IDF routing. v2 adds interpretations of positive NLP backward transfer and task-order effects, while removing the quantitative zero-shot-collapse interpretation. The stated applicability limitation shifts from instruction tuning versus future continual pre-training to image/text coverage versus future additional modalities and scenarios.

D1.justification: v2 supplies complete instruction-template and grouping tables, identifies sklearn's TfidfVectorizer, and provides codebook/pool pseudocode and adapter-use details. It newly states the Truth Alignment evaluation criterion without establishing a change from v1. Hardware changes from eight A100s to eight H100s, while the main LoRA hyperparameters remain unchanged. Runtime reporting is removed, the grouping threshold is unspecified, and both PDFs only promise future code release.

E1.justification: The main continual evaluation expands from six VQA datasets to eight tasks: ImageNet becomes a trained classification task rather than only a held-out zero-shot evaluation, and visual grounding is added. Appendix M adds 19 language-only dialogue tasks. The earlier quantitative evaluation on successive unseen VQA/ImageNet datasets is removed, although qualitative zero-shot dialogue cases remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds EProj, Model Tailor (MT) and Multi-Task to the LLaVA-7B comparison, removes v1's separate full-fine-tuning and Upper-Bond entries, and no longer reports the baseline panel for the ten-template setting. The new InstrDialog comparison includes FT variants, L2, AGEM, replay and AdapterCL (Table 8).

E3.justification: v2 adds LLaVA-13B, Qwen-VL and T5-small configurations. The robustness protocol changes from four combined order/instruction settings to separate comparisons of three task orders and three instruction regimes. Final task accuracy replaces ADA/ADF in the headline plots, and the new NLP evaluation uses ROUGE-L and forward/backward transfer. These changes preclude treating the main version-to-version scores as equivalent-setting comparisons.

E4.justification: v2 adds an incremental instruction-grouping ablation and matching-accuracy analysis, revises order/instruction robustness tests, and replaces the main qualitative examples. v1's quantitative zero-shot-collapse analysis and EMA-weight trajectory plots disappear. The fixed-weight sensitivity experiment is retained with expanded reporting in Appendix F; the four appendix dialogue cases are retained and reordered.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty information. v2 Table 8 introduces means and standard deviations for InstrDialog, including the proposed method. Neither version states run counts or seeds, and v2's main multimodal tables still report point estimates.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports 61.89 Avg.ACC and 2.68 forgetting for LLaCA; v2 Table 1 reports 64.64 and 1.93 for the revised method on eight tasks. These are replaced results under different conditions, not demonstrated same-setting gains. v2 adds other-backbone, NLP, ablation and matching results, including InstrDialog AR of 39.8 with SD 0.5, while removing earlier zero-shot, runtime and intermediate learning-score tables.

M1.justification: v1 continually updates one LoRA/projector parameter set. v2 adds TF-IDF instruction encoding, cosine-similarity grouping, a codebook and parameter pool, conditional parameter reuse or expansion, and instruction-based selection at inference (Section 4.4). It also adapts the procedure to T5 adapters and revises the implemented EMA approximation in Appendix E.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title and terminology, substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, method overview and experimental narrative, moves the task definition into Preliminary, and reorganizes the appendices from A.1–A.11 into A–P. Much mathematical prose survives, but the overall narrative is extensively restructured. Several new citation locations display unresolved question marks.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the headline radars, redraws the workflow around instruction grouping, adds an instruction-reuse illustration, expands the benchmark tables and introduces large instruction/grouping tables. The fixed-EMA bar chart becomes an expanded appendix table, and the EMA trajectory plot series is removed. Existing dialogue figures are reordered and relabeled.

R1.justification: Although the bibliography is largely retained, v2 explicitly credits L2P and EProj as inspiration for grouping and adds substantial comparisons with their selection mechanisms in Appendix G. Its positioning shifts from avoiding model expansion to distinguishing lightweight, limited expansion through TF-IDF routing, stored instructions and no learned routing keys.

T1.justification: The ideal-state proposition, Taylor/Lagrange derivation and supporting EMA proofs are largely retained under renumbering. However, v2 Appendix E, Eq. 45 adds an approximation of the form ||1-X|| approximately equal to 1-||X||; v1 Appendix A.6, Eq. 58 stops at ||1-X||. This changes the mathematical approximation used for implementation.

improvement.justification: v1's broad applicability claim was tested only on LLaVA-7B with VQA training. v2 substantially strengthens its support through additional model configurations, language-only tasks, relevant EProj/MT comparisons, and direct grouping ablation and matching tests. Full instruction templates and NLP uncertainty reporting also improve transparency. These gains outweigh the removed quantitative zero-shot and runtime analyses, although efficiency evidence is weaker and the unspecified grouping threshold and unresolved citations limit reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research lineage, retaining the authors and central dynamical EMA derivation despite the changed title and expanded scope. All 24 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including appendices, figures, equations and rotated tables, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original results for the revised method across multiple multimodal model configurations, eight multimodal tasks and the 19-task InstrDialog benchmark, plus ablations and instruction-matching results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLaCA experiments on six VQA datasets, including accuracy, forgetting, ablations, zero-shot evaluations and dialogue examples.

results.title: Large Continual Instruction Assistant

C1.justification: The model-selection objective, kernel/RFF contributions and regret claims remain. V2 extends the introduction's empirical superiority claim from greedy baselines to standard LinUCB and KernelUCB, and more explicitly presents per-arm prediction as addressing their shared reward-model restriction.

C2.justification: V2 expands the explanation of arm-specific reward functions and interprets beating One-arm Oracle as outperforming a user who knows the best single model. Section 6.2 also emphasizes nonlinear kernels. V1's blanket kernel-approximation motivation is removed; the proposed future extensions to language models and other quality criteria remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies eta=1 alongside the retained alpha=1, adds UniDiffuser access information and reports execution times. Existing CLIP features, cached RFFs and default feature counts remain. However, Section 6's unscaled polynomial kernel conflicts with Appendix D's retained gamma=5, leaving its experimental scale ambiguous.

E1.justification: The MS-COCO and MSR-VTT generation tasks remain, including the synthetic experiments moved into Appendix D. V2 adds dedicated train/baseball-bat and elephant/fire-hydrant prompt categories and scenarios where generators or prompt categories arrive during operation, substantially extending the earlier stationary coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds actual plotted comparisons against LinUCB, KernelUCB-poly3 and One-arm Oracle, including in retained experiments such as Figure 2 and the synthetic tasks. Naive-KRR remains, and PAK-UCB-lin matches the earlier SCK-UCB-lin rather than constituting a new comparator.

E3.justification: New protocols introduce UniDiffuser after 2,500 iterations and additional prompt categories every 1,000 iterations. V1's four-generator static test is absent; v2 includes a three-generator carrot/bowl test. Reporting narrows from O2B, OPR and 100-iteration moving-average OPR to the first two metrics.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining the RFF bandwidth and feature-count studies, v2 adds tests of adaptation to arriving models/categories, polynomial-kernel scale sensitivity, KRR regularization sensitivity and measured computational efficiency (Figures 4 and 11–17). These address substantial additional robustness and practical-efficiency questions.

E5.justification: Both versions report curves averaged over 20 trials and use ± values for illustrative mean CLIPScores. V2 follows the same reporting practice without adding seed information, defined confidence intervals, significance tests or an increased repeated-run count.

E6.justification: V2 adds results for new generator pairs, baselines, adaptation and sensitivity tests, plus approximately 10 versus under 2 minutes for 2,000 iterations in Figure 17. V1's four-generator and moving-average OPR results disappear. Adaptation results have an internal inconsistency: Figures 11–12 duplicate curves, and Figure 11(a) differs from Figure 4(a).

M1.justification: SCK-UCB is renamed PAK-UCB. Algorithms 2–4 retain the same per-arm kernel regression, optimistic selection, RFF approximation and staged theoretical variant. Expanded explanations and new evaluation scenarios do not establish a changed method.

P1.justification: V2 revises the method explanations and terminology throughout, restructures Section 6 into experimental details, summary and setups, and moves the synthetic experiments into an expanded Appendix D. The former proof appendices B–D become A–C. This substantially changes the experimental narrative and document organization.

P2.justification: Figure 1 becomes a two-example overview, with the earlier detailed example retained as Figure 5. Experimental plots are broadly redrawn from three panels to two, with expanded legends and numerous added displays; synthetic illustrations are relocated. Figures 11 and 12 incorrectly reuse identical plots under different scenario captions.

R1.justification: V2 more explicitly positions per-arm prediction against the shared-weight formulation of prior linear and kernelized contextual bandits. The related-work survey remains largely intact. Bao et al. (2023) is added, while the Lin et al. MS-COCO reference is removed despite continued dataset use.

T1.justification: The assumptions, regret bounds, RFF approximation bounds and proofs remain substantively unchanged. V1 Appendices B–D match v2 Appendices A–C. Restating the existing lower-bound quantity c in the variance proof and correcting notation do not introduce new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked direct experimental comparisons with standard contextual-bandit algorithms. V2 adds these controls across real and synthetic tasks and broadens the real-generator comparisons, substantially strengthening evidence for the proposed approach's usefulness. New sensitivity and timing results further support its practical claims. Duplicated adaptation plots and conflicting polynomial-kernel disclosures weaken portions of the added evidence, but the central comparative-validation gains remain substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete text, algorithms, equations, figures and appendices are readable and can be matched despite renaming and substantial experimental reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and reports additional model comparisons, adaptation experiments, sensitivity studies and execution-time measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-selection experiments using real text-to-image generators and synthetic image, captioning and video tasks, plus hyperparameter studies.

results.title: PAK-UCB Contextual Bandit: An Online Learning Approach to Prompt-Aware Selection of Generative Models and LLMs

C1.justification: v1 claims a learned reconstruction function, a continuous-message compression bound, and promising preliminary toy results. v2 broadens the central contribution to learning model representations across PAC-Bayes, sample compression, and their hybrid. Its introduction and conclusion additionally claim that these representations support tight bounds across differing tasks where existing PAC-Bayesian meta-learning approaches struggle.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability distinctions: noisy MNIST tasks are described as unsuitable for its task-representation approach, whereas binary tasks expose limitations of shared-prior methods. Appendix C explains why full-dataset bounds help only in unfavorable high-loss/high-KL regimes. v1's interpretation of the size sweep and suggestion to regularize the KL term are removed.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds learning-rate, network-architecture, compression-size, and message-size search grids for the image experiments; Table 3 supplies selected representation sizes. Existing moons architecture, GPU, optimizer, initialization, and 200-epoch information are largely retained or relocated. However, v1's explicit batch size of 20 is omitted, without evidence that the actual batch size changed.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only transformed synthetic moons tasks. v2 retains moons and adds MNIST classification with 100/200/300 pixel swaps, binary MNIST class-pair tasks, and binary CIFAR100 tasks, substantially expanding domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: v1 has no external baseline experiments. v2 Tables 1–2 add comparisons with Pentina and Lampert (2014), Amit and Meir (2018), Guan and Lu (2022; kl and Catoni variants), Zakerinia et al. (2024), and an opaque-encoder control. Rezazadeh (2022) additionally participates in the binary-task comparison.

E3.justification: The moons generation procedure and 300-training/100-test-task split remain unchanged. New protocols specify 10 training and 20 test tasks for pixel-swapped MNIST, and class-based partitions with 34/50 test tasks for binary MNIST/CIFAR100. Appendix C also introduces controlled numerical bound comparisons at m = 10000, delta = 0.01, and KL values of 100 and 10000.

E4.justification: v1's compression-size/message-size sensitivity heatmaps are removed. v2 adds latent-coordinate interventions in Figure 3, the opaque-encoder control and noisy-task comparison, numerical analysis of full-dataset versus complement-set bounds in Appendix C, and alternative-bound comparisons in Table 4. The original compression-point decision-boundary examples survive as Figure 4.

E5.justification: v1 reports task-averaged moons results without empirical uncertainty estimates. v2 Tables 1, 2, and 4 introduce 95% confidence intervals for bounds and test errors across 20, 34, or 50 test tasks. This establishes new cross-task uncertainty reporting, not increased training repetitions; neither version specifies repeated-training counts or seeds.

E6.justification: The quantitative moons sweep in v1 Figure 2 disappears, while v2 Tables 1, 2, and 4 add extensive benchmark and alternative-bound results. For example, binary-MNIST SCH+ reports a bound of 0.280 ± 0.148 and test error of 0.155 ± 0.109. These are newly reported results under added settings, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Beyond retaining the sample/message/reconstructor pipeline, v2 revises the stated continuous-message training objective from v1's deterministic Equation 3 to an expectation over Gaussian-perturbed messages in Equation 9, with a corresponding latent-only objective in Equation 4. Definition 4.1 also adds multiclass label encoding. Binary STP-to-DeepSet renaming and the zero-compression-set special case alone are not new methods.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around model representations and three theoretical frameworks. Theory and architecture sections are reorganized, terminology is standardized into PBH/SCH/PBSCH variants, and Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix G. This substantially changes the narrative beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with new tables, architecture diagrams, latent-space plots, and appendix bound-comparison heatmaps. v1 Figure 1 is redrawn, Figure 3 is retained as v2 Figure 4, and Figure 2 is removed. Appendix G relocates the algorithm and redisplays architecture schematics.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around PAC-Bayesian meta-learning, information bottlenecks, and disintegrated bounds, adding works such as Pentina and Lampert, Amit and Meir, Tishby and Zaslavsky, and Viallard et al. It contrasts latent-space distributions with prior approaches and adds an Appendix C critique of an earlier theorem's scope. v1's Pick-to-learn discussion and citation disappear.

T1.justification: v2 substantially extends v1's continuous-message theorem and corollaries. Appendices B–D derive general bounds over joint compression-set/message distributions and rederive the retained continuous-message result. Theorem 2.5 and Appendices E–F add disintegrated bounds for a single sampled predictor, with proofs and corollaries. Several bounded-loss corollaries are also replaced by sub-Gaussian formulations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's important limitation of toy-only evidence without external comparisons through image-task benchmarks, an informative opaque-encoder control, uncertainty reporting, and explicit discussion of failure conditions. The expanded theoretical derivations and bound comparisons also strengthen the contribution. These gains outweigh losing the moons size sweep and some reporting weaknesses. The superiority language remains too broad: Table 1 reports a tighter 300-swap bound for Zakerinia et al. (0.149) than SCH+ (0.177).

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, retaining the reconstruction-hypernetwork framework, continuous-message bound, and moons examples despite substantial expansion and retitling. All 11 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: Sections 4.2–4.4 report original moons, MNIST, and CIFAR100 experiments. Appendices C and H additionally report numerical bound comparisons.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figures 2–3 report original moons experiments, including test errors, computed generalization bounds, and learned decision boundaries.

results.title: Generalization Bounds via Meta-Learned Model Representations: PAC-Bayes and Sample Compression Hypernetworks

C1.justification: The benchmark's central scalability and representation-learning claims remain, but v3 adds prominent claims that several specialized representation methods underperform standard SAC and that trained agents generally fail to transfer to unseen images. Its introduction and conclusion substantially broaden v1's principal empirical message about DreamerV3 outperforming PPO and degradation with visual diversity.

C2.justification: v3 adds method-specific hypotheses for CURL, DBC, SPR, SB and VAE failures, interpretations of augmentation benefits, and an early-stopping versus solution-quality tradeoff (Section 5 and Appendix D.1). It newly qualifies comparisons by architectural differences and limited tuning. The earlier limitation about missing representation-focused agents is replaced, while the five-seed limitation remains.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands implementation documentation with preprocessing, architectures, augmentation procedures, auxiliary optimization and SAC hyperparameters, plus a separate experiment-code link. Appendix D.2 adds SAC runtimes and revises PPO's longest reported runtime from 30 to 90 minutes. Some details conflict: Table 10 lists crop-based augmentations, whereas Section 4 and Appendices B–C specify grayscale and channel shuffling.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates 3×3 puzzles using ImageNet-1k validation images. v3 adds DiffusionDB images, 4×4 PPO puzzles and direct evaluation of trained policies on unseen images (Section 5, Figure 5, Tables 3–4). The latter goes beyond v1's encoder-transfer experiments, which involved training on the new image pool.

E2.justification: v3 retains the three PPO and two DreamerV3 variants and adds discrete SAC plus RAD, CURL, SPR, DBC, SAC-AE, SAC-VAE and Simple Baseline variants to the reported comparisons (Tables 1–2). RAD and CURL were discussed but explicitly not evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: Reported PPO environment instances change from 1,024 to 64 and rollout steps from 4 to 16; DreamerV3 replay capacity changes from 5 million to 500,000 (v1 Table 1; v3 Tables 7 and 9). v3 also revises sampled pool sizes and adds 100-episode unseen-image evaluation, episode-length metrics and a control without early stopping. These are reported protocol changes, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retained pretraining and decoder-gradient comparisons, v3 adds SAC representation-component comparisons, entropy-temperature/autotuning sweeps and augmentation ablations (Appendix C, Figures 7–8). Section 5 additionally examines unseen-image generalization and tests whether continued PPO training after successful convergence improves solution length.

E5.justification: Sample-efficiency uncertainty changes from v1 Figure 3's bootstrap confidence intervals with 1,000 resamples to v3's mean ±1.96 standard errors. v1 already used normal-based intervals for learning curves, and both versions retain five independent seeds for the main comparisons; increased replication is not reported.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial numerical results: at pool size 5, SAC+RAD requires 0.42M steps versus SAC's 0.91M and DreamerV3's 1.23M (Table 2); unseen-image success is near zero, and 4×4 PPO success is 51.4±39.3% (Tables 3–5). Existing curves are revised and some entries, including v1's 500-image DreamerV3 result, disappear. Changed settings prevent same-setting cross-version performance claims. Some PPO success values disagree between v3 Tables 3 and 5.

M1.justification: Section 3 changes the stated solved-puzzle reward from +10 to +1 and revises Manhattan-distance normalization. This changes the benchmark's learning signal locally; image-pool construction, tile movements and the two initialization procedures remain substantially unchanged. Expanded descriptions of retained agents do not establish architectural changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, benchmark description, results and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Results are reorganized around five research questions, benchmark mechanics receive named subsections, and appendices expand into A–F with hyperparameters moved to E. The NeurIPS checklist is removed, while acknowledgements and a dedicated impact statement are added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns. v1's combined sample-efficiency chart becomes separate algorithm panels in v3 Appendix Figure 9, and scaling curves gain a SAC panel. v3 adds visual-diversity and augmentation illustrations, result tables and analysis plots. The existing modality illustration is retained and renumbered from Figure 2 to Figure 3.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to puzzle benchmarks, including Estermann et al., classical heuristic search and deep-RL puzzle solvers. Additional literature supports SAC and its representation-learning variants. Several earlier references, including DrQ, CBM, CycAug and two puzzle-solving sources, disappear. This substantially revises positioning relative to closely related puzzle research.

T1.justification: v3 introduces an explicit POMDP specification and revises the reward mathematics in Section 3. In particular, its normalization expression omits v1's explicit exclusion of the blank tile. These are limited formal changes; neither version develops theorem or proof results.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked representation-focused comparators and left direct unseen-image testing to future work. v3 addresses both central gaps and adds analyses of augmentation, tuning and solution quality, supported by much fuller implementation documentation. This substantially strengthens the benchmark's empirical assessment. Conflicting PPO success summaries in Tables 3 and 5 and augmentation instructions in Table 10 reduce confidence in specific details, but the broader evidence and diagnostic analyses provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPGym research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original PPO, SAC and DreamerV3 experiments, including unseen-image evaluation, additional puzzle configurations and sensitivity analyses in Section 5 and Appendices C–D.

before.justification: v1 Figures 3–4 report original five-seed experiments with PPO and DreamerV3, including pretrained-encoder and decoder-gradient variants.

results.title: Sliding Puzzles Gym: A Scalable Benchmark for State Representation in Visual Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes LLMs' failure to integrate logical reasoning and factual knowledge. V2 adds a central claim that formal-logic enhancements can increase divergence from human-like reasoning, making this trade-off prominent in the abstract, introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of prompting trade-offs, DS/MT structural similarity, logic enhancement and neuron activation, and revises familiarity/attention explanations around changed exceptions. It removes v1's explicit scope-limitations discussion and warning that the findings do not establish internal symbolic reasoning.

D1.justification: V1 promises a future code/dataset release; v2 reports a public dataset release and supplies its repository address. V2 also documents GPT-4o's version and evaluation dates, generation/parsing procedures, comparator implementations and fallback behavior. Existing hardware, batching, runtime and license information is retained.

E1.justification: The same English geographical/categorical MT/DS dataset is retained. Appendix I adds premise-only conclusion generation to supplied-conclusion judgment, extending task requirements within the existing domains and reasoning patterns.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's six LLMs, v2 evaluates GPT-4o and adds Llama-3.1-8B before/after logic fine-tuning, plus GPT-3.5-turbo with direct prompting, two-shot CoT, LogicLM and SymbolicCoT (Appendix K, Table 10). This substantially expands the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: V2 adds factual-knowledge instructions, alternative questions and prefixed premises; conclusion generation with a 50-token limit, output parsing and sampling temperatures of 0.1, 0.5 and 1.0; and logic-system execution/fallback protocols (Appendices H–K). The original ten-phrasing evaluation remains documented.

E4.justification: V2 substantially extends the original sensitivity and attribution analyses with instruction/premise-framing controls, decoding sensitivity, controlled logic-enhancement comparisons and layerwise neuron-activation analysis (Appendices H, I, K and N). These test additional robustness and mechanism questions.

E5.justification: V1 already reports 95% confidence intervals, Welch tests and attribution-ratio standard deviations. V2 additionally reports standard deviations for confidence and familiarity in Tables 2–3, previously presented as plots. This expands dispersion reporting without establishing additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results for new models and experiments. Table 10 reports GPT-3.5-turbo paired accuracy of 50.80% directly, 65.36% with CoT, 30.81% with LogicLM and 9.53% with SymbolicCoT. Retained results also change: Gemma's paired accuracy changes from 0.096 to 0.071 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 4), alongside revised attribution values and rankings.

M1.justification: The dataset-construction procedure, entity inventories and four rulebreaker templates are retained. The added prompting variants and external logic systems are experimental conditions and comparators; no new proposed algorithm or model component is introduced.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. V2 incorporates worked explanations into the introduction, reorganizes retained appendix material, removes the standalone Limitations section and introduces several new appendix sections.

P2.justification: V2 changes conference formatting and appendix layout, redraws Figure 1, replaces confidence/familiarity plots with Tables 2–3, expands accuracy plots to seven models and adds comparison tables and generation/activation figures. These are substantial changes to visual organization, beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands cognitive-science grounding, including Table 5 linking templates to prior human experiments. It adds detailed comparisons with human–LLM reasoning research and Holliday et al., and develops its positioning against logic-enhancement approaches, replacing much of v1's textual-entailment framing.

T1.justification: The principal logical rules and metric definitions remain substantively equivalent. However, v2's redrawn Figure 1 introduces an inconsistent symbolic inference: 'A or B' and 'Not B' produce 'Not A', although its text correctly gives conclusion A. V1's illustration correctly presents modus tollens.

improvement.justification: Appendices H–I test whether the original findings depend on question wording or supplied conclusions, while Appendix K directly investigates logic-enhancement trade-offs. Together with clearer cognitive-science grounding and reported dataset access, these substantially strengthen the paper's evidence and usefulness. Removing explicit limitations and introducing the Figure 1 inference error are regressions, but they do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RULEBREAKERS study despite the changed title. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds GPT-4o evaluations, prompting and generation experiments, logic-enhanced model comparisons and neuron-activation analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original accuracy, confidence, familiarity and attribution experiments on six LLMs, with additional prompt-sensitivity and qualitative analyses.

results.title: RULEBREAKERS: Challenging LLMs at the Crossroads between Formal Logic and Human-like Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction now include alpha-renaming augmentation as an explicit alternative, with an originality claim in the introduction. The central generalization and inductive-bias claims remain. Alpha-covariance is newly foregrounded in the abstract but was already a claimed contribution in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds hypotheses about shared semantic embeddings and avoidance of token-specific biases to explain advantages over alpha-renaming. It questions the significance of copying differences because of training variance, elaborates the in-distribution/generalization tradeoff, and identifies meaningful variable names as an unexplored applicability issue.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies retained LTL evaluation sample counts, embedding selection and reuse during alpha-covariance evaluation, and constant epochs with approximately tenfold fewer steps for limited-data training. It also documents baseline augmentation, reproduction from scratch, and computing facilities. The main hyperparameter table is relocated with its numerical values retained.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same synthetic copying tasks and vocabulary/length ranges, LTLRandom35, its perturbed and limited-data variants, and LTL generalization to 10 APs and length 50. New comparisons and alpha-covariance measurements use this existing coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds an evaluated alpha-renaming augmentation baseline alongside the original and full-vocabulary fixed-embedding baselines. It participates in copying, LTL perturbation, limited-data, and generalization comparisons, providing a substantial alternative explanation for the proposed method's benefits.

E3.justification: v2 adds a larger-vocabulary alpha-covariance protocol using 1,000 examples with 120 random alpha-equivalent variants each, alongside the retained exhaustive five-AP evaluation. It also reports LTL RoPE/AdaCos validation controls. Section 5.2.3 changes the stated configuration from dα=5 to dβ=5 without establishing that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: New Table 3 tests alpha-conversion robustness in the vocabulary-generalization regime, substantially extending evidence about whether invariance survives expansion. v2 also extends perturbation, limited-data, and normalization analyses to the alpha-renaming baseline and reports LTL RoPE/AdaCos controls. The existing embedding-randomness and 277-model correlation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain best-of-at-least-three training-run reporting, ten embedding randomizations, the same standard-deviation analysis, and correlation p-values. Moving the correlation analysis to Appendix A.3.1 does not change statistical practice. The new copying-variance caveat adds interpretation rather than a new uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: v2 adds alpha-renaming results, including copying edit distance 1.85 and LTL generalization correctness 85.81%, plus the larger-vocabulary alpha-covariance table. Existing LTL values also change: normal-baseline correctness goes from 97.96% to 98.23%, and limited-data proposed correctness from 87.62% to 87.32% (v1 Table 4; v2 Tables 2 and 7). The original Figure 4 scores, including proposed correctness 92.87%, remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed dual-part embeddings, random-vector generators, normalization, three-way weight tying, and adapted AdaCos loss remain unchanged. Alpha-renaming augmentation is introduced as a comparison method, not a modification of the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the narrative around a new Problem Definition, moves language-model preliminaries, hyperparameter analysis, and limited-data discussion into appendices, and centralizes baseline descriptions. It also edits the abstract and introduction, expands experimental discussion, and adds acknowledgments.

P2.justification: The opening copying visualization moves into Section 5.1. Figure 3 replaces the full-length copying panel with an alpha-renaming panel, while retaining the former result in text. Figure 4 changes from three panels to a four-panel grid. Tables are relocated, split, and expanded, including new Table 3 and the combined appendix comparison in Table 7.

R1.justification: The cited works are unchanged. v2 adds positioning through its claimed novel internal alpha-renaming baseline, an explicit assertion that no existing metric measures the targeted robustness, and discussion of reproducing Hahn et al. (2021).
