T1.justification: New Section 3 formally defines the vocabulary partition, semantics-preserving token bijections, and post-training vocabulary-extension requirement. No theorem or proof is added. Equation 2's replacement of n with |P| is equivalent under the existing definition; the embedding and LTL syntax equations are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central evidential gap in v1 by testing whether simple alpha-renaming augmentation can provide the same benefits. The added baseline matches scaled-up copying performance and exceeds the proposed method on reported five-AP LTL tests, but trails in LTL generalization (85.81% versus 92.87% in Figure 4). This makes the comparison substantially more informative and exposes meaningful tradeoffs. Formal task definitions and clearer evaluation details further strengthen the paper, although best-run selection and limited uncertainty reporting remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same interchangeable-token embedding work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison, including matching material moved into v2's appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds alpha-renaming baseline evaluations and larger-vocabulary alpha-covariance results, with additional results in Appendices A.3–A.4.

before.justification: v1 reports original Transformer experiments on copying and LTL solving, including edit distances, correctness rates, alpha-covariance, and sensitivity to embedding randomness.

results.title: Interchangeable Token Embeddings for Extendable Vocabulary and Alpha-Equivalence

C1.justification: Vocabulary generalization and alpha-covariance remain the central contributions. The rewritten abstract explicitly claims improved generalization over alpha-renaming across three tasks, and the introduction adds negligible computational overhead to its contribution statement. These extend the claims without redefining the central research contribution.

C2.justification: v2 briefly discusses in-distribution degradation and meaningful variable names. v3 substantially expands applicability limits to semantic information in natural language, manually specified interchangeable-token sets and training from scratch. It also adds interpretations of task-dependent normalization benefits, computational scaling and general-purpose LLM performance.

D1.justification: v3 adds its own code/project-page link, propositional-data generation details, and explicit normalization settings for the logic experiments. Appendices H and I disclose timing hardware and configurations, Llama quantization, Ollama version, sampling settings, output formatting and complete prompts. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v2.

E1.justification: v3 adds propositional-logic assignment prediction using PropRandom35 and generated generalization and perturbation datasets (Section 5.3; Appendices C and G). Predicting possibly partial Boolean assignments introduces distinct task requirements beyond copying and temporal-trace generation, both of which are retained.

E2.justification: v2 compares three conventional-embedding baselines. v3 retains these and adds prompted Llama 3.2 3B comparisons on the logic benchmarks and generalization sets (Tables 2 and 8; Figure 6), substantially broadening comparator coverage. Figure 7 also adds a naive uniqueness-checking runtime comparator.

E3.justification: v3 introduces propositional-logic protocols, including order-insensitive assignment matching and a 132-dimensional, six-layer model trained for 50K steps. New LLM protocols use infix inputs, constrained JSON assignment outputs and top-k/top-p sampling; efficiency experiments add controlled timing procedures. Retained copying and LTL training settings in Table 4 match v2.

E4.justification: v3 adds normalization/AdaCos ablations on both logic tasks, propositional-logic perturbation tests and an LLM seed-sensitivity comparison. It also evaluates random-vector generation efficiency and revises the trace-generation scaling analysis. The copying ablations, embedding sensitivity and limited-data LTL study remain, largely relocated to appendices.

E5.justification: Appendix I newly specifies seed 42 for every LLM sample and reports comparison with an unfixed seed. Existing training-repeat counts, ten-draw embedding evaluations, standard deviations and correlation p-values are retained; no increase in those existing run counts is reported.

E6.justification: LTL generalization accuracies change from 92.37% to 90.76% for the proposed method, 47.07% to 41.97% for the vanilla baseline, 95.33% to 92.82% for full vocabulary, and 85.81% to 82.71% for alpha-renaming (v2 Figure 4; v3 Figure 3(a)). Their ranking and stated settings remain unchanged, without an explanation for the revisions. v3 adds substantial propositional-logic, LLM, ablation and efficiency results. It also replaces the trace-generation length-scaling curves with differently labeled evidence. Retained entries in Tables 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 match.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the shared/random embedding construction, resampling schedule, three random-vector generators, weight tying, normalization and sequence-adapted AdaCos with its scale cap of 100. Expanded explanations and additional task configurations do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Detailed copying experiments move from Section 5.1 into Appendix E, where they are combined with the former hyperparameter-search appendix. The appendix structure is extensively reorganized, limitations are separated from the conclusion, the abstract is rewritten, and the introduction gains an explicit contribution list.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws Figure 2 annotations, moves the copying heatmaps to Figure 8, and combines LTL and propositional-logic heatmaps in Figure 3. It adds ablation, LLM and runtime figures, expands tables and adds prompt listings. The timing figure is rearranged vertically and replaces its two length-scaling curves with one.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for the Llama model family and py-aiger, and explicitly positions its language-modeling adaptation of AdaCos as previously unexplored. The related-work discussion otherwise remains largely intact; the Sanh and RoFormer publication updates concern existing cited works.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds a formal propositional-logic grammar, Equation 4, and defines the partial-assignment prediction problem. Existing alpha-equivalence, embedding and alpha-covariance definitions remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical support by adding a second logic task and testing component necessity directly on both logic tasks, addressing v2's reliance on copying-task ablations. Efficiency measurements, reproducibility details and explicit applicability limits further improve the paper. The LLM comparisons remain contextual because training and inference settings differ, and the revised LTL averages are unexplained; these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds propositional-logic experiments, Llama evaluations, logic-task ablations and computational-efficiency measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original copying and LTL experiments, including generalization, perturbation, limited-data evaluation, embedding sensitivity and hyperparameter analyses.

results.title: Interchangeable Token Embeddings for Extendable Vocabulary and Alpha-Equivalence

C1.justification: The synthetic-framework contribution and central representation-shattering hypothesis remain. The abstract and introduction expand the claimed naturalistic replication from GPT-2-XL to GPT-2-XL and Mamba, and the introduction adds preliminary evidence involving non-cyclic city–country relationships.

C2.justification: V2 interprets newer editors as less damaging while sharing ROME's failure modes, and speculates that Mamba's complexity explains fluctuations in shattering. Appendix F.6 acknowledges that city–country representations do not yield a clean tree. The conclusion newly advocates synthetic testing before trusting editors at scale, while retaining the simplified-model limitation.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies random permutations for constructing cyclic orders, identifies the Mamba-2.8B variant and adaptation reference, and documents the city–country selection and editing procedure. The original training and ROME hyperparameters and the promise of a future code release remain unchanged; detailed implementations of the added editors are not supplied.

E1.justification: V2 retains the synthetic cyclic-graph tasks and calendar experiments, but adds geographical editing involving 25 cities and five countries in Appendix F.6. This substantially extends coverage to a different domain and non-cyclic, tree-structured ground-truth relationships; Mamba's calendar evaluation itself does not add task coverage.

E2.justification: V1's editing experiments evaluate ROME. V2 adds MEMIT, AlphaEdit, and PMET to the retained synthetic comparisons: Table 3 reports corrective and counterfactual accuracy changes, and Table 4 compares counterfactual representation distortion. MEMIT's earlier citation did not constitute an evaluated comparison.

E3.justification: The shattering measurement changes from an unnormalized change in Isomap geodesic distances to normalized Frobenius distortion of Euclidean representation distances. Prediction aggregation also changes from three sampled contexts in v1 Section 4.1 to five in v2 Section 3.3, without establishing that Table 1 was rerun. Added experiments introduce Mamba-2.8B and paired closest/farthest-country editing procedures.

E4.justification: Appendix F.5.2 newly tests whether the distortion–edit-distance relationship persists across alternative editors, and F.5.3 tests architectural robustness using Mamba. Appendix F.6 adds a non-cyclic case study and closest-versus-farthest edit analysis across 25 cities. These substantially broaden the tests of the central hypothesis; earlier appendix analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: Figure 5c adds a displayed regression fit and reports r² = 0.905, whereas v1 presents the relationship without a reported fit statistic. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-based uncertainty; the three-to-five-context change concerns prediction aggregation rather than independent experimental runs.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical entries are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results. Table 3 newly reports corrective edit-subgraph direct-recall changes of -9.51 for MEMIT, -6.05 for AlphaEdit, and -3.97 for PMET. Appendix F.6 reports a mean farthest/closest distortion ratio of 1.1483. New Mamba and distortion results extend the evidence; scores under the revised distortion definition are not directly comparable to v1's values.

M1.justification: V2 reports using an architecture-specific adaptation of ROME for Mamba-2.8B in Appendix F.5.3, although its detailed steps are not provided. The synthetic generator, nanoGPT architecture and loss, and original ROME implementation in Appendices A–D remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify cyclic orders, relation names, and the training/editing distinction. Section 3.3 becomes Experimental Setup, the hypothesis moves into a new Section 3.4, and Discussion becomes a revised Conclusion. Terminology and author order also change, but most existing prose and the appendix organization are preserved.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 2–4 and Figures 16–18, substantially expanding the visual presentation of comparisons and generalization tests. Figure 5 gains revised metric axes and a regression line; Figure 6's projections and annotations change; the GPT-2 month visualization is redrawn; and Figures 7–8 exchange order. Figures 1 and 3 also receive explanatory revisions.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for AlphaEdit, PMET, Mamba, and factual editing in Mamba, supporting its expanded experimental positioning. The related-work narrative remains largely intact. The additional Meng et al. 2022b entry describes the already cited MEMIT work and is not a distinct new research reference.

T1.justification: V2 Equation 1 substantively revises the mathematical distortion definition by normalizing the Frobenius difference and using Euclidean rather than Isomap geodesic distances. The knowledge-graph definitions and ROME derivation remain substantially unchanged. The representation-shattering hypothesis is mostly retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: V1's broad hypothesis relied mainly on ROME and cyclic knowledge. V2 substantially strengthens its support by testing three additional editors, Mamba, and city–country edits, addressing important limits on generality. The explicit normalized distortion definition and quantified association with accuracy also make the central evidence more assessable. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses, although Table 4's nonmonotonic values require more cautious claims about increasing edit distance, and the tree results remain preliminary.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same representation-shattering study and retain its core synthetic framework and experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's added Appendices F.5–F.6.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds evaluations of other editors, Mamba experiments, and city–country editing analyses in Appendices F.5–F.6.

before.justification: V1 reports original Transformer training, knowledge-editing evaluations in Table 1, representation analyses, and GPT-2 experiments in Section 4.5.

results.title: Representation Shattering in Transformers: A Synthetic Study with Knowledge Editing

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contribution: using unlabeled trajectories for both skill pretraining and online high-level learning to improve sparse-reward exploration. Expanded experiments do not redefine that contribution or its stated core claim.

C2.justification: Appendix J.1 adds consequential applicability qualifications: noisy data can yield unusable skills, while expert data reduces the need for structured exploration and thus SUPE's advantage. Section 5.3 interprets HILP's Scene performance as support for the broader data-reuse principle. These substantially extend the interpretation despite retaining Section 6's original limitations.

D1.justification: Appendices A-C substantially expand hardware and compute reporting, domain-specific architecture and hyperparameter tables, and Diffusion BC + JSRL tuning details. Appendix J.1 documents expert-data collection and its VAE KL-coefficient sweep. Existing code-access statements remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The main evaluation expands from 19 tasks across three domains to 42 across seven, adding HumanoidMaze, AntSoccer, Cube and Scene. These introduce harder humanoid control, ball manipulation and additional sequential manipulation tasks. Appendices H.3 and J.1 also add AntMaze play and expert-to-random data scenarios.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in matched experiments is retained, including the KL, ICVF and ExPLORe-without-online-RND comparisons. HILP with Offline Data already appears in v1; the new SPiRL discussion clarifies an existing baseline. Added datasets use existing comparison methods.

E3.justification: Main figures switch from mean summaries to interquartile means. Added OGBench experiments introduce larger networks, a 0.995 discount and domain-specific KL and baseline-tuning settings; new studies vary skill horizons and RND coefficients. Retained-domain settings largely persist. V2's blanket -1/0 reward statement conflicts with its detailed Kitchen description, so a Kitchen reward-protocol change is not established.

E4.justification: Section 5.5 and Appendix G add seven-task sensitivity studies for RND coefficients and skill horizons. Appendix J.1 tests dependence on expert, navigate, stitch and noisy exploratory data. The original ICVF, KL, coverage and data-corruption analyses remain, with several relocated.

E5.justification: V2 introduces explicit IQM summaries with 95% stratified bootstrap confidence intervals and specifies t-tests at p=0.05 for Table 3's significance markings. Appendix shading is explicitly defined as standard error. Kitchen's 16 seeds were already documented in v1, so this is not an established increase. V2 contains conflicting four-versus-eight-seed statements for manipulation and AntSoccer experiments.

E6.justification: New results include SUPE's success on large and giant HumanoidMaze tasks where evaluated baselines fail, HILP with Offline Data's advantage on Scene, and SUPE's failure on noisy Explore data. Sensitivity and play-dataset results are also added. Every numerical entry in v1 Table 1 is retained in v2 Table 3; changed IQM aggregates are different summaries, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, trajectory-VAE training, optimistic relabeling, frozen low-level skills and high-level online learning remain unchanged. The larger networks and different hyperparameter values are configurations for added experiments.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative and appendices are substantially reorganized. Detailed domain descriptions move to Appendix D, coverage analysis leaves the main text, and Section 5.5 becomes a hyperparameter study. Appendices regroup D4RL, OGBench and data-quality results, while introductory and method prose largely persist.

P2.justification: The domain montage and aggregate-results grid expand substantially, and first-goal times gain an IQM interval plot. New sensitivity and data-quality displays accompany relocated figures and tables: v1 Table 1 and Figures 4-5 become v2 Table 3 and Figures 10 and 13. Plot styling and hyperparameter-table layouts also change.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantial hierarchical-RL positioning, contrasting jointly learned primitives with frozen pretrained skills and citing additional classical HRL and motor-primitive work. OGBench and statistical-evaluation references are added, while Liu and Abbeel (2021) is removed.

T1.justification: The MDP formulation, VAE loss, trajectory-relabeling equations and RND/reward-model objectives are retained. No substantive mathematical assumptions, definitions, derivations or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis by testing qualitatively harder domains and directly examining previously untested hyperparameter and data-quality dependencies. Reporting failures and explaining applicability boundaries makes the evidence more informative, while explicit confidence intervals and significance procedures improve assessability. Conflicting seed counts and the Kitchen reward-summary inconsistency weaken reproducibility, but these localized defects do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SUPE research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds OGBench evaluations, hyperparameter studies and offline-data-quality experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments on AntMaze, Visual AntMaze and Kitchen, including exploration measurements and appendix ablations.

results.title: Leveraging Skills from Unlabeled Prior Data for Efficient Online Exploration

C1.justification: V2 promotes expected computational cost and quantitative robustness to initial step size into central contributions in the abstract, introduction and conclusion. V1 established finite termination and energy-jump bounds without this cost claim. The empirical pitch shifts toward robustness of the simplified selector, while the main invariance, irreducibility, aperiodicity and competitiveness claims remain.

C2.justification: V1's recommendations that tuned jitter prevents catastrophic failures and its interpretation of erratic NUTS behavior on mRNA disappear. V2 explains robustness through logarithmic adaptation cost and discusses its efficiency penalty. Appendix B.4 adds qualifications that MALA acceptance still declines in the tails and that large Cauchy jumps can reflect rare extremes rather than good mixing.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents several comparator settings, explicit Kilpisjarvi prior parameters, orbital-model access information and reference-sample counts in Appendices B–C. V1's detailed hit-and-run configuration and AutoStep-HMC leapfrog tuning instructions disappear. The main code/data access link remains unchanged. Newly disclosed settings alone do not establish changes to previously used implementations.

E1.justification: V2 adds Laplace and Cauchy targets and the Gliese 229 orbital posterior, while removing banana and sonar/horseshoe experiments. Gaussian testing shifts from multivariate ablations to one-dimensional tests. Funnel, mRNA and Kilpisjarvi coverage is retained; Kilpisjarvi already appeared in v1's appendix and jitter experiments.

E2.justification: The adaptive comparison expands from NUTS and hit-and-run slice sampling in v1 Appendix B.8/Figure 13 to those methods plus adaptive RWMH, adaptive MALA and delayed-rejection HMC in v2 Section 5.4/Figure 5. Fixed-step RWMH/MALA comparisons remain, while the corresponding HMC comparison disappears.

E3.justification: V2 replaces the principal autocorrelation/known-moment minESS metric with KSESS using reference CDFs and 40 batches; supplementary ESS uses Geyer's estimator. New protocols include 20-round tuning and million-step robustness runs across initial step sizes from 10^-7 to 10^7, unlike v1's tuned-step multipliers and default minESS > 100 stopping criterion. Appendix B.1 also changes funnel variance, scale and dimensional settings.

E4.justification: V1's jitter ablations, jitter-convergence analysis and fixed-versus-tuned jitter tests are removed. V2 substantially revises the symmetry analysis into acceptance-versus-state-norm tests across three tail behaviors, and adds initial-step-size tuning and robustness analyses with cost, acceptance and jump-distance diagnostics. The comparative mRNA pair-plot case study and Gaussian-hole scatter plots are also removed.

E5.justification: V1 Section 5 specifies 30 independent trials by default; v2 omits this statement without supplying an equivalent trial count for its benchmark summaries. This reduces statistical reporting detail without establishing that fewer runs were performed. Both versions retain the three-chain calibration and 2% error-tolerance description for cost-scaling estimates.

E6.justification: Substantial jitter and AutoStep-HMC results disappear. V2 Figures 1–4 report RWMH acceptance above 10% across the tested state norms, tuned initial step sizes stabilizing around 1 despite widely varying initialization, and robustness/cost trends. Figures 5 and 9 provide revised adaptive-comparison results. Changed methods, metrics and target settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: V2 removes Gaussian step-size jitter and its adaptation, prescribing the zero-jitter case already permitted in v1. Section 3.2 and Algorithm 3 replace averaging selected step sizes with median log-step-size tuning. The reported RWMH proposal also changes from x + theta*z to x + theta*M^{-1}*z. These revise the sampling procedure, beyond clarification or renaming.

P1.justification: Section 5 is substantially rewritten and reorganized around symmetry, initial-step-size tuning, robustness and adaptive comparisons. The adaptive comparison moves from the appendix into the main narrative. Method explanations and introduction paragraphs are revised, and the experimental appendix is reorganized with new reference-plot and diagnostic appendices. Much of the background and augmented-space exposition remains recognizable.

P2.justification: The empirical displays are extensively replaced: v1's explanatory schematic, jitter plots and comparative sampler pair plots give way to robustness curves, revised benchmark summaries and five reference-sample pair plots. Table 1 changes from two blocks of model configurations to one compact table. Figure placement, legends, plotting styles and document layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: V2 expands the existing discussion of concurrent Gibbs self-tuning work, explicitly acknowledging the same general augmentation technique while distinguishing its selector and theoretical analysis. It adds focused references for adaptive comparators, orbital modeling and the Kolmogorov diagnostic, and removes references associated with discarded experiments. The Modi citation's year update concerns the same work.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 4.9's expected selector-cost bound and Corollary 4.10's logarithmic dependence on initial step size, with proofs in Appendix A. It revises termination assumptions and removes the positive-jitter alternative from Corollary 4.6. Appendix D introduces mathematical definitions and a heuristic derivation of KSESS. The earlier energy-jump bound is retained as Proposition 4.11.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for automatic adaptation: v1 established finite termination, whereas v2 quantifies expected computational overhead and connects its logarithmic bound to systematic initialization tests. Expanded comparator coverage and a documented CDF-based diagnostic also improve evaluation of the central claims. KSESS remains heuristic, and removing HMC/other benchmarks and the independent-trial count creates tradeoffs, but the stronger theoretical support and targeted validation provide a substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoStep by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support a reliable comparison despite substantial methodological and experimental revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports original acceptance-probability, tuning, robustness and benchmark experiments in Section 5 and Appendix B, together with reference-sample analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original sampling experiments on synthetic distributions and Bayesian posteriors, including sampler comparisons, jitter ablations and sampling diagnostics in Section 5 and Appendix B.

results.title: AutoStep: Locally adaptive involutive MCMC

C1.justification: The title, abstract and contributions shift from demonstrating constrained LLM optimization against a GA to comparing generalist and specialized solvers. v4 adds claims about prompting limitations and solver tradeoffs, emphasizing LLOME's advantage on medium-difficulty functions while acknowledging comparable specialist performance on easier and harder cases.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantial interpretation of computational overhead, specialist steerability and hyperparameter sensitivity, and develops the biological motivation through binding and epistasis examples. It also warns that DPO's aggregate hypervolume is artificially favorable because some experiments terminate after generator collapse. Earlier calibration and reward-related qualifications largely remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.7 adds LaMBO-2 architecture, eight-head ensembles, optimizer settings, hyperparameter ranges and cortex/poli-baselines implementation provenance. Appendix A.4 adds the prompting template, while Section 6.1 identifies the prompted model versions. These substantially extend reproducibility information, although the template leaves the transition matrix as a placeholder. Existing LLOME training details remain.

E1.justification: v3 evaluates LLOME mainly on 32- and 16-token Ehrlich instances, alongside a broader GA-only parameter sweep. v4 expands solver evaluation to four vocabulary/length/motif configurations and a half-quantization case, adds full-specification prompting, and briefly reports testing a Rough Mt. Fuji function. This substantially broadens the synthetic test conditions.

E2.justification: LaMBO-2 is newly evaluated in regret, diversity/feasibility and Pareto comparisons alongside the retained GA and LLOME variants. Its citation in v3 was not an evaluated comparison. REINFORCE remains an objective comparator; o1 and Gemini are evaluated separately through prompting.

E3.justification: New protocols include eight-sample prompting with the full function specification and a randomly initialized, 314K-parameter LaMBO-2 model using the same 10K GA seed evaluations and 2K evaluations per round as LLOME. v4 specifies tuning on f2 and transferring configurations across functions, and expands the Pareto aggregation. Existing LLOME model size, training epochs and oracle budgets are retained.

E4.justification: v4 adds an explicit half-quantization sensitivity experiment and extends diversity and Pareto analyses to LaMBO-2 and additional functions. Most oracle-selection, calibration, refinement, SFT/MargE scheduling and REINFORCE analyses are retained. Figure 13 drops the earlier 12K-evaluation refinement panel.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 6 defines calibration shading as mean plus or minus two standard errors. The identical plots retained in v4 Figures 5a and 14 lose this explanation. The 95% confidence-interval descriptions in Figures 11 and 12 remain. No increase in independent evaluation runs is reported.

E6.justification: v4 adds LaMBO-2 and additional-function results, plus prompting minimum regrets of 0.9375 for o1 and 0 for Gemini. The original f2 result, including MargE reaching zero regret at 24K evaluations, is retained. Pareto values change under expanded experiment coverage, not as same-setting performance gains. v3's per-round average-regret plot and 12K refinement panel are omitted.

M1.justification: The LLOME bilevel loop, PropEn formatting, refinement/filtering, temperature adjustments, MargE loss and clipped reward margin are retained. Moving Algorithm 1 and renaming its evaluation-budget variable from k to j do not change the procedure. LaMBO-2 is an added comparator, not a new LLOME component.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, the abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the contribution narrative is reorganized. Related work moves before the method, evaluation follows it, results receive a separate section, and substantial original discussion and analysis move into the appendices.

P2.justification: v4 switches the main text to two columns, redraws the LLOME overview, adds biological illustrations, expands benchmark figures and regroups or relocates numerous existing plots. These are substantial visual changes beyond renumbering. Some presentation defects remain, including a clipped legend in Figure 10.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning against biophysical benchmarks and theoretical fitness landscapes, discussing GuacaMol, Therapeutics Data Commons, ProteinGym, FLEXS and Rough Mt. Fuji. LaMBO-2 becomes central to the generalist-versus-specialist framing. Much of the original LLM optimization and controllable-generation literature is retained in the extended related-work appendix.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2.3 adds a quantitative argument that uniformly sampled sequences become infeasible as length grows and explicitly requires q to divide k. The original MargE derivation and translation-invariance lemma remain. The newly displayed geometric-series equality contains an indexing error.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses an important weakness of v3's primarily GA-based external evaluation by adding a specialized solver under matched oracle budgets and examining difficulty-dependent performance. This supports clearer, more qualified conclusions about when LLM optimization is useful, reinforced by additional implementation detail and biological motivation. Lost calibration-band definitions, the clipped legend and the indexing error are limited regressions that do not outweigh the substantial gains in comparative evidence and interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Ehrlich functions, LLOME and MargE. Their main texts and appendices support a reliable comparison despite the changed title, expanded experiments and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results and adds LaMBO-2 comparisons, additional Ehrlich evaluations and an o1/Gemini prompting experiment.

before.justification: v3 reports original LLOME and genetic-algorithm experiments, including regret, feasibility, calibration, refinement and training-objective analyses.

results.title: Generalists vs. Specialists: Evaluating LLMs on Highly-Constrained Biophysical Sequence Optimization Tasks

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the central claim that LLOME outperforms LaMBO-2 on medium-difficulty tasks to conditional competitiveness or superiority. This materially qualifies the generalist-versus-specialist contribution, while retaining the benchmark and preference-learning contributions.

C2.justification: v5 revises LaMBO-2's interpretation from diverse but less feasible designs to strong diversity and feasibility. It adds explanations of reverse-KL exploration, possible capacity/pretraining causes of small-model failure, and explicit limitations concerning symmetric epistasis modeling and the absence of experiments with nonzero epistasis factors.

D1.justification: v5 newly specifies reference-policy updates, LaMBO-2's recency-weighted data partitions and sampling procedure, and candidate-selection pseudocode in Algorithms 8–9. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Newly documenting reference updates and data rebalancing does not establish that those practices were newly adopted.

E1.justification: v5 adds evaluations on TFBind8, TrpB, and DhfR biological lookup benchmarks to validate Ehrlich functions (Appendix A.2.7). These evaluate GA variants, not LLOME on biological data. The existing main Ehrlich tasks and half-quantization experiment remain.

E2.justification: The principal comparator roster remains unchanged, but v5 explicitly introduces an FFT expansion factor and associated candidate-selection procedure for the evaluated LaMBO-2 comparator (Appendix A.8.2). This is a limited adaptation of an existing comparison method.

E3.justification: LaMBO-2's reported kernel width changes from 3 to 5, and its selected design steps, mutations per step, and training epochs change from 64, 16, and 16 to 32, 4, and 100. v5 also adds the 226K-parameter model experiment and a 64-configuration GA rank-correlation protocol.

E4.justification: v5 adds a substantive test of whether Ehrlich optimizer rankings predict biological benchmark rankings, plus an f2 analysis using a small, unpretrained LLaMA model. Existing calibration, reward-objective, refinement, and Pareto analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The new biological validation specifies median cumulative regret estimated from eight trials and Spearman correlations across GA configurations. Existing 95% confidence-interval reporting is retained. This does not establish increased repetitions of the earlier experiments.

E6.justification: Figure 3 replaces medium-task results under revised LaMBO-2 settings: LaMBO-2 now reaches zero regret on f2 and leads on f3, where v4 favored MargE. Diversity and feasibility results also change. Table 1 adds correlations of 0.61–0.89, and Figure 11 reports the small model's plateau.

M1.justification: The Ehrlich construction gains an optional cubic motif-response function allowing non-monotonic scoring (Appendix A.2.3). All experiments use a=0, reproducing the original scoring function. LLOME's pseudocode and implemented MargE loss remain unchanged; the FReKL presentation mainly reorganizes their explanation.

P1.justification: Section 4 is extensively rewritten and expanded from two subsections into four separating the algorithm, theoretical motivation, computable loss, and margin reward. The LaMBO-2 appendix is also reorganized into dedicated subsections, substantially changing the explanatory structure.

P2.justification: v5 adds the response-function plot, model-size plot, and Table 1; revises comparison captions and diversity-plot axes and legends; and relocates the unchanged Pareto figure from Figure 17 to Figure 10. The overall visual format and most existing displays are retained.

R1.justification: v5 adds focused positioning through maximum entropy, generalized variational inference, and comparison with Steinberg et al.'s forward-KL approach, alongside biological benchmark sources. The broader related-work organization and principal research positioning remain largely intact.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.3 states SIC conditions and develops limiting-policy, convexity, and stationarity arguments with explicit representational and support assumptions. The Ehrlich definition also gains the cubic response function. The earlier MargE derivation and translation-invariance lemma are retained in Appendix A.4.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens the central comparison through revised, better-documented LaMBO-2 evaluation and appropriately narrower claims. Table 1 adds quantitative biological validation missing from v4, while the small-model analysis and technical disclosures address important evaluation and reproducibility gaps. Validation remains limited to GA variants, and the small-model comparison jointly changes size, architecture, and pretraining; some comparison prose is still inconsistent. These limitations do not outweigh the gains in evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Ehrlich benchmark, LLOME solver, and MargE objective. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v5 retains original experiments and adds biological benchmark rank correlations in Table 1 and a small-model comparison in Figure 11.

before.justification: v4 reports original solver benchmarks, prompting experiments, and analyses of calibration, refinement, and training objectives in Section 6 and the appendices.

results.title: Generalists vs. Specialists: Evaluating LLMs on Highly-Constrained Biophysical Sequence Optimization Tasks

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: xLSTM-based LRAM, favorable performance and inference efficiency, evaluation of fine-tuning and in-context learning, and dataset/pipeline release. The new controls support these existing headline claims.

C2.justification: V2 develops a domain-specific copycat explanation tied to action smoothness and explains when sLSTM state tracking and layer placement help. Section 5 adds Transformer exact-recall advantages and task-dependent backbone selection, including the relevance of less powerful edge hardware. Existing real-robot, offline-fine-tuning, and grid-world limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C.3 newly explains extracting environment-specific action dimensions from joint predictions, and Appendix A states that source code accompanies the submission. V1's explicit full-fine-tuning disclosure is omitted. Most implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware, training times, and the repository location are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same six-domain mixture of 432 training tasks, 37 held-out tasks, and Dark-Room 10 × 10 with 80 training and 20 held-out goals. The added studies reuse this coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding backbone comparisons retain DT, Mamba, xLSTM [1:0], and xLSTM [7:1]; fine-tuning still compares pretrained and randomly initialized xLSTMs. New behavior-cloning comparisons use the same backbones. Additional block ratios are internal ablations, while newly cited decision-model papers are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V2 adds full-mixture action/context sweeps, controlled removal of RTG or RTG plus reward tokens, and block-ratio and placement sweeps. These substantially expand experimental configurations while retaining the original main training and evaluation protocol. The ratio study has inconsistent size reporting: 16M in Appendix E.3 versus 206M in Figure 29's caption.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's Meta-World action-history, dropout, and layer-count ablations, v2 tests action history across all 432 tasks, adds xLSTM context-length sweeps and adjacent-action MSE analysis, and investigates return conditioning and block composition/placement on the task mixture and Dark-Room (Appendix E, Figures 23–30).

E5.justification: The existing three-seed means and 95% confidence intervals, and single-run 408M qualification, are retained. V2 specifies single-seed exceptions for new full-task DT context and block-ratio sweeps and reports standard deviations for adjacent-action MSE in Table 7. This does not establish changed run counts for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Retained plots are unchanged, but Figures 23–30 and Tables 7–16 add substantial results. New action-free context sweeps report normalized scores rising approximately from 0.3 to 0.7 for DT and 0.4 to 0.8 for xLSTM as context increases from 1 to 50. Appendix G adds per-task scores at the 206M scale.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 retains the same recurrent backbones, action-free state/RTG/reward sequences, shared discretized action head, cross-entropy objective, and recurrent inference procedure. Token-removal and block-composition alternatives are introduced as ablation conditions, without replacing the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain recognizable. V2 makes local rewrites, expands the ablation subsection hierarchy, renames the ethics statement, moves reproducibility from Section 7 to Appendix A, removes the appendix contents list, and updates affiliation text.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with extensive figure resizing and relocation. V1's separate memory plot becomes Figure 6c in v2. Eight new ablation figures, the action-MSE table, and nine raw-score tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds Ota and Dai et al. on Mamba-based decision models, Wen et al. on copycat behavior, and Ni et al. on memory/recall. It removes Di Palo et al. and selected fine-tuning and ICL references. These are targeted contextual updates rather than a wholesale repositioning.

T1.justification: The MDP formulation, trajectory definitions, and conditioning equations (1)–(2) remain unchanged. V2 adds empirical and conceptual discussion without new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for important design choices. V1's action-history justification relied mainly on a Meta-World ablation; v2 tests the full task mixture, measures action smoothness, and checks return-conditioning and block-composition alternatives. Per-task scores and task-dependent qualifications make the retained claims easier to scrutinize. Single-seed sweeps and the Figure 29 model-size inconsistency limit parts of the added evidence but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LRAM study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Existing content can be matched across reformatting and renumbering, including identical retained plot images.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds controlled ablations, action-smoothness measurements, and per-task results in Appendices E and G.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendices C–E report original multi-domain evaluations, fine-tuning, Dark-Room in-context learning, inference measurements, and ablations.

results.title: A Large Recurrent Action Model: xLSTM enables Fast Inference for Robotics Tasks

C1.justification: The original claims about steering, robustness, bias mitigation, and unseen-feature generalization remain. V4 adds a distinct fourth introductory contribution claiming preservation of pretrained instruction-following and zero-shot QA capabilities, together with favorable scaling across model sizes.

C2.justification: V2 describes the training independence conditions as necessary; v4 explicitly recasts them as an ideal controlled setting that BBQ need not satisfy. V4 also clarifies why unseen genre-label mappings cannot be known despite maintained steerability, expands discussion of incomplete feature annotation, and identifies simultaneous control of multiple features as future work.

D1.justification: V4 adds a project-page pointer for code and datasets, dataset split counts, explicit identification of SHANS's held-out subsequence heuristic, and BBQ-NLG prompts, learning rate, and epoch budget. These improve documentation without establishing changes to previously undisclosed settings. The contradictory NLG adapter description limits reproducibility.

E1.justification: V4 adds free-response BBQ-NLG, which removes answer choices and requires generated answers, plus Alpaca-GPT instruction-following and MMLU transfer evaluation. SS, SMNLI, ordinary BBQ, and SHANS remain; moving SS into Appendix E does not remove coverage.

E2.justification: The baseline families remain substantially unchanged, including PoE. However, v4 Figure 15 and Table 6 add zero-shot and SFT(y) comparisons on held-out BBQ bias features; v2 Figure 9 reports these comparators only on trained features. The few-shot count change belongs to evaluation settings.

E3.justification: Reported settings change from five to four in-context examples, eight to four decoding beams, and an 80/20 to 90/10 training/validation split. V4 Table 3 nevertheless lists 80/20 counts for SS and SMNLI, leaving the actual split inconsistent. New protocols include LLM-judged free-response answers, GPT-4o ratings of 500 prompts, and Qwen models at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B.

E4.justification: V4 Sections 5.3–5.4 add analyses of instruction-following preservation, zero-shot transfer after FIT, and sensitivity to model capacity. These address questions not tested in v2. The prompt-paraphrasing analysis and SHANS feature-overlap analysis were already present and are retained.

E5.justification: V4 newly specifies four independent repeats, reports standard deviations in result captions and model-size error bars, and adds Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for instruction ratings. Tables 4–5 additionally report between-split variability, rather than confidence intervals. V2 does not document comparable repeat counts or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V4 adds BBQ-NLG, model-size, capability-preservation, and held-out baseline results. For example, its new pretrained-versus-FIT comparisons report Llama instruction ratings of 3.51 versus 3.45 and MMLU accuracy of 30.4% versus 29.6% (Tables 1–2). These are newly reported experiments, not v2-to-v4 performance gains; existing benchmark results also receive new numerical summaries.

M1.justification: The core FIT objective and instruction-sampling procedure are retained. However, v4 Definition 1 omits v2's standalone ignore(C) target case, while Appendix H.1 claims expanded LoRA coverage but names value projections twice and conflicts with Appendix D.1. Whether these represent procedural changes or documentation errors is unresolved.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and methodological explanations are extensively rewritten. V4 introduces a more explicit subsection structure, reorganizes the appendix into thematic lettered sections, moves the main SS experiment into Appendix E, and expands the ablation narrative.

P2.justification: V4 adopts a two-column main-paper layout, redraws introductory schematics and causal graphs, combines standard and shifted SMNLI plots, and relocates the paraphrasing display. It also adds numerical tables and NLG/model-size figures and reformats prompt templates as figures.

R1.justification: V4 substantially expands positioning around conditional SFT, SteerLM, alignment tax, sycophancy, and latent steering. It also cites Wu et al. (2025) to justify selecting SFT rather than latent-steering baselines. These are substantive additions beyond bibliographic updates to retained references.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds a general SS predictivity derivation for unbalanced labels, retaining the balanced case as a corollary. Appendices E–F remove unnecessary balance assumptions and replace independence proofs, correcting erroneous steps in v2. The SS causal graph also changes from a hidden common cause to a direct C-to-S relationship (v2 Figure 13; v4 Figure 11b).

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens the paper by addressing v2's undocumented uncertainty, limited validation beyond classification, and errors in its independence proofs. The new generation, capability-retention, and scaling studies provide meaningful additional evidence. Split and adapter inconsistencies remain, and nonsignificant rating differences do not establish capability equivalence, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the experimental and mathematical improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FIT study. Their main texts, figures, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V4 retains original FIT experiments and adds BBQ-NLG, instruction-following, MMLU, and model-size results.

before.justification: V2 reports original FIT experiments on SS, SMNLI, BBQ, and SHANS, including distribution-shift and feature-generalization results.

results.title: Focus On This, Not That! Steering LLMs with Adaptive Feature Specification

C1.justification: Beyond v1's central claim of improved T5 mathematics performance, v2 explicitly claims compatibility with multi-digit tokenizers, performance comparable to a regression head, preservation of text-task performance, and effectiveness at billion-parameter scale. These broaden the contributions stated in the abstract, introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning equal weighting of digit positions and instability from large multi-digit tokens, recommending digit-level tokenization. It also interprets accuracy–R2 discrepancies, task-dependent benefits of combining GCE with NTL, and generalization behavior. V1's explanation for the lack of benefit from adding NTL-MSE to RT is removed.

D1.justification: V2 expands Algorithm A2 and supplies task-specific training iterations, loss weights, subset sizes, module choices, MultiRC processing instructions and runtime-benchmark controls. Appendix A.6 adds A100 and A40 hardware alongside A6000. The original software version, core mathematics settings and repository link are retained; the additions substantially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The original DeepMind mathematics coverage is retained. V2 additionally evaluates humor-score regression on rJokes, generative reading comprehension on MultiRC, GSM8K mathematical reasoning, and controlled multiplication scenarios, substantially broadening the represented tasks and data.

E2.justification: V2 adds Gaussian Cross Entropy comparisons (Tables 3 and A6), a T5 regression-head control (Table 4), and P10, P1000, B1999 and FP15 encoding comparisons (Table A1). The RT-plus-NTL-MSE comparator is removed from the retained mathematics comparison in Table 1.

E3.justification: The original mathematics splits and 1.05M-step budget remain. New protocols include 100,000-example T5-small ablations trained for 2.5M iterations, tokenizer controls, decoder-only model configurations, T5-3B evaluation, and MultiRC reformulated as answer generation. For the retained benchmark, v2 changes xVal accuracy from exact matching to matching predictions rounded to two decimal places.

E4.justification: V2 adds loss-weight and loss-family ablations, Gaussian smoothing and combination tests, tokenizer controls, runtime and sample-efficiency analyses, and GSM8K digit-boundary and error-distribution studies. Appendix Figures A2–A4 and Example 1 add generalization analyses, token-distribution evidence and a worked comparison beyond v1's limited analyses.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates without repeated-run uncertainty. V2 introduces means and standard deviations across runs for multiple evaluations, including four-run ablations. Some counts conflict: rJokes uses three runs in Section 4.3 and Appendix A.6.3, five in Table 4's caption, and four in Table 6's caption. These discrepancies limit interpretation but do not obscure the substantial reporting change.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive benchmark and analysis results, including GSM8K accuracy of 13.5% for CE versus 17.7% for NTL (Table 9). In corresponding Table 1, NTL-MAE entries replace RT-plus-NTL-MSE entries, and T5 extrapolation accuracy changes from 0.3686 to 0.367 beyond rounding. xVal's new 0.10/0.058 accuracies use the revised rounding criterion; Figure A1 still displays zero, creating an internal inconsistency.

M1.justification: The CE-plus-NTL framework and MSE branch remain, but v2 replaces the default Wasserstein CDF computation with a direct one-hot formulation that supports irregularly spaced, multi-digit tokens. It also introduces flexible transport costs and a tested cost-squashing variant (Sections 2 and 4.5; Algorithm A2). These extend the procedure beyond v1's digit-level formulation.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion, adds an explicit contribution list, separates experimental setup from the method, and organizes results around distinct claims. The appendices are reorganized into model descriptions and experiment-specific subsections. These are substantial narrative and structural changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. V2 redraws and combines the NTL schematic and loss illustration, rearranges the loss heatmaps, and moves the original performance plot to Figure A1 with altered rows. Numerous new tables, runtime plots, generalization heatmaps and error-distribution figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands its positioning through discussion of regression as classification, optimal transport, Gaussian label smoothing, decoding order, tokenizer direction and modular arithmetic. New references such as Shah and Aamodt, Stewart et al., Cuturi, and Wang et al. support substantive comparisons and distinctions beyond v1's narrower positioning.

T1.justification: V2 adds an optimal-transport definition with explicit token-distance costs, the one-hot reduction, and conditions for the CDF formulation (Equations 2–5). Appendix A.5 adds an algebraic normalization argument for xVal's incompatibility with T5. These substantially extend v1's directly stated loss formulas and informal normalization discussion.

improvement.justification: V1's broad applicability and efficiency claims rested mainly on one T5 mathematics benchmark. V2 substantially strengthens their assessment through measured runtime, additional architectures and tasks, regression-head and tokenizer controls, repeated-run reporting, and explicit limitations. Conflicting run counts, table–figure discrepancies and removal of the RT-plus-NTL comparison weaken transparency, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support and scrutiny of the method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Number Token Loss work and retain the original mathematics benchmark. Their complete main texts and appendices support comparison of equations, experiments, tables and figures despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on regression, reading comprehension, multiplication, GSM8K, computational efficiency and several ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original training and evaluation of T5, NTL variants, Regression Transformer and xVal on mathematics interpolation and extrapolation tests (Table 1).

results.title: Regress, Don't Guess -- A Regression-like Loss on Number Tokens for Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the residual-generalization contribution, low-overhead improvements for vision and language, and advantages over naive scaling. The new experiments support these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: Adds explanations of adaptive residual weighting, allocation of linear learning capacity and access to previous activations. It also supplies rank/variant recommendations and hypotheses about deeper baselines needing retuning or more tokens, while acknowledging LAUREL-40's slightly higher step time.

D1.justification: Section 3.3 supplies a concrete column-orthogonal initialization formula where v3 only named orthogonal initialization. Section 4.3 documents C4 hardware, token budget, layer counts and r=32/k=3 settings. These improve documentation without establishing changes to older experiments.

E1.justification: Section 4.3 adds a C4 language-modeling experiment. Existing ImageNet-1K and text, multilingual and multimodal task coverage remains. The new 40/41-layer comparison reuses the LLM-4B task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 6–7 introduce an extra-layer LLM comparator, BASELINE-41, alongside BASELINE-40 and LAUREL-40. v3's empirical naive-scaling comparison was confined to ResNet; its LLM tables compared ordinary residual connections with LAUREL.

E3.justification: Adds a roughly 10B-token, 24/28-layer experiment using test loss, measured peak memory and average step time, plus a separate modified 40/41-layer LLM comparison. These substantially extend evaluation design; the original ImageNet and large-LLM protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Section 4.3/Table 5 newly compares RW, LR, PA and two combinations on a common small-LLM baseline, testing their quality/resource tradeoffs. Section 4.5 adds an empirical LLM scaling analysis. The existing ResNet rank-sensitivity study remains.

E5.justification: v4 explicitly identifies statistical significance in Tables 1, 3 and 7 and adds ± uncertainty estimates in Table 7. Five-trial ImageNet reporting remains. The new estimates and testing procedures are unspecified, and an increase in training runs is not established.

E6.justification: Tables 5–7 add loss, resource and downstream results under new configurations. For example, C4 RW+LR+PA loss is 2.9499 versus BASELINE-28's 2.9963. Existing raw scores in Tables 1–3 remain, while reported relative gains change for TyDi QA (6.07% to 6.76%) and MGSM (6.07% to 15.45%).

M1.justification: The RW, LR, PA and combined variants retain their operations and formulations in Sections 2.1–2.4. Expanded explanations and initialization documentation do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: Prose is edited across sections, LLM-1/LLM-2 become LLM-1B/LLM-4B, and subsection titles are shortened. Explanatory paragraphs, an ablation subsection, acknowledgments and an impact statement are added; the overall narrative order remains.

P2.justification: Adds three result tables, redraws Figures 1–2, compacts Table 4, revises highlighting and caption explanations, and relocates Figure 3. These substantially expand and revise the displays, although the existing rank curve and most original table content remain.

R1.justification: Section 5 replaces broad compression, pruning, distillation and progressive-training coverage with detailed comparisons to DenseNet, gated residual connections, Highway Nets and Residual Gates. LoRA and AltUp remain, but positioning now focuses substantially on LAUREL's relationship to closer residual architectures.

T1.justification: LAUREL's mathematical formulations and Table 4's parameter, memory and latency bounds remain equivalent. Reordered sums, explicit PA input notation and reformatted expressions do not add theoretical results or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses an important gap in v3's efficiency evidence through measured variant-level loss, memory and timing comparisons and a direct extra-layer LLM comparison (Tables 5–7). Its focus on closer residual architectures also improves research positioning. These substantially strengthen the paper despite remaining limitations: uncertainty procedures and the large-model configuration change are underexplained, and LAUREL-40 is slightly slower than BASELINE-41 rather than uniformly more efficient.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LAUREL work, with readable text, equations, figures and tables through the references. Complete inspection found no separate appendices in either version.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds C4 variant experiments and LLM scaling comparisons in Tables 5–7.

before.justification: v3 reports original ResNet-50/ImageNet-1K and 1B/4B LLM experiments in Tables 1–3, plus the rank-sensitivity experiment in Figure 3.

results.title: LAuReL: Learned Augmented Residual Layer

C1.justification: Both versions retain the same central contributions: full-rank gradient splitting, SGDM/SGD convergence guarantees, effective memory-efficient language-model training, and output-layer sensitivity. v1 already claims success with the same or smaller memory budget, so v2's emphasis on less memory does not introduce a substantively new core claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about hyperparameter tuning, iteration-based versus wall-clock comparisons, untested 7B-plus pre-training, language-only applicability, and potentially better subspace-selection strategies (Appendices B and F). It also interprets new precision experiments as showing that larger bfloat16 models can fail to compensate for precision-related degradation. These substantially expand v1's interpretations and limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds PyTorch-like Algorithms 4–5 documenting projected/block updates and Adam/signSGD internals, plus settings for the new experiments. The code pointer changes from GitHub to an anonymous hosting address, and the removed 7B setup details disappear. The new documentation has a concrete inconsistency: Algorithm 4, line 11 uses grad_full instead of grad in the residual calculation, conflicting with Algorithm 1.

E1.justification: v2 retains C4 and GLUE and adds Commonsense170K training with evaluation on BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e, ARC-c, and OBQA (Section 7.2, Table 7). This substantially extends fine-tuning coverage to decoder-language-model commonsense reasoning.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with AdaMeM, Fira, and LDAdam (Tables 20–21), Lion and GaLore with Lion (Table 11), and a full-parameter GLUE reference row (Table 6). Removing v1's 7B experiment also removes its comparisons with 8-bit Adam and 8-bit GaLore. Adam/AdamW relabeling is not counted as a new comparator.

E3.justification: v2 adds 3B training for 300k steps with weight decay and clipping, rank-32 commonsense fine-tuning, GPT-2 tokenization, and precision/model-size controls. Its Fira/LDAdam comparison enables decay and clipping or norm limiting, unlike the retained main C4 protocol. The 20k-step standalone SGD/signSGD experiment becomes a 200k-step FRUGAL comparison, while v1's pure-bfloat16 7B protocol is removed.

E4.justification: New analyses test precision versus model size, GPT-2 architecture, beta2 = 0.95, and Lion as the state-full optimizer. v1's standalone SGD/signSGD learning-rate sweep is replaced by a comparison of those optimizers within FRUGAL (v2 Table 10). Existing scheduler, density, block-selection, update-frequency, output-head, and state-reprojection analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Section 6.3 explicitly reports a single training run for the new 3B experiment because of computational constraints. The existing three-run GLUE mean/standard-deviation reporting and five-run quadratic experiment remain unchanged. Neither version establishes increased repetition for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Retained primary C4/GLUE values remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results. Table 7 reports commonsense averages of 84.89/84.94 for FRUGAL ranks 32/0, versus 84.65 for GaLore and 84.18 for LoRA. Under Table 21's modified protocol, 350M perplexities are 13.99 for FRUGAL, 13.74 for Fira, and 13.54 for LDAdam; these are new comparisons, not same-setting changes from v1. v1's 7B results, standalone optimizer sweep, and Table 1's 20k/100k columns are removed.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the gradient splitting, complementary updates, and optimizer-state management procedures. Blockwise pre-training and columnwise fine-tuning already appear in v1. Lion experiments instantiate the existing configurable framework; the added pseudocode does not establish a revised method.

P1.justification: Existing introductory and methodological prose is extensively condensed and reorganized. Empirical motivation and the framework become separate sections, pre-training and fine-tuning become separate major sections, and zero-density training receives its own subsection. Appendix organization, terminology such as Logits/Output layer, and publication headers also change.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column ICML layout. The three original figures retain their graphics but are resized or relocated. Table 1 is restructured around projection type and residual updating, numerous tables are added or rearranged, and two substantial pseudocode displays are introduced.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix B substantially revise positioning through detailed comparisons with Fira, LDAdam, and AdaMeM, including residual handling, state reprojection, preconditioning, and computational tradeoffs. AdaMeM is positioned as a special case of FRUGAL. Additional experimental references and removal of some earlier PEFT/coordinate-descent citations accompany this expansion.

T1.justification: v2 Section 5.1 explicitly requires continuous differentiability and Lipschitz gradients, beyond v1's explicit one-sided quadratic-upper-bound definition in Appendix E. This refines the formal smoothness requirements. The convergence rates, appendix proofs, and memory derivations otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through decoder-LLM fine-tuning, targeted optimizer and architecture ablations, and comparisons with closely related full-gradient methods, addressing important gaps in v1. Appendix B reports unfavorable comparisons and tuning caveats, while Appendix F clarifies applicability limits. These gains outweigh the removal of preliminary 7B pre-training evidence, although the blanket superiority claim and the inconsistent residual calculation in the new pseudocode remain weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FRUGAL and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Content can be reliably matched despite substantial reformatting, reorganization, additions, and removals.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments including 3B pre-training, LLaMA-3.1-8B commonsense fine-tuning, and concurrent-optimizer comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original C4 pre-training, GLUE fine-tuning, ablation, and quadratic optimization results, including Tables 2–4 and Figure 3.

results.title: FRUGAL: Memory-Efficient Optimization by Reducing State Overhead for Scalable Training

C1.justification: V2 leaves Hopper implementation to future work. V4's abstract, introduction, and conclusion add the substantive claim of matching FlashAttention3-FP8 speed on Hopper while achieving substantially higher accuracy. The original technique contributions and broad plug-and-play accuracy claims remain.

C2.justification: V4 newly explains why transferring outliers with SmoothQuant is ineffective when both Q and K contain outliers, and why numerous small softmax values favor floating-point over integer quantization (Sections 3.1 and 3.3). The conditional benefits and optional status of V smoothing are retained.

D1.justification: V4 adds details about fused preprocessing, on-chip correction, register accumulation, and the 128-by-64, four-warp quantization-group example in Appendix A.5. It also identifies the long-context checkpoint. CUDA implementation and code access remain, but v2's Ubuntu 22.04 environment disclosure is omitted.

E1.justification: V4 extends existing long-context coverage with InfiniBench, including summarization, QA, code debugging, mathematical search, and retrieval tasks (Appendix A.7, Table 14). The original language, image/video generation, image classification, and Needle-in-a-Haystack coverage remains.

E2.justification: V2 cites FlashAttention3 without evaluating it. V4 adds FlashAttn3-fp8 to the CogvideoX-1.5, HunyuanVideo, and Mochi comparisons in Table 2 and to long-context comparisons. Hopper kernel plots also evaluate FlashAttention3 in FP16 and FP8. This introduces a directly relevant competing attention implementation.

E3.justification: V4 adds H100/H20 kernel measurements and evaluates Llama-3-262k (8B) up to 262k tokens on H100, extending the existing context-length/needle-depth evaluation. Original head dimensions, causal/noncausal configurations, benchmark metrics, and end-to-end latency settings are retained.

E4.justification: Table 18 adds component-overhead profiling beyond v2's single smoothing-overhead estimate. V4 also extends NIAH robustness comparisons to longer contexts with FlashAttn3-fp8 and adds its video failure examples in Figure 8. Existing smoothing, quantization-granularity, datatype, and optional V-smoothing ablations largely remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, run-to-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Retained averages and worst cases across layers summarize quantization accuracy rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: V4 adds Hopper timings, FlashAttn3-fp8 video scores, component-overhead results, and long-context outcomes. Table 14 newly reports InfiniBench averages of 43.05 for full precision, 41.53 for FlashAttn3-fp8, and 43.06 for SageAttention2. Most existing end-to-end values remain unchanged; v4 Table 5 omits v2 Table 1's CogvideoX VQA-a column.

M1.justification: V2's Equation 4 and Algorithm 1 use a sequence-wide Q mean before tiling; v4's Equation 2 and Algorithm 1 use a separate mean and correction for each query block. This revises one component of the retained quantized-attention procedure. Two-level accumulation describes the existing FP32-buffer strategy.

P1.justification: The preliminaries and method explanations are substantially rewritten and reorganized. FP8 quantization receives a dedicated subsection, while detailed per-thread formulas, dataset/metric descriptions, optional V-smoothing discussion, and several experiments move into Appendix A. Terminology and kernel names are standardized.

P2.justification: V4 adopts a two-column main layout, repartitions large benchmark tables between the main text and appendices, relocates many displays, and rearranges distribution plots. It adds Hopper charts, FlashAttention3 video comparisons, and a memory-layout diagram, while removing v2's standalone naive-INT4 video illustration.

R1.justification: V4 adds CUTLASS, DeepSeek-V3, and InfiniBench references. Section 3.4 acknowledges earlier two-level accumulation for linear layers and locates the claimed novelty in attention. Positioning against FlashAttention3-FP8 becomes explicit, while most existing literature coverage remains; numerous publication updates are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: V4 Section 3.1 replaces v2 Equation 4's abbreviated smoothed-product equality with an explicit expansion containing a row-constant bias and explains why softmax permits discarding it. It also defines block-specific Q means. These are limited mathematical revisions; the per-thread formulas and accumulation principle largely remain.

improvement.justification: V4 resolves v2's explicitly deferred Hopper evaluation and missing direct FlashAttention3-FP8 comparison, substantially strengthening its practical speed-and-accuracy evidence. Longer-context testing and the more explicit smoothing derivation further improve support and clarity. These gains outweigh the limited loss of one ablation metric and the operating-system disclosure; most earlier experimental evidence is preserved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SageAttention2 and provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures. All 19 pages of v2 and 20 pages of v4 were inspected, including v4's Appendix A. Material relocated from v2 can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V4 retains original experimental results and adds Hopper GPU comparisons, FlashAttention3-FP8 evaluations, and long-context results in the appendices.

before.justification: V2 reports original kernel benchmarks, end-to-end model evaluations, and quantization ablations, including Figures 8–11 and Tables 10–13.

results.title: SageAttention2: Efficient Attention with Thorough Outlier Smoothing and Per-thread INT4 Quantization

C1.justification: Both versions propose local denoising as a mechanism for diffusion generalization. V2 expands the central contribution to two PSPC variants, claims better approximation than previously proposed methods, and adds the claim that complete PSPC samples share structural similarities with neural-network samples (Abstract, Introduction, and Conclusions).

C2.justification: V1's explanation that patch errors compound into unrealistic samples is retained and elaborated through v2's trajectory discussion. V2 additionally proposes using patch posterior probabilities for training-image attribution and discusses copyright, licensing, and computational-efficiency implications (Section 8 and Impact Statement). The central mechanism and sampling-quality limitation remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents nearest-neighbour patch-mean estimation, gradient-map construction using 1,000 samples, flexible-patch thresholds, FFHQ/AFHQ schedules, U-ViT checkpoint conversion, and SSCD checkpoint and sampling instructions. The original DiT training budget and hyperparameter table are retained.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates CIFAR-10. V2 adds denoising and sampling experiments on 64×64 FFHQ faces and AFHQv2 animal images, substantially expanding domain and resolution coverage. The translated and partially noise-replaced input examples from v1 Figure 3 are removed.

E2.justification: V2 adds U-ViT to the CIFAR-10 architecture comparison in Figure 2. It also evaluates a Gaussian denoiser attributed to Wang and Vastola and Li et al. in Figure 6, introducing an alternative generalization mechanism beyond v1's empirical-denoiser comparison.

E3.justification: The 150-noise-level, 10,000-sample CIFAR-10 architecture analysis is retained. V2 adds 40-step schedules and 2,000 samples per noise level and process for FFHQ/AFHQ. It also introduces SSCD evaluation using 1,000 shared initial latents and deterministic Euler sampling (Appendix C.1), materially expanding the evaluation design.

E4.justification: The gradient-locality and patch-size analyses are retained, while v1's translation and noise-replacement case study is removed. V2 adds comparisons testing flexible patch geometry, gradient-derived mask visualizations, and complete sampling-trajectory analyses examining accumulated errors (Figures 6–8).

E5.justification: V1 Figure 6 displays mean MSE with intervals labelled 50% and 95% confidence intervals. V2's replacement Figure 6 removes these intervals and reports mean curves only; its SSCD comparison also reports point averages. This withdraws uncertainty reporting from the central comparison, although v1 does not explain the interval construction.

E6.justification: V2 adds U-ViT results, PSPC-Flex and Gaussian-denoiser MSE curves across three datasets, and complete sampling results. Figure 9 reports average SSCD similarity to neural-network samples of 0.55 for PSPC-Flex versus 0.34 for both optimal and Gaussian denoisers. These are newly reported comparisons; the eight original appendix denoiser grids are retained.

M1.justification: V1 averages overlapping square patch posterior means with noise-dependent patch sizes. V2 retains this construction as PSPC-Square and introduces PSPC-Flex, which selects non-square patches from network gradient sensitivity maps using time-dependent thresholds (Section 5). This adds a substantive denoising component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, and method narrative are extensively rewritten. Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 7, the method is reorganized into local mechanisms and PSPC variants, Results becomes a separate section, and the appendices are reordered and expanded.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main layout, reorganizes image comparisons, moves the composite diagram from the appendix into the main text, and expands Figure 6 into a multi-dataset display. New mask, trajectory, similarity, and schedule figures are added. The eight existing appendix grids are enlarged to one per page rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against alternative mechanisms, discussing Gaussian-score explanations and distinguishing PSPC's flexible patches from the concurrent square-patch method of Kamb and Ganguli. It also adds discussion of patch-based diffusion training and data-replication research, beyond v1's narrower related-work coverage.

T1.justification: V2 extends the formal composite from square crops in v1 Equation 6 to arbitrary patch sets in Equation 11 and introduces the gradient-threshold cropping definition in Equation 12. The underlying posterior-mean reasoning remains, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the mechanistic hypothesis through flexible patches, comparisons with a Gaussian alternative across three datasets, and quantitative validation of complete sampling trajectories and outputs. These address v1's narrow empirical scope and lack of quantitative sample-level validation. Removing confidence intervals and the input-transformation case study weakens parts of the evidence, and poor final sample quality persists, but the added methodological and empirical support provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renamed in v2.
