after.justification: V2 retains original empirical analyses and adds experiments on FFHQ and AFHQv2, flexible patch denoising, and generated-sample similarity.

before.justification: V1 reports original CIFAR-10 experiments measuring denoiser approximation errors, gradient locality, input-transformation responses, and patch-composite outputs.

results.title: Towards a Mechanistic Explanation of Diffusion Model Generalization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: shared local inductive biases, patch denoising as a partial generalization mechanism, and PSPC's similarity to network outputs. Additional evidence supports these existing claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: Appendix D.3 explicitly discusses PSPC's remaining approximation gap relative to other neural denoisers and identifies closing it as future work. Section 7 newly explains why localized patch sets can benefit spatially aligned FFHQ images. The existing sampling-artifact limitation remains.

D1.justification: The introduction adds access information for an open-source implementation of PSPC and other denoisers. Section 4 explicitly clarifies that square cropping excludes patches requiring boundary padding. Existing architecture tables, training hyperparameters, and patch schedules are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CIFAR-10, FFHQ at 64×64, and AFHQv2 at 64×64 through denoising and diffusion sampling. Additional network configurations introduce no new dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: CFDM moves from citation-only coverage in v2 to evaluated comparisons in v3 Figures 7 and 9. Figure 9 also adds PSPC-Square, while Appendix D adds neural-to-neural MSE comparisons and additional reference networks, substantially broadening direct comparisons.

E3.justification: Section 3.1 changes the reported gradient-analysis sample count from 10,000 to 1,000; whether experiments were rerun is unspecified. v3 also introduces 50k FID reporting and patch-error evaluations using additional networks' reverse processes. Existing training settings and the SSCD protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix D tests whether gradient locality and patch-size behaviour extend beyond DDPM++, adding NCSN++ and DiT gradient analyses and additional transformer patch-error analyses. Figures 9 and 25 also extend the Square-versus-Flex comparison to generated samples, materially expanding validation of the proposed mechanism.

E5.justification: The reporting practice remains point estimates and averages, including SSCD averages over 1,000 shared initializations. No repeated-training results, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests are added. The gradient sample-count revision concerns evaluation sample size.

E6.justification: v3 adds CFDM error curves, extensive cross-network results, FID scores in Table 3, and new sampling comparisons. Figure 9 adds CFDM's mean network similarity of 0.23 and PSPC-Square entries, while retaining the original submatrix and PSPC-Flex mean of 0.55.

M1.justification: PSPC aggregation, square-patch scheduling, gradient-based flexible patches, and nearest-neighbour posterior estimation remain unchanged. The new boundary-handling explanation documents the existing cropping definition.

P1.justification: v3 edits grammar and expands explanations of locality, gradient indexing, and patch posterior means. It inserts Appendix D, renumbers the retained qualitative appendices, and adds acknowledgements and publication information. The main section sequence and narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds a FID table and several analytical figures, expands Figure 9 from a 7×7 to a 9×9 matrix, and adds Figure 25. Retained denoiser grids are arranged two per page, and v2 Figures 21–23 are consolidated into v3 Figure 24 without changing their samples.

R1.justification: Section 7 substantially expands positioning within classical patch synthesis and single-image GAN/diffusion research, adding works such as PatchMatch, SinGAN, SinFusion, and SinDiffusion. It also develops the comparison with Kamb and Ganguli around localized patch sets and architectural scope.

T1.justification: Equation (8) corrects the denoiser argument from x to noisy input z in the formal gradient-sensitivity definition, resolving its inconsistency with differentiation with respect to z. The posterior definitions, PSPC equations, and mathematical reasoning otherwise remain unchanged; no proofs are added.

improvement.justification: Appendix D addresses an important evidential weakness: v2's locality and patch-error analyses focused on DDPM++, despite the central claim spanning architectures. Direct checks on additional CNN and transformer denoisers substantially strengthen that claim. CFDM and neural-peer comparisons better establish PSPC's strengths and remaining gap. Some new baseline documentation remains incomplete, but the improved empirical support and added code-access information provide a substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PSPC diffusion-generalization work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, and added content.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds CFDM comparisons and further architecture-dependent analyses in Appendix D.

before.justification: v2 reports original denoiser-error and gradient analyses, PSPC-generated samples, and CIFAR-10 SSCD comparisons.

results.title: Towards a Mechanistic Explanation of Diffusion Model Generalization

C1.justification: Both versions claim a causal interpretation of masked GPT attention, zero-shot causal structure recovery, and an association between structural confidence and legal generation. The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain these claims; the new experiments supply additional support.

C2.justification: v2 interprets pruning as evidence that high-confidence heads contribute to legal generation and connects the illustrated graph's relations to move-enabling conditions. The short-sequence memorization explanation remains, while v1's speculation about endgame memorization is omitted.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility details: partial-correlation/Fisher-z CI testing, alpha = 0.01, averaging across eight heads, common prefix trimming of the 1,000 sequences, and explicit restricted-ICD pseudocode. These are newly documented details, not demonstrated changes to existing settings. However, v1's Causality Lab package link is removed.

E1.justification: Coverage remains Othello move sequences, legality and attention-derived structures, using the retained pretrained model and random legal-sequence evaluation. The new pruning and n-gram analyses do not introduce a distinct domain or task; held-out real-world sequences constitute a split within existing coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 5 adds reverse-order pruning of high-confidence heads as a comparator to pruning low-confidence heads. The four existing CI-conditioning variants remain unchanged. Voita et al. is cited for pruning motivation, not evaluated as another baseline.

E3.justification: The new pruning experiment pools 8,000 sequence/head scores, applies thresholds at the 10th–90th percentiles, skips heads without retraining, and compares normalized legality under opposite pruning orders. Appendix B adds a protocol comparing 2–6-gram frequencies using training, random-test and held-out real-world sequences.

E4.justification: v2 adds a head-removal intervention testing the functional importance of structural confidence, an Othello graph-recovery case study in Figure 1, and training/test distribution analysis in Appendix B. The original conditioning-set ablation is retained as Figure 4.

E5.justification: v1 already reports 95% confidence intervals and statistical significance for the CI ablation. v2 specifies that these intervals use an unpaired t-test. Neither version reports additional repeated runs or seeds establishing an increase in replication.

E6.justification: New results show that pruning low-confidence heads generally preserves legality better than reverse-order pruning, and that random test sequences have lower training n-gram match frequencies. Figure 1 adds a recovered four-move graph. The reported 95% overall accuracy, 88% after 15 moves, and original CI-ablation findings are retained.

M1.justification: The covariance construction, entropy-difference confidence score and recursive discovery procedure remain unchanged. v2's modified-ICD pseudocode documents the restriction to newly added edges already specified in v1 Algorithm 1. Head pruning is introduced as an experimental ablation.

P1.justification: The title, author list and wording are revised, while the main five-section narrative remains intact. Definitions, the covariance derivation and algorithm explanation move into the main text; appendices and references are reorganized. Some section cross-references become inaccurate.

P2.justification: The paper switches from single-column to two-column layout and adds Figures 1, 5 and 6 plus colored modified-ICD pseudocode. Existing plots are resized and rearranged: CI-ablation panels change from a 2-by-2 grid to one row, and the length-10 confidence plot loses its connecting line.

R1.justification: Voita et al. (2019) is newly cited to support pruning without retraining. Positioning relative to ABCD, BERT and prior Othello world-representation studies remains substantially unchanged; other reference changes mainly concern formatting and bibliographic metadata.

T1.justification: The SCM assumptions, Markov/faithfulness definitions and covariance derivation are retained, with some material moved into Section 2. Appendix B newly states a finite-context conditional-dependence assumption in Equation 11 and defines its n-gram frequency estimator, constituting limited formal additions.

improvement.justification: v1 relies largely on confidence–legality associations. v2's head-pruning intervention tests whether the identified heads matter for generation, substantially strengthening this central evidence, while expanded CI/ICD details improve reproducibility. The removed package link and cross-reference errors are limited drawbacks. The intervention supports functional importance without establishing the correctness of every recovered causal relation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GPT-attention causal-world-model research. All 11 pages of each version, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison despite substantial layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original head-pruning results, an illustrated recovered graph, and training/test n-gram analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of a pretrained Othello GPT on 1,000 random legal sequences, including confidence–legality relationships and conditional-independence ablations.

results.title: A Causal World Model Underlying Next Token Prediction: Exploring GPT in a Controlled Environment

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and Discussion retain the central warnings about non-conservative forces and the recommendation to combine conservative and direct-force predictions for reliable acceleration. The added experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving receptive range and descriptor degeneracies, extends the discussion to stress/enthalpy conservation, explains why energy rescaling does not restore equipartition, and attributes the tested GLE's failure to insufficient damping of near-diffusive modes. These substantially broaden the mechanism and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v3 specifies PET-MAD version 1.1 for stress tests, identifies the barostat and GLE parameters, and discloses that its MTS implementation does not reuse conservative/direct computations. A practical MTS example link supplements the existing Zenodo archive. Earlier software versions and hardware disclosures remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds molecular-dynamics evaluations of benzene on graphene, alanine dipeptide in water, and oxygen on a Sc-Co-Al alloy surface, plus NPH/NPT direct-stress tasks (Appendices G and I). OC20 training already appeared in v2; the adsorbate dynamics evaluation is new task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds PET-MAD comparisons involving conservative, direct and MTS stress treatments, and conservative versus velocity-rescaled direct-force dynamics (Appendices G.3–G.4). Earlier comparator membership is retained. The ORB-v2 wording is a clarification: v2 already specifies orb-v2.

E3.justification: New protocols include a two-versus-three-message-passing-layer comparison, constant-pressure tests holding forces conservative while varying stresses, stepwise velocity rescaling, and a specified high-pass GLE thermostat (Appendices C and G). These substantially expand the evaluation design; existing training splits, budgets and optimization criteria are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds a receptive-range/depth ablation, controls isolating direct-stress errors, tests of velocity rescaling and GLE stabilization, and MTS stride/stability analysis for adsorbed oxygen. These examine several additional failure mechanisms and mitigation strategies beyond the retained v2 analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report parenthesized temperature uncertainties and structural-correlation bands spanning two standard errors. The new GLE table follows the existing reporting practice; v3 adds no reported seed counts, repeated-run counts or statistical estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Matched existing tables retain their numerical entries. New results include depth-dependent force errors (Table 3), GLE temperatures of 1181.5 K for ORB and 524.1 K for PET-NC (Table 9), stress/rescaling trajectories, and MTS-8 slowdowns of 1.19 for oxygen/alloy and 1.18 for water (Table 10). These are additional results under their stated conditions.

M1.justification: v3 extends hybrid multiple time stepping to periodic conservative-stress corrections in constant-pressure dynamics (Appendix G.3). The PET architectures, conservative fine-tuning procedure and existing force-based MTS updates remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose are retained. Changes include local grammar and terminology edits, expanded explanations, inserted appendix subsections, updated cross-references, and reversal of the Acknowledgements/Impact Statement order.

P2.justification: v3 adds displays for interaction range, stress dynamics, velocity rescaling, GLE results and MTS timings/adsorbate dynamics. The materials plot expands from three to five panels. Retained displays are largely relocated or renumbered, with some axis, legend and caption edits; Figure 9 retains an outdated three-material caption.

R1.justification: Section 2.4 adds discussion of Eissler et al., Loew et al. and Fu et al. concerning conservation, system size, phonons and downstream reliability. Additional citations support PET-MAD, velocity rescaling, interaction range and GLE analyses, while the overall research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: New Appendix C derives the receptive-range difference between differentiated and directly predicted forces using three-body forms (Equations 10–11). Appendix I adds MTS cost expressions and computation-sharing assumptions. The original conservation criterion, harmonic-mode analysis and MTS update equations remain intact.

improvement.justification: v2's MTS simulation evidence centered on water; v3 measures practical overhead and validates the approach for adsorbed oxygen and constant-pressure stress dynamics. Controlled stress tests and evaluations of rescaling/GLE remedies substantially strengthen the investigation of failure mechanisms, while Appendix C explains an additional architectural limitation. These gains materially improve the support and usefulness of the paper's recommendations, despite the outdated Figure 9 caption.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, title, core sections and experiments. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds interaction-range experiments, heterogeneous-system simulations, stress-prediction tests, stabilization analyses and measured simulation timings.

before.justification: v2 reports original model-training results, geometry-optimization success rates, molecular-dynamics trajectories, and fine-tuning and multiple-time-stepping experiments.

results.title: The dark side of the forces: assessing non-conservative force models for atomistic machine learning

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the DSP account of spectral damage and the two-part FoPE method for improving length generalization. The newly named downstream experiments support the broad applicability claim already present in v1 rather than redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: Section 4 revises the zero-frequency rationale to emphasize short- and long-term dependencies and avoidance of positional bias. v3 adds interpretations of its mechanism simulation and low-pass argument. It also removes v1's explicit qualification that applying the modeling to cache compression, model collaboration and semantic communication requires further work.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 documents the new fine-tuning recipe: approximately 350k samples, one epoch, AdamW, learning rate 3e-4, cosine scheduling, 0.1 warmup ratio and four hours of training. Section 5.5 newly specifies the retained ablations' 5B-token Gutenberg setting. The repository pointer, pseudocode, hardware and original model hyperparameters remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds downstream summarization and few-shot evaluation on GovReport, MultiNews, TREC, TriviaQA and SAMSum. This substantially extends coverage beyond the retained C4/Gutenberg perplexity and synthetic Passkey Retrieval tasks.

E2.justification: The retained experiments use the same RoPE, ALiBi, YARN and normalization-related comparators. The new downstream evaluations reuse RoPE. The new mechanism illustration uses a constructed Ground Truth signal as its target, rather than introducing another baseline algorithm.

E3.justification: v3 introduces SmolLM-1.7B fine-tuning at context length 4096, followed by evaluation in 0–4k, 4–8k and 8k+ groups. The earlier 512-to-1024 extrapolation procedure remains, renamed continual pre-training. Appendix B.3 also changes the budget associated with reported pre-training runtimes from 20B to 10B tokens, aligning with the retained main-text setting without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: v3 Section 5.6 and Figure 3 add a two-dimensional, single-layer MLP simulation comparing FoPE and RoPE against frequency-matched attention signals. This supplements the retained FS/CF ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity studies and QK-normalization analyses with a focused mechanism check.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 1,000 Passkey Retrieval trials per context length and the same sampling information for activation and Gaussian-vector analyses. v3 adds no training-run replication counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: v3 Table 1 adds downstream results: for example, TREC at 8k+ scores 36.00 for RoPE versus 51.00 for FoPE, while TriviaQA at 0–4k scores 36.50 versus 33.26. Figure 3 adds the finding that FoPE better follows the constructed reference signal. The retained benchmark curves and toy-model loss table match v1.

M1.justification: FoPE retains the same Fourier-series construction, coefficient initialization and clipping of frequencies below 2π/N to zero. Equations (11)–(13) and the appendix implementation listing are unchanged apart from formatting.

P1.justification: Related work moves to Appendix A, implementation explanations move to Appendix C, and experimental settings are regrouped in Appendix B.3. The earlier fine-tuning section becomes continual pre-training, while Limitations is replaced by an Impact Statement. Prose revisions are localized; most of the existing narrative is retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds the mechanism plot and downstream-results table, redraws and reorders the Q/K heatmaps, expands several captions and moves the attention-decay plot into the appendix. ICML formatting and full-width appendix text and equations substantially revise the presentation beyond simple renumbering.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to Barbero et al.'s RoPE analysis, HOPE and SMR, alongside citations supporting the new model and benchmarks. The positioning that earlier approaches primarily address attention while FoPE considers other LM components remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D.3 adds sampling-theorem statements and a corollary supporting a low-pass interpretation of RoPE. Equation (22) also corrects the Fourier-transform kernel from a positive to a negative exponent. The central NUDFT formulation and spectral-damage derivations otherwise remain.

improvement.justification: v1's broad length-generalization claims relied mainly on perplexity and synthetic retrieval. v3 Section 5.4 and Table 1 address an important practical-validation gap by testing instruction-fine-tuned models on downstream tasks, reporting both advantages and the TriviaQA exception, with supporting training details in Appendix B.3. This substantially strengthens empirical support for applicability. The removed applicability caveat and continued absence of run-level uncertainty limit transparency, but do not outweigh that gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Fourier Position Embedding (FoPE) work. Their complete text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds downstream evaluations using SmolLM-1.7B and a simulated attention-mechanism comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original C4/Gutenberg training experiments, Passkey Retrieval evaluations, component ablations and toy-model normalization results.

results.title: Fourier Position Embedding: Enhancing Attention's Periodic Extension for Length Generalization

C1.justification: The central critique of aleatoric–epistemic terminology is retained. However, v1’s contribution of a minimal entropy-based clarification becomes a broader claimed unification of uncertainty, predictive performance and data dispersion through decision theory. v2 also makes explaining BALD’s practical acquisition utility a principal contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explains errors arising from simulated future data and approximate model updating, deemphasizes infinite-data decompositions for practical acquisition, and proposes a short-run explanation of BALD’s usefulness. It adds substantive qualifications about loss choice, imperfect reference systems and the non-universality of the observed estimation-error ranking.

D1.justification: New Appendix C supplies Gaussian-process training points, kernel and noise scale, reference distributions, conjugate-model specifications and error calculations. It also provides a code link for Figures 3–4; v1 has no comparable implementation or code-access information. Figure 5’s detailed setups are delegated to cited papers.

E1.justification: v1 has no original experimental coverage. v2 adds a Gaussian-process regression example, Bernoulli and Gaussian prediction simulations, and active learning on Curated MNIST and Coarse ImageNet (Figures 3–5 and Appendix C).

E2.justification: Figure 5 introduces evaluated comparisons among BALD, predictive-entropy acquisition and random acquisition on both image tasks. v1 discusses acquisition methods but reports no experimental comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 introduces experimental protocols: a two-point Gaussian-process example evaluated under two losses; exact conjugate inference at n = 1, 10, 100 and 1000 using squared estimation errors; and test negative log likelihood versus acquired labels. These are new settings, not revisions of experiments reported in v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantive diagnostic analyses: Figure 3 tests how uncertainty, predictive performance and data dispersion differ under two losses; Figure 4 examines sample-size sensitivity and compares short-run versus long-run information-gain estimation errors. v1 offers analytical discussion and cites external findings instead.

E5.justification: Figure 4 and Appendix C.2 newly specify averaging over 50 repeats with different random-number seeds and display predictions across seeds. v1 contains no corresponding repeated-run or statistical reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds all empirical result curves. They demonstrate distinct uncertainty/performance/dispersion behavior, smaller short-run than long-run information-gain estimation errors in the studied conjugate models, and BALD’s advantage over entropy acquisition in Figure 5. These are newly reported findings, not same-setting performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The proposed uncertainty-estimation framework expands from predictive entropy and BALD-based estimators to loss-derived uncertainty and policy-dependent expected uncertainty reduction. v2 Sections 5.1–5.3 introduce an estimator with separate proxies for future-data generation and model updating, substantially broadening the framework’s inputs and computations.

P1.justification: The introduction, key-concept exposition, alternative perspective and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Sections 3 and 5 become detailed numbered subsections, the former related-work section is integrated into Background, and examples, proofs and implementation details are organized into three appendices.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the earlier decomposition schematic with a broader decision-theory diagram, revises and renumbers v1’s ambiguity diagram as Figure 2, and adds experimental Figures 3–5. Main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout, while appendices use full-width presentation.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from making minimal changes to existing uncertainty discussions toward unifying them through decision theory. v2 substantially adds decision-theory, model-selection and estimation literature, including Dawid, DeGroot, Neiswanger and Huang, while removing much of v1’s engineering-history discussion and associated references.

T1.justification: v2 generalizes the entropy decomposition to loss- and policy-dependent expected uncertainty reduction, adds scoring-rule and discrepancy derivations, and establishes additional Bayes-estimator results. v1’s first two propositions correspond to v2’s Propositions 4–5 with explicit posterior-concentration assumptions. Proposition 6 and the derivations in Appendices A–B substantially extend the theory.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly acknowledged abstracting away dependence on the actual data and learning algorithm. v2 addresses that important limitation through its policy- and update-dependent framework, clarifies estimator assumptions, and adds original demonstrations with implementation details. These changes substantially strengthen precision and evidential support, despite limited local documentation of Figure 5’s experimental settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching title, authors and central critique. All pages are readable and support comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendices; v2 includes Appendices A–C.

after.justification: v2 reports original Gaussian-process and conjugate-model computations in Figures 3–4, documented in Appendix C. Figure 5 additionally reports active-learning outcomes.

before.justification: v1 contains conceptual diagrams, theoretical propositions and analytical examples. Its discussion of empirical estimator failures explicitly attributes those results to earlier work.

results.title: Rethinking Aleatoric and Epistemic Uncertainty

C1.justification: The central contributions remain controllable feature-tree synthesis, 433k instruction examples, strong function/file-level EpiCoder performance and potential repository-level synthesis. The introduction's explicit 7.4-point BigCodeBench-Hard comparison foregrounds results already present in v1 without changing the contribution's scope.

C2.justification: V2 Section 4.3 explicitly interprets comparable-data-size results as evidence for data quality and evolutionary enhancement beyond training quantity, including improved generalization. The existing complexity, diversity, leakage and repository-scalability interpretations largely remain, with no substantive new limitations discussion.

D1.justification: V2 supplies an explicit code-and-data repository link in the abstract, whereas v1 only refers to released code. Appendix B.2 adds manual-review criteria and reviewer qualifications. Most implementation information and prompts persist, although some displayed feature-extraction prompt details are further abridged.

E1.justification: The training sources, five function-level benchmarks, Python cross-file completion task and LLaMA-Factory repository case are retained. Smaller training subsets and XFileDep quality filtering change sample selection without establishing new task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds comparisons with Magicoder-DS, distinct from Magicoder-S-DS, and SelfCodeAlign-CQ-7B in Tables 5–6. EvoEval adds Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and Codestral-22B-v0.1. The consolidated Table 1 also substantially changes comparator membership, including removing GPT-3.5-Turbo from HumanEval/MBPP and replacing GPT-4o with GPT-4-Turbo in BigCodeBench.

E3.justification: V2 Appendix B.2 adds manual question–solution consistency checks, reducing XFileDep from 930 to 466 problems and changing the evaluation sample. Section 4.3 introduces 75k-example DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B and 74k-example CodeQwen-7B training comparisons. These are substantive evaluation changes; the existing greedy decoding and XFileDep execution settings remain.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds a focused analysis testing whether EpiCoder's advantages persist with comparable training-data quantities against Magicoder, WaveCoder and SelfCodeAlign. Existing scaling, leakage, complexity, diversity and repository case analyses are retained, often relocated to appendices.

E5.justification: Neither version introduces repeated-run counts, random-seed reporting, confidence intervals or significance tests. The same complexity means, medians and standard deviations appear in v1 Table 6 and v2 Table 12; these describe variation across code samples.

E6.justification: V2 Tables 5–6 add results for the 75k and 74k models, with reported averages of 51.2 and 62.6. Figure 4 replaces XFileDep scores of 65.7/68.8 for EpiCoder-DS/Qwen with 68.2/69.7 on the reduced test set, so these are not same-setting gains. Complexity-score percentage comparisons are corrected from 1.08%/1.74% to 32.6%/52.5% without changing table scores. V2 retains old XFileDep values in Figure 1 and inconsistently reports WaveCoder EvoEval as 43.6 in Table 5 versus 42.0 in Table 7.

M1.justification: Feature extraction, tree evolution, frequency estimation, temperature-based sampling and execution-guided refinement remain unchanged. V1 Algorithms 1 and 2 correspond to v2 Algorithms 2 and 1. The retained appendix prompts establish that compatible-feature selection and task/code generation already existed despite revised main-text descriptions.

P1.justification: The abstract and main narrative are extensively condensed and reorganized. Benchmark descriptions, feature-evolution pseudocode, the file-generation illustration, and scaling/leakage analyses move into reorganized appendices. Section headings and explanations are revised, the appendix contents page is removed, and an Impact Statement is added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column preprint layout to two-column conference layout. Benchmark results are consolidated into Table 1, Tables 5–6 are added, Figure 1 becomes a radial chart, and a new FullStackBench bar chart redisplays existing results. The XFileDep flowchart adds human checking, while numerous retained displays are relocated and resized.

R1.justification: V2 adds SelfCodeAlign and OctoPack citations and expands coverage of code search, retrieval-augmented generation and tree-based code-generation research. The LIMA citation is removed. The central positioning around feature-based synthetic instruction data remains; publication updates and consolidated duplicate references are not new works.

T1.justification: Equation 1, sibling-frequency estimation, sampling mathematics and the Halstead-derived metric definitions are retained. Algorithm relocation and explicit output labels do not introduce new mathematical reasoning, assumptions or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens two central aspects of empirical validity: expert question–solution review supplements v1's automated XFileDep filtering, and matched-size Magicoder/SelfCodeAlign comparisons address the previously uncontrolled role of training-data quantity. These changes improve confidence in the benchmark and the synthesis approach's benefits; explicit code/data access also helps reproducibility. Stale XFileDep overview scores and inconsistent WaveCoder results are material reporting flaws, but do not outweigh those gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EpiCoder research. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds training-data-size comparisons, manual XFileDep validation and revised file-level evaluation results.

before.justification: V1 reports original EpiCoder fine-tuning and benchmark evaluations, XFileDep results, and quantitative analyses of synthesized code complexity, diversity, leakage and data scaling.

results.title: EpiCoder: Encompassing Diversity and Complexity in Code Generation

C1.justification: MCG becomes an additional central contribution in the abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion. The generalist-generation claims remain, while statements that parallel decoding improves efficiency without degrading quality are removed.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly acknowledges the quality loss from unmasking multiple tokens and the assumption of a supplied high-quality fragment vocabulary. It also adds Gibbs-sampling and context-calibration explanations and interprets the new GPT-remasking control. These materially qualify applicability and expand the account of why the method works.

D1.justification: Section 4.2, Algorithm 1, and Appendix D newly specify fragment scoring and selection, distinct decomposition rules, unlimited lead vocabulary size, seed provenance, SAFE split counts, and guidance settings. Baseline implementation links are added, and reported training time changes from approximately six to five hours.

E1.justification: The added DiGress comparisons introduce a GuacaMol-trained model (Appendix E.1). The four task families, ten-drug fragment benchmark, 23 PMO objectives, and five lead-optimization targets remain. Newly identifying DUD-E and ChEMBL documents the retained seeds' provenance rather than establishing new target coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds JT-VAE and DiGress to de novo comparisons, DiGress to fragment-constrained comparisons, and standard-diffusion and GPT-remasking controls. SELFIES-REINVENT and GP BO in the main PMO table were already in v1's appendix. GenMol-TR and GenMol-NR are retained under new names.

E3.justification: V2 adds guidance searches with w=2 and gamma from 0 to 0.5, a ten-fragment initialization condition, and alternative QED/SA thresholds. Table 1 also replaces one temperature/randomness configuration. Main training budgets, generation counts, and the 10,000-call PMO budget remain; 15 versus 30 lead tasks counts the same seeds under two similarity thresholds.

E4.justification: New analyses test confidence sampling, diffusion versus GPT fragment regeneration, MCG, quality-threshold sensitivity, and reduced fragment availability. Conversely, the GenMol-ZINC250k training studies disappear, and lead-remasking ablations retain only delta=0.4 rather than both similarity thresholds. Existing token/no-remasking controls are renamed, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 Tables 4 and 17 newly describe lead-optimization scores as means over three runs; v1 did not specify this aggregation or run count. This does not establish an increase in runs. Other experiments retain three-run mean/standard-deviation reporting, and lead-score dispersion remains unreported.

E6.justification: The new MCG variant reports PMO sum 18.362 versus the retained unguided 18.208, and motif-extension quality 30.1% versus 27.5%. V2 adds baseline, sensitivity, and ten-fragment results while removing ZINC250k-trained results. Lead scores also change under newly specified aggregation; v2 Tables 4 and 17 disagree for the guided 5ht1b seed -9.8 at delta=0.4 (-11.6 versus -11.8).

M1.justification: V2 introduces molecular context guidance (MCG), which combines predictions from the current sequence and a further-masked sequence to modify inference logits (Section 4.3). The BERT/MDLM backbone and fragment remasking remain; expanded documentation of fragment scoring and decomposition does not itself establish further procedural changes.

P1.justification: Section 4.2 is reorganized around scoring, attaching, and remasking; confidence-sampling details move to Appendix B; and the appendices are reorganized into A–E. The abstract, introduction, baseline descriptions, and ablation narrative are also substantially reworked.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with explicit axis scales, and the lead-results table is restructured beside a new ablation summary. V2 adds Algorithm 1, dataset and parameter tables, baseline and sensitivity displays, and molecular examples in Figures 7–8. Detailed ablations are reorganized into appendix tables.

R1.justification: V2 positions MCG relative to Karras et al.'s autoguidance and Nisonoff et al.'s discrete guidance, and adds Gibbs-sampling, fragment-design, and dataset references. Bohacek et al. and Tang et al. are removed. The broader positioning around SAFE, discrete diffusion, and generalist molecular generation remains.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's masked-diffusion background, v2 adds a CTMC-based derivation of MCG in Appendix C, a formal fragment-scoring definition, and a Gibbs-sampling formulation of fragment remasking in Section 4.2. These extend the mathematical content beyond notation or explanatory restatement.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves reproducibility and tests the method's explanations more directly: Algorithm 1 and Appendix D clarify the previously underspecified fragment pipeline, while new confidence-sampling, GPT-remasking, MCG, and threshold controls strengthen the evidence. Explicit limitations also correct the speed-quality overstatement. These gains outweigh the removed ZINC250k and strict-similarity ablations and the localized lead-score inconsistency between Tables 4 and 17.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GenMol and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Renamed and relocated material can be reliably matched across the versions.

after.justification: V2 retains original GenMol experiments and adds guidance evaluations, comparison methods, and supplementary analyses in Section 5 and Appendix E.

before.justification: V1 reports original GenMol experiments on de novo generation, fragment-constrained generation, PMO optimization, and docking-based lead optimization, including appendix results.

results.title: GenMol: A Drug Discovery Generalist with Discrete Diffusion

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same core claims: optimal feature-entry and feature-exit criteria, enhancement through meta-substitution, preservation of theoretical guarantees and computational complexity, and empirical gains. The added theory and extensions do not revise these central statements.

C2.justification: Appendix N adds substantive interpretations concerning suppression of correlated true features and removal of spurious correlated features. Appendix Q connects CoSaMP failure to pruning without subsequent least-squares refinement. Section 6 newly discusses prohibitive least-squares costs at very high dimensions and the applicability of gradient updates, CSS adaptations, and complex-domain extensions.

D1.justification: v2 adds a MATLAB implementation URL in Section 5 and image-source URLs in Appendix V. It also documents Toeplitz covariance and block-sparse signal construction for the new stress test. These improve access information and experimental documentation; the original algorithm pseudocode is largely retained.

E1.justification: Regression coverage expands from three to six datasets, adding House 16H, Prostate.v8.egen, and Spectra. New evaluations include correlated, block-sparse compressed-sensing scenarios, column subset selection on eight grayscale images, and complex line-spectrum estimation with closely spaced frequency components.

E2.justification: The original OMP, CoSaMP, and (A)BESS comparisons are retained. v2 adds Gradient Pursuit comparisons in Figures 11–12 and leverage-score selectors using 128 or 256 singular vectors in Table 3. Table 3 separately reports an optimal rank-K SVD reference bound, rather than treating it as a column-selection algorithm.

E3.justification: New protocols include five-fold prediction evaluation, a p=2000 correlated-feature test with n/p=0.05–0.10 and SNR=5–15, and task-specific CSS and complex-signal metrics. Section 5.2 also changes stated polynomial expansion from the first two regression datasets to the first five, including Superconductivity, although its reported dimension remains 80. This establishes a reporting revision, not that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix P adds robustness tests combining correlated features, low sampling rates, and noise. The brief CoSaMP failure discussion in v1 Appendix M becomes an empirical diagnosis in v2 Appendix Q, comparing pruning with least-squares refinement and plotting residual evolution under strong and weak correlations. Appendix U additionally analyzes gradient-pursuit residual convergence.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 500-run recovery/runtime reporting and 100 AudioSet trials with mean and standard deviation. The added runtime comparison uses the same 500-run boxplot practice. No new seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing practice appears; five-fold prediction averaging introduces an evaluation protocol without reporting fold variability.

E6.justification: Figure 3, Table 1, and Figure 5 retain their original results. v2 adds substantial regression, prediction, robustness, gradient-pursuit, CSS, and complex-signal results. For example, Table 3 reports Barbara K=10 error of 0.1730 for OP-(A)BESS versus 0.2437 for (A)BESS. It also contains exceptions to improvement: Cameraman K=3 gives OP 0.2767 versus OMP 0.2749. These are newly reported comparisons, not gains over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: The original criteria and Algorithms 1–4 remain essentially unchanged. However, Appendices S–U introduce Optimal Gradient Pursuit, including a selection criterion accounting for gradient updates and an optional threshold for retaining the current support. Appendix V also introduces matrix-residual selection and trace-based elimination criteria for column subset selection.

P1.justification: The title and publication information change, acknowledgements are added, and a new Discussion section organizes the extensions. The CoSaMP explanation is expanded and appendix references are updated. Most existing prose, including the abstract, introduction, and conclusion, is retained; much of the expansion consists of new scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1's elimination panels are redrawn, and Figure 4 is reorganized from nine panels into eighteen panels covering six datasets. v2 adds correlation heatmaps, failure diagnostics, prediction plots, OGP diagrams and plots, a CSS table, and complex-signal visualizations. The retained runtime Figure 5 is relocated from Appendix L to Appendix O.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and brief positioning for Gradient Pursuit, column subset selection/PCA, line-spectrum estimation, and the added datasets. The original positioning relative to greedy subset-selection methods and the independently developed SMP criterion in Remark 3.8 remains unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorems 4.10–4.11 on correlated-feature selection and elimination, their proofs and a counterexample in Appendices L–M, and OGP derivations and a residual-convergence theorem in Appendices T–U. Appendix I also revises its support assumption to use the best K-sparse approximation instead of the coefficients restricted to the selected support.

improvement.justification: v1's sparse-regression evaluation reported explanatory R2 without held-out prediction tests. v2 adds five-fold prediction evaluation and targeted correlated-feature robustness and failure analyses, substantially strengthening assessment of generalization and the proposed mechanism. It also supports new algorithmic extensions with derivations and experiments and supplies a code URL. The inconsistent preprocessing statement and uneven detail for some new experiments remain limitations, but the gains in validation and explanatory support are substantial.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same work despite the revised title. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison: Appendices A–M in v1 and A–W in v2. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds regression datasets, correlated-feature tests, cross-validation, gradient-pursuit experiments, image column subset selection, and complex-signal estimation.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic sparse-recovery experiments, AudioSet reconstruction results, regression results on three datasets, and runtime measurements in Section 5 and Appendix L.

results.title: Best Subset Selection: Optimal Pursuit for Feature Selection and Elimination

C1.justification: The main contributions remain scaling analysis, affordable multi-objective multi-fidelity tuning, competitive open-weight judges, and analysis of judge design choices. The new title foregrounds an approximately 1,000-fold cost reduction, but v1 Appendix B.3 already supplied the roughly $2.1K versus $2M estimates supporting that claim.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly qualifies that fine-tuning might improve PandaLM performance while hurting generalization. Its new Impact Statement discusses propagation of human and group biases and limits the reassurance obtainable from its small LMSys inspection. Existing explanations involving model capacity, prompt complexity and distribution shift are largely retained.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents synchronous scheduling across two cluster queues, epsilon-net tie-breaking, and per-model runtime-derived token prices in Table 6. It also revises hardware-price and annotation-time assumptions. Prompt examples and split instructions remain, and both versions still promise future code and annotation release.

E1.justification: Both use Alpaca-Eval, Arena-Hard, Chatbot Arena ratings, LMSys and PandaLM for preference judging and model ranking. v3 evaluates tuned judges on the already-covered Arena-Hard ranking task; changes in model subsets and annotation counts concern evaluation settings.

E2.justification: v3 adds a direct comparison against Arena-Hard judges using Claude Opus and GPT-4-1106-preview in Table 4, substantially expanding comparison with frontier judges. The LMSys comparator set is retained: its shortened Arena-Hard label still denotes GPT-4o mini. A Random comparator is also added to the PandaLM table.

E3.justification: Test-judge selection advances from v1's explicitly preliminary 1,200-instruction stage to the full 3,548-instruction validation set. Table 1 replaces 400 instructions times 24 models versus 6,400 human-agreement battles with 6,500 annotations for each metric, using 26 models for Spearman correlation. v3 also introduces the tuned-judge comparison on 20 models and 500 Arena-Hard instructions. Appendix B.1 replaces TogetherAI token prices with runtime-derived self-hosting estimates, materially changing the cost evaluation.

E4.justification: New Figure 13 tests split-half stability of judge scores at the three fidelity sizes, providing focused evidence about ranking reliability. Figure 7 updates the existing prompt-stability analysis, and the Impact Statement reports a limited qualitative inspection of LMSys data. The main hyperparameter-survival analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 reports variability for scaling metrics but only point estimates in its test-comparison tables. v3 adds 100-bootstrap uncertainty reporting for LMSys and the Arena-Hard comparison, plus coefficients of variation in Table 1. These are resampling procedures, not evidence of 100 independent tuning runs. LMSys prose calls the uncertainty standard errors while its caption calls it standard deviation.

E6.justification: Test results are substantially expanded and revised. LMSys JudgeLM-7B changes from 0.440 to 0.42, and a large tuned judge is added at 0.49. The largest tuned judge's PandaLM score changes from 0.74 to 0.76. New Table 4 reports Arena-Hard correlations of 0.81, 0.93 and 0.86 for the three tuned judges, versus 0.82 for Claude and 0.90 for GPT-4. Scaling and prompt-correlation values also change. Revised selection, sampling and cost assumptions prevent treating these collectively as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: Both retain the 4,480-configuration search, prompt options, three-stage successive halving and non-dominated sorting for accuracy and cost. Synchronous execution and epsilon-net tie-breaking are newly documented in v3, without evidence that they replace an earlier procedure.

P1.justification: Paragraphs across the introduction, related work, metric explanations, test-results discussion and conclusion are extensively edited or rewritten. v3 changes the title, replaces the preliminary-results narrative, and adds Impact Statement, Acknowledgments and multi-objective-background sections, while retaining the main numbered section sequence.

P2.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the displays: the search-space table moves to the appendix, Figure 6 combines separate model-size panels into grouped bars, and Table 1 replaces cost entries with variability columns. Test tables gain uncertainty and revised cost units. New displays include the Arena-Hard comparison, token-price table, sorting illustration, recolored configuration plots and fidelity-stability plots.

R1.justification: v3 adds Zhang et al. on summarization, Ni et al. on LEVER, and Elshin et al. on translation, while removing the Verga et al. jury reference. The positioning relative to zero-shot judges, fine-tuned judges and prompt optimization remains substantially unchanged. The Llama 3 author correction identifies the same cited work.

T1.justification: New Appendix C formally defines multi-objective optimization, dominance and the Pareto front, and discusses scalarization restrictions and non-dominated sorting. This adds mathematical background and reasoning, but no new theorem or proof about the proposed tuning method.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly bases its preliminary test results on an unfinished search. v3 reports selection using the full validation set, directly evaluates the tuned judges' Arena-Hard rankings, and adds bootstrap uncertainty and fidelity-stability evidence. These substantially strengthen validation of the proposed approach. Changed cost assumptions limit interpretation of the lower dollar figures, and the PandaLM prose still claims outperformance where the small judge and PandaLM-70B both score 0.67, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same judge-tuning study despite the changed title. All 14 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v3, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original scaling and tuning experiments, updated test results, an additional Arena-Hard comparison, and fidelity-stability analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original scaling experiments, analysis of 4,480 judge configurations, and preliminary LMSys and PandaLM test results.

results.title: Tuning LLM Judge Design Decisions for 1/1000 of the Cost

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion now explicitly restrict superiority over RFNNs and E2E ResNets to the small- to medium-scale regime, whereas v1 states this without that explicit qualification. The central methodological, analytical-solution, and theoretical-guarantee contributions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 and Appendix E.5 introduce substantive large-data limitations and motivate RFRBoost initialization followed by E2E fine-tuning as future work. Appendix E.4 adds an interpretation of modest initialization benefits versus training cost. However, its claim of 32 classification wins for i.i.d. features conflicts with Table 10 and Figure 7, which assign those wins to SWIM RFRBoost.

D1.justification: V2 supplies dataset identifiers with individual results, detailed larger-dataset splits and hyperparameter grids, Gaussian-scale settings, and NVIDIA RTX 6000 hardware information. It newly specifies the point-cloud allocation of 5,000 training/validation and 5,000 test points, classification solver, PyTorch implementation, and official XGBoost implementation. The code-access location is unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds CoverType classification and YearPredictionMSD regression in Appendix E.5 while retaining the 91 OpenML datasets and concentric-circle task. Larger-sample experiments on OpenML IDs 23517 and 44975 revisit existing datasets; their increased sample counts are protocol changes rather than additional coverage.

E2.justification: The main OpenML and point-cloud comparator sets are retained. Appendix E.4 adds evaluated i.i.d.-Gaussian RFNN and RFRBoost variants alongside their SWIM counterparts in Tables 9–10. The larger-dataset experiments reuse existing baseline families.

E3.justification: Table 4 changes the E2E learning-rate search from 10^-7–10^-2 to 10^-6–10^-1 and XGBoost depth from 3–10 to 1–10. Point-cloud settings also change, including RFRBoost's boosting rate from 0.1 to 1.0 and E2E batch size from 64 to 128. New experiments introduce Gaussian-scale tuning and GPU learning curves using hold-out tests and 20% validation splits, alongside the retained nested five-fold benchmark protocol.

E4.justification: V1 already compares scalar, diagonal, and dense mappings and examines point-cloud representations. V2 adds an initialization ablation across regression and classification in Appendix E.4 and training-size sensitivity analyses of predictive performance and runtime in Appendix E.5. These address previously untested dependence on feature initialization and data scale.

E5.justification: Figures 2–3 change the significance threshold from 0.10 to 0.05 while retaining Wilcoxon testing with Holm correction. New scaling experiments report five different random seeds and 95% confidence bands in Figures 9–10. The point-cloud experiment retains its ten-run mean and standard-deviation reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 revise scores and timings: E2E regression RMSE changes from 0.4167 to 0.412, and point-cloud accuracy from 0.519 to 0.732, alongside changed settings; RFRBoost's point-cloud accuracy remains 0.997. V2 also adds dataset-level OpenML scores, initialization results, and scaling curves. Figure 10 shows E2E outperforming RFRBoost on three of four datasets at the largest tested sizes.

M1.justification: The residual architecture, exact-greedy and gradient-greedy procedures, objectives, gradient fitting, and line search remain unchanged in Section 3 and Algorithms 1–2. Renaming the learned map from Delta to A and evaluating Gaussian features within the already supported arbitrary-feature framework do not introduce a new method.

P1.justification: The existing narrative and section sequence are largely retained. V2 makes local prose corrections, renames mathematical symbols, adds short time-complexity and larger-dataset sections, extends Appendix E, and includes an impact statement. Author affiliations and publication information are reformatted.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the presentation with dataset-level tables, distribution plots, initialization-comparison displays, and scaling curves with confidence bands in Tables 5–7 and 9–11 and Figures 5–10. Existing main results are regrouped and Figure 4 is redrawn. V1's point-cloud settings table is retained as v2 Table 8.

R1.justification: V2 adds scattering-network literature, statistical-comparison references, and citations for software and the new datasets. It also identifies sandwiched least squares as a special case of generalized Sylvester equations. The broader positioning relative to boosting and random-feature research remains intact.

T1.justification: V2 adds a formal serial time-complexity expression in Section 3.5 and corrects the empirical-measure normalization in Section 2 by including 1/n. The principal closed-form solutions, excess-risk bound, and proofs in Appendices A–D are retained, largely with notation changes.

improvement.justification: V1's tabular evaluation was capped at 5,000 observations and did not isolate initialization dependence or expose individual dataset results. V2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny through initialization ablations, seeded scaling experiments, detailed results, and reproducibility information. The larger-data findings reveal important limits and appropriately narrow the abstract and conclusion. The erroneous classification-win summary weakens reporting accuracy, but the overall gains in validation and claim calibration are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Random Feature Representation Boosting by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across notation changes and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds feature-initialization ablations and larger-dataset experiments, including performance, timing, and uncertainty results.

before.justification: V1 reports original OpenML regression and classification experiments and a synthetic point-cloud experiment, with measured performance and training times in Tables 1–3.

results.title: Random Feature Representation Boosting

C1.justification: v2 removes the abstract's priority claim that comparable performance to semi-structured pruning is achieved 'for the first time.' The central claims about lossless PIFA compression, M's error correction and MPIFA's performance and efficiency remain in the introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: New appendix discussion interprets cross-method results as evidence for plug-in applicability, describes the tradeoff against LLM-Pruner, and explains compression costs through rank searching and CPU staging. It explicitly limits ESPACE evaluation to pruning variants that avoid backpropagation. Existing explanations about overfitting, conditioning and PIFA requiring prior rank reduction remain.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the anonymous code link with a named GitHub repository, newly specifies 2048-token calibration/perplexity evaluation, and details compression hardware, timing scope and CPU staging. Appendix B.2 corrects the density-search value. The existing fine-tuning recipe, including its 1024-token sequence length, remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates model quality on WikiText2 and uses C4 in fine-tuning data. v2 additionally evaluates C4 perplexity with WikiText2 calibration and eight zero-shot SuperGLUE tasks (Appendices C–D), substantially broadening evaluation domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: LLM-Pruner, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated comparator for perplexity and layer efficiency in Appendix E. Appendix G adds four ESPACE pruning-only comparators: MSE, MSE-NORM, GO-MSE and GO-MSE-NORM. The original low-rank and semi-structured comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include zero-shot SuperGLUE evaluation using accuracy and ReCoRD F1, compression-time and peak-memory measurements with explicit stage boundaries, and structured-layer comparisons at 55% and 70% density. Appendix B.2 also corrects the reported attention-density search from global density minus 1 to minus 0.1; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix G/Table 15 adds a substantial component analysis comparing X, X plus PIFA, X plus M, and X plus MPIFA across SVD-LLM and four ESPACE pruning variants. It newly isolates PIFA without M and tests component benefits beyond SVD-LLM. Existing mix-ratio, calibration-size and conditioning analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added experiments continue reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: The original WikiText2 tables, efficiency measurements and plotted results are retained. Tables 8–15 add C4/SuperGLUE scores, LLM-Pruner results, compression costs and component results. For example, the new 50%-density LLaMA2-7B comparisons report C4 perplexity of 52.01 versus 129.8 and SuperGLUE means of 52.9 versus 50.5 for MPIFA versus SVD-LLM.

M1.justification: The PIFA representation, M reconstruction objectives and updates, regularization, and inference procedure are retained. Algorithms 1 and 2 are moved and renumbered. Applying the existing components to ESPACE introduces no documented change to their procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract receives limited editing, affiliations and publication information are updated, acknowledgements are added, and Appendices C–G extend the document. The original section sequence and most existing explanatory prose remain essentially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial tabular presentation for C4, SuperGLUE, structured pruning, compression resources and component combinations. It moves the factorization algorithm, original component table and sensitivity plots into the main text, reduces the calibration plots to column width, and reorganizes appendix displays. The eight figures retain their underlying content.

R1.justification: Related work adds references including SLEB, ShortGPT, DISP-LLM, LORD and Dobi-SVD; new appendices discuss ESPACE and evaluated relationships to structured pruning. These extend the existing positioning without replacing its central low-rank versus semi-structured framing. The abstract also drops its first-time priority assertion.

T1.justification: The factorization identities, parameter and FLOP derivations, reconstruction equations, regularized objective and module-density formula are retained. Appendix A's closed-form derivation and invertibility assumptions are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 evaluates model quality only on WikiText2 and demonstrates component benefits in LLMs using SVD-LLM's pruning step. v2 adds downstream tasks, C4 evaluation and component combinations across ESPACE variants, addressing substantial gaps in generalization and component attribution. LLM-Pruner and compression-resource comparisons also strengthen practical assessment. ESPACE coverage remains pruning-only and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the expanded validation provides a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MPIFA work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, allowing reliable comparison despite relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds C4, SuperGLUE, LLM-Pruner, compression-resource and ESPACE experiments in Appendices C–G.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLaMA compression experiments, WikiText2 perplexities, fine-tuning outcomes, measured GPU efficiency and component ablations.

C1.justification: V1's abstract claims provable robustness to both prior and likelihood misspecification. V2 retains robustness to both but specifically limits its provable-robustness claim to likelihood misspecification. The principal framework, generalization, cavity-distribution, conjugacy, and predictive-performance contributions remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds the qualification that robust losses can underperform under correct likelihood specification and explicitly identifies proving prior robustness as an open problem. It also interprets the new sensitivity and runtime evidence, conjectures that contamination exacerbates baseline instability, and discusses challenges in extending FedGVI to personalized and hierarchical FL.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the promised future code release with an explicit repository pointer. Appendix D substantially expands documentation with loss, kernel, and divergence formulas and newly specifies 99 observations plus one outlier and convergence-based execution for the retained influence experiment. Some added details contain inconsistencies, including the Alpha-Renyi formula's sign relative to Section 3.3.

E1.justification: All datasets and tasks are retained. Fashion-MNIST adds an explicitly evaluated 10% random-label-contamination condition to the earlier 0%, 20%, and 40% conditions, as documented in v1 Appendix C.3.2 and v2 Appendix D.3.2.

E2.justification: The Fashion-MNIST comparison expands from PVI versus FedGVI variants in v1 Figure 2 to include FedAvg, FedPA, and beta-PredBayes in v2 Tables 2 and 6. These methods already participated in the MNIST comparison; the other principal comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds comparisons controlling network architecture across methods using one 200-neuron layer versus two 100-neuron layers (Table 3). It also introduces three-client learning-rate experiments, five-client MNIST sensitivity experiments, and error-versus-per-client-wall-clock evaluation. These substantially expand evaluation controls and procedures while retaining the original Table 1 setting.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained influence and contamination analyses, v2 adds a joint loss/divergence parameter ablation (Figure 6), architecture controls, learning-rate sensitivity, and small loss-parameter perturbations (Tables 3–5). Figures 10–12 examine convergence stability and computational overhead, addressing whether gains depend on architecture, tuning, or additional computation.

E5.justification: Fashion-MNIST gains explicit plus/minus uncertainty reporting in v2 Tables 2 and 6, whereas v1 Figure 2 showed accuracy curves without uncertainty bars. The existing MNIST standard deviations, five-run information, and CoverType split counts are retained; no increase in repetitions or new significance-testing procedure is specified.

E6.justification: MNIST Table 1 is numerically unchanged, but v2 adds substantial architecture, tuning, convergence, and timing results and expands and revises Fashion-MNIST results. For example, new Table 3 reports 96.77 ± 0.10% for combined FedGVI versus 96.64 ± 0.07% for FedAvg in the two-hidden-layer, ten-client setting. These are newly reported controlled comparisons.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and the client/server updates in Equations 3–7 are retained. The additional loss and kernel formulas document existing components, while the new experiments vary existing architecture and hyperparameter choices.

P1.justification: The main section order and most methodological and proof prose are retained. V2 rewrites the notation setup, expands explanatory passages, completes unfinished appendix prose, and introduces a contextual Appendix C while moving the experimental appendix to D. These are localized revisions rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 adds relationship diagrams, a parameter heatmap, architecture and sensitivity tables, and convergence/runtime plots. The Fashion-MNIST plot becomes expanded tables, with Table 6 redisplaying Table 2 at higher precision. Retained experimental figures are repositioned closer to their corresponding discussions, substantially changing the visual organization.

R1.justification: V2 expands positioning around personalized and hierarchical Bayesian FL and adds references including Kim and Hospedales, Hassan et al. (2023), Swaroop et al., and Yonekura and Sugasawa. Section 4.7 also attributes the robust losses to GVI instead of FedGVI. The central relationship to PVI and generalized inference remains.

T1.justification: V2 restores beta in Equation 2's normalizing constant and specifies beta = 1 for recovering ordinary Bayes. It adds the convexity/global-optimality statement in Remark 4.5 and makes Proposition 4.4 explicitly local. The corresponding Appendix B proofs remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1's principal comparison used different network depths across methods; v2's Table 3 directly addresses that confound. The sensitivity, convergence, and runtime analyses substantially strengthen practical validation, while the narrowed provability claim improves scientific precision. Expanded documentation also helps reproducibility. Ambiguous labels in Tables 4–5 and the Appendix D Alpha-Renyi sign inconsistency detract from precision, but these localized defects do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and claim calibration.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FedGVI research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison across renumbering and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds architecture controls, hyperparameter sensitivity experiments, convergence comparisons, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic outlier experiments and evaluations on CoverType, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST, including supplementary results.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central contribution: an electrostatics-based method for both noise-to-data and data-to-data transport, with theoretical justification and toy/image demonstrations. The expanded evidence and revised formal construction do not change this overarching contribution claim.

C2.justification: V1 discusses dimensionality, plate distance, and training-volume selection. V2 additionally explains that first-crossing termination can distort the target distribution and that omitting backward trajectories can leave target support uncovered, particularly with shifted distributions. Section 5 and Appendix C make the gap between theoretical transport and practical implementation explicit.

D1.justification: V2 adds sampling pseudocode, CIFAR-10 hyperparameters including L=500 and sigma=0.05, and code-source links for Cycle-GAN, DDIB, and DSBM. Existing optimizer, solver tolerances, EMA, GPU, and training-time disclosures are retained in the relocated experimental-details appendix.

E1.justification: V2 expands generation from colored digit 2 to all MNIST digits and adds CIFAR-10 natural images. Appendix C.2 also adds transport to a separated two-Gaussian target. Gaussian-to-Swiss-roll transport and colored 3-to-2 translation remain.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 23 adds Cycle-GAN, DDIB, and DSBM outputs for the retained colored MNIST translation task, substantially expanding comparison beyond v1's Flow Matching baseline. PFGM remains the image-generation comparator.

E3.justification: Toy inference is now specified through the z-parameterized Algorithm 2 rather than v1's raw-field Euler update in Eq. (40). Added protocols vary CIFAR-10 plate distance over 50, 500, and 5000 and compare interpolation-based training points with a uniform cube mesh. Existing Table 1 parameter values and image RK45, Adam, and EMA settings remain unchanged; rerunning retained experiments is not established.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Swiss-roll distance example, v2 adds CIFAR-10 distance sensitivity, a Gaussian-to-two-Gaussians boundary-crossing failure case, and an interpolation-versus-cube-mesh training-volume comparison (Appendix C, Figures 19, 20, and 22). These substantially expand evidence about sensitivity and failure mechanisms.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed or repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's references to significant visual differences do not introduce statistical testing.

E6.justification: V1's digit-2 generation panels are replaced by full-MNIST samples, and v2 adds CIFAR-10 samples and three translation-baseline outputs. New findings include degraded CIFAR-10 generation at L=5000 and similar Swiss-roll recovery with two training-volume constructions. Retained Swiss-roll and translation comparison panels are unchanged; the expanded results do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The stated training objective changes from matching E to matching E/||E||, and the interpolation and noise-sampling formulas are revised. The ideal transport is redefined through flux-weighted stochastic forward/backward and stopping choices. V2 explicitly distinguishes this construction from its practical forward-only sampler, which stops at the first target-plane crossing.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reworks the electrostatics and transport exposition, restructures the main proof into auxiliary lemmas and numbered steps, and expands explanations throughout the retained material. An extended limitations appendix is inserted, with experimental details moved from Appendix C to D. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: V2 adds stochastic-map and proof diagrams, CIFAR-10 panels, sensitivity/failure illustrations, and additional baseline panels. MNIST generation panels are replaced, the original multipart flux illustration is simplified, and Table 1 gains a CIFAR-10 row. Retained figures are largely renumbered, but the new and revised displays substantially change the presentation.

R1.justification: References add Peluchetti (2023), Su et al. (2023), and De Bortoli et al. (2024), while removing the variational-diffusion and adversarial Schrödinger-bridge works cited in v1. Appendix C.4 adds a specific contrast with Flow Matching's interpolation-dependent loss. The overall electrostatic/PFGM positioning remains.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 now explicitly assumes compact support and concerns the stochastic transport map. Appendix B replaces v1's half-charge-flux argument with field-jump, branching, and termination lemmas plus flux accounting across multiple plane crossings. This substantially revises the definitions and proof, although the replacement proof introduces an unexplained Φ0 in Eq. (56).

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important omission in v1: how field-line direction and repeated plane crossings affect distribution transfer. Its explicit stochastic construction, revised proof, and candid explanation of the practical approximation substantially improve scientific precision. Targeted failure and sensitivity experiments strengthen that explanation. Results remain qualitative, and the revised proof has notation problems such as unexplained Φ0 in Eq. (56), but the clearer theoretical scope and experimentally illustrated limitations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Electrostatic Field Matching work. Their main text, equations, figures, table, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved from v1 Appendix C to v2 Appendix D.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices C–D report original transport and image-generation results, including full MNIST, CIFAR-10, sensitivity experiments, and additional baseline outputs.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original Gaussian-to-Swiss-roll transport, colored MNIST 3-to-2 translation, and digit-2 generation experiments, illustrated in Figures 5–10.

results.title: Field Matching: an Electrostatic Paradigm to Generate and Transfer Data

C1.justification: v2 narrows the broad IAR–DM privacy comparison to empirical findings under current attacks and models with similar FID. It also describes IAR image quality as matching or surpassing DMs. The three attack contributions and headline IAR outcomes remain.

C2.justification: New Appendix A offers mechanisms involving likelihood access, prediction targets and token-level signals. Expanded limitations discuss unavailable large-scale training data and confounding by model size, training duration, objectives and tokenizers. v2 also attributes VAR-CLIP leakage to richer conditioning and explicitly qualifies the proposed diffusion-based mitigation direction.

D1.justification: v2 newly tabulates DM parameter counts, training steps and batch sizes; supplies Min-K%, Min-K%++ and SURP search grids and selection rules; and documents the unified control and DI's MinMaxScaler implementation. This substantially expands reproducibility information. The code link, hardware disclosure and original IAR training details remain.

E1.justification: v1 excludes text-conditioned models from its privacy evaluation. v2 adds MIA and DI evaluation of VAR-CLIP trained on captioned ImageNet-1k (Appendix B.1, Table 6), extending conditioning requirements within the retained image domain.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated LFM and DiT-MoE models as supplementary diffusion reference architectures (Table 9), although explicitly excluding them from the primary comparison. The original LLM-MIA and DM-MIA comparator sets, including CLiD, remain.

E3.justification: Appendix C adds a common training-loss evaluation across 19 models, using random diffusion timesteps, fewer noise draws, training-style MAR masking and loss-only DI without DM-specific scoring. Table 7 additionally reports MIA accuracy. These are new controls; the main experiments retain 10,000 members and 10,000 nonmembers.

E4.justification: v2 adds cross-model correlation analysis of architecture, size and training duration, plus a unified-loss control testing whether leakage differences persist without tailored attacks (Appendices A and C). The original MAR ablations, DI aggregation ablation, mitigation experiments and prefix/SSCD analyses remain.
