E5.justification: Appendix A.2 adds pairwise Pearson correlation estimation across 11 IARs and eight DMs. Both versions retain reporting over 100 randomized MIA experiments, uncertainty entries and Welch tests at 0.01. Changed numerical uncertainties do not establish increased repetitions.

E6.justification: The improved MAR results are substantially replaced: MAR-H Min-K% TPR changes from 49.19% to 3.40%, and AUC from 96.40 to 59.98 (v1 Tables 11–12; v2 Tables 16–17). SiT-XL/2 CLiD changes from 0.91% to 6.38% TPR and from 43.58 to 78.65 AUC, making SiT the strongest reported DM result. v2 also adds correlation, VAR-CLIP, unified-attack and additional DM results. The headline IAR attack and extraction outcomes remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The conditional-output MIA features, MAR adjustments, normalized feature-sum DI, prefix-based extraction and output-noising defense are retained. v2 clarifies probability-based scoring and per-sample aggregation. The added unified Loss Attack serves as an evaluation control.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized rewrites to the abstract, introduction, attack explanations and conclusions, expands terminology explanations and reorganizes the opening appendices. The main section sequence and most existing exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a DI workflow diagram (Figure 4) and new correlation, comparison and model-detail tables (Tables 5–9). It restyles trade-off plots with square DM markers and separate legends, expands captions and consolidates appendix result tables into a denser layout. The extraction image galleries are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds diffusion-architecture background and citations, alongside references on privacy auditing and distribution mismatch. It explicitly distinguishes its attack from CLiD's loss-based scoring and fitted scaler, and removes the VAR-CLIP issue citation. The central research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: The objectives, numbered MIA equations, DI null hypothesis and IID assumption are retained. The explicit conditional-probability difference clarifies the existing attack. New architectural explanations and empirical correlations introduce no substantive formal derivation, theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves a serious internal inconsistency: its revised MAR-H Min-K% result of 3.40% agrees with the main tables, replacing v1's conflicting 49.19%. The unified-attack control, text-conditioned evaluation and fuller settings documentation substantially strengthen the evidence and reproducibility. Architectural causes remain unisolated, as Appendix B.2 acknowledges, so some mechanism interpretations remain inconclusive; nevertheless, the gains in consistency and empirical support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and retain matching core methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds VAR-CLIP evaluation, unified loss-attack experiments, additional diffusion-model evaluations and correlation analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet experiments on membership inference, dataset inference, training-image extraction and privacy defenses, including appendix ablations.

results.title: Privacy Attacks on Image AutoRegressive Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: an instance-dependent PAC lower bound, worst-policy–reward-pair complexity, a tractable relaxation including reward-free evaluation, and an MR-NaS adaptation with asymptotic guarantees and tabular evidence.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 corrects v1's interpretation that increasing accuracy tolerance or decreasing the discount factor may increase confusing models and sample complexity; v2 gives the opposite direction. It also qualifies the empty-alternative case as a minimal learning challenge, explains the 2ε separation, and acknowledges possible lower-bound looseness.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code-repository link and documents target-policy generation, sampling without replacement, finite reward-set size, and fixed single-policy targets. Appendices B.2.5 and C.4 also add warm-started CVXPY solver information and value-computation details. These are additional disclosures rather than established changes to the experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Riverswim, Forked Riverswim, DoubleChain, and NArms under finite-reward multi-policy, reward-free multi-policy, and reward-free single-policy scenarios. Figure 5's Riverswim analysis with cube and norm-bounded reward sets is also retained.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same methods: SF-NR, GVFExplorer, and both noisy-policy variants for finite rewards; SF-NR and both noisy variants for reward-free multi-policy evaluation; and both noisy variants for reward-free single-policy evaluation. Newly cited methods are not added as experimental comparators.

E3.justification: v2 Appendix C.4 describes batched evaluation every F steps, but leaves F unspecified and retains Section 6's statement that evaluation occurs at each time-step. The new sampling details are not identified as changes to earlier experiments. Consequently, a change in the evaluation procedure cannot be reliably established.

E4.justification: The existing state-size sensitivity evidence in Figures 10–11 is revised. For example, at the largest NArms size in Figure 10, MR-NaS changes from finishing above several comparator error curves to below them. The size ranges and analytical questions remain the same, with no new ablation or robustness axis.

E5.justification: Both versions report 30 seeds and bootstrap-based 95% confidence intervals. Changed confidence-band widths do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figures 3 and 10 substantially revise finite-reward learning curves across the four environments and multiple sizes. In Figure 3's NArms panel, MR-NaS finishes above GVFExplorer and the noisy-policy curves in v1 but below them in v2. Some reward-free multi-policy curves also change in Figures 4 and 11. These are revised reported outcomes; the PDFs do not establish identical underlying settings for attributing cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: MR-NaS retains the same relaxed-rate objective, certainty-equivalent allocation, forced exploration mixture, model updates, and stopping rule. The revised optimization derivations and additional solver documentation do not establish a different exploration algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the prose remain intact, with targeted explanatory rewrites. Section 5 is renamed to 'MR-NaS for Policy Evaluation,' computational material is organized into Appendix B.2.5, Appendix C.4 gains experimental-detail subsections, and an Impact Statement is added.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main paper and references from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout, with running headers and extensive resizing and relocation of figures, algorithms, and theorem boxes. Several result plots change legend order and axis ranges. The numbered figure set and notation table are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of Mukherjee et al. on tree-MDP evaluation, Weissmann et al. on bandit excess-risk guarantees, and Papini et al. on behavioral-policy optimization, alongside additional bandit and CVXPY citations. This broadens the contextual comparison while preserving the paper's central positioning relative to Best Policy Identification.

T1.justification: Proposition 4.1 replaces an exact equivalence with separate necessary and sufficient bounds. Lemma B.2 changes its discount dependence from (1−γ)^2 to (1−γ)^4, and Proposition B.7 replaces recurrent-class indicators with hitting-probability vectors. The old Lemma B.8 is qualified and reproved as Lemma 4.4/B.8; Proposition B.9 and the relaxed-rate proof are substantially revised. v1's erroneous polytope optimization in Equation 14 is also replaced by a revised formulation in v2 Equation 16.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantial mathematical deficiencies in Proposition 4.1, Lemma B.2, Proposition B.7, and the relaxed-rate argument, and replaces v1's unbounded polytope formulation with a meaningful linear program. These repairs materially strengthen the theoretical foundation of the paper. Added computational and experimental documentation also helps reproducibility. Evaluation-frequency ambiguity and unexplained curve revisions remain limitations, so the improved assessment rests principally on the theoretical repairs rather than higher plotted performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multi-reward multi-policy evaluation work and MR-NaS framework. The main text, equations, figures, algorithms, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 reports original tabular simulations in Section 6 and Appendix C, including revised learning curves and retained sample-complexity calculations.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations in four tabular environments, including learning curves, experiments across environment sizes, and a numerical sample-complexity analysis.

results.title: Adaptive Exploration for Multi-Reward Multi-Policy Evaluation

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the principal theoretical, methodological and empirical claims. The conclusion modestly qualifies applicability: it explicitly frames the method around text and presents healthcare and protein applications as future extensions, also adding images as a prospective direction.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the new ablations as evidence that SAE monosemanticity supports higher-fidelity, less redundant interpretations. It also replaces the earlier sampling rationale with an explanation that weakly activating texts act as hard negatives that improve precision. Existing diagnostic interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies temperature 0 for GPT-4o-mini concept annotation and documents the human-rating questions, evaluator eligibility and aggregation procedure. It supplies configurations for the new controls. Existing SAE hyperparameters, prompts and code, data and demo access information remain.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate WIKI-5, WIKI-15, BILLS, HEADLINES, YELP and CONGRESS. The added ablations reuse the three real-world datasets, and human evaluation assesses existing HEADLINES and CONGRESS hypotheses. Images, proteins and healthcare extensions remain prospective.

E2.justification: Section 6.3 and Table 7 add end-to-end comparisons against direct Embedding features, PCA features and a supervised Bottleneck, substantially expanding controls for the SAE's contribution. BERTopic, NLParam, HypoGeniC and the prior-work novelty comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v3 introduces human evaluation of helpfulness and interpretability: three nonauthor researchers rate significant hypotheses from two datasets in randomized order. New ablation settings include PCA reduction from 1536 to 256 dimensions and a 20-neuron supervised bottleneck. Existing dataset splits and benchmark protocols are retained.

E4.justification: v2 already analyzes interpretation fidelity, prompting choices, omitted fidelity validation and losses across pipeline stages. v3 adds controlled non-SAE ablations that test whether the SAE specifically improves interpretation fidelity and nonredundant hypothesis discovery, plus structured human assessment of hypothesis quality.

E5.justification: The new human evaluation specifies three ratings per hypothesis and majority-vote aggregation, adding a limited estimation procedure. Existing Bonferroni corrections, paired t-tests and stochastic interpretation disclosures remain unchanged. No confidence intervals, inter-rater agreement estimates or repeated model-run counts are added.

E6.justification: Existing results in Tables 1–6 and the retained plots are unchanged. New Table 7 reports 45/60 significant SAE hypotheses versus 30/60 for Embedding, and mean fidelity 0.836 versus 0.640 for Bottleneck. Human evaluation adds 24/30 SAE hypotheses rated helpful, 29/30 interpretable and 23 satisfying both, versus at most 7 for a baseline.

M1.justification: The proposed k-sparse autoencoder, L1-based feature selection and LLM interpretation with fidelity-based selection are unchanged. The new Embedding, PCA and Bottleneck variants are evaluation controls, not revisions to the proposed pipeline.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized revisions to related work, method explanations, costs and the conclusion, adds a non-SAE ablation subsection and qualitative-evaluation appendix, and expands acknowledgements and funding disclosures. The overall narrative and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the two-panel human-evaluation Figure 2 and ablation Table 7, refines the cost-table caption and reflows material. Existing figures and tables retain their displays and results, with subsequent figures renumbered. The conference footer replaces the preprint footer.

R1.justification: Related work adds Lam et al. on concept induction and Koh et al. and Feng et al. on concept bottlenecks; the new ablation cites Yang et al. The conclusion adds application references and removes Pierson et al. on health equity. The central positioning relative to hypothesis generation and SAE interpretability is retained.

T1.justification: The separation and fidelity definitions, Proposition 3.1 and its derivation are unchanged. The proof moves from Appendix E to Appendix F; this is renumbering rather than new mathematics.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens two central validation gaps: matched non-SAE controls test whether the SAE itself provides the benefit, and nonauthor researcher ratings directly assess real-world helpfulness and interpretability beyond predictive significance. These additions support the paper's defining contribution without displacing earlier evidence. The three-rater evaluation covers only two datasets, and aggregate ablation results lack uncertainty estimates, but the evidential improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Sparse Autoencoders for Hypothesis Generation. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original non-SAE comparisons in Table 7 and researcher evaluations in Figure 2 and Appendix E.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic and real-world experiments, baseline comparisons, hypothesis discoveries and supporting analyses in Appendix C.

results.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Hypothesis Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the central claims: intrinsic dimension and teacher–student discrepancy explain variance reduction in W2S, with implications for relative performance and sample sizes. Their principal contribution statements are not redefined.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 changes the interpretation from non-monotonic PGR and OPR bounds sharing an optimal labeled sample size to a decreasing PGR bound and a separately optimized, non-monotonic OPR bound. Appendix C replaces the claim that increasing nN compensates approximation-related terms with the qualification that increasing N cannot eliminate inherited teacher parameter noise.

D1.justification: Appendix E.3 clarifies and corrects the sketch dimensions, oversampling and QR implementation used for correlation estimation. It also revises SST construction to parse-tree subsampling while removing the explicit neutral-sentence filtering description. Other training and computing-resource disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Synthetic regression, UTKFace and ColoredMNIST coverage is retained. Appendix E.3 replaces the description of full-sentence SST-2 with a dataset subsampled from SST parse trees, retaining the same sample counts and results. The PDFs do not establish whether sentence/phrase coverage changed or the existing dataset description was corrected.

E2.justification: The weak teacher, strong SFT baseline, strong ceiling and evaluated teacher architectures are retained. Appendix E.2 corrects a CLIP-B32 mention to DINOv2-s14, which v3 already identifies as the student in its setup and Table 2; this is not a comparator replacement.

E3.justification: Appendix E.3 revises the stated correlation-estimation procedure: the Gaussian sketch changes from dimension d_s by D to N by (d_s+p), with oversampling and truncated column-pivoted QR specified. This is a reported procedure correction without evidence of reruns; experimental split sizes, training budgets and performance metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Both versions retain the same sample-size and feature-discrepancy sweeps, synthetic noise-regime comparisons, and injected-label-noise analyses on UTKFace, ColoredMNIST and SST. No empirical ablation, robustness test or case study is added or removed.

E5.justification: Both specify standard-deviation error bars over 40 synthetic runs and 10 UTKFace runs. The plotted uncertainty and other repeated-run or statistical reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: Figures 1–13 retain identical plotted content, and Tables 1–3 retain their numerical entries. The reported empirical rankings and noise/discrepancy trends are unchanged; the revised analytical bounds are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The teacher fitting, pseudo-label generation and student fitting procedures remain unchanged, including the ridge objectives and sentiment finetuning losses. The substantial revisions concern their analysis and diagnostic measurements.

P1.justification: The overall outline, abstract, introduction and experimental narrative are retained. Focused reorganization moves the risk definition into Section 2.2 and finite-sample approximation-error definitions into Appendix B, alongside revised technical explanations, cross-references and acknowledgements.

P2.justification: All figure designs and table structures are retained. Appendix pagination and placement change, including Figures 7 and 9 moving earlier and Table 3 moving from page 50 to page 49; there is no substantive visual redesign.

R1.justification: v6 adds Mourtada (2022) for the revised inverse-covariance argument, removes Vershynin (2010), and removes Xue et al. (2025) and its representation-based W2S discussion. The broader research positioning and related-work coverage remain intact.

T1.justification: Sections 2–3 revise feature-coupling assumptions, specify S-based evaluation and condition the bias–variance decomposition on training inputs. Weak-teacher variance changes from sigma² d_w/n to sigma² d_w/(n-d_w-1), with corresponding strong-baseline and finite-sample bias corrections. PGR/OPR bounds and their optimizing sample sizes change substantially. Appendix B replaces Lemma 2 with a small-ball argument; Appendix C replaces the ridge bound and proof, adding fourth-moment and proportional-asymptotic conditions and changing the leading dependence from nN to n with an N-dependent correction.

improvement.justification: v6 substantially repairs the paper's central theoretical accounting: it corrects reference-model evaluation errors and finite-sample bias, states additional assumptions, replaces the inverse-covariance argument, and removes the ridge claim that more pseudo-labels can eliminate inherited noise. These are important gains for a theory-centered paper, despite narrower guarantees. Integration remains incomplete: Figures 1–4 retain earlier theoretical curves, including Figure 4's non-monotonic PGR bound, despite the revised formulas.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same W2S generalization work. Their main text, Appendices A–E, equations, 13 figures and three tables are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v6 retains these original experiments, including measured risks, PGR, OPR, dimension estimates and label-noise analyses.

before.justification: v3 reports original synthetic regression experiments and evaluations on UTKFace, ColoredMNIST and SST sentiment classification in Section 4 and Appendix E.

results.title: Discrepancies are Virtue: Weak-to-Strong Generalization through Lens of Intrinsic Dimension

C1.justification: v2 adds asymptotically accurate posterior sampling as an explicit central contribution in the introduction and Theorem 4.1. v1 claims an approximate sampling method and empirical advantages without this guarantee. The emphasis on improved inpainting remains, with v2's contribution statement more specifically emphasizing perceptual quality.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for inconsistent improvements at small particle counts, relates Gibbs-iteration tradeoffs to threshold s, and discusses unoptimized code and computational scaling. Appendix C acknowledges that its gradient assumptions may fail even for linear transformations. These extend the existing interpretations of perceptual-versus-distortion tradeoffs and auxiliary guidance without replacing their central meaning.

D1.justification: v2 adds a stated public code link, selected hyperparameters for each dataset/task in Table 3, the 64-image tuning-sample size, initialization details, and comparator-specific settings in Appendix A. Table 4 supplies concrete runtime and memory information where v1 offered only qualitative computational limitations. These substantially expand reproducibility information; actual code availability was not externally verified.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ImageNet and FFHQ on box inpainting, Gaussian deblurring and 8× super-resolution. v2 adds free-form inpainting on both datasets, introducing irregular missing-pixel patterns within the existing image-restoration coverage (Tables 1–2; Appendix H).

E2.justification: v2 adds PFLD and LatentDAPS to the benchmark comparisons, substantially broadening the evaluated alternatives. PFLD was discussed but explicitly not compared in v1. Latent DPS/TDS become LDPS/LTDS, and Resample becomes ReSample; these renamed comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v2 revises hyperparameter-search grids and evaluates LD-SMC with both one and five particles, adding particle-count, Gibbs-iteration and computational-cost protocols. Appendix A specifies settings for the new baselines. Section 5.1 also states CIN256-V2 for ImageNet instead of v1's VQ-4; this is a reported setting revision, although the PDFs do not establish whether it corrects documentation or reflects a model change in executed experiments.

E4.justification: v1's principal ablation varies the guidance-switch threshold (Table 3). v2 revises that sweep and adds particle-count sensitivity, multiple Gibbs iterations on super-resolution and deblurring, and prior-versus-DPS-versus-LD-SMC proposal comparisons (Figures 5–6; Appendix F, Table 5). Appendix E additionally measures computational scaling with particles and Gibbs iterations.

E5.justification: v2 newly states that runtime and memory measurements are averaged over 10 trials (Appendix E). v1 provides no corresponding repeated-trial reporting. Neither version reports image-quality confidence intervals, error bars or seed-based uncertainty; the new trial count concerns computational measurements.

E6.justification: Numerous retained benchmark entries change alongside substantial new results. For five-particle LD-SMC, ImageNet box-inpainting FID/NIQE changes from 51.81/5.103 to 50.67/6.891, and FFHQ deblurring FID changes from 32.18 to 29.47. v2 also adds free-form, new-baseline, one-particle, ablation and computational results. Because the procedure and reported settings change, these are revised results rather than isolated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v2 changes the Gibbs procedure to update full latent trajectories, initializes SMC particles from the standard-normal prior instead of around the forward trajectory's endpoint, and samples the final chain by weights instead of selecting the highest-weight particle (Section 4.2; Algorithm 1). Below threshold s, it combines both guidance terms using rho, whereas v1 switched exclusively to auxiliary guidance. Initial and final weighting rules also change.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the introductory motivation and sampling exposition, organizing the latter around target distributions, weights, proposals and Algorithm 1. Derivations move into dedicated appendices, the appendix structure is expanded and reorganized, and the separate Limitations section is incorporated into the conclusion. These changes exceed local language polishing.

P2.justification: v2 expands benchmark tables with another task and additional method rows, adds hyperparameter, cost and proposal-ablation tables, and replaces the threshold table with a plot alongside new sensitivity plots. Reconstruction grids are revised to include free-form masks and additional baselines. Existing graphical-model and appendix illustrations are also relocated or revised; they are not all new content.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against ADIR, variational approaches, DAPS, MGPS and SILO, alongside additional SMC references. It reframes SMC-Diff's limitation around expensive prior proposals and explicitly distinguishes LD-SMC's claimed asymptotic guarantees from PFLD (Section 3). This goes beyond citation or bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v1 contains posterior approximations and a recursive derivation but no convergence proof. v2 revises the generative and target distributions, derives endpoint cases, and adds Theorem 4.1 and Appendix C's Gibbs-stationarity and SMC-convergence arguments with explicit assumptions. Separately, Eq. 7 replaces squared-error gradients with log-likelihood gradients while retaining subtraction, which is not equivalent with Appendix D's positive coefficients.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the method's component choices and practical tradeoffs: v1's single threshold study and qualitative cost warning are supplemented by particle, Gibbs and proposal ablations, measured costs, broader comparisons and selected implementation settings. These gains make the empirical contribution considerably easier to assess and reproduce. The improvement is qualified by Eq. 7's guidance-sign inconsistency and by the convergence proof's larger-proposal-variance assumption, which does not cover the stated equal-variance default.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LD-SMC with the same title and authors. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and rendered figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction experiments, expanded benchmark comparisons, component ablations, and runtime and memory measurements in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet and FFHQ reconstruction experiments, quantitative results in Tables 1–2 and Appendix D, and a guidance-threshold study.

results.title: Inverse Problem Sampling in Latent Space Using Sequential Monte Carlo

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the claimed empirical applicability to protein structure completion. The central contributions—generalized decoupling, asymptotically exact SMC, and the discrete extension—remain.

C2.justification: Remark 3.2 explicitly distinguishes consistency for the chosen prior from equality with the standard diffusion prior, materially qualifying the interpretation of exactness. New discussion attributes the improvement over DAPS to the SMC component and explains particle-versus-ODE budget tradeoffs, including why score-evaluation counts need not track runtime under parallelization (Appendix G.1.3–G.1.5).

D1.justification: V2 adds a DDSMC code-access link, explicit FFHQ downsampling information, and image attribution details. It also documents Chroma weight access and protein implementation settings, including noise-dependent ADP-3D learning rates and sampling budgets, and expands the explanation of ODE execution and computational cost.

E1.justification: V2 retains Gaussian mixtures, FFHQ restoration, and binary MNIST, while adding backbone structure completion for five PDB proteins. Section 5.3 and Appendix G.3 introduce a biological domain with varying observation sparsity and noise conditions.

E2.justification: ADP-3D is added as an evaluated protein-completion comparator in Figures 4 and 15. The existing GMM and FFHQ comparator sets are retained; the additional DDRM step-count variants change settings rather than comparator identity.

E3.justification: FFHQ evaluation increases from 100 to 1,000 images and adds PSNR. New experiments vary particle counts, ODE steps, and DDRM sampling budgets; protein evaluation uses RMSD with 200 DDSMC versus 1,000 ADP-3D steps. The printed FFHQ time/noise schedules also change from v1 Equations 67–68 to v2 Equations 79–80, without establishing whether those corrections reflect changed implementations.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained reconstruction-function and decoupling ablations, v2 tests single-particle DDSMC against DAPS, allocation of score-evaluation budgets between particles and ODE steps, and DDRM step sensitivity (Tables 4–8 and 9–10). Protein experiments additionally examine sensitivity to noise, observation sparsity, and particle count.

E5.justification: The GMM reporting of 20 seeds and 95% CLT intervals is retained. V2 newly reports image-level standard deviations for FFHQ LPIPS and PSNR across 1,000 images. Protein experiments report eight seeds and display shaded bands, although the bands' precise statistical definition is not stated.

E6.justification: GMM Tables 1–2 retain their numerical values, but v2 adds substantial particle/step results, FFHQ PSNR scores, and protein RMSD curves. FFHQ Table 3 contains revised averages under the expanded evaluation, such as MCGDiff middle-inpainting LPIPS changing from 0.12 to 0.10; this is not evidence of a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The core DDSMC and D3SMC procedures are retained. Appendix F newly adapts DDSMC to Chroma's correlated-noise protein prior through whitening, an SVD transformation, and coordinate-dependent observation noise, providing a bounded extension of the inference procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose are retained. V2 locally rewrites the PF-ODE and SMC explanations, adds protein and computational-analysis subsections plus an Impact Statement, and reorganizes the experimental appendix around the new protein appendix.

P2.justification: V2 adopts an ICML layout with running headers, revised typography and table styling, and extensive reflow of existing displays. It adds Tables 4–11 and protein Figures 4 and 15. Earlier qualitative figures are retained but relocated, renumbered, or resized, with FFHQ captions expanded to identify image sources.

R1.justification: V2 adds Gibbs-sampling references by Coeurdoux et al. and Wu et al., an SMC foundation reference, and protein-related work including ADP-3D, Chroma, and PDB sources. The established positioning relative to DAPS, TDS, and MCGDiff remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The original marginal-equality proof is retained, with its forward/backward inversion assumption made explicit in Remark A.2. V2 corrects the VP proposal covariance (v1 Equation 54 versus v2 Equation 57) and DDIM coefficient (66 versus 78), and derives the protein whitening transformation. Proposition 3.1 mainly formalizes the existing SMC consistency argument.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence through single-particle and matched-score-budget controls, addressing v1's limited analysis of computational tradeoffs and the contribution of SMC. Corrected equations and explicit qualification of the target prior improve technical clarity. Expanded FFHQ reporting, protein experiments, and code-access information strengthen evaluation and reproducibility. Real-data reconstruction metrics still do not establish posterior fidelity, but the central claims are substantially better supported and easier to assess.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DDSMC/D3SMC research by the same authors. Their readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved from Appendix F to G.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds protein structure completion experiments, computational ablations, and expanded image-restoration measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original Gaussian-mixture experiments, FFHQ restoration measurements, and qualitative binary-MNIST denoising results.

results.title: Solving Linear-Gaussian Bayesian Inverse Problems with Decoupled Diffusion Sequential Monte Carlo

C1.justification: The introduction lowers the headline GPU-hour saving estimate from 15% to 12%. The central contributions remain training acceleration, modest generalization benefits, and the inability of the studied averaging schemes to fully replace learning-rate decay. The revised conclusion foregrounds approaching Pareto optimality and the remaining challenge of accessing optimal intermediate models.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes robustness even with suboptimal baselines; v2 adds substantive qualifications that averaging typically cannot rescue failed trajectories. Appendix B and Section 7 explain interactions between sampling interval and averaging memory and suggest why earlier EMA configurations underperformed. Appendix C discusses overfitting and shorter-schedule advantages, while Appendix E attributes poor competition performance to API and CPU-GPU transfer overheads.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds a plainLM code reference, tokenizer and architecture details, and hyperparameter search ranges with the selected configuration in Table 3. Appendix B provides concrete averaging recommendations, and Appendix E adds LAWA/EMA pseudocode and implementation constraints. The original hardware, precision, and CPU-offloading disclosures are largely retained or relocated.

E1.justification: v2 adds decoder-only causal language modeling on FineWebEdu, a distinct next-token prediction task beyond v1's machine translation and other AlgoPerf tasks. All seven original AlgoPerf workloads remain. The newly explained exclusion of ImageNet-ResNet documents an omission already present in v1.

E2.justification: v2 systematically adds EMA to retained comparisons that previously evaluated LAWA alongside the baseline: learning-rate sweeps in Figures 4 and 6, the WMT Shampoo comparison in Figure 5, and annealing comparisons in Figure 7. It also introduces a tuned AdamW baseline for the language-modeling comparisons in Table 4.

E3.justification: The new language-modeling protocol uses a 124M-parameter model, 5B training tokens, a 5M-token held-out split, a target loss of 3.28, and evaluation every 40 steps. Table 3 defines a grid search selecting the fastest-to-target baseline. Figure 8 also adds an unaveraged, constant-learning-rate control, and the Criteo1TB learning-rate sweeps include additional settings.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds joint sampling-interval and averaging-memory sweeps with individual seed failures on four AlgoPerf workloads. Appendices C–D add shorter-schedule analyses for FastMRI, OGBG, and WMT, plus language-modeling sensitivity analyses. These substantially extend v1's pooled horizon analysis and selected learning-rate sweeps. The WMT learning-rate sensitivity panel from v1 Figure 6 is removed.

E5.justification: Table 2 changes from median/IQR to mean/standard deviation, explicitly exempting ViT from the three-seed summary and omitting its uncertainty. Figures 4 and 6 now specify standard error, while Figure 8 replaces boxplot spreads with mean-only points. Table 4 explains zero step-count standard deviation through evaluation resolution. The usual three-seed practice remains; an overall increase in runs is not established.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes estimated GPU-hours from 636/548/540 to 612/550/541 for NadamW/+LAWA/+EMA; Figure 2 changes average relative steps from 78% to 82%. Table 2 reports different validation summaries, with changed aggregation preventing direct performance-gain interpretations across versions. Substantial new results include expanded Shampoo comparisons and Table 4's 3200/2240/2200 steps to the language-modeling target for AdamW/+LAWA/+EMA.

M1.justification: Both versions use LAWA's rolling checkpoint average and EMA, updated at configurable intervals without feeding averaged weights into optimization updates. v2 Algorithms 1–2 document these existing procedures; applying them to language modeling does not introduce a new averaging method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main argumentative sequence are retained, with localized rewrites and terminology corrections. v2 inserts a language-modeling section and Impact Statement, revises the conclusion, and organizes the expanded appendix into A–E, moving the previous online/offline discussion into Appendix E.

P2.justification: Figures 4–7 receive revised panels, legends, and arrangements; Figure 8 changes from three-condition boxplots to four-condition point plots and includes ViT. Table 2 is reordered and reformatted. New Figures 9–14, Tables 3–4, and two algorithm displays substantially expand the visual presentation beyond numerical updates alone.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Arpit et al., Portes et al., Singh et al., and works supporting the language-modeling setup. It revisits Sanyal et al.'s EMA comparison through a sampling-and-decay explanation. The overall positioning as an empirical evaluation of existing averaging techniques remains; publication-year updates to retained works do not constitute new references.

T1.justification: The averaging-horizon definition and quadratic fit in Figure 3 are retained. v2's pseudocode expresses the previously described averaging operations, without adding a new theoretical result, formal assumption, proof, or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: v1's pooled horizon analysis and brief implementation appendix leave joint tuning and failure cases largely undocumented. v2 supplies direct evidence about these issues, demonstrates when tuned EMA can match LAWA in causal language modeling, and strengthens optimizer coverage through additional Shampoo tests. The expanded experimental and implementation details substantially improve practical usefulness and evidential support. Figure 8's loss of variability displays and Table 2's omission of ViT uncertainty are reporting drawbacks, but they do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same weight-averaging study. Their text, figures, tables, and mathematical material are readable, including v1 Appendix A and v2 Appendices A–E, supporting reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original AlgoPerf results and adds causal language-modeling experiments and extensive hyperparameter analyses, including Figure 9, Table 4, and Appendices B–D.

before.justification: v1 reports original AlgoPerf experiments measuring training efficiency, validation performance, and sensitivity to averaging and learning-rate settings, including Tables 1–2 and Figures 1–8.

results.title: When, Where and Why to Average Weights?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims: integrating the four MCTS stages with diffusion planning through tree rollout, guidance meta-actions, and fast simulation, with improved planning and compute scalability. Replacing TTC terminology with inference-time wording does not change their meaning.

C2.justification: The added analyses substantially expand interpretation: diverse guidance options matter more than precise scales, excessive tree depth can exhaust search budgets, greedy search suffers from limited backtracking, and aggressive denoising jumps impair value estimation on harder tasks. These mechanism explanations and speed–accuracy qualifications are new; Section 6's existing limitations are largely retained.

D1.justification: V3 adds specific reproducibility details, including the default UCT weight of 1.141, five-child branching, one-shot decoding from fully denoised predictions, and automatic cube release and arm pre-positioning in Appendix A.6.7. Existing architecture and training hyperparameter tables and repository access information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate pointmaze and antmaze navigation, one-to-four-cube manipulation, visual pointmaze, and short-horizon stitch datasets. The new ablations reuse PointMaze navigate tasks without adding datasets, task requirements, or input-environment conditions.

E2.justification: The original benchmark comparator sets, including the appendix goal-inpainting variants, are retained. V3 adds component-focused controls: a greedy tree-search baseline in Table 4 and Diffusion Forcing and MCTD variants without causal denoising in Table 7.

E3.justification: V3 substantially expands the controlled evaluation design: greedy branching widths of 5–20, five guidance sets, subplan counts of 1/3/5/20, causal-denoising and tree-search controls, UCT weights from 0 to 10, and jumpiness settings including one-shot decoding. These are new experimental protocols; previously stated benchmark settings are retained.

E4.justification: V2's compute-scaling, stitching, goal-inpainting, and visual-failure analyses are retained. Section 5.6 and Appendix D add systematic tests of greedy search, guidance-set sensitivity, subplan length, causal denoising and tree search, UCT weighting, and simulation jumpiness, directly examining MCTD's central design choices.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five tasks per environment, ten seeds per model/task, and mean ± standard deviation reporting in Appendix A.4. V3's A.5.7 newly discloses three AntMaze trials per task/seed with the best outcome retained. This adds run-count and aggregation information without establishing an increase in trials.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark results remain unchanged, including Tables 1–3, Figure 6, and v2 Tables 8–9 becoming v3 Tables 12–13. New ablation results are substantial: Table 7 reports giant-maze success of 18 ± 11% without causal denoising versus 100 ± 0% for MCTD; Table 15 reports 10 ± 21% for one-shot simulation versus 100 ± 0% at C=10. These are new comparisons, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The core tree rollout, guidance meta-actions, jumpy denoising, architecture, training objective, and Algorithms 1–10 remain substantively unchanged. Appendix A.6.7 newly documents cube-release and arm-positioning operations in the existing manipulation setup without establishing that the procedure changed between versions.

P1.justification: Existing prose and narrative organization are largely retained. V3 revises TTC/test-time terminology, expands DDIM, updates publication and reference text, and adds cross-references. It inserts Section 5.6 and an additional-results Appendix D, moving the existing algorithms appendix to E without extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the experimental displays with four main-text ablation tables and two appendix tables covering success, runtime, and search counts. Figures 1–7 are retained, existing appendix tables are renumbered and relocated, and algorithm comments are realigned with changed spacing.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds Jurgenson et al. (2020) on subgoal trees and de Waard et al. (2016) on high-level MCTS to acknowledge earlier planning approaches. Most other reference changes update existing works' publication information, including Anonymous becoming Ye et al. for the chess diffusion paper.

T1.justification: The existing equations and mathematical reasoning are retained, with no new theorem, proof, or formal assumption. Appendix D.1 explicitly states the standard UCT formula for the already-used selection criterion to explain its parameter sweep.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses an important gap in v2 by directly testing MCTD's central components and quantifying sensitivity and computational tradeoffs in Section 5.6 and Appendix D. Execution and trial-selection disclosures also improve transparency. Unexplained Diffusion Forcing score differences between Tables 1 and 7 limit cross-experiment interpretation, but the added component evidence substantially strengthens the paper's empirical justification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MCTD study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite added sections and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains these original empirical results and adds component ablations and sensitivity experiments in Section 5.6 and Appendix D.

before.justification: V2 reports original evaluations of MCTD and baselines on maze navigation, cube manipulation, and visual planning, including success rates, runtime measurements, and appendix experiments.

results.title: Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion for System 2 Planning

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion narrow the claim of outperforming state-of-the-art methods in lip synchronization to competitive or strong performance. The central framework, video-quality and controllability claims remain intact.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 explicitly acknowledges Sonic's better lip-sync scores and discusses Playmate's greater control flexibility alongside higher implementation complexity. The existing limitations concerning facial scope, extreme head movements, rendering artifacts and backgrounds remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The promised code-access location changes from the project homepage to a specific GitHub repository. Both versions still describe future availability, so this does not establish a release. Hardware, training times, preprocessing and disclosed hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The represented datasets and portrait-animation, emotion-control and pose-control tasks remain unchanged. MEAD already supplied emotion-training data in v2; its new test comparison and the additional ratings and control analyses extend evaluation within existing coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 newly evaluates EAMM, DreamTalk, EDTalk and EAT against Playmate, substantially expanding comparison methods for the central emotion-control contribution. The five existing video-generation baselines remain unchanged and also participate in the new user study.

E3.justification: v3 adds a MEAD emotion-comparison protocol, a 10-participant study using 1–5 ratings for four perceptual metrics, APD measurements in Appendix A.3, and fixed-latent controls in A.4. Existing training and preprocessing settings remain unchanged; Emo-A was already used in v2's CFG ablation.

E4.justification: Appendix A.4 and Figure 10 add a targeted disentanglement analysis: generated poses with fixed facial dynamics, and generated facial dynamics with fixed or predefined spinning poses. The adaptive-normalization, CFG and Gaussian-noise ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new user study reports mean ratings and participant count without variability or uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results: emotion accuracy of 0.550 versus EDTalk's 0.460 in Table 2; user-study rankings favoring Playmate for video definition and visual appeal, but Sonic for lip sync and naturalness; and pose APD results and disentanglement examples. Table 1 and the CFG results, renumbered from Table 2 to Table 4, are numerically unchanged.

M1.justification: The latent representation, motion-decoupled module, diffusion transformer, two-stage emotion controller, CFG procedure and appendix noise augmentation are unchanged. The new disentanglement demonstrations test existing capabilities rather than introduce a method component.

P1.justification: Changes include localized wording and typo corrections, revised abstract and conclusion passages, expanded results discussion, and new appendix subsections A.3–A.4. Most prose and the main section sequence remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Three new tables present emotion comparisons, user ratings and pose accuracy, while the new multirow Figure 10 displays disentanglement controls. This substantially expands the visual evidence. All nine earlier figures are retained; some material moves, and the renumbered CFG table gains best/second-best highlighting.

R1.justification: v3 adds the EDTalk reference and expands positioning against Sonic by discussing controllability and complexity. The remaining cited works and the related-work organization are retained; the Tan 2024 citation suffix changes reflect the added reference.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(10), covering latent transformations, losses, normalization, diffusion guidance and noise augmentation, are unchanged. No new formal assumptions, mathematical derivations or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central controllability contribution: v2 offered emotion demonstrations and CFG sweeps, whereas v3 adds comparisons against four emotion-control methods, quantitative pose evaluation and direct disentanglement checks. The user study provides complementary perceptual evidence, and the narrowed lip-sync claims better match Table 1. Sparse new protocol details and absent uncertainty reporting limit confidence, but the added validation and better-calibrated claims constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Playmate framework. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds emotion-control comparisons, a user study, pose-accuracy measurements and disentanglement examples.

before.justification: v2 reports original video-generation benchmarks, CFG and adaptive-normalization ablations, and a Gaussian-noise augmentation experiment in Appendix A.2.

results.title: Playmate: Flexible Control of Portrait Animation via 3D-Implicit Space Guided Diffusion

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claims of logarithmic regret for online KL-regularized contextual bandits and MDPs without the earlier coverage requirement. The correction does not broaden or strengthen these claims.

C2.justification: The interpretations of KL regularization and optimism remain unchanged. Remark 3.1 retains the discussion of absolute versus preference feedback, and the conclusion retains the additional horizon dependence as a limitation.

D1.justification: Algorithm specifications and parameter information are unchanged. Neither version adds implementation instructions, hardware details, training times, or code and data access information.

E1.justification: Neither version actually trains or evaluates on datasets or benchmarks. The abstract contextual-bandit and MDP settings remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates comparison methods. Table 1 retains the same theoretical comparators, including Online Iterative GSHF, Two-Stage Mixed-Policy Sampling, Online Iterative M-GSHF, and XPO.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental evaluation protocols. No splits, metrics, training budgets, sample sizes, or testing procedures are added or revised.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, sensitivity studies, robustness tests, or case studies. The changed appendix passage is a theoretical proof.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. The theoretical probability guarantees and concentration results remain unchanged.

E6.justification: The regret and sample-complexity entries in Table 1 and the guarantees in Theorems 4.1 and 5.1 are unchanged. No empirical results are added, removed, or revised.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1 and 2 retain the same estimation procedures, exploration bonuses, objectives, and policy updates. The appendix revision changes their analysis, not their operation.

P1.justification: v4 adds an Acknowledgements section crediting help identifying a proof error and locally rewrites the explanation and notation in Lemma A.1. The main narrative and section organization otherwise remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Eq. (A.3) now marks the full sum with an underbrace, and the replacement proof introduces expanded equation displays. These additions and the acknowledgements reflow later material; Table 1 and both algorithm displays remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion, cited works, bibliography, and positioning against earlier analyses are unchanged. Reference entries merely shift between pages.

T1.justification: The central monotonicity argument in Lemma A.1 is substantively replaced. v1 uses a single-coordinate partial derivative to justify the bound following Eq. (A.3). v4 instead defines an aggregate U(lambda), differentiates along the interpolated reward function, and proves E[X^3] - E[X^2]E[X] is nonnegative for X >= 0. This changes the reasoning supporting both main regret guarantees, while retaining the assumptions and theorem statements.

improvement.justification: v1's Lemma A.1 leaves a central gap by inferring monotonicity under simultaneous reward changes from a single-coordinate derivative. v4 supplies the aggregate interpolation and nonnegative-covariance argument that addresses this gap. Because this bound supports Theorem 4.1 and the MDP reduction in Lemma B.1, the correction substantially strengthens the paper's main theoretical contribution. The unchanged Section 4.2 sketch and small algebraic slips in the new display, including a dropped eta factor, still need cleanup, but do not outweigh this substantive repair.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Logarithmic Regret for Online KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning. All 29 pages of each version, including equations, Table 1, algorithms, and Appendices A–D, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 remains a theoretical paper. The revised appendix supplies mathematical reasoning, with no original empirical outcomes added elsewhere.

before.justification: v1 reports algorithms and theoretical guarantees, including appendix proofs. Its empirical RLHF examples are attributed to cited work; it reports no original experiments, simulations, or data analyses.

results.title: Logarithmic Regret for Online KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and results summary expand the headline comparison from primarily Llama-3-8B versus SpinQuant to claimed uniform superiority across models through 70B. Section 1.1 identifies QA-LDLQ as an innovation and claims full quantization can outperform prior methods retaining full-precision KV caches. The original drop-in quantizer claim and 6.6-perplexity example remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds activation-noise amplification as a large-model failure mechanism and explains QA-LDLQ's tradeoff between noise robustness and output bias. It also explains NestQuantM's altered shaping region and qualifies the comparison against W4A4KV16 methods with a Llama-2-7B exception. These extend v1's interpretations centered on lattice shaping and ordinary LDLQ.

D1.justification: Appendix E replaces the earlier operation-count discussion with concrete CUDA implementation information: an integer basis for 2E8, packed vector representations, bit-mask operations, beta-index decoding and code listings. Hardware and kernel-benchmark details are added. The original calibration and beta-search disclosures remain in relocated Appendix G.

E1.justification: Both versions use WikiText2, ARC-Easy/Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande and synthetic Gaussian matrix data. The added Llama configurations, precision settings and GEMV timings extend evaluation within the retained language and matrix-product tasks; they do not introduce another dataset or domain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds reported comparisons with QuIP#, OstQuant and DuQuant, and includes QuaRot in weight-only comparisons. Appendix E.1 adds kernel comparisons with QuIP# and uniform int4. The original Table 1 comparator set remains, so these are substantive extensions rather than renamed or replaced baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-2 7B/13B/70B and Llama-3-70B configurations, W3A3KV16 evaluation with q=7 and k=4, and an 8192-by-8192 GEMV benchmark on an A100. Its noise diagnostic adds an epsilon sweep using ten 2048-token sequences. Existing WikiText2 split, context and calibration settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds a substantial failure analysis: poor Llama-3-70B quantization is traced to four activation-sensitive layers, with a full-precision-layer intervention and Figure 6 examining the noise-amplification versus output-error tradeoff. The earlier LDLQ, rotation, scaling-count and First-beta/Opt-beta analyses remain, including those relocated to appendices.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed or repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates. The new activation-noise covariance model and epsilon sweep concern the method and sensitivity analysis, rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive result entries, including Llama-3-70B full-quantization perplexity of 3.61 in Table 2 and three-bit results in Appendix J. Table 4 reports NestQuantM at 60 microseconds versus 97 for FP16 and 31 for uniform int4; the approximately 75-microsecond QuIP# four-bit value is extrapolated. Original benchmark and ablation tables retain their values.

M1.justification: Section 4.5 introduces QA-LDLQ, replacing ordinary LDLQ with transformed weights and a Hessian incorporating activation-noise covariance. Appendix D adds NestQuantM, whose decoder repairs parity using a fixed coordinate instead of argmin/argmax searches while retaining the original encoding oracle. These change the quantization procedure.

P1.justification: The overall introduction–prior work–method–experiments structure and much of the prose remain. v2 rewrites the codebook explanation and results summary, clarifies terminology, and moves the Llama-3.2-1B and scaling-count discussions into appendices. This is targeted editing and reorganization rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds a central multi-model comparison table, kernel-timing and three-bit tables, and a paired noise-amplification figure. Figure 4 corrects the Hadamard/output-projection order. Existing Llama-3.2-1B and scaling-count displays move to appendices, while the other original plots are retained. Together these substantially extend the evidence displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to lattice quantization noise, Optimal Brain Compression, DuQuant and OstQuant, and positions QA-LDLQ as a correction to LDLQ/GPTQ when activations are quantized. The existing information-theoretic and LLM-quantization survey remains largely intact; many other reference edits only update bibliographic metadata.

T1.justification: v2 adds Lemma 4.2 and its QA-LDLQ derivation under independent, zero-mean activation noise, plus Lemma D.1 proving translation equivariance of the modified oracle. It also introduces the amplification-ratio definition and NestQuantM shaping argument. The earlier crude runtime derivation is removed.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's practical case: QA-LDLQ responds to a documented large-model failure, Table 2 validates configurations through 70B, and Appendix E supplies CUDA code and measured kernel timings where v1 mainly offered cost estimates. These substantially strengthen applicability and reproducibility. Some superiority wording exceeds the tables, including a QuIP# tie, and the timing comparison uses unequal bitrates and an extrapolated baseline; these limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NestQuant, with matching authors, core algorithms and original experiments. All 16 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable and support matching text, equations, figures and tables across relocations.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds larger-model evaluations, activation-noise diagnostics, NestQuantM results and GPU kernel timings.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian-matrix simulations, Llama perplexity and zero-shot evaluations, and quantization ablations.

results.title: NestQuant: Nested Lattice Quantization for Matrix Products and LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract, main observations, and conclusion move tokenizer choice from a dominant determinant alongside pretraining data to a generally minor or negligible factor. V2 also foregrounds the implication that similar training losses on the same data yield closely matched downstream performance across training setups.

C2.justification: V1 attributes tokenizer differences to special-token handling and interprets deduplication as preserving the data distribution. V2 instead proposes weight tying as an untested explanation for exceptional pretrained-model curves and interprets deduplication as meaningfully changing the distribution. These revise substantive explanations of central findings.

D1.justification: V2 specifies SciPy curve_fit and fallback estimation, lists pretrained model names, sizes, datasets, and tokenizers, and clarifies tokenizer-ablation details in Tables 2–3. Conversely, v1's code-website statement and link are removed; this establishes lost access guidance, not that the code itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: OpenBookQA is removed from the reported task list and corresponding appendix scaling plots. The pretraining and validation corpora and remaining nine downstream tasks are retained. COPA appears in v2 Figure 2 but was already evaluated in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the GPT, Llama, Mamba, and Mamba2 architecture groups and the same tokenizer alternatives. The new point-wise comparison uses the existing Llama–Mamba pairing; the pretrained-model inventory adds identification details rather than establishing new comparators.

E3.justification: Cross-tokenizer evaluation changes from token-based loss to byte-normalized BPB, materially changing the basis of a central comparison. V2 also reports few-step Llama-7B checkpoints, point-wise comparisons after approximately eight billion tokens, and a new curve-area metric evaluated over [0, 2].

E4.justification: V2 supplements the retained intervention suite with matched-loss architecture comparisons in Section 5/Table 1, quantitative curve-separation analysis in Appendix D/Table 4, and a larger-model check in Figure 1. Existing alternative-axis and individual-task analyses remain in the appendices.

E5.justification: Figure 1 newly reports R-squared goodness-of-fit values of 0.998–0.999. The existing statements about 200–800 checkpoints and varying seeds remain; no increase in independent runs or new confidence intervals is documented.

E6.justification: BPB-based results replace the moderate tokenizer-effect finding with generally minor differences; these are not same-metric performance gains. Figure 4 and Section 4.1 change the Pile/deduplicated-Pile finding from coincident to separated curves. New tables add concrete results, including base-to-data and base-to-tokenizer curve areas of 0.22 and 0.01; OpenBookQA results disappear.

M1.justification: The model architectures, training objectives, intervention framework, and central shifted-power-law fitting approach are retained. Appendix B provides additional fitting documentation without establishing that the underlying procedure changed; BPB normalization changes evaluation.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized revisions to the abstract, introduction, tokenizer discussion, and conclusion, adds a short Point-wise Comparisons section, and expands appendix explanations. Most of the original prose and narrative sequence are retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds three tables and a compute-to-loss contour figure, redraws the central tokenizer plots and appendix counterparts with BPB axes, and adds fit annotations and highlighted checkpoints to Figure 1. It also corrects several model-size, context-length, and optimizer captions in the final appendix figures.

R1.justification: V2 adds the SciPy reference and removes the OpenBookQA reference. It also drops v1's novelty assertion about special-token effects. The main positioning relative to loss-to-loss scaling and robustness research remains intact; the OLMo publication update identifies the same work.

T1.justification: Appendices A–B add explicit mathematical specifications for compute-to-loss fitting, including the minimum-observed-loss fallback estimator in Equation 5, which v1 did not specify. The central shifted-power-law equation and irreducible-error interpretation remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: BPB normalization addresses a central cross-tokenizer comparability problem underlying v1's headline conclusion, and v2 revises that conclusion while acknowledging exceptional models. Numerical intervention comparisons and clearer fitting documentation make the evidence substantially easier to assess. Removing the code-access link is a drawback, but the correction to this central scientific comparison outweighs it.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original experiments and supplementary analyses can be matched despite renumbering and additions.

after.justification: V2 retains original training and scaling experiments and additionally reports numerical model comparisons and quantified intervention effects.

before.justification: V1 reports original Llama and Mamba training experiments and loss-to-loss scaling analyses across model checkpoints, including intervention results in the appendices.

results.title: LLMs on the Line: Data Determines Loss-to-Loss Scaling Laws

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions and conclusion retain the same claims: efficient, FM-agnostic online forecast adaptation using a linear forecaster and dynamic weighting improves forecasting. Renaming the approach and adding supporting experiments do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: V3 newly qualifies the fixed-FM recommendation by acknowledging conditions where simultaneous finetuning helps at additional computational cost. The weighting discussion replaces the simpler-versus-complex-dataset explanation with a suggested mechanism for defaulting to one component. The frequency-removal discussion drops the earlier 5%-retention superiority statement alongside new curves showing failures under heavy filtering.

D1.justification: V3 adds explicit DFT/RFT processing, frequency cropping, zero-padding, initialization timing and three forecaster/Woodbury algorithms in Appendix A.1.3. Appendix B documents new comparator initialization, normalization, update settings and memory-driven TAFAS restrictions, plus statistics and seasonalities for the added datasets. Core hyperparameter values are retained.

E1.justification: V3 Appendix C.1 adds systematic evaluation on Wind-PerSec, Solar-PerSec and Cloud-PerSec, extending coverage to second-resolution forecasting scenarios where computational latency matters. The nine original benchmark datasets remain. V2 already included qualitative cloud examples, which are retained rather than newly introduced.

E2.justification: V3 adds evaluated comparisons with TAFAS, FSNet, OneNet and OneNet-TTM in Tables 2 and 5. Forecaster ablations additionally compare OGD, FITS, FSNet and residual-prediction alternatives, while the weighting ablation adds Hedge. The original unadapted-FM and TTM-finetuning comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New comparator experiments introduce initialization on the first 2,000 steps, RevIN normalization, method-specific update intervals and restrictions on TAFAS prediction adjustment and calibration modules. The weighting ablation changes from per-dataset MASE averaged across FMs to per-FM relative MASE averaged across datasets. The original main experiment's context length, horizons and update interval remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 adds tests of continually finetuning TTM alongside ELF and replacing the auxiliary forecaster with four alternatives. It expands the weighting ablation with Hedge and extends frequency-removal sensitivity analysis from Weather/ETTm1 to ECL/Solar. These investigate additional design choices and failure conditions beyond the retained analyses.

E5.justification: V2 Table 5 contains unspecified plus/minus quantities. V3 explicitly identifies standard errors in Tables 9 and 10, with aggregation across datasets. Neither version supplies seed or repeated-run counts, so this does not establish that additional runs were performed.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial results in Tables 2, 4, 5, 8 and 9 and replaces the weighting summaries in Table 10. For example, Table 8 reports that frozen TTM+ELF beats continually finetuned TTM+ELF in 9 of 12 conditions. The original main MASE, RMSSE, finetuning and standalone-forecaster tables retain their numerical values; the reaggregated weighting scores are not same-setting improvements over v2.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains the Fourier-domain ridge forecaster, frequency filtering, Woodbury updates and fast/slow/merge exponential weighting. AdapTS becomes ELF. Expanded transform, initialization and pseudocode descriptions document the existing approach; alternative forecasters and simultaneous finetuning are experimental variants.

P1.justification: The central forecaster exposition in Section 4.1 is substantially rewritten around separate forecasting and online-fitting stages. Section 3 is streamlined, Section 5.3 is recast around continual-learning comparisons, and the methodological appendix gains a dedicated algorithm subsection. Paper-wide renaming, acknowledgements and an impact statement accompany this restructuring.

P2.justification: V3 adds five result tables and three algorithm displays, expands Figure 8 from two to four panels, and rebuilds the weighting table with FM-based rows and a Hedge column. The single-finetuning and weighting tables replace checkmark columns with bolded best values. Retained figures and tables are also relocated and relabeled.

R1.justification: Section 5.3 adds targeted positioning against TAFAS, FSNet and OneNet, with additional references for TAFAS, OneNet, RevIN, Monash datasets, gating and convolutional models. Section 2 and the broad research framing remain largely unchanged. The added 2023 FSNet reference represents work already cited in its 2022 form.

T1.justification: Section 5.1 corrects the printed MASE definition's context summation limit from H-S to L-S and consistently uses H for the forecast horizon. The regret theorem and OLS/Woodbury reasoning remain unchanged. The added DFT formula and algorithm descriptions primarily provide explanation.

improvement.justification: V2 left comparisons with other online adaptation approaches and the choice of auxiliary forecaster largely untested. V3 substantially addresses these validation gaps through Tables 2, 5 and 9, adds deployment-relevant per-second evaluations, and makes implementation substantially more explicit. Disclosed TAFAS restrictions limit the comparison's generality, and the reaggregated weighting table loses dataset-level detail, but these tradeoffs do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with AdapTS renamed ELF in v3. Inspection of all 23 and 29 pages, respectively, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds online-method comparisons, per-second dataset evaluations and further ablations in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: V2 reports original forecasting experiments, computational measurements, finetuning comparisons, ablations and case studies in Section 5 and Appendix C.

results.title: Lightweight Online Adaption for Time Series Foundation Model Forecasts

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution summary, and conclusion retain the same central claims: characterizing and correcting inversion bias for random sampling and SRHT, and establishing problem-independent local SSN convergence. Their high-level scope is unchanged despite the revised quantitative guarantees.

C2.justification: Remark 3.5 incorporates logarithmic factors into the threshold determining when scalar debiasing matches fine-grained debiasing, changing that applicability boundary. The two-regime interpretation, empirical explanations, and future-work limitations otherwise remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix G retains the same leverage-score and SJLT construction details, Armijo line search, preprocessing, regularization parameters, and reference to the Newton-LESS repository. No implementation or resource-access information is added.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate logistic regression and inversion bias using MNIST and CIFAR-10. Appendix G retains the same binary grouping of image classes; no dataset or test scenario is added.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged: Newton-LESS in Figure 2; GD, SGD, LESS, SRHT, ARLev, ALev, and SLev in Figure 3; and RLev, ARLev, DARLev with their non-debiased counterparts in Figure 4.

E3.justification: Empirical settings remain unchanged, including dataset dimensions, preprocessing, regularization, timing conventions, Figure 2's five/seven iterations, and Figure 3's sketch sizes of 300/400. Revised theoretical sample-size requirements are not changes to the experiments.

E4.justification: The sketch-size sweep in Figure 2 and Appendix G.3's comparisons of exact versus approximate leverage sampling, with and without scalar debiasing, are retained without additional ablations or robustness analyses.

E5.justification: Figures 2, 3, and 4 retain averaging over 30, 10, and 500 independent runs, respectively, with deterministic GD excepted. No empirical uncertainty-reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: Figures 2–4 retain the same numerical curves, comparisons, and reported findings, including ARLev's favorable convergence–time tradeoff and reduced inversion bias under scalar debiasing. The theoretical bound revisions are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The sampling reweighting in Equation (5), scalar debiasing, approximate-leverage variants, and SSN updates remain unchanged. The revised theoretical guarantees do not change these procedures.

P1.justification: The document retains its organization and most prose, with local proof expansion, added tilde asymptotic notation, and an updated date. Numerous cross-references now incorrectly say Theorem while their targets remain labeled Definition, Lemma, Proposition, Remark, or Assumption.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes its asymptotic axis annotations to include tilde-O and tilde-Theta. Figures 2–4 retain their plots and panel structures; revised equations and text cause local reflow and changes in placement relative to surrounding paragraphs.

R1.justification: The bibliography removes Burkholder (1973) and adds de la Peña and Giné (1999) for the replacement martingale inequality. The broader related-work discussion and research positioning remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Lemma A.4 replaces Burkholder's inequality with a martingale Rosenthal inequality. Lemma D.1 replaces an individual variance bound with an expected-maximum bound using moments of order log(n), correcting the expectation/maximum step in Appendix D.2. The resulting log(n)/log(log(n)) factor propagates through Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.2, and Appendices E–F, changing sample-size requirements, bias bounds, and SSN convergence errors and neighborhoods.

improvement.justification: V3's Equation (27) unjustifiably moves a maximum outside an expectation. V4's Equation (28) retains the expected maximum and supplies a high-moment argument in Lemma D.1, propagating its logarithmic cost into the central guarantees. Addressing this foundational proof gap substantially improves the mathematical support for this primarily theoretical paper. The more conservative bounds reflect that correction; the introduced cross-reference errors are a smaller presentation drawback.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their complete main texts, equations, four figures, and Appendices A–G support reliable comparison, including the expanded proofs in v4.

after.justification: V4 retains the original logistic-regression and inversion-bias experiments in Section 5 and Appendix G.3.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original logistic-regression experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10. Appendix G.3 reports original numerical inversion-bias experiments.

results.title: Fundamental Bias in Inverting Random Sampling Matrices with Application to Sub-sampled Newton

C1.justification: V2 withdraws SnapKV++ as a separately proposed contribution and instead emphasizes adopting SnapKV, adaptive compression decomposition, and RocketKV-MT. The abstract and introduction add multi-turn applicability and near-oracle accuracy claims, plus a 400× compression claim and revised efficiency claims on A100.

C2.justification: V2 explains why permanent eviction fails across turns and explicitly states that RocketKV-MT sacrifices storage savings to preserve context. It adds reasoning for adaptive compression allocation, discusses disaggregated serving, and interprets A100/H100 speedup differences through their memory-bandwidth-to-compute ratios.

D1.justification: V2 documents integer page-size rounding, a worked 64× compression allocation, revised pooling parameters, and SCBench observation-window settings. A100 hardware information is added, while the Python/gpt-fast implementation, FP16 precision, batch size one, and existing benchmark preprocessing remain documented.

E1.justification: LongBench, NIAH, and RULER coverage is retained. V2 adds SCBench multi-turn evaluation on Llama3.1-8B-Ins, testing retrieval, question answering, global operations, and mixed tasks across successive queries. Reusing context across turns introduces a substantial new evaluation scenario.

E2.justification: The separately evaluated SnapKV-GQA variant in v1 Figures 6 and 9 disappears from v2's comparisons. Otherwise, corresponding benchmark tables preserve Full-KV, Exact-TopK, DuoAttention, SnapKV, Quest, SparQ, and standalone Hybrid, renamed HSA. SCBench extends this existing roster.
