E3.justification: V2 introduces SCBench budgets of 1024–16384, a 128-token observation window, and a 127,500-token prompt limit; efficiency testing adds A100 alongside H100. The new qasper analysis examines 200 questions using layer 31, head 0. Appendix A.3 also removes v1's explicit generated-token deduction from SnapKV's budget description, leaving that accounting less explicit.

E4.justification: V2 adds a CDF analysis of unique Exact-TopK token selections and compares adaptive compression splitting against fixed factors 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. V1's GQA-enhancement and pooling-kernel sensitivity studies are removed. Standalone Hybrid/HSA comparisons remain supported by the appendix tables, despite fewer plotted models.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or performance uncertainty estimates. V2's new CDF characterizes token-selection behavior across questions rather than introducing uncertainty reporting for experimental results.

E6.justification: RocketKV and SnapKV values change throughout the retained appendix tables. For example, RocketKV's Llama3.1 RULER-96K average at budget 256 changes from 57.5 to 73.2 under revised method settings (v1 Table 7; v2 Table 9). V2 adds SCBench results and reports maxima of 3.3× on H100, 3.7× on A100, and 32.6% memory savings, versus v1's 3× on H100 and 31.4%.

M1.justification: V2 replaces equal square-root compression splitting with an adaptive split factor and replaces sequence-dependent 63/511 pooling with fixed pooling size 63. It also introduces RocketKV-MT, which preserves the full KV history and selects a new subset each turn. Hybrid attention is renamed HSA with its underlying selection steps retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and method exposition are substantially rewritten. Existing baseline motivation moves into the introduction, cost analysis is reorganized into adaptive compression and system implications, and the main-text ablation section is restructured within Appendix B.1. Acknowledgment and impact sections are added.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column conference layout and rearranges the HSA diagram and pseudocode side by side. It removes the first-stage pseudocode, adds CDF, SCBench, and split-factor displays, expands the efficiency figure to three panels, redraws heatmaps, and reorganizes appendix tables.

R1.justification: V1 claims GQA-compatible SnapKV++ as a contribution; v2 explicitly adopts SnapKV and credits Ada-KV for groupwise selection, materially revising the novelty attribution. Research positioning also expands to SCBench, MLA/DeepSeek, XAttention, and disaggregated serving systems.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.6 generalizes the storage derivation from 1/sqrt(c) + 2/c^(3/4) to 1/c^r + 2/c^((1+r)/2), and derives the corresponding RocketKV-MT expression. This extends the existing analytical cost model without introducing a new theorem or proof framework.

improvement.justification: V2 exposes a multi-turn failure untested in v1 and evaluates a targeted remedy: at budget 1024, Table 4 reports 44.3 for RocketKV-MT, 26.6 for RocketKV, and 45.0 for Exact-TopK. Explicit storage tradeoffs, compression-split ablations, and clearer attribution substantially strengthen applicability and scientific support. These gains outweigh the removed GQA/kernel ablations, although SnapKV budget accounting becomes less explicit and the headline speedup includes newly tested hardware.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RocketKV and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–B. The retained experiments and method components can be matched reliably despite substantial revision and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark and efficiency results, including new SCBench multi-turn evaluations, A100 measurements, token-selection analysis, and compression-split ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and RULER evaluations, H100 efficiency measurements, and component ablations in Section 4 and Appendix B.

results.title: RocketKV: Accelerating Long-Context LLM Inference via Two-Stage KV Cache Compression

C1.justification: The abstract and five introductory contributions retain their central claims about narrow finetuning, controls, backdoors, and number sequences. The revised conclusion additionally claims emergent misalignment in base models, extending applicability without redefining the central finding.

C2.justification: v1's speculative grokking/regularization explanation is revised using training-dynamics and weight-decay/extended-training evidence. v5 develops the malicious-persona explanation, argues that alignment post-training is unnecessary, and adds substantive qualifications about Flask results overlapping with insecure-code behavior and evaluations potentially failing to predict practical harm.

D1.justification: v5 explicitly reports availability of training/evaluation code and OpenAI reproduction instructions beyond v1's dataset disclosure. It also documents chat templates and the default system prompt, and explains the retained GPT-4o loss plot's random-run selection and 50-step smoothing. These disclosures do not establish changes to earlier training.

E1.justification: The coding and number datasets, Ruby/paraphrase variants, main and preregistered questions, and external benchmark suite are retained. The new analyses reuse these tasks with different model configurations and evaluation formats, including Flask wrapping and token-probability measurements.

E2.justification: v5 adds a direct comparison between Qwen2.5-Coder-32B base and Instruct models under matched Flask evaluation conditions (Figure 14). The original comparisons against unfinetuned, secure, educational-insecure, and jailbroken models remain intact.

E3.justification: Sections 4.7–4.8 introduce evaluation every 10 training steps, 100 held-out coding prompts, 1,000 sampled answers per question, and multiple-choice/pivotal-token measurements. New conditions include zero weight decay, extended training, and Flask evaluation with a coherence threshold of 95 instead of the usual 50. These additions do not establish rerunning the earlier experiments.

E4.justification: v5 adds substantial analyses of when misalignment emerges relative to coding performance, whether weight decay and extended training support the grokking analogy, whether post-training is necessary, and how assistant versus neutral chat templates affect base models. The earlier diversity, backdoor, formatting, and in-context-learning analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v5 specifies globally that error bars represent bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals; v1 already reported seeded runs and identified confidence intervals for the backdoor experiment. New dynamics plots show ranges across five seeds, and Figure 38 specifies model counts by template. The original main-experiment run counts remain unchanged.

E6.justification: New results document training trajectories, little effect from removing weight decay, plateauing beyond one epoch, and base-model/template differences under Flask evaluation. Table 1 also changes Machiavelli values from 119.3 ± 1.30 to 0.196 ± 0.013 for insecure models and 99.4 ± 1.61 to -0.004 ± 0.016 for jailbroken models, correcting normalization and reference rather than demonstrating a performance gain.

M1.justification: The core supervised finetuning procedure, code/number dataset construction, and rs-LoRA approach are retained. The added base-model, weight-decay, and chat-template experiments vary experimental conditions without introducing a new core algorithm or training objective.

P1.justification: Related work, discussion, limitations, safety implications, and the conclusion undergo substantial rewriting and narrative reorganization. The related-work discussion gains thematic divisions, while Sections 4.7–4.8 and Appendix G extend the document structure. Most earlier experimental descriptions remain intact.

P2.justification: v5 adds paired training curves, log-probability panels, base-model and chat-template comparisons, prompt illustrations, and Tables 10–11. Original figures are largely retained and renumbered. Additional presentation edits include axis/legend wording, an expanded loss-plot caption, code syntax highlighting, and appendix line numbers.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially expands research positioning through comparisons with reward tampering, alignment faking, Bing Chat, emergent preferences, and out-of-context reasoning. New references include Mazeika, Davies, Roose, and Treutlein; several earlier bibliography entries are removed.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs. The added log-probability measurements and grokking discussion introduce empirical analyses and mechanistic hypotheses, without substantive formal derivations or mathematical assumptions.

improvement.justification: v1's tentative grokking explanation gains direct empirical scrutiny through training trajectories and weight-decay/extended-training controls, substantially strengthening the analysis of possible mechanisms. Base-model and chat-template comparisons further constrain explanations, while clearer statistical and reproducibility disclosures improve assessability. The Flask results remain partly confounded by insecure-code outputs, as v5 acknowledges; this limits their interpretation but does not outweigh the stronger mechanistic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including material renumbered between versions.

after.justification: v5 retains those empirical results and adds training-dynamics experiments, base-model evaluations, and chat-template comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original finetuning experiments, benchmark evaluations, control comparisons, and ablations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and concluding contribution statements retain the same central claims: synthetic interaction training develops transferable decision-making abilities, and curriculum sampling improves data efficiency. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining the core contribution.

C2.justification: v3 clarifies task-directed curiosity and amortized exploration, explicitly identifies Wordle as a case of absent or negative transfer, and discusses limitations associated with lengthy reasoning and starting-model quality. Existing caveats about environment hacking, Minesweeper preference pairs, and limited standard-bandit transfer remain.

D1.justification: New appendices disclose environment/judge temperature and token limits, agent token limits, Gemma training hardware, and explicit code, dataset, and checkpoint access links. These materially expand reproducibility information. The inference settings are newly documented, rather than demonstrated changes to existing experiments; Gemma training-data counts remain unspecified.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same ten task groups, LMRL-Gym evaluations, modified Wordle scenarios, standard-bandit test, and six standard benchmarks. The additional model configurations and controls operate within retained task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds PAPRIKA trained on a single task group to the generalization comparisons in Figures 3 and 13, providing an important task-specific comparator absent from v1. It also adds comparisons with unmodified Gemma-3-12B-IT. GPT-4o-mini and WildChat fine-tuning additionally enter the best-arm-selection comparison in Figures 5–6.

E3.justification: v3 adds Gemma-3-12B-IT experiments and single task group training controls, reports pass@k for k=1–4, and removes the best-of-four turn-count metric. Table 1 also revises the twenty-questions training count from 1,500 to 1,499; this reported correction does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Generalization analysis expands from five displayed task groups to all ten and adds single-group versus joint training controls. The SFT/RPO ablation expands from four groups to six, adding Minesweeper and Wordle. Appendix I.11 adds starting-model comparisons and observations about unsuccessful DeepSeek-R1 distilled-model inference.

E5.justification: v1 Figures 2 and 5 explicitly identify their bands as standard errors over three seeds. Their expanded counterparts in v3 Figures 6–7 retain bands without that explicit caption information, while the new main summary uses bars without uncertainty indicators. Three-seed reporting remains elsewhere; no increased run count or new statistical procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive Gemma, pass@k, single-group training, and expanded ablation results. Figure 3 reports LOO improvement on nine of ten groups and joint training outperforming single-group training on seven. The best-of-four turn-count results disappear. These additions coexist with unchanged standard-benchmark values in Table 2.

M1.justification: The described self-generated trajectory collection, filtering, SFT followed by RPO, action-token optimization, and coefficient-of-variation/UCB curriculum remain unchanged. Corrected equation signs and applying the pipeline to Gemma do not establish a changed training procedure.

P1.justification: Most methodological prose and detailed task prompts remain intact. v3 makes localized introduction and results rewrites, adds explanatory and reproducibility sections, moves WildChat discussion into the appendix, and regroups standard-benchmark details. The principal section sequence remains stable.

P2.justification: Figure 2 changes from six temperature curves to a ten-task bar-chart comparison, and Figure 3 expands its panels and comparator display. Numerous appendix plots are added, recolored, resized, and rearranged; the best-of-four efficiency figure is removed. A new table summarizes initial states, actions, and observations.

R1.justification: The introduction and new Appendix A substantially position PAPRIKA relative to intrinsic motivation and exploration research. Section 5 and Appendix B.2 also expand connections to agent training and text environments, including ReAct, Aviary, TextWorld, and DiscoveryWorld. This extends research positioning beyond isolated citation additions.

T1.justification: v3 adds the missing leading minus signs to the SFT and DPO loss equations in Section 3.3, correcting their mathematical loss formulation. The POMDP framework, curriculum definitions, and coefficient-of-variation estimator remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evaluation of the central generality claim through a second model family and direct comparisons with task-specific training, addressing important gaps in v1. Corrected losses, explicit inference settings, and release information also improve reproducibility. Losing the best-of-four efficiency analysis and some explicit uncertainty labeling are limited drawbacks relative to these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PAPRIKA research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds Gemma-3 experiments, single task group controls, additional metrics, and starting-model analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original training and evaluation results, including task success, generalization, curriculum learning, ablations, and qualitative trajectory analyses.

results.title: Training a Generally Curious Agent

C1.justification: The central market-induction and differentiable-learning contributions remain. The introduction narrows the claim that accurate classifiers must associate positive predictions with high budgets to a tendency that occurs often. It also emphasizes that raising the threshold can increase crossing, where v1 emphasized its limited effectiveness.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a broader cluster hypothesis, explains how accurate classification can occur without budget-label correlation, and discusses where the surrogate loss struggles. It explicitly notes that prior generalization bounds do not immediately transfer to dependent users. The Adult discussion adds market-readjustment interpretations and drops v1's low-budget overfitting discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds Folktables feature, label, and budget mappings; scaling and feature-flipping instructions; budget filtering; and dataset-specific learning rates and epoch counts. Existing Adult implementation and preprocessing details remain substantially unchanged, as does the code URL.

E1.justification: v2 adds Folktables employment-status classification using personal income as the budget proxy, extending coverage beyond Adult income classification with capital-gain-based budgets. Appendix B.2 also adds a scenario with heterogeneous budgets independent of labels.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparisons retain naive, strat, and the non-strategic benchmark. Folktables uses this same comparator set. The new short/long distinction evaluates strat under different price conditions rather than introducing another comparison method.

E3.justification: v2 separates fixed-price short-term and re-equilibrated long-term evaluation of strat. New diagnostic experiments introduce threshold sweeps and exact-versus-smoothed price comparisons on 1,000 samples. Folktables adds its own preprocessing and 1,000-epoch training protocol; Adult retains its previously stated splits, metrics, and 100-epoch budget.

E4.justification: New Appendices B.1–B.3 test the market-hinge approximation to 0-1 loss, classification without budget-label correlation, and price-setter jumps while varying mixture separation, location, and variance. Earlier price-sensitivity and inverted-data analyses remain, with some empirical revenue plots revised.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard errors over 10 random data splits. Folktables adopts the same split/repetition scheme. No new uncertainty-estimation procedure, significance test, or increase in repeated runs is reported.

E6.justification: Adult curves change between v1 Figure 6 and v2 Figure 7, which also adds separate strat short/long results. New Figures 13–15 and 17 report loss landscapes, cluster behavior, and Folktables outcomes. The budget-independent example reports accuracies of 0.83 for h2 and 0.63 for h1. Some retained empirical revenue examples also have changed plotted values.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and the market-hinge objective remain unchanged. Equation (6) now explicitly returns x plus the purchased features, consistent with v1's existing response procedure. The negative-weight discussion provides additional justification for the existing computation.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence and much existing prose remain. Local rewrites clarify the introduction, setup, learning approach, and experiments; appendices gain descriptive subsections. Author contribution and publication notices change, and acknowledgements move before the impact statement.

P2.justification: v2 adds a five-panel market schematic and four experimental figures, expands the Adult comparison legend, and rearranges several retained appendix figures into side-by-side layouts. These substantially expand the visual presentation. Figure 14 introduces a mismatched caption describing increasing sample size instead of its classifier comparison.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on strategic learnability, practical strategic classification, recommendation incentives, competing classifiers, and feature-based market decongestion. It explicitly distinguishes its setting from Nahum et al. The externalities citation changes from Chen et al. to Hossain et al. for the same work, rather than adding another research contribution.

T1.justification: Proposition 1 changes from asserting proportional market prices to asserting existence of a proportional equilibrium. New Appendix A.1 introduces Proposition 2 and a proof relating projected demand to single-feature purchases, addressing classifiers with negative weights when at least one weight is positive. The earlier revenue theorems and proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond Adult's largely imputed budgets through Folktables, direct surrogate-loss diagnostics, and a budget-independence example that supports narrowing v1's necessity claim. Separating short- and long-term baseline outcomes also clarifies the central comparison. Some new reporting is imperfect: Appendix B.5 claims dominance from scale 2² although Figure 17 shows strat short ahead at several lower scales. Nevertheless, the added checks and substantive qualifications provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Learning Classifiers That Induce Markets. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, and appendices A–D are readable and support comparison across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Folktables experiments, loss-landscape comparisons, and analyses of budget independence and demand clusters.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic market experiments, Adult classification results, and appendix analyses of empirical prices and induced separability.

results.title: Learning Classifiers That Induce Markets

C1.justification: The central sparse-compression contribution and broad efficiency claims remain. The introduction reduces the stated ImageNet advantage from 17% to 9% and replaces the claim that MRL requires training from scratch with a requirement for full-parameter updates. The conclusion additionally claims complementarity with other acceleration techniques.

C2.justification: v3 gives more specific backend and nonzero-overlap explanations for sparse retrieval speed, removes the Johnson–Lindenstrauss analogy, and interprets the new zero-shot results as evidence of scalability and transfer. The dead-latent limitation already appeared in v1. Some overgeneralization remains: Figure 7's all-dimensions superiority wording conflicts with Table 5 at larger dimensions.

D1.justification: v3 identifies FF2048, explains SVD and random-feature baseline construction, specifies Figure 1(c)'s averaging range, and adds CC3M hyperparameters and trainable-parameter counts. It removes v1's sentence-transformer implementation note for Int8 quantization. Hardware, core code-access information, and most existing implementation details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds CC3M training and zero-shot transfer to MS COCO and Flickr30K, substantially extending evaluation beyond target-dataset training in the multimodal experiments. Existing ImageNet and text coverage remains. Appendix B.1 mentions few-shot results, but no separately identifiable outcomes support counting additional few-shot coverage.

E2.justification: MRL-LP enters the linear-probing accuracy comparison in v3 Figure 7(a) and Table 5, whereas v1 included it only in Figure 1(c)'s training-cost comparison; it disappears from that revised cost plot. The text and multimodal comparator sets remain unchanged after matching shortened model names.

E3.justification: v3 adds ImageNet comparisons using the FF2048 ResNet50 backbone alongside the retained stronger-backbone results, and adds linear-probing evaluation. Table 3 changes the reported image-training batch size from 1024 to 4096 and gamma from 1.0 to 0.1. Appendix D introduces separate CC3M training protocols for zero-shot evaluation. These are substantive experimental-setting changes, without establishing that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The new CC3M-to-COCO/Flickr30K evaluation tests cross-dataset multimodal generalization. Appendix E.4 and Table 11 additionally test the runtime explanation by counting multiplications across hidden dimensions and sparsity levels. Existing backbone-size, hidden-dimension, loss, and dead-latent analyses in Figures 4–6 and 8 are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report three random seeds and mean performance for the Appendix E.1–E.2 studies. They also retain the same 2000 timing rounds and 100 warm-up rounds in E.3. No new uncertainty-reporting practice or significance test is introduced.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial matched-backbone, linear-probing, zero-shot retrieval, and operation-count results. In Table 4, v1's CSR accuracy of 73.84 at eight active dimensions remains under the stronger-backbone label; the new FF2048 result is 67.78, not a same-setting deterioration. Retained entries also change: CSR's NFCorpus score rises from 37.06 to 38.06 in Table 1, and several stronger-backbone ImageNet scores are revised. Table 2's existing in-distribution scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Both versions use frozen embeddings, a TopK sparse autoencoder, auxiliary and Multi-TopK reconstruction losses, and a contrastive objective. v3 explicitly writes ReLU after TopK, clarifying the nonnegative latents already assumed in v1; this does not establish a changed procedure.

P1.justification: Sections 3.2 and 4 undergo extensive explanatory rewriting, including renamed method subsections and a reorganized timing discussion. Section 5 gains a baseline-description paragraph and substantially revised analyses, while the conclusion becomes Conclusion & Discussion. These changes exceed local copyediting despite retaining the overall section and appendix organization.

P2.justification: Figures 1, 3, and 7 are substantially revised, including backbone distinctions, timing axes, and replacement of Figure 7's retrieval-time panel with linear-probing results. Table 2 expands to full width with zero-shot and parameter columns; Table 4 separates backbone settings; Tables 5 and 11 are added. Table 1 gains method categories, while Figures 4–6 and 8 retain their plotted content.

R1.justification: The sparse-coding discussion adds Gamma-prior models and concept bottlenecks, and the conclusion relates CSR to pruning, quantization, and distillation. SAE background gains the k-sparse autoencoder citation. Duan et al. (2024) changes from Contrastive Factor Analysis to A Non-negative VAE, while several earlier citations are removed. The overall MRL-versus-sparse-coding positioning remains.

T1.justification: The objectives and cited NCL identifiability theorem retain their mathematical substance, with no new proof or formal guarantee. Explicit ReLU notation clarifies existing nonnegativity. The removed Johnson–Lindenstrauss analogy and added runtime explanation are informal interpretations rather than formal derivations.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important weakness in v1's central ImageNet comparison: CSR's stronger pretrained backbone confounded attribution of its advantage. The FF2048 comparisons and separate stronger-backbone columns make the method's contribution substantially more assessable. Zero-shot multimodal experiments and operation-count analysis further strengthen generalization and efficiency evidence. Blanket superiority wording still conflicts with some linear-probing results, but the improved controls and supporting analyses provide a substantial net gain in credibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Contrastive Sparse Representation (CSR) work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–E are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds matched-backbone ImageNet evaluations, zero-shot multimodal retrieval, and multiplication-count analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet, text, and multimodal experiments, including retrieval measurements and ablations.

results.title: Beyond Matryoshka: Revisiting Sparse Coding for Adaptive Representation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims about cross-model intervention transfer, corrupted capabilities, lightweight behavioral switches and tokenizer-dependent cross-architecture transfer. The additional experiments do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 8 and Appendix L newly qualify activation replacement through severe out-of-distribution capability losses and unintended backdoor responses. Appendix H interprets feature-transfer effects relative to substantial reconstruction and mapping noise. Section 6 also removes v2's qualification that affine mappings were competitive for the Llama pair and its proposed distillation explanation.

D1.justification: v3 clarifies SAE patch timing and placement before Top-K activation, and supplies task-specific data preparation and judging details. Appendix J adds the MediQA generation prompt, dataset access information and fine-tuning settings: ten epochs, batch size three, learning rate 3e-5 and sequence length 512. Existing core configurations and repository links remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds humorous-response generation and curated MediQA medical question answering, plus AlpacaEval instruction-following evaluation (Appendices I, J and L). The OpenWebText examples used to interpret SAE features in v2 are removed. These changes substantially broaden coverage beyond the retained safety tasks.

E2.justification: Appendix H adds reconstruction-only and mapped-reconstruction-only baselines to the SAE transfer comparison, alongside explicit random-noise comparisons. These controls were absent from that experiment in v2, although noise comparisons existed elsewhere. Existing affine, native-steering and mean-ablation comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The SAE transfer evaluation changes from 1,000 prompts to 100, with feature scaling and a noise-conditioned success measure. Added protocols include 20 held-out humor prompts, a three-point MediQA judging rubric, reduced zero-shot MMLU using four questions per domain, and 100 AlpacaEval instructions. The original benchmark protocols remain documented separately.

E4.justification: v3 substantially revises the SAE analysis through reconstruction/mapping-noise controls, comparisons across features, scaling sensitivity and the Gaussian-noise sweep in Figure 24. It removes the old feature-activation examples and patching case study. New analyses examine humor-data sensitivity and out-of-distribution failures, including results restricted to non-backdoored outputs.

E5.justification: The new noise sweep specifies averaging ten random-noise samples per prompt and then averaging across 50 prompts. This adds a statistical estimation procedure, without establishing increased repetition of earlier experiments. The standard-deviation reporting in Table 27 is retained; no new confidence intervals or significance tests are supplied.

E6.justification: v2's SAE report of 83% source triggering, 80% target triggering and 94.22% conditional transfer is replaced by differently conditioned results. v3 reports 8%/63% reconstruction-only triggering and 81%/89% with factor-three feature scaling; these are not comparable performance gains. New results include approximately 60% humor success, a reported 7.14% MediQA improvement, and MMLU declines from 0.605 to 0.101 for Qwen and 0.373 to 0.004 for Llama after mapping.

M1.justification: Appendix I introduces an intervention adaptation for humor: a mapped steering direction derived from middle-layer activations is applied uniformly across all target-model layers. The core autoencoder architecture, affine alternative and training losses remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 edits the introduction and background, adds a roadmap, subdivides Appendix H, moves the steering sweep from C.1 to B.1, and condenses resource information into a footnote. The overall narrative remains recognizable, and the long completion appendix is unchanged apart from relocation and renumbering.

P2.justification: Main figures and tables are repositioned, Figure 24 and new judging-prompt boxes are added, and the old SAE example table and patching-example box are removed. The probe-accuracy table changes from Table 31 to Table 30 without changing its scores. Most existing displays retain their content.

R1.justification: The background adds explicit positioning against Lindsey et al.'s crosscoders and Lee et al. (2025a)'s linear steering transfer. New benchmark citations accompany MediQA, MMLU and AlpacaEval, while several background references are removed. Bibliographic updates to retained works do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: The autoencoder equations, steering and projection definitions, and reconstruction-loss formulations in Section 3.3 and Appendices A and D are retained. v3 adds no formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps: Appendix H quantifies reconstruction and mapping noise that could confound v2's SAE-transfer evidence, while Appendix L exposes previously untested capability losses and unintended backdoor activation. These changes substantially improve evidential rigor and clarify applicability. The smaller SAE sample, 20-prompt humor evaluation and still-broad headline claims limit the revision, but the added controls and explicit failure evidence provide a clear overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same activation-transfer study and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices sufficient for comparison. Relocated material was matched, including v2 Appendix I becoming v3 Appendix K.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds humor steering, MediQA transfer, noise-control experiments and out-of-distribution evaluations.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments on backdoor removal, refusal transfer, corrupted capabilities, activation reconstruction, model switching and SAE feature transfer.

results.title: Activation Space Interventions Can Be Transferred Between Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central sequential-validity claim is substantially narrowed to bag-sufficient distributions, with an explicit correction notice attached to the introductory contribution statement. The practical claims about adaptation, fast detection, and root-cause diagnosis remain.

C2.justification: New Remarks B.4–B.6 explain how dependence can permit profitable betting under the null despite marginally uniform p-values, why using the p-value filtration does not resolve this, and why the stated covariate-shift null satisfies bag sufficiency. This materially clarifies the guarantees' applicability boundary; Appendix C's existing fixed-calibration caveat remains.

D1.justification: v5 newly states that accompanying code reproduces the counterexample's exact rational calculations (Appendix B.3, footnote 12). The experimental repository information, model and hyperparameter disclosures, and algorithm pseudocode are otherwise retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic scenarios, MEPS, Bike Sharing, Superconductivity, MNIST-C, and CIFAR-10-C tasks and shifts. v5 Appendix D.1 reproduces existing benign-shift results from v4 Figure 2 rather than adding dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain CTM, PR-ST, PR-CD-online, and PR-CD-50 comparisons and the same ablation alternatives. The new online-compression-model correspondence table is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Splits, corruption mixtures, alarm thresholds, training settings, and evaluation procedures match. The enlarged validation set and 200-point smoothing described in v5 Figure 10 were already documented in v4 Figure 9.

E4.justification: The shift-severity, density-ratio-estimator, and betting-function ablations are retained, together with runtime, corruption-specific, and root-cause analyses. The added counterexample is theoretical, not a new empirical robustness experiment.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same seed/run counts, standard-error reporting, and interval-width interquartile ranges. These include 200 seeds for tabular comparisons, 20 for runtimes, five runs for Figure 3, and ten seeds for aggregate corrupted-image results.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the matched runtime and image-results tables (v4 Tables 2–3; v5 Tables 4–5) are numerically unchanged, and the plotted experimental data are retained. For example, MEPS WCTM detection delay remains 115.8 ± 3.8. The new counterexample supplies theoretical evidence.

M1.justification: The weighted p-value computation, X-CTM-triggered adaptation, density-ratio estimation, betting procedures, and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. The added bag-sufficiency requirement restricts theoretical validity rather than changing the implemented procedure.

P1.justification: Section 3.2 is reorganized to distinguish one-shot validity from sequential independence, with expanded proof explanations and correction notices. v5 also adds an AI-assistance disclosure and revises the Appendix D.1 heading, while retaining the overall narrative and section order.

P2.justification: v4 Figure 2 moves intact to v5 Figure 5, while main-text Figure 2 retains only MEPS. v5 adds two theoretical tables and adjusts captions and figure sizing. The overall design remains similar, but product operators in Appendix C are newly malformed.

R1.justification: v5 substantially expands v4's brief online-compression-model mention through Remark 3.4, Appendix A, and Table 2. It connects oracle weights to Vovk (2003)'s backward kernels and discusses the central theorem's relationship to existing conformal-validity theory, while explicitly leaving a formal reduction unresolved. The reference list itself is unchanged.

T1.justification: v4 Theorem 3.1 asserts independence for arbitrary joint distributions with exact weights; v5 Theorem 3.3 adds the formally defined bag-sufficiency assumption. Appendix B repairs the conditioning and randomized-smoothing arguments, removes reliance on score bijectivity, and adds an exact three-observation counterexample disproving the unrestricted statement.

improvement.justification: v5 addresses an important flaw in the paper's central theoretical foundation: the unrestricted independence assertion in v4. The explicit restriction, repaired proof, and checkable counterexample substantially improve correctness and transparency without removing empirical evidence. These gains outweigh the localized typesetting deterioration in Appendix C; the practical implementation's previously documented limitations remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WATCH research. Their complete main texts and appendices A–F support reliable comparison of methods, equations, experiments, tables, and figures despite localized typesetting defects in v5.

after.justification: v5 retains these original empirical results, including the main experiments and appendix ablations.

before.justification: v4 reports original synthetic, tabular-data, and corrupted-image experiments evaluating adaptation, detection delays, alarms, coverage, runtime, and root-cause analysis.
